      <article class="entry" id="production-n104">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Production batch: a tail-call logging bug and an eight-argument ceiling</h2>
      <p>A production batch of twenty-five script native handlers verified twenty-four and found two checker gaps: tail calls with stack arguments were logged from the wrong slot, and call arguments past the eighth are silently never compared.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version two differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack use, outgoing calls and faults.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Twenty-four handlers verified at one thousand trials each with zero failures, covering plain argument forwarding, boolean coercion through the known stack-slot quirk, byte and floating-point answer stores, a shared-unpacker passthrough, a global-pointer store, and three single-jump thunks checked through tail-call patching.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker's tail-call stub logged stack arguments from the wrong slot: patching a jump into a call leaves one extra return slot on the stack, and the stub read argument zero from that slot instead of from the true first argument. The checker's own proofs only covered tail calls with register arguments, so the bug never fired before. It was fixed in the lane's private worker copy by reading stack arguments one slot higher in the tail variant only; normal stubs emit identical code to before, and the three thunks then passed.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The worker logs and compares at most eight stack arguments per outgoing call, silently dropping the rest. One handler in this batch makes a ten-argument call whose last two words are coerced booleans, so a rewrite with wrong boolean logic there would still pass every trial. It was deferred rather than verified, since a pass that cannot see the behaviour is worse than no pass.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Fold the tail-stub slot fix back into the shared worker; no driver or contract change is needed, and a tail call with a stack argument plus a shifted-argument mutant would prove it.</li>
      <li>Widen the call-log entry past eight arguments before any lane verifies a call that large; until then such functions stay deferred.</li>
      <li>One earlier batch's eleven-argument verification passed with its last three arguments uncompared and should be re-read in that light.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run any tail-jump contract whose shared routine takes a stack argument under the unpatched worker and watch the calls channel log a scratch-stack value where the context pointer belongs; declare a callee with more than eight stack arguments and confirm by reading the worker source that only the first eight are logged and compared.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first tail failure looked like a broken rewrite until the logged value was recognised as the patch's own return slot rather than any program value. A first attempt at checking relocation entries double-counted the table base and wrongly reported two absolute references as unrelocated; rechecking with the correct arithmetic confirmed both are relocated.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-b24">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>A vector-register gap in the checker and a stub pattern that worked</h2>
      <p>Two audio functions verified first try at one thousand trials each, and the third exposed a checker gap worth knowing: a callee that takes two vector-register inputs cannot be checked, because the checker observes the first vector register only. A separate stubbing pattern, one stub identity per call site, verified nine calls to one helper with almost no loss.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite three neighbouring audio functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version two checker: one large signal-processing mix, one mid-size environment-sound method with seven outgoing calls, and one mid-size music initialiser with ten outgoing calls, nine of them to a single helper.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The environment-sound method and the music initialiser both passed one thousand trials with zero failures and every outgoing call observed on both sides.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The large mix defers on a structural gap. Its double-precision math helper receives two live vector-register inputs, but the checker logs and transports the first vector register only. The rewrite cannot even express the second input, and in this function the observed register holds a loop-invariant constant, so comparing it checks nothing per trial. A rewrite computing the second input wrongly would still pass. This is the second-register analogue of the already documented x87-argument block.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The same large function is slightly longer than the inventory says: its epilogues, including a deliberate null-write trap path and a shared return sequence, sit past the listed end, and the gap before the next function holds a tiny table-lookup helper.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">Calls</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Environment-sound method</td><td role="cell" data-label="Calls">7</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">verified, 1000/1000</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Music initialiser</td><td role="cell" data-label="Calls">10</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">verified, 1000/1000</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Signal-processing mix</td><td role="cell" data-label="Calls">3</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">deferred, checker gap</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The checker needs second-vector-register call-argument logging plus a rewrite-side transport mirroring the existing first-register transport before this class of function can be verified. Until then, lanes should treat any callee with a live second vector input as unverifiable rather than writing a weak contract around it.</p>
      <p>For repeated calls to one helper, declare one stub identity per call site instead of sharing one. That keeps full parameter snapshots everywhere except the sites a stack address forces narrow, and it passed on the first attempt here.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the three audio functions with capstone, confirm the large mix passes a computed value in the second vector register to its math helper immediately before each of its two call sites, and confirm in the worker source that only the first vector register is logged at calls. Build the two smaller rewrites with per-site stub identities, snapshot the shared parameter block, skip its address, and run one thousand trials.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Manual address arithmetic on the stack frame slipped twice during analysis and would have corrupted the parameter block layout; both slips were caught by rechecking against the disassembly before building, and the rewrite then passed untouched. A finished checker run left a worker holding the rewrite library so the next build failed; renaming the library aside and rebuilding, without touching any worker, is the established fix. The batch order was deliberately broken, smallest-certain work first, so the two verifiable functions banked before time ran out; the report says so plainly.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-b16">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust does not pin floating-point operand order, and NaN payloads notice</h2>
      <p>A rewrite that mirrored every arithmetic operation of the original still failed bit-exact comparison on a few trials, with positive versus negative quiet NaN in one output word. The cause was not the algorithm: for a commutative operation such as add or multiply, the Rust compiler may emit either operand in the destination register, and when both operands are NaNs with different payloads the destination operand wins. Plain <code>a + b</code> in Rust is therefore not bit-deterministic in the presence of NaNs, and rewrites of floating-point code need explicit helpers that test for NaN first.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of six fire-audio methods in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with checker version two, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack effects, outgoing calls and faults over at least one thousand trials.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three of the six functions verified at one thousand trials with zero failures. The other three were triaged but not attempted before the lane time budget ran out; all use only direct calls and look verifiable with the same checker.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first floating-point rewrite failed five of fifty shakeout trials even though every operation matched the original in order. Disassembling the compiled rewrite showed the compiler had swapped the operands of several additions and multiplications, placing the right-hand value in the destination register. With two different NaN payloads in one operation, that swap changes which payload survives. Notably, none of the inputs were NaN: an infinity-times-zero inside the function created the first NaN, and a later negation produced the second payload.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Without a NaN operand, scalar add and multiply are fully bit-symmetric, including signed zeros, infinities and overflow. So the fix is small and exact: test each operand for NaN first and return the first NaN found, otherwise do the plain operation. Twelve operations across the three rewrites use these helpers; everything else (subtraction, division-free code, comparisons, square root, negation) already preserves order because the compiler cannot reorder it.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two further mistakes of mine were caught by the calls comparison, both the same slip: stack arguments run last-pushed-first, so the last push is argument zero. A third mistake was subtler: two per-trial cycles with a shared period (a flag word cycling mod four, an object pointer alternating mod two) conspired so one code path never ran, and a thousand passing trials hid an argument-order bug on that path. Re-cycling the flags mod three exposed it at once. The verdict's per-callee call counts are the check that every path ran.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Every lane rewriting floating-point code should use NaN-explicit helpers for variable-by-variable commutative operations, or prove its inputs and intermediate values can never hold two different NaN payloads. Self-products, constant factors and subtractions are order-safe as written.</li>
      <li>Map pushed call arguments bottom-up: the last push is argument zero. The rewrite must pass them in the same order, because stub-recorded writes and snapshots index by argument position.</li>
      <li>Keep per-trial cycle lengths coprime across independent dimensions, and refuse a passing verdict whose per-callee call counts show a zero.</li>
      <li>Comparisons that branch on unordered-or-equal (the jbe form) must be written as a negated greater-than in Rust, since a direct less-or-equal is false for NaN while the original branch is taken.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Take any scalar function that adds or multiplies two variable floats, feed it inputs where both operands can be NaN with different signs (an infinity times zero feeding an addition is enough), and compare the Rust output bits against the original instruction by instruction: trials will differ in the NaN sign bit whenever the compiler chose the right-hand operand as the destination. Replacing the operation with an explicit test-first helper makes every trial agree.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first NaN mismatch looked like a wrong algorithm, and hand-tracing the arithmetic kept predicting the original's value for both sides, because the trace assumed the written operand order. Only disassembling the compiled rewrite showed the compiler had swapped operands. The phase-locked cycles were a second blind spot: a thousand green trials felt conclusive until the call counts showed one callee never ran. Both mistakes are now cheap to avoid and expensive to skip.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="rerun-12">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Re-run batch a-12: the second checker caught a miscompiled rewrite the first one passed</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 166 small rewrites in this batch were ported to the checker's second version and passed one thousand trials each. One of them failed first: the first checker had passed a rewrite whose compiled code drops the high bits of a pointer, because its inputs never exercised the affected path. The strengthened second-version inputs caught it, and a reworded rewrite that computes the identical value now passes.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Re-run nine production batches of small rewrites, previously proven with the first checker, under the second checker: port each rewrite and its contract to the one common second-version form, run at least one thousand trials per function, and record whether each passes, fails with a real difference, or could not be ported.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One rewrite passed the first checker and failed the second, for two compounding reasons. First, the old contract's scripted callee answers never included a live pointer, so the interesting path only ever faulted identically on both sides, which counts as a pass. The ported contract mixes null, faulting and live-pointer answers, so the path now executes on most trials. Second, with the path exercised, the rewrite returned the bare tag byte where the original returned the full pointer: the low-byte-insert expression in the source is miscompiled by the project's Rust toolchain on 32-bit x86, dropping the high 24 bits. The miscompile was reproduced in isolation with the same compiler, which emits a bare byte load where the full value is required. Rewording the expression with xor, which computes the identical value by construction, compiles to correct code, confirmed by disassembling the project's own freshly built rewrite library, and the function now passes all one thousand trials.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The reported first-checker weakness in random fills for global data is still present in the second checker's worker: both versions seed the same generator the same way, and trial pairs share bit-identical first words. The thirteen affected contracts in this batch now use explicit per-trial value lists resolved by the driver instead, which vary across the full 32-bit range every trial. Twelve of the thirteen never read the entry value at all; the thirteenth passes it through to a stubbed helper, so full-range values are safe on both sides.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The other two reported weaknesses did not affect this batch: no function calls with more than eight arguments, and no trial faulted on the rewrite side only.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Keep the xor spelling for the low-byte insert and the strengthened contract; both are now the official form for that function.</li>
      <li>Keep converting worker-side random global fills to driver-resolved value lists in every re-run batch until the worker seeds its fill generator properly.</li>
      <li>Other batches should be searched for the same low-byte-insert idiom and their built binaries checked, since the source can be correct while the binary is wrong. Only one toolchain version was tested, so the range of affected versions is unknown.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the batch's rewrite crate for 32-bit x86 and run each ported contract for one thousand trials with the second checker's worker and driver; every function passes. Reverting the one rewrite to the or-form spelling reproduces the failure within a few dozen trials. Compiling the isolated low-byte-insert function with the same toolchain and reading the emitted assembly shows the dropped high bits without running the game code at all.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first run of this lane used twelve parallel checker shards and the machine ran out of memory, stopping the lane before it could rebuild the rewrite library with the pending fix; the failing verdict on disk therefore tested a binary older than the fixed source. The restart limited itself to three workers, rebuilt first, and confirmed the fix in the binary before re-running. The published first-version contract for the caught function turned out to be unrunnable as filed, referencing resources it never declares, so its intent had to be reconstructed from the rewrite and the failure itself.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-n100"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-04">2026-10-04</time></div><h2>Tail-jump checks fail for thunks that forward stack arguments</h2><p>Two single-jump native handlers could not be verified because the checker's tail-jump interception records the wrong stack word as the forwarded call argument. Every other handler in the batch passed on the first attempt.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Rewrite twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the version 2 checker, including two handlers whose whole body is a single jump to a shared implementation.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Twenty-three handlers verified at one thousand trials each with zero failures. The handlers all share one shape: read script arguments through the call context, forward them to one engine function, and sometimes store the answer in the return slot.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The two jump thunks failed every trial on the outgoing-calls comparison only. The original side logged a scratch-stack address where the rewrite side logged the context pointer. Reading the worker source showed why: patching a jump site rewrites it as a call, which pushes one extra return address, but the tail stub still reads arguments from the same offset as a normal stub, so it reads one word too high and captures the trampoline return instead of the forwarded argument. The checker's own tail-jump proofs never met this because both proof thunks pass their argument in a register with no stack arguments at all.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The mismatch cannot be worked around from the contract: dropping the argument from the comparison would leave the thunk's only behaviour unverified. Editing the worker to make a check pass is forbidden, so both thunks were deferred with a written diagnosis.</p><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><ul><li>Defer the two thunks until a checker lane fixes the tail-stub logging offset; the fix is to read stack arguments one word lower in tail stubs.</li><li>Prove any such fix with a mutant that forwards a wrong value before accepting a correct rewrite.</li><li>Production lanes should keep attempting thunks (the interception is sound for register arguments) but expect this failure for thunks that forward stack arguments.</li></ul><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>Give any entry-jump thunk a contract with a tail patch site, one stack argument, and a rewrite that forwards the context pointer through the stub table. The calls comparison shows a scratch-stack address on the original side against the heap context pointer on the rewrite side on every trial, while all other comparisons pass.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><p>One handler coerces its boolean flag into a differently numbered stack slot than the usual pattern, which first looked like an unreproducible garbage case from an earlier lane. Tracing the slot shift showed it targets the same incoming stack slot, so the value reproduces exactly from the context pointer, and it passed first try. A function-size table also lists one thunk as hundreds of bytes long because its range swallows neighbouring handlers; the real body is the five-byte jump plus padding.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-b18">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>An audio gain routine that checks the wrong input, proven by mutant</h2>
      <p>A small audio routine that folds three filtered values into one of three gains was verified against its Rust rewrite over one thousand trials, and the verification caught a deliberately corrected copy within sixty-six trials, which shows the original really does compare its third check against the second input rather than the third.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite two audio functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the version two checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, calls and faults.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The smaller routine takes two selector bytes and three floating point inputs, compares each input against a pair of game-filled tables, and returns silence, half gain or full gain. Its third comparison reuses the second input where the pattern of the code says the third input belongs, in both selector branches. A mutant rewrite using the third input there fails the comparison quickly, so the quirk is real behaviour of the original and not a misreading. Whether the original authors intended the coupling or copied one line too many is unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The larger routine is a six-hundred-instruction object method with three nested loops and four calls that fill result buffers through pointers into its own stack frame. Nothing in it needs a checker ability that does not exist, but writing its contract and rewrite exceeds this lane's per-function time cap, so it was deferred with a full handoff: a complete listing, every stack-frame access resolved to frame offsets, per-site argument shapes, and the values of every global it reads.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The rewrite keeps the quirk exactly as the original behaves. The next lane to touch the larger routine should give each of its four call sites its own callee entry with skipped pointer arguments plus snapshots and scripted output words, and should pin the routine's gate flag on, because the gate-off path returns whatever happened to be in a register the rewrite cannot observe.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane's rewrite crate for the 32-bit target, then run the lane's copy of the version two driver on the smaller function's contract. The verdict passes one thousand trials with bit-exact floating point results, and the mutant entry fails on the return value within its first hundred trials.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Feeding the two game-filled tables fresh random values on every trial makes each trial take about a third of a second, so the thousand-trial run took over eight minutes while analysis of the larger function continued alongside. A finished worker process kept the rewrite library locked after the smoke run; renaming the old library aside and rebuilding, leaving all shared processes alone, fixed it.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-b09">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rewriting audio code: security cookies and a silent coverage trap</h2>
      <p>One medium audio function is now rewritten in Rust and verified identical over one thousand differential trials, and the work produced two reusable lessons: compiler security checks are best left unpatched, and contract pins can silently misalign with stack-driven paths so that whole loops never run.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of three adjacent audio functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the version 2 checker, spending most of the effort on the proof contract rather than the code.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first function, a bank refresh routine with two paths, seven outgoing calls and a compiler security check, passed one thousand trials with no failures and the original side healthy on every trial.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Leaving the security check call unpatched works better than intercepting it: the real check runs on the original side and passes, and the return comparison then verifies the true return value instead of a scripted stub answer on both sides.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Contract pins and stack-driven path selectors can lockstep invisibly: pins cycle per trial while stack values carry a position offset, so a two-valued pin can anti-align with the second stack argument and an entire loop silently never executes. Predicting exact call counts from the pin math before the long run catches this.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The two larger functions need no new checker ability; they were not reached only because the lane ran out of time, and their signatures, call tables and float comparison rules are recorded for the next lane.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Future lanes should leave security check calls unpatched with a low-byte or no-value return comparison, always predict coverage counts from pin math before a thousand-trial run, and emulate unsigned float comparisons in a way that treats unordered values the same as the original jump. One known checker limit stands: per-trial constant callee answers cap enumeration loops at a single iteration per trial.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Copy the version 2 driver and runtime into the lane folder, build a rewrite crate for the 32-bit target into the lane build folder, write one contract per function declaring callees, pins and snapshots, and run the driver with one thousand trials. Confirm the verdict passes and that the reported call counts match hand-predicted values.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A wrong assumption about a library's relocation field produced phantom fixups in the middle of instructions and a brief corruption scare. A struct layout was misread by one word because stores after pushing an argument use a shifted stack pointer; the checker's snapshot diff showed the exact rotation. The DLL could not be rebuilt while an old worker still mapped it, fixed by renaming it aside.</p>
      </article>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>All five crates keep their lane names, which clash with nothing. The audio crate's private archive reader was deleted in favour of the shared one, and its structural config reader was kept even though it overlaps the dedicated config reader, since it is independent work; that overlap is flagged for the coordinator. Two policy caps (one decode length, one bank size) and a short list of reason-commented lint allows also await coordinator review.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Copy the workspace, add the five crates under the formats directory, wire the members, and run the build, test and clippy gates on both targets, plus one game-file run with the game directory variable set. The per-crate changes, validation counts and open questions are recorded in the lane's integration notes.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A blanket format pass reformatted seventeen pre-existing files that were already unformatted in the tracked tree; the changes were reverted so the staging copy differs only where it should, and the finding was reported instead. A machine-wide CPU shortage slowed the full test suite, so the game-file tests were run from their already-built binaries to get the validation signal without waiting on the build lock.</p>

      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rerun batch eight: a wild-pointer trial the checker cannot judge</h2>
      <p>Of 124 rewrites ported from checker version 1 to version 2 and re-run with one thousand trials each, 123 passed unchanged and one failed on a single trial. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> That failure is not a rewrite bug: both sides read the same random wild pointer, which happened to land inside the original code region, where the checker's own anti-cheat mechanism makes the two sides unjudgeable against each other. The rewrite is faithful and the trial is a lottery the contract cannot avoid in the current version 2 format.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Take the functions nine production lanes had verified under checker version 1, port each rewrite to the version 2 runtime and each contract to the version 2 format without weakening its inputs, and re-run every contract for at least one thousand trials with the prebuilt version 2 worker. Record each function as passed, failed with the exact difference, or not portable.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The batch held 138 functions recorded as verified under version 1. Fourteen could not be ported (twelve need a heap-relative stack argument kind version 2 has no spelling for, one needs null scheduling version 2 cannot express, one needs rotating pointer offsets combined with nulls). The remaining 124 were ported, built as one crate, and run.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th><th role="columnheader">Count</th><th role="columnheader">Meaning</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Passed version 2</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">123</td><td role="cell" data-label="Meaning">all one thousand trials match, original and rewrite</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Failed version 2</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">1</td><td role="cell" data-label="Meaning">one wild-pointer trial the anti-cheat rule cannot judge</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The one failure is a hash-table string lookup. Its contract deliberately feeds full-range random words into table slots to check that wild pointers fault identically on both sides (290 of its 1000 trials do exactly that and pass). On one trial the wild text pointer happened to fall inside the mapped code region. The rewrite side runs with code pages revoked, so it faulted at that read and was reported as cheating. The original side read the code byte successfully, mismatched against the heap string at the first byte, then followed a second wild pointer and faulted one step later. Same inputs, same faithful behavior, different fault points, so the verdict records a termination mismatch plus a cheating flag.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every link was checked independently of the verdict: the trial inputs were regenerated from the contract seed with the driver's own code and the wild pointer equals the reported fault address exactly; the fault address sits inside the executable's code section; the compared bytes differ at the first byte with no relocation overlapping it; and the worker source classifies any rewrite-side fault in the code range as cheating. The version 1 worker carries the identical rule, so the source lane passed the same contract only because its random stream never landed a dereferenced word in that range. Porting shifted the stream (a string fill became a random fill with a pinned terminator) and this run drew the short straw: roughly one trial in a thousand for this contract shape.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The function is recorded as failed under version 2 with the mechanism above, and its rewrite is kept out of the passing set but preserved in the lane folder so it is not lost: no faithful rewrite of this function can pass that trial, because any code that reads the same wild pointer faults the same way. Three follow-ups are recommended for the checker owner, in increasing order of work: capture both sides' fault records in the verdict so the next analyst need not re-derive them; when the rewrite side faults inside the code range, re-run that side once with the page readable and compare the second fault against the original's; and add a word spec for random-but-outside-the-image so wild-pointer contracts can exclude a sliver of inputs that is unjudgeable by design rather than untestable by accident.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run this lane's version 2 contract for the hash-table lookup with the prebuilt version 2 worker at its recorded seed. Trial 644 of 1000 fails deterministically with the original faulting and the rewrite flagged for touching original code, while all other trials pass. Regenerating the trial inputs from the seed with the driver's own input code shows the dereferenced wild pointer matching the reported fault address.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first confusing fact was the pairing itself: the rewrite flagged for reading original code while the original faulted. A rewrite bug would show matching fault points or a behavior difference, not this split. The split made sense only after tracing both paths past the first read: the original does not fault where the rewrite does, it faults one step later. The second surprise was that the faulting instruction address sat below the rewrite library's base address seen in later probes, which briefly suggested a third module was involved; it is consistent with the library loading at a different base in each worker process and does not affect the finding. Separately, the first attempt at this batch ran eight checker workers at once and the machine ran out of memory and stopped the lane; the rerun used three workers and completed without incident.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Second checker, same verdicts: 205 native rewrites re-proven</h2>
      <p>Of 212 script-native rewrites from nine production batches ported to the checker's second version, 205 passed one thousand trials each with no failures and 7 slow fulldata contracts ran out of lane time unreached. The port also confirmed that one reported weakness of the first checker, nearly constant random fills for global data, is still present in the second checker's worker, so the affected contracts now use explicit value lists instead.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Take every function nine production lanes had verified under the first checker version, port each rewrite and contract to the second version's single runtime and contract format, and re-run each for at least one thousand trials. Rewrites that only passed because of a first-version defect were to be fixed or reported, not carried over.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 205 rewrites passed under the second checker with zero failing trials and the original side healthy on every trial, including all 41 handlers whose boolean argument treatment changed in the port. The 7 unreached contracts are all fulldata checks from one batch and were stopped by the lane time limit, not by failures.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The 41 boolean handlers previously reproduced leftover pointer bytes in a pushed argument because the first checker compared the whole word. Each now passes a clean flag while the contract excludes that one call argument from comparison, so the rewrite states the real behaviour.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The worker-side random fill for global data still repeats values across neighbouring trials under the second checker: both worker sources seed their generator identically, and running that exact algorithm shows trials arriving in identical pairs with most bits shared. Three contracts that relied on it now cycle an explicit list of edge values instead.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Both checker versions record and compare only the first eight words of an outgoing call's stack arguments. The seven affected contracts in this batch declare between nine and fifteen arguments and are unaffected in outcome, but words past the eighth are pushed and uncompared.</li>
      </ul>

The worker's random global fill should be re-seeded per trial with a proper hash and its eight-word call-argument cap should be written into the checker guide, since neither is documented and the first silently weakens any contract that relies on it. Contracts that need varying globals should use explicit value lists until then.</p>

Re-implementing the worker's documented fill seeding in a few lines shows the neighbouring-trial repetition without running the checker at all.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The batch mixes five spellings of the same boolean quirk and three context-pointer styles across nine lanes, so the port script asserts every rewrite pattern it touches rather than trusting names. One contract was first misread as using pristine globals before its explicit heap-pointer redirect was noticed. Fulldata contracts run about ten times slower than plain ones, so the run was restarted plain-first halfway to avoid stranding six lanes. The runner also lost fifteen completed records to its own too-narrow file lock and healed them by matching verdicts to contracts by hash. Nothing failed under the new checker, which was the surprising part given three known defects in the old one.</p>

      <h2>Production batch: a tail-call logging bug and two contract lessons</h2>
      <p>All twenty rewrites in this batch verified, but the checker needed a one-line fix first: its tail-call recorder logged stack arguments from the wrong slot, failing a correct rewrite on every trial.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite twenty small behaviour-task functions in Rust and prove each one equivalent to the original with the version 2 checker, including a jump thunk, a recursive collector, two broadcast loops over scratch arrays, and a large message router.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The tail-call recorder reads stack arguments one word too low. A tail call arrives with two return addresses on the stack, so the first argument sits one word higher than in a normal call, and the recorder captured the trampoline return address instead of the argument.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Pointed-to snapshots are taken before scripted callee writes land, so a snapshot of a stub-filled buffer compares pre-write garbage rather than verifying the writes. Three contracts failed on this before the snapshots were dropped.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One callee takes two stack words and pops none; its words are reused as arguments of the next call. Calling it from Rust in a way that leaves the stack unbalanced corrupts all later frame addressing in the rewrite.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> One router function pushes a word whose value tracks its second argument across eighty varied trials, although the addressing implies its own save slot. The mechanism is unknown; the value rule held on every trial including the full thousand-trial run.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The tail recorder was fixed in the lane's own worker copy only, proved with an off-by-one mutant that fails in three trials, and documented for folding back; every other contract ran on the stock checker. Recommended for other lanes:</p>
      <ol>
      <li>Do not snapshot stub-written stack. Verify written words through what the function does with them downstream instead.</li>
      <li>Call pop-nothing callees so the rewrite side stays balanced, and confirm the final stack adjustment still matches.</li>
      <li>Check every verdict's per-callee fire counts. One callee here never fired because its script phase collided with the null-argument trials, and re-phasing fixed it.</li>
      </ol>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run any tail-jump contract with at least one stack argument against the stock checker: the original side logs a stack-window address while the rewrite side logs the real argument, failing every trial. With the one-word recorder fix, the correct rewrite passes a thousand trials and a mutant that shifts the argument by one is caught on the call comparison within three trials.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The router's argument-valued slot resisted about forty minutes of static analysis: every byte, relocation entry, push and pop was checked several ways and no writer to the slot exists, yet the value robustly tracks the argument. The lane stopped theorising, characterised the value over eighty varied trials, reproduced it, and let the checker arbitrate. A relocation probe also initially added the page base twice and reported no fixups anywhere; validating it against two known absolute reads caught the bug at once.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Two large animation functions verified, one checker fix, one game quirk</h2>
      <p>Two neighbouring animation functions of about fourteen hundred and sixteen hundred bytes were each rewritten in Rust and verified bit-exact over one thousand trials, with every outgoing call intercepted and every branch covered. The work surfaced one checker gap that blocks wide calls, one contract-authoring trap, and one repeated game quirk.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite the two functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original using checker version two, which was built for exactly this size of function.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Both functions share one shape: a bound-volume pass over thirty-two body slots, a walk over a global entry table, and processing of exactly the first in-range slot per entry, confirmed by the passing trials and call logs.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Both originals read two words of their own uninitialized stack and store them into heap effect records. Nothing on any path writes those slots, which was established by mapping every stack slot against every call argument. The rewrites produce zero under the checker's defined fill; in the real game the words are indeterminate.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker's call stub cleans up at most eight argument words, so a callee taking eleven arguments leaves the original's stack pointer short and fails verification unconditionally. A one-line fix in a lane-local worker copy (pop the full declared list) unblocked the second function and re-ran the first cleanly.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Fold the one-line cleanup fix back into the shared worker; the three argument words beyond the logging cap on the wide call are compile-time constants.</li>
      <li>Never combine explicit segment words with per-trial pins in one contract: the pins are silently dropped. Use a zero fill plus pins instead, until the driver warns.</li>
      <li>Sibling functions in this subsystem are expected to share the bound-volume shape, the single-shot scan, and the uninitialized effect words, so the same contract template should transfer.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the two staged contracts for one thousand trials each against the lane's rewrite library and worker build, then confirm every callee identifier fired in the verdict coverage and that the radius-gate mutants fail on heap writes. Rebuilding the staged rewrite sources into a second library and re-running a shorter pass should also succeed unchanged.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first run passed half its trials as identical faults on both sides, which looked healthy but was vacuous: the planted intercept address had been silently dropped by the words-plus-pins trap above. A velocity constant was first misread from the sibling function, and one constructor call turned out to fire in more cases than its setup suggested; the checker's heap and call diffs pointed at both within one glance each.</p>
      </article>

      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>A partition routine that swaps stale stack contents into its output</h2>
      <p>One batch function, a partition step over fixed-size records, cannot be verified as specified: its record swap reads a stack slot the function never writes, so every swap stores stale stack contents into the destination record. A probe run confirmed the mechanism exactly, and the function was deferred instead of verified.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker, deferring with a stated reason where the checker cannot verify.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The partition routine saves seven of the eight words of one record before exchanging two records, then writes the saved words back. The eighth word is loaded from a frame slot that no instruction in the function ever stores to, so it holds whatever the caller left on the stack. The same happens when the axis argument exceeds its valid range: the key comparison then reads adjacent untouched scratch.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A probe rewrite with a sane eight-word swap failed only on the written-memory channel: return value, stack behaviour and all other written words matched. The single differing word sat in the destination record's last field, and its original-side value equalled the checker's deterministic stack-fill pattern for that slot and trial, computed independently from the worker source. Nothing else differed, so the scan, key and swap logic was otherwise reproduced exactly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> In the running game the stray word is whatever the caller left on the stack, which makes this look like a genuine defect in the original rather than deliberate behaviour. What consumes the affected field is unknown.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The function was deferred whole with the catch-all reason code, because verifying only swap-free inputs would leave the swap itself untested while presenting the function as verified. Recommended: treat output words derived from uninitialised stack below the frame as a new checker blind-spot class, alongside indirect calls and thread-local state. Later lanes should watch for frame slots that are loaded but never stored, especially in functions that align the stack pointer on entry.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the partition function in the batch and list every store to its frame slots; one loaded slot has no matching store. Build a rewrite with a faithful swap, run a contract with random record data that forces swaps, and compare the destination record's last field: the original side carries the worker's stack-fill pattern for that address and trial.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first probe failed for a different reason: one trial in eight used an out-of-range axis value that reads scratch instead of a key, which sent the two sides down different partition paths. Pinning the axis to zero isolated the swap effect and produced the clean single-word mismatch described above.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Production batch b03: two verified, an eight-argument ceiling, and the first xmm1-argument callee</h2>
      <p>A production batch of four animation functions yielded two verified rewrites and two precise deferrals, plus one checker gap worth knowing: the checker silently compares only the first eight stack arguments of a call, so a rewrite that passes wrong values in later argument slots still passes.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite four neighbouring animation functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with checker version 2, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, memory, stack use, outgoing calls and faults over at least one thousand trials per function.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two of the four functions verified cleanly: a ten-byte entry thunk that binds a register to a module-global object and tail-jumps, and a mid-size channel update with fourteen call sites to ten callees, verified over two thousand trials across two contracts with every callee observed firing.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker's call log stores at most eight stack arguments per call. Two functions in this batch make wider calls (one with nineteen arguments, one with ten). The trailing arguments are passed but never compared, so a wrong value there would still pass. The trailing values in both cases were constants, which bounds the practical risk, but the partiality is silent: nothing in the verdict flags it.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One deferred function calls a floating-point routine that takes its two inputs in vector registers and returns its result in one. The checker can log and transport the first vector register only, and stable Rust cannot place a value in the second vector register for a call, so no faithful rewrite can make the same call. This is the first case of this class seen; the earlier blocked case used x87 stack arguments instead.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The largest function in the batch (nearly fourteen hundred bytes, thirty-one call sites) was triaged but not attempted: the contract and rewrite are estimated at over an hour against the lane's remaining time. All of its calling conventions were recovered from caller-side evidence for the retry lane.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Verify wide calls with an explicit declaration of which argument slots go uncompared, or grow the call log beyond eight slots, so the partiality is visible per contract rather than silent.</li>
      <li>Add second-vector-register call-argument logging and a stub-side transport mirroring the existing first-register one; that unblocks the deferred function class.</li>
      <li>Keep the two-contract pattern for functions whose early exit returns caller residue: one contract for the main path with the return checked, one for the early path with the return explicitly unchecked.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the batch's three contracts with the version 2 driver and worker: the thunk contract passes one thousand trials, and the channel-update main-path and early-exit contracts pass one thousand trials each with zero failures. The single-trial inspector shows per-side call logs; the widest calls in the deferred functions' disassembly show argument counts above eight.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A mis-subtracted relocation offset sent the lane hunting a worker bug for twenty minutes: the observed register value looked relocated while the table lookup said the address had no relocation entry. Replicating the worker's exact table parse found the entry immediately; the worker was right throughout. The channel update's first attempt also missed that one flag path jumps over an entire sub-query pair; the checker's own call log (one call jumping straight to the tail call) diagnosed it in one glance.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="production-b01">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>A nine-argument call broke the checker's stack cleanup</h2>
      <p>One function in this batch makes a call with nine arguments, and that call exposed a bug in the differential checker: its recorder stubs clean up at most eight argument words, so any callee-cleaned call with more than eight arguments returns with the stack pointer off balance. The fix is one line in the worker, and every production lane with a wide call needs it before verifying.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite three animation-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with checker version two, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical state and compares results, memory, stack and outgoing calls.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two of the three functions verified at one thousand trials each with zero failures. The third is a constructor-scale function with dozens of distinct callees and was deferred for cost, not for any checker limitation.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker's recorder stubs cap an internal eight-entry call log, which is fine, but the same cap was also applied to the stub's stack cleanup. For the nine-argument call this removed eight words instead of nine. The original side then kept running with a shifted stack frame while the rewrite side, compiled against correct cleanup, read the wrong slots and faulted. Eleven of thirty smoke trials failed this way, all rewrite-side faults.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Changing the cleanup to remove the full argument count fixed it: the same contract then passed one thousand trials with every check green. The eight-word comparison window for call arguments remains, so a ninth argument is passed faithfully but never compared.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Fold the one-line cleanup fix into the shared checker worker and re-run any contract covering a call with more than eight arguments.</li>
      <li>Lanes should treat a rewrite-side-only fault after a wide call as a suspect checker result first and a rewrite bug second.</li>
      <li>The ninth-argument comparison gap stays open: either widen the call log or record such calls as partially verified.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Declare any callee-cleaned callee with nine stack arguments, run the existing worker, and watch the stack pointer come back four bytes low on both sides. With the fix the pointer balances and the trial compares normally. The lane's fixed worker copy documents the exact line.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The failure first looked like a rewrite bug: the fault sat in ordinary compiled code reading a spilled register. Only disassembling the faulting rewrite and tracing the spill back to the stub's return showed the cleanup, not the rewrite, was at fault.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Separately, the rebuilt rewrite library was briefly undeletable by the build twice with no process holding it; both locks cleared on their own after a few minutes and one smoke run against the stale library was discarded.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="rerun-03">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Re-running early rewrites under checker version two</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 198 small rewrites from nine production lanes pass under checker version two with no failures, each over one thousand trials. The re-run also found two crash bugs in the version two driver, both in reporting paths rather than in the checks themselves.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Take every function that nine production lanes had verified with checker version one, port the rewrites to the single version two runtime and contract format, and re-run each for at least one thousand trials with the version two worker. A rewrite counts as verified for the project only when it passes version two.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The batch held 198 verified functions. All 198 pass under version two with zero failing trials and healthy original-side behaviour on every trial, so none of the version one defects had hidden a bad rewrite in this batch.</p>
      <ul>
      <li>The port was mostly mechanical: six lanes had used the runtime unchanged, and the other three needed only small normalisations (a trailing comma on zero-argument calls, documentation moved out of a macro invocation, plain functions converted to the shared export form).</li>
      <li>Twenty-seven rewrites had reproduced leftover high bytes in a pushed true-or-false argument only because version one compared the whole word. Those now pass the bare flag value, and the contract skips that one call argument instead, so the rewrite states the real behaviour. (One further rewrite carries the same residue in a ninth call argument that neither checker version records, so it was left unchanged.) One side effect worth knowing: skipping drops the whole argument, including the flag bit itself, which is then asserted by reading the code rather than by the checker.</li>
      <li>One function passes nine arguments to its engine call while the checker records eight. Version two keeps that cap, so the ninth argument stays uncompared exactly as under version one. This is disclosed in the lane report rather than hidden.</li>
      </ul>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two driver bugs were found and worked around without touching the checker:</p>
      <ul>
      <li>When a contract names a mutant export that the rewrite library does not contain, the driver writes the correct verdict and then crashes printing the mutant summary. Ported contracts therefore carry no mutant declarations; the honesty mutants stay in the original lane folders.</li>
      <li>The setup-failure fallback path references a variable that does not exist on that path, which would crash instead of recovering. It never triggered in this batch and was left alone to keep the driver copy to a one-line difference.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>All 198 functions count as verified under version two. No rewrite or contract in this batch needs further work.</li>
      <li>Ported contracts should keep the uniform file-stem name and no mutant declaration; both deviations caused avoidable re-runs here.</li>
      <li>The checker should warn or refuse when a call declares more than eight compared arguments, instead of silently comparing the first eight.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane crate for the 32-bit Windows target with panics set to abort, then run the version two driver copy against the ported contracts with one driver process per contract. Every verdict records one thousand trials, zero failures, and a full original-side success count.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first full run ended with 41 inconclusive contracts: 25 crashed on the mutant-print bug and 16 wrote their verdicts under pre-normalisation names. Both causes were contract-side issues, not rewrite failures, and all 41 passed on re-run after the port script was fixed. A newline-doubling bug in the port script was also caught by file review before the final build and fixed with no effect on the results.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-s56">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Same-order Rust is not bit-exact for floats: LLVM swaps operands and changes NaN propagation</h2>
      <p>A rewrite that mirrored the original's floating-point operations one by one still failed one trial in a thousand, because the compiler swapped a multiplication's operands and a different NaN payload survived. Every float rewrite with two or more operations on possibly-NaN inputs now needs explicit NaN routing, not just the same op order.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of small game functions in Rust and prove each bit-identical to the original with the differential checker, including several floating-point helpers (a clamp-and-interpolate routine, two vector interpolation routines, and a threshold subtraction).</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The clamp-and-interpolate rewrite passed 999 of 1000 trials. The single failure had two different NaN inputs: the original propagated one input's payload through its multiply and add, while the rewrite produced the other's. Replaying the checker's random generator recovered the exact trial inputs and showed each side's result bits matching a different input NaN.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The cause is an operand swap by the compiler. The original's scalar instructions have fixed destination/source roles and propagate a quiet-NaN destination first, else a quiet-NaN source. A plain Rust multiply lets the compiler exchange the operands, which is unobservable for ordinary numbers but selects the other NaN when both are NaN.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The fix is a small explicit router around every float operation: if the destination is NaN return it, else if the source is NaN return it, else perform the operation, using the original's exact roles. After the fix all four float rewrites pass 1000 of 1000 trials, including the previously failing trial.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row">
      <th role="columnheader">Case</th>
      <th role="columnheader">Plain same-order Rust</th>
      <th role="columnheader">Explicit NaN router</th>
      </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row">
      <td role="cell">Ordinary numbers</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Plain same-order Rust">Matches</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Explicit NaN router">Matches</td>
      </tr>
      <tr role="row">
      <td role="cell">One NaN operand</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Plain same-order Rust">Matches (only one payload to propagate)</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Explicit NaN router">Matches</td>
      </tr>
      <tr role="row">
      <td role="cell">Two different NaNs</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Plain same-order Rust">May diverge (compiler picks the roles)</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Explicit NaN router">Matches (roles pinned)</td>
      </tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Float rewrites pin NaN routing explicitly wherever two NaNs can meet at one operation. Same-order source alone is not a bit-exactness argument.</li>
      <li>Single-NaN trials prove nothing about this class; only trials where two different NaNs reach the same operation discriminate. Input generators should include such pairs deliberately rather than waiting for random chance (here, one trial in a thousand).</li>
      <li>Inline assembly would also pin operand roles but is forbidden; the router is plain safe code with no performance cost on the game path.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Take any routine that multiplies or adds two values that can both be NaN with different payloads, rewrite it with plain Rust operators in the original's order, and run the differential checker with float edge inputs until a two-NaN trial reaches the operation. Recover the failing trial's inputs by replaying the checker's seeded generator, then compare which input payload each side's result carries.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first fix attempt blamed the wrong layer: the return-type conversion from 32-bit to 64-bit float, which does re-encode NaN payloads. It failed on the identical trial with identical bits, which proved the divergence was in the computed value, not the conversion. Only the input replay showed the swapped-operand mechanism.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-n77">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>A wrong calling convention, and two checker weaknesses it exposed</h2>
      <p>A production lane rewriting script native handlers found that one handler's engine routine pops its own argument instead of using the usual convention, and that declaring the wrong convention makes the checker run the original into wild code; the same investigation showed faulting trials can report zero failures while comparing almost nothing, and that the shared checker binary disagrees with its own source on what counts as a pass.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each one equivalent to the original with the differential checker, deferring with a reason code any function the checker cannot verify.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Handlers verified</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">22 of 25, 1000 trials each, 0 failures</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means"><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> rewrites behave identically on every trial</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Handlers deferred</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">3 (two carry entry-register garbage in a call argument, one calls through a float register)</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means"><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the checker cannot script these shapes today</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Popping engine routine</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">one handler performs no caller-side stack cleanup</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means"><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> its engine routine pops its own argument; every other handler in the batch uses the normal convention</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Wrong-convention symptom</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">original returns to a register value instead of its caller, then runs wild</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means"><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the fault address equalled the register input on every probed trial</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Silent worker death</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">worker stopped responding at the same trial number on repeated runs</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means"><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> wild execution corrupted the worker; deterministic per seed because inputs are seeded</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Faulting trials compare little</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">a faulting trial emits 2 of 9 comparisons, and same-code fault pairs pass</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means"><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> a run can show zero failures while comparing almost nothing</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Binary disagrees with source</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">binary returned pass with a failed termination check, which the source cannot produce</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means"><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the shared binary was built from different logic than the tracked source</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Call-site cleanup decides the declared convention: no cleanup after the call means the routine pops, so declare that convention; the one misdeclared handler passed fully once corrected.</li>
      <li>Lanes should read the per-comparison totals in verdict files, not just the failure count, before calling a function verified.</li>
      <li>The accept gate should keep requiring every comparison to pass, which is what blocks the vacuous fault-only runs from counting as verified.</li>
      <li>The shared worker binary should be rebuilt from the tracked source, or the source difference documented, before wider rollout.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Take any handler whose call site has no caller-side cleanup, declare its engine routine with the normal convention, and run the checker: every trial faults at an address equal to one of the register inputs, and the worker eventually stops responding mid-contract at a seed-determined trial. Declaring the popping convention instead yields a clean full-comparison pass.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The silent mid-contract death first looked exactly like the known shared-worker flake seen by earlier lanes, and a re-seed only moved the death to a different trial. Probing single trials showed every trial was faulting for the same reason, which pointed at the contract rather than the worker. The deeper confusion was a run that reported zero failures while the original faulted on every trial; reading the worker source showed that faulting trials skip nearly all comparisons by design.</p>

      <h2>A relocation lookup bug the checker caught, and 24 verified native handlers</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A production batch of 25 script native handlers finished with 24 rewrites verified at 1000 out of 1000 differential trials each and one jump thunk deferred, and the single failure along the way exposed a relocation-table lookup bug that is now copied through several lanes' recon scripts.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite 25 script native handler functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack use, outgoing calls and faults.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Twenty-three handlers passed on the first attempt. One handler that passes an engine address to its callee failed all of its trials on the outgoing-calls comparison: the original pushed a relocated address while the rewrite pushed the raw word. A probe script had reported no relocation entry at that instruction, but re-reading the raw relocation bytes showed the entry exists. The probe added the page base to a value that already included it, so every lookup missed and every result was silently false. The same expression is present in the first production lane's recon script, which later lanes copied, so their relocation flags are affected too.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The batch also contained two shapes not seen in earlier native batches: a handler whose engine answer arrives as a floating point value rather than an integer, verified bit-exact with a script free of signaling not-a-number patterns, and a handler that makes no engine call at all and instead files data into the call context using a counter, verified with every comparison channel enabled.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th><th role="columnheader">Count</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Verified handlers</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">24</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Deferred jump thunks</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">1</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Trials without a mismatch</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">24000</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Derive the pushed address from the relocated image base like any other original address; the corrected rewrite passed all of its trials. Lanes that copied the affected recon snippet should fix the lookup to use the entry address as given instead of adding the page base again, and any past claim of the form "no relocation entry here" that rests only on that snippet should be re-checked against the raw bytes.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable's relocation directory two ways and compare: once with the library's entry addresses used directly, and once with the block page added a second time. Then dump the raw block covering the instruction in question and confirm which of the two parses matches the bytes. The checker's mismatch line for the failing contract names both pushed words, which points straight at the relocation question.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The wrong probe result was convincing because it agreed with a plausible story: the pushed word looked like a leftover constant, and the absence of an entry would have explained it. What broke the story was the checker's side-by-side comparison, which showed the original pushing a relocated value on every single trial. The lesson is that a relocation lookup that never returns true is not evidence of absence, and the raw bytes settle it in seconds.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>A relocation-table trap and a bit-exact vector rewrite</h2>
      <p>Verifying one batch of script handlers caught a wrong assumption about a pushed constant, traced it to a relocation-lookup bug that silently reports nothing as relocated, and proved a floating-point handler bit-exact with explicit SSE operations.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each one behaves identically to the original with the differential checker.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Twenty-three handlers verified, each over one thousand trials with zero failures. One handler is a single jump to a shared implementation with nothing of its own to rewrite, and one pushes boolean bytes whose upper bytes are leftover stack contents rather than behaviour, which the checker cannot mask per argument.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One handler passes a constant tag together with the call context itself, leaving argument unpacking to the engine. The tag looked like a plain constant but the checker showed the original pushing the relocated address; a direct parse of the relocation table confirmed the entry, and deriving the address at load passed every trial.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The relocation lookup snippet used for reconnaissance adds the table block base to a value that already includes it, so it matches no entry anywhere and every address looks unrelocated. The checker's failure was the only thing that exposed the wrong conclusion.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One handler does its own arithmetic instead of calling the engine: a three-component vector magnitude. Rewriting it with the same scalar SSE operations in the same order is bit-exact across edge inputs including zeros, infinities and quiet NaN.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two handlers stage a float value through a scratch register push, but overwrite the whole word before the call, so no register garbage survives; plain forwarding matches with all comparisons enabled.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Reconnaissance code should use the relocation entry value directly as the full address, never add the block base to it, and any earlier not-relocated conclusion drawn with the doubling formula should be treated as unknown until rechecked against a raw table parse.</li>
      <li>Pure-compute floating-point handlers should be rewritten with explicit SIMD operations in the original order rather than plain arithmetic, so the result is identical by construction on every input class.</li>
      <li>Handlers whose pushed call words contain leftover bytes the rewrite cannot observe stay deferred until the checker can mask individual call arguments.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane's checker contracts for the batch: the tag-forwarding handler fails every trial with a plain constant and passes every trial once the address is derived at load, and the vector handler passes every trial over float edge values with the SIMD rewrite. The lookup bug is visible by comparing the entry values against a raw walk of the relocation table.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A rebuild failed because a lingering worker held the output file open, and the failure was missed because only the output length had been captured, so the next checker run tested the stale file and failed identically. Comparing file timestamps exposed it; renaming the locked file aside and rebuilding fixed it. The lesson is to always capture build output and compare timestamps before re-running after a rebuild.</p>
      </article>
