      <h2>One verified, and a checker gap: loops that poll a callee until done</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A production batch of three animation-system functions yielded one verified rewrite, one deferral on the time cap, and one function the checker cannot verify at all: it calls a tokeniser in a loop until the tokeniser returns null, and the checker scripts only one fixed answer per callee per trial, so the loop either never ends or never starts.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite three neighbouring animation-system functions in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the version 2 differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, memory, stack, calls and faults over at least one thousand trials each.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The middle function, a registry that matches two key words and otherwise allocates a record, registers fourteen parameters and appends it, verified clean: one thousand trials, zero failures, every callee fired, and a planted mutant caught through the globals comparison within eight trials.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The largest function dispatches each token from a tokeniser against twenty-one flag names and sets bits in an output word. The tokeniser is called in a loop until it returns null. The checker's answer scripts are indexed by trial, and the worker fills each callee slot once per trial, so every call within a trial returns the same value: a non-null script hangs the loop and a null script tests only the empty path. No contract can drive this shape under version 2.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first function, with about twenty direct call sites, three table-driven calls and a float loop, looks verifiable in principle but needs roughly an hour of contract and rewrite work against a thirty-minute single-function cap, so it was deferred with a full call-site map for the next lane.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The registry rewrite was accepted. The tokeniser loop was deferred with the missing ability named exactly: per-call answer sequencing, where a callee's script is a list consumed in call order within a trial rather than one value fixed per trial. Until the worker stub advances its answer slot per call, lanes should defer any function that polls a scripted callee until a sentinel instead of spending attempts on it. A table of the batch outcome is below.</p>

      </tr>
      <tr role="row">
      <td role="cell">Object setup with float loop</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Size class">Medium</td>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">Deferred, single-function time cap</td>

Separately, a null word inside heap and pin specs silently becomes random bits rather than zero, so literal zero must be written instead.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="swarm-memory-limit">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-04">2026-10-04</time></div>
      <h2>The swarm ran the machine out of memory: what the real limit is</h2>
      <p>At 74 lanes the laptop came within about 1 GB of its commit limit, lanes began to fail, and the coordinator had to stop six lanes by hand. The limit that mattered was not free memory, which is what every guard had been watching.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>The project owner asked for as many agents as the laptop's memory can handle. Through the evening the swarm ran at 55 to 65 lanes with 4 to 8 GB of memory free, and self-refilling slots paused whenever free memory fell below 3 GB.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <table>
      <thead><tr><th>Fact</th><th>Value</th><th>What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
      <tr><td>Lanes running at the time</td><td data-label="Value">74</td><td data-label="What it means">Thirteen of them were the new re-run lanes</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Commit in use</td><td data-label="Value">85.6 of 86.8 GB</td><td data-label="What it means">The operating system had already grown the page file twice; the next large allocation anywhere would fail</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Free physical memory</td><td data-label="Value">0.7 GB at the worst point</td><td data-label="What it means">It had read 8 GB twenty minutes earlier</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Checker worker processes</td><td data-label="Value">107</td><td data-label="What it means">Each re-run lane had started about a dozen at once to run its batch in parallel</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Shell processes</td><td data-label="Value">215, about 13 GB of private memory</td><td data-label="What it means">Every lane and every slot keeps several shells alive; together they were the largest single consumer</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Agent processes</td><td data-label="Value">62, about 9 GB</td><td data-label="What it means">The number the earlier estimates were based on</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The per-lane cost is not the agent process. Earlier estimates took about 230 MB per lane from the agent's own memory. Counting the shells, Python processes and checker workers a lane starts, a production lane costs closer to 600 MB of commit, and a re-run lane running twelve workers costs well over 1 GB.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Free memory is the wrong gauge. The slots' guard read free physical memory, saw more than 3 GB, and kept starting lanes while commit climbed to the limit. Free memory only collapsed in the last few minutes.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Slots now wait for both at least 5 GB of free memory and at least 14 GB of commit headroom before starting a lane, with a random delay so they do not all start in the same second. Lanes that run a batch through the checker are told to use at most three worker processes at a time. The working ceiling on this machine is about 45 lanes, not 60 to 70.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>The numbers come from the operating system's memory counters and per-process private memory, grouped by process name, read while the machine was under pressure.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Six re-run lanes were stopped mid-work to recover; their ported rewrites were on disk and they were restarted one at a time with instructions to continue. Several production lanes and slots failed with errors during the squeeze and their batches will need to be handed out again. Stopping the lanes took over ten minutes because the machine was thrashing. The coordinator had described 60 lanes as the ceiling on the strength of free memory alone and then added a wave of heavier lanes on top; it should have measured what a lane of the new kind costs before launching thirteen of them.</p>
      </article>

      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Production batch: eighteen small functions verified, one checker anomaly</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A production batch of twenty small file and memory subsystem functions yielded eighteen verified Rust rewrites, each passing one thousand differential trials with zero failures, and two deferrals caused by a checker anomaly in which the original is reported as finding its argument at index zero on every trial where the argument sits anywhere in a scripted table.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, written memory, stack effects, outgoing calls and faults.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Eighteen functions verified on the first attempt with no fixes needed. The batch split into init loops over heap objects, pure queries, global table resets and queries, a constructor mixing a global sequence number into an id slot, a guarded activation wrapper, flag-gated clears, a global scan driving a ten-argument engine call, a name-to-hash pool search, and a handle dereference. Eleven use a register-plus-stack convention and nine use a stack-only convention. Two functions had merged symbol names that matched their disassembly; the rest were given descriptive names.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two twin functions that scan a ten-entry global table for a query value could not be verified. Twelve dedicated probe contracts narrowed the symptom to a precise rule: the original is reported as returning index zero whenever the query value is present anywhere in the explicitly scripted table, and agrees with the rewrite on misses and on genuine index-zero hits. The rewrite returns the true index on every trial. The probes ruled out fill size, fill entry shape, junk values, stale fills, request encoding, and instruction decoding as causes; the worker source reads correctly on every path inspected, so the root cause is still unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Under this anomaly a wrong rewrite that returned a bare membership flag would pass a full-coverage contract, while the correct rewrite fails one. Narrowing the contract to index-zero hits plus misses would pass but would leave the other nine indexes untested, which is not verification, so both functions were deferred instead.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Both table scans are deferred with reason other and a pointer to the lane report, which holds a three-trial minimal repro and the full probe table.</li>
      <li>The checker owner should reproduce the minimal case with per-side logging of the table words, the entry register and the exit register, and compare the built worker binary against the checked-in source on the result observation path.</li>
      <li>After any worker change, the two table contracts should be re-run unchanged: they plant all ten hit indexes deterministically and should then pass with no rewrite change.</li>
      <li>One six-line driver extension was added to this lane's driver copy only: a stack argument kind that cycles a fixed value list, for indexes that must be negative on some trials and small on others. No worker change was needed for anything else.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Script the ten table words to fixed values with the query value at index one and anything else at index zero, pass the query value as the sole argument, and run three trials. The rewrite returns the index-one encoding on all three; the original is reported as returning the index-zero encoding on all three. Replacing the fill with a uniform table makes both sides agree, in both the hit and the miss direction.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The anomaly investigation took about forty minutes because every natural theory died to exactly one observation: same-memory theories cannot produce disagreement from a shared request, shifted-read theories die to the passing index-zero trial, and alias theories die to the passing miss trials. The eventual pattern, that the original reports membership as index zero, only emerged after mapping every table position with distinct values. Nothing else went wrong: the rewrite crate built first try, no worker flakes occurred, and the riskiest contract, a pool search over a fully scripted heap pool, passed immediately.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>An audio initialiser that reads a word it never wrote</h2>
      <p>One small audio initialiser in this batch copies the same uninitialised word from its own fresh stack frame into four fields of the record it builds, so no faithful rewrite can be verified against it and it was deferred.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty small audio-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical starting state and compares everything observable.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seventeen of the twenty functions verified cleanly at one thousand trials each with zero mismatches. They are ordinary small routines: two entity constructors, three flag predicates, three float conversion routines, a list drain, three guarded releases and four block resets.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One initialiser reads the same stack word four times and stores it into four record fields, but nothing in the function ever writes that word. The slot sits inside the function's own freshly reserved frame, below the saved frame pointer on every possible stack alignment, so the value is leftover stack garbage from previous calls, not an argument and not a constant.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> This looks like a genuine bug in the original: four record fields are seeded with whatever happened to be on the stack. The game presumably tolerates or overwrites the values later.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two further functions are large floating point routines over game data tables that exceed the twelve minute single-function budget and were deferred for a lane with more time.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The initialiser was deferred with reason other and no rewrite was attempted: reproducing caller stack garbage would need inline assembly, which project rules forbid, and pinning the value would be a fake pass. This needs a checker-level decision, not a better rewrite: either such functions stay permanently deferred, or the harness gains an explicit rule for uninitialised stack words. Until then, lanes that find a function reading a word it never wrote should defer it with the same reason rather than guess.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the function with capstone from the project copy of the executable and list every stack read and write: the four reads of the same frame slot have no matching write anywhere in the body. The frame arithmetic shows the slot always lands below the frame base, which rules out a hidden argument.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first reading looked like a possible hidden float argument, since the value is moved with vector instructions into four evenly spaced fields. Checking the frame arithmetic slot by slot ruled that out: no alignment makes the read land on an argument, the return address or the saved frame pointer. A second trap in the same batch was a conversion loop that skips one source offset; the first rewrite assumed contiguous inputs and the checker caught it on the first run.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Production lane traps: a misleading mnemonic, a short size, and an unsolved float divergence</h2>
      <p>Seventeen of twenty audio functions verified first, then three lessons worth sharing: a disassembler mnemonic that means the opposite of what it says, a function that runs past its listed size in two inventories, and a float divergence on denormal-heavy inputs that resisted half an hour of probing and is left reproducible for the checker owners.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty small audio-subsystem functions in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, deferring with a reason code where the checker cannot verify.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Capstone prints SSE predicate six as cmpnless, which reads as not-less-than but is not-less-or-equal. The two differ only when the operands compare exactly equal, which produced a thirteen-in-a-thousand failure that the checker caught and a one-line fix cured.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The batch's large mixer evaluator continues past its listed size in both the batch list and the repaired inventory: two more stores, the epilogue and the return sit beyond the listed end, followed by padding and the next batch function. The rewrite covers the full body.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A zero-length guard idiom recurs in float code: an unordered compare, a flags-to-register move, a mask test and a parity jump together mean not-equal, guarding a square-root plus reciprocal against zero input including negative zero, with NaN taking the compute path.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The batch interpolator fails about a tenth of trials, every failure on denormal-heavy table rows in one of its two modes while the other mode passes completely. The rewrite matches a strict software emulation bit for bit, minimal tables pass, and the failure bisects to a single table word, but the original-side intermediate values were never captured so the mechanism is unknown.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Trust the SSE predicate byte, never the printed mnemonic, when porting scalar float compares; check equality-boundary behaviour explicitly.</li>
      <li>Disassemble past the listed end before trusting any batch size, and treat the repaired inventory as advisory where it repeats the same number.</li>
      <li>The interpolator case stays deferred with its failing contract and four probe scripts in the lane folder; whoever continues should capture original-side intermediates through worker-side tracing or ask the checker owners whether denormal-heavy vector math is a known gap.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Read the lane report for the batch analysis and the per-function verdict table. Rerun any verified contract with the lane's driver copy and the stock worker binary for a thousand trials. Reproduce the interpolator divergence with the probe scripts, which drive the worker directly with hand-built single trials and bisect the failing table word by word.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two self-inflicted issues: a shell append that wrote Unicode into the Rust sources and broke the build, repaired by truncating at the first null byte with a script; and two rebuilds blocked by a locked output file while a worker held it mapped, worked around by renaming the old file aside and rebuilding. The unresolved item is the interpolator divergence above: every simpler hypothesis (wrong branch, wrong address, misread opcode, uninitialised input) was eliminated by probes, and the lane stopped past its per-function cap rather than guess.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>A wrong stub arity passes vacuously through identical faults</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A contract that declares one stack argument too many for an intercepted callee makes the stub clean up too many stack words, so the original and the rewrite both return to a garbage address and fault identically on every trial, and the checker counts that as passing with no behavioural comparison run at all.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty small audio functions and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker, one contract per function, one thousand trials each.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Eleven of the twenty functions are thin wrappers that move their first argument into a register and forward the rest to a callee. The contracts declared the callee's stack argument count equal to the wrapper's, which is one too many, because the first argument travels in a register, not on the stack.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> With the arity overstated by one word, the recorder stub popped one word too many on return. Both sides then returned into their own first argument instead of to the caller. Since that argument is a random test value, both sides faulted on essentially every trial, at the same address with the same fault code.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker treats a fault on both sides with equal codes as a pass and skips every other comparison for that trial. One wrapper's verdict read 995 of 1000 passing with only the termination checks present; the return value, stack, heap, call and undeclared-write checks ran on zero trials. The verdict file gives no signal that nothing behavioural was compared.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Signal</th><th role="columnheader">Vacuous verdict</th><th role="columnheader">Genuine verdict</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Comparisons present</td><td role="cell" data-label="Vacuous verdict">termination only</td><td role="cell" data-label="Genuine verdict">return, stack, calls and the rest</td></tr>

      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Any contract bug that makes both sides fault identically, not only an arity slip, passes the same silent way.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Fixed the eleven contracts to declare one fewer stack argument for the callees and re-ran them; every re-run shows the full set of behavioural checks passing.</li>
      <li>Recommended for the checker: record per-trial end states and require a floor of cleanly-returned trials before a verdict can pass, so a contract bug can never again pass through universal faulting.</li>
      <li>Recommended for lanes until then: after every run, confirm the verdict lists the behavioural checks, not just termination. A verdict with only termination checks proves nothing.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Declare one callee stack argument too many in any wrapper contract and run the checker. Nearly every trial passes on termination alone; a few fail where the random first argument happens to point into the mapped image, which is the only visible symptom. The worker source shows the comparison returning early once both sides fault with equal codes.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first symptom looked like a rewrite defect: a handful of trials reported the rewrite touching original code. Tracing the fault address showed it always equalled the wrapper's first argument on both sides, which pointed away from the rewrite and toward the stack discipline, and from there to the overstated arity. The same mistaken count had been copied into all eleven wrapper contracts from one generator function, so all of them needed re-running.</p>

      <h2>A wrong fifteen-argument rewrite passes the checker</h2>
      <p>Twenty-five script native handlers were rewritten and verified this shift, but the most important result is a gap: a rewrite with two of its fifteen call arguments swapped still passes, because the checker's call stub records only the first eight stack arguments. The same shift also found that several handlers reuse their own incoming stack slot as scratch space, which safe Rust cannot reproduce and the checker must therefore exclude.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, running at least one thousand trials per function.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All twenty-five handlers take a single call-context pointer, make exactly one direct call to an engine function, and touch no globals. Fourteen are plain argument forwards; the rest normalise a boolean, return a byte, word or float through the return slot, or pass one float argument.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five handlers write scratch data over their own incoming stack slot: four normalise a boolean into its low byte, one spills a float result across the whole slot. The pushed call bytes were reproduced exactly, but the slot clobber itself is unwritable from safe Rust, so the stack comparison is disabled for those five contracts and the exclusion is documented in each one.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A deliberately wrong rewrite of the fifteen-argument handler, with two late arguments swapped, passes all two hundred honesty trials. The worker stub stores at most eight stack arguments per call, so late arguments are never compared. Two other mutants, with a wrong boolean encoding and a missing byte mask, fail as required, which shows the surrounding checks are working.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The twenty-five rewrites are accepted, with the late arguments of the fifteen-argument handler covered by construction and an independent argument-order cross-check rather than by the checker. The recommended follow-up is a worker extension that records more than eight stack arguments per call, after which that handler should be re-verified with no code changes.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build any contract whose callee takes more than eight stack arguments, run the correct rewrite to confirm it passes, then swap two arguments past the eighth position and run again: the checker still passes. The same procedure with an argument inside the first eight fails on the calls comparison.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A contract regeneration silently reverted an intended configuration flip, so the main runs used the stronger full-discovery mode throughout; four earlier verdicts were rerun so the batch has uniform rigor. A duplicate of the lane's own runner appeared under a different interpreter and was killed after its nature was established. Throughput fell to roughly a tenth of the pilot figure under more than thirty concurrent workers, so the remaining contracts were split across two workers to finish inside the timebox.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Assembling the format readers into one workspace</h2>
      <p>The thirteen finished format-reader crates now build and test as one workspace, with no warnings under the project's strictest lint set. Assembly found and fixed six abort-class robustness bugs the lane tests had missed, all of them unbounded allocations or unguarded reads on hostile input.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Collect the workspace scaffold and every finished format-reader crate into a single workspace that builds, tests and lints cleanly on two Windows targets, with game-file tests skipping cleanly when no game folder is configured. Audit every crate for material that must never be published, review code quality as a senior reviewer, add hostile-input tests for each reader, and propose a commit sequence for integration.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Thirteen lanes had finished; five were still running and were left out. One reader had to be renamed because it shared a name with an engine-subsystem crate. Seven example programs shared one filename and would have overwritten each other in a shared build folder, so each got a unique name.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The strict lint set produced about five hundred diagnostics across the thirteen crates, almost all mechanical: missing documentation sections, unmarked must-use functions, and integer casts. Each cast site was read. Harmless ones became explicit conversions; value-changing ones on hostile input became checked conversions that return the crate's error type.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The audit found nothing to remove. No decompiled code, no disassembly listings, no key material, no machine paths, no verbatim game data. Text fixtures were compared against the matching real game files and none appears there. The key-locating hash and offset list are the documented run-time mechanism, not key material, and nothing prints or logs keys.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Six abort-class bugs were fixed: three readers inflated compressed data without any size bound, and three pre-allocated collections directly from raw file counts. Each fix got a regression test proving hostile input now returns an error. A further three panics on truncated or mis-indexed input were fixed the same way.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game-folder tests were unified on one convention: the install folder that holds the game directory. Two lanes had assumed one level deeper and were changed. Four optional lane variables were renamed to the same project prefix.</p>
      <ul>
      <li>Integration should land as thirteen commits, one crate per commit in dependency order; only the save-game reader depends on others.</li>
      <li>Four decisions need the coordinator: the MIT licence choice, the renamed script crate, keeping the key-locating constants, and the game-folder convention.</li>
      <li>Follow-up work: an iterative rewrite of one recursive table walk, unit tests for the one crate that has none, and checked arithmetic in two 32-bit edge cases.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>From the staging copy, run the workspace build, the workspace tests with and without the game-folder variable set, and clippy with warnings denied, on both the host target and the 64-bit Intel target. Then run the per-crate hostile-input suites, which need no game files. All gates pass with zero diagnostics.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The panic-documentation lint fires on any public function containing an unwrap or expect, including ones proven dead by validation elsewhere. Each of the eighteen sites was verified by hand before documenting the invariant, which took longer than the mechanical fixes.</p>
      <p>The formatter turned several long match arms into blocks without trailing semicolons, which the lint set then rejected. The failures only appeared on the second target because its build cache was fresh, which briefly looked like a target-specific lint before the real cause was found.</p>
      <p>The hostile-input sweeps start from synthetic patterns, so they mostly exercise early rejections. The deep-state allocation bugs were found by reading every allocation site, not by the sweeps. A corpus fuzzer over real files would go further and does not exist yet.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>A matrix routine that copies stack garbage, and a compiler trap for rewrites</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One large matrix-transform routine in this batch reads a stack slot it never wrote and stores the result into the object, so three output fields receive whatever the caller left on the stack; it cannot be faithfully rewritten and was deferred.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, deferring any function the checker cannot verify.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seventeen of the twenty functions verified with one thousand trials each and zero failures. They are flag-gated float updates, small vector copies, and single-call forwarding wrappers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two functions end in a tail jump to shared code after doing a little work of their own, which the checker cannot follow, so both were deferred.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The matrix routine reserves a sixteen-byte stack area, never writes to it, then loads one float from it three times into three output fields. The slot always lies below the frame, in caller-owned stack, so the values are caller residue. A rewrite has no way to observe that memory, and copying whatever the test harness happens to leave there would be a fake pass.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The stack read looks like an uninitialized-variable bug in the original code rather than anything deliberate.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The matrix routine was deferred as unverifiable, and the two tail-jump functions likewise. Sibling lanes should treat any function whose output depends on uninitialized stack or register state as unrewritable rather than encoding harness-specific residue.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the routine and list every write to the stack between the frame setup and the three float loads: there are none, and the loaded slot is always at a lower address than the frame pointer. Any input state gives the same verdict, since the value comes from outside the function.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One rewrite failed two trials in a thousand with no visible cause: the Rust compiler had packed three independent scalar float operations into vector instructions and swapped their operands, which changes the result only when both sides are not-a-number values with different payloads. The fix computes through small helpers that settle the not-a-number cases explicitly. Any lane rewriting parallel independent float arithmetic should check its compiled output for the same repacking.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-s07">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>A faithful rewrite can fail the cheat check</h2>
      <p>Twenty small leaderboard routines were rewritten and all twenty passed a thousand differential trials each, but the runs also showed that the checker can wrongly accuse a correct rewrite of cheating: when both sides perform the same wild pointer read and the address lands in the original program's own code pages, the original reads them fine while the rewrite faults, because the checker revokes those pages while the rewrite runs, and the fault is reported as cheating.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty small game routines that share one helper-call pattern, and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All twenty rewrites passed one thousand trials each with zero mismatches, covering the helper-call protocol, the failure paths, value-returning paths through controlled memory, and fault parity on wild reads. A deliberately wrong rewrite was caught within three trials.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One trial in a thousand failed a correct rewrite as cheating. Recomputing the trial input from the recorded seed showed the rewrite read exactly the address the original read; the address happened to sit inside the original code pages, which are readable when the original runs and revoked when the rewrite runs. The mismatch is a checker artifact, not a rewrite bug. Steering wild inputs away from the code range removed it with the comparison itself unchanged.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> A second, rarer asymmetry (two trials in about four thousand, only in the fulldata phase) saw the original read an address outside the program image successfully while the rewrite faulted on the same address. Input replay again showed the rewrite read exactly the intended address; reading the worker source points at its per-phase snapshot buffers, which are allocated fresh for each side and freed in between, so an address mapped during the original phase can be gone during the rewrite phase.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Finding</th><th role="columnheader">Rate</th><th role="columnheader">Status</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Rewrite behaviour mismatch</th><td role="cell" data-label="Rate">none in twenty thousand trials</td><td role="cell" data-label="Status">all verified</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">False cheat verdict on code-page reads</th><td role="cell" data-label="Rate">about one in a thousand wild trials</td><td role="cell" data-label="Status">worked around in the lane driver</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Read asymmetry outside code pages</th><td role="cell" data-label="Rate">two in about four thousand fulldata trials</td><td role="cell" data-label="Status">mechanism identified, worker fix proposed</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Wild-read inputs should avoid the original code range until the worker changes; the comparison on all other trials stays strict.</li>
      <li>Recommended worker fixes: only treat faults at the rewrite's own instruction address inside original code as cheating, or treat a fault at the same address on both sides as agreement; and reuse snapshot buffers across both phases instead of allocating them per phase.</li>
      <li>Recommended driver fix: a lost worker should restart the batch from the next contract instead of abandoning the run, since the watchdog can fire on slow trials under load.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run any wild-reading rewrite whose input address can land in the original code pages: the original side reports success while the rewrite side reports a fault inside the code range, flagged as cheating. Recomputing the trial input from the contract seed confirms both sides addressed the same location.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first false cheat looked like a real bug until the fault address was matched against the recomputed input. A later batch run died partway when a worker was lost under load; the verdict it left behind records zero failures with an error flag, because the error path drops the counters, so the per-check totals are the only reliable record of those trials.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-n29">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Native handlers that stash a flag in their own doorstep</h2>
      <p>Five script-native handlers coerce a true/false argument by writing the 0/1 byte over the low byte of their own incoming argument slot on the stack, then pass that whole slot to the engine, high bytes and all. The high bytes are the caller's own context pointer, so the engine receives a flag fused with a pointer. Rewrites reproduce this exactly, and a deliberately wrong rewrite was caught by the checker on its first trial.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of 25 script-native handlers in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs both from identical state and compares results, memory, calls and faults.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 25 handlers in the batch take one call-context pointer holding a return slot and an argument array, forward their arguments to one engine function, and optionally store the answer. All are short straight-line wrappers with no branches.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five of them normalize a true/false argument with an unusual trick: instead of pushing a clean 0 or 1, they overwrite the low byte of the stack slot that holds their own incoming context pointer and push that slot. The engine therefore receives the context pointer's high bytes fused with the flag bit. One more handler uses the same slot as scratch space for a float result on its way to the return slot.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker cannot compare that scratch slot for these six handlers, because a Rust function cannot address its own incoming stack slot. The pushed value is instead verified exactly through the outgoing-call comparison, and the slot is dead after return. The six contracts record this choice explicitly.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Future lanes should watch for this pattern: any handler that writes into its incoming stack slot needs the stack comparison off and an exact-value proof through the call comparison instead. The batch generator built for this lane documents the rule and can be reused for further native batches.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane's contracts with the project checker: every rewrite passes one thousand trials with zero tolerance, and two deliberately introduced bugs (a dropped byte mask, a raw flag instead of the fused value) are both caught within a few trials.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The checker worker process was twice lost mid-run with no failing trial, apparently under machine load, and the driver then crashed talking to the dead worker instead of recovering. Both contracts passed cleanly on rerun. The lane's driver copy now restarts the worker in that case.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Twenty native handlers verified, and three traps for the next lanes</h2>
      <p>Twenty of twenty-five script native handlers now have Rust rewrites proven identical to the originals over one thousand trials each, with a fulldata second phase confirming none of them touch global state. The five that could not be verified taught us more than the twenty that could.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original using the differential checker, which runs the original and the rewrite from identical starting state and compares return values, memory writes, stack effects, outgoing calls and faults.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Most handlers in the batch are thin wrappers: read script arguments from the call context, forward them to one engine function, and either return its answer or store one byte of it into the return slot. Twenty followed shapes the checker handles well and all passed.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two console-debug stub handlers store a fixed word to the return slot. That word is a relocated image address, not a plain magic constant: an early rewrite that stored it literally failed every trial, and resolving it through the mapped image base passes. A wrong relocation-table script had claimed otherwise; the checker settled it on the first trial.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One handler passes its engine argument in a register with no stack arguments at all, unlike its four lookalikes which push. Modelling it as a stack-argument call failed every trial on the call comparison; modelling the register call passes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Four handlers coerce a script argument to a boolean by writing the flag into the low byte of their own incoming stack-argument slot, then push that clobbered word to the engine function. The pushed value therefore carries address bits from the caller's stack slot alongside the flag. That stack-slot write is covered by the checker's stack comparison but is not reachable from stable Rust without inline assembly, so all four are deferred with a stated reason rather than fudged.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One handler passes a pointer to its own stack frame as a call argument. Stack call arguments are always compared in full and frame addresses cannot match across code generation, so it is deferred too.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Deferring with a precise reason beats weakening a comparison. Five functions are recorded as deferred with the exact blocker, so a future worker extension can unblock them honestly.</li>
      <li>Lanes hitting a boolean-coercion handler should check for the write into the incoming argument slot first: if it is there, the function cannot be verified as the checker stands, and no rewrite attempt will change that.</li>
      <li>The lane driver now survives the check worker dying mid-batch under load by starting a fresh worker and continuing; that change is proposed for foldback into the shared driver.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the checker driver in the lane scratch folder over the twenty contracts: each must report one thousand passing trials with zero failures, plus a two-hundred-trial fulldata confirmation each. The honesty mutant, which drops the low-byte mask on one return-value handler, must fail on the heap comparison within a few trials.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A relocation-table script repeated a documented pilot mistake and wrongly cleared two relocated addresses as plain constants; the checker caught it immediately. The check worker died once mid-batch under the shared host load and once the driver crashed the whole run on a malformed contract of our own making (a heap segment index off by one); both are handled now. Build throughput is several times slower than the pilots measured because dozens of lanes share the host.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Production batch n20: twenty-five native handlers, one compiler surprise</h2>
      <p>Twenty-three of twenty-five script native handlers were rewritten in Rust and proven identical to the originals with the differential checker, a thousand trials each and every honesty mutant caught. The surprise was in four of them: the original coerces a script boolean by scribbling the 0/1 result into the low byte of its own incoming argument slot and pushing the whole dword to the engine, so the engine call receives the call-context pointer with its low byte replaced instead of a clean boolean.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original using the project checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every handler in the batch follows one calling pattern: a single pointer to a call context holding a return slot and an argument array, one direct engine call, and either no stored result or one store through the return slot. They fall into a few shapes:</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Shape</th><th role="columnheader">Count</th><th role="columnheader">Behaviour</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">

      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Count">Byte result</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">6</td><td role="cell" data-label="Behaviour">Store the low byte of the engine answer through the return slot</td></tr>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The four boolean handlers reuse their own dead argument slot as scratch: the 0/1 result overwrites the low byte of the incoming context pointer, and that modified dword is what the engine receives. Since a real context address is never small, the value the engine sees is always nonzero even when the script passed false. Whether the engine reads the full dword or only the low byte decides whether the false branch works at all.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One further handler passes eleven argument words to its engine call, which exceeds the checker's eight-word call record, so its last three arguments could never be compared and it was deferred rather than stamped with a gap.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Rewrites reproduce the slot-surgery value exactly, and the pushed value is compared on every trial with the context placed at an address with a nonzero low byte so the masking is exercised.</li>
      <li>The stack comparison is disabled for those four contracts only, because the original's write lands on its own incoming slot where no Rust rewrite can follow without inline assembly; the value itself is still checked through the call record.</li>
      <li>The jump thunk and the eleven-argument handler were deferred with explicit reason codes instead of verified with holes.</li>
      <li>The checker driver should restart a lost worker mid-run and resume remaining trials; two runs died environmentally with zero failures and passed cleanly on rerun.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble any of the four boolean handlers and watch the incoming argument slot between the comparison and the engine call: the low byte changes to 0 or 1 while the upper bytes keep the old pointer value, and the pushed engine argument is that combined dword. The lane scratch folder holds the contracts, verdicts and rewrites behind these numbers.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first full-batch run died twice with the worker process vanishing mid-contract and no failures recorded; both contracts passed a thousand trials on immediate rerun with identical inputs, which pointed at machine load rather than the trials. Running one contract per worker process contained it.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The slot reuse looks like a compiler saving one stack slot by recycling dead space, not hand-written code: it is identical in all four handlers and serves no purpose a plain push would not.</p>

      <h2>Some native handlers cannot be rewritten without assembly</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A production batch of twenty-five script native handlers yielded eighteen verified rewrites, and the seven deferrals share only two causes: six handlers normalize a boolean argument by writing into their own incoming stack slot, which safe Rust cannot reproduce, and one handler is a bare jump to engine code with no body to rewrite.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handler functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, running at least one thousand trials per function including edge values.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Eighteen handlers verified cleanly: each passed one thousand standard trials plus two hundred full-data undeclared-write discovery trials with zero failures, all on the first attempt. Three deliberate mutants were all caught quickly, confirming the checks are sensitive to swapped call arguments, unmasked return bytes and inverted flag logic.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Six handlers share a surprising idiom: to pass a true or false value to the engine, they write the normalized byte directly into the low byte of their own incoming argument slot on the stack, then push that corrupted slot as the call argument. Both effects are visible to the checker, so a rewrite must reproduce the stack write exactly, but naming that slot from safe Rust is impossible: taking the argument's address gives a compiler-made frame copy instead, and inline assembly is forbidden. These six were deferred.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One handler is a five-byte jump to engine code with padding after it, so there is no handler body to rewrite. It was deferred as a jump thunk.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Defer slot-scratch handlers rather than weaken any comparison; record the exact reason so a future checker extension can revisit them as a class.</li>
      <li>Other native batches will contain the same boolean idiom, so lanes should check for it during disassembly before writing contracts.</li>
      <li>Under heavy machine load, run one contract per driver invocation with retry on failure: two contracts here lost their worker mid-run with zero failures and passed fully on same-seed retry.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble any deferred handler from the original executable and look for a boolean test whose result is stored into the incoming stack argument slot before the engine call. Compare against a Rust rewrite that computes the same call argument but cannot touch the slot: the call comparison passes while the stack comparison reports the missing write. Attempting the C-variadic workaround fails at compile time on this toolchain.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The relocation check initially reported that absolute addresses had no fixup entries, which would have broken every global read. The bug was in the check script: the parsing library already returns full addresses, and the script added the page base a second time. A pilot lane report described this exact trap, and re-reading it fixed the issue in minutes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first full-batch run aborted partway when its worker process went silent; the driver then crashed while tearing down instead of continuing. Splitting the run into one invocation per contract with a single retry made the rest of the batch proceed unattended.</p>
      </article>

      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>A whole batch that ends in jumps, not returns</h2>
      <p>This production batch verified nothing, and that is the finding: all twenty functions were destructor fragments that hand off to the next destructor with a tail jump, a shape the checker cannot intercept, so the only honest outcome was to defer every one.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite twenty small game functions from the animation task subsystem in Rust and prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every function in the batch takes an object pointer, writes one or two table pointers into the object, sometimes releases one owned field, and then jumps to another destructor instead of returning. There is not a single return instruction in the batch. About half make one ordinary call first; the rest only store and jump.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker's worker only intercepts ordinary call instructions and refuses anything else, which its own source states plainly. A tail jump therefore cannot be observed or scripted: running the original would execute unrewritten game code, including further chained jumps, and no honest rewrite can reproduce that.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The batch had been classified as checkable. The classifier counts ordinary calls but does not look at the final instruction, so it mistakes jump-chained destructors for plain checkable functions.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>All twenty functions were deferred with a stated blocker and no checker runs were made, since there was nothing the checker can express. Two recommendations went to the coordinator: exclude functions ending in a jump from checkable batches, and consider a future worker feature that turns a terminal jump into an observed call so this whole class becomes verifiable.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble any function in the batch and read its last instruction: it is a direct jump to another destructor, which itself ends the same way. Read the worker source function that installs call patches: it rejects any site that is not an ordinary call. The batch list, the repaired inventory sizes, and the merged destructor names all agree on what these functions are.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A first relocation check wrongly reported that none of the table addresses are relocated, because the script added the page base twice. The corrected check confirms they all are. The lesson, already learned by earlier lanes in both directions: when a small script disagrees with an established proof, suspect the script.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Nine-argument native calls exceed the checker call log</h2>
      <p>One native handler in this batch forwards nine words to its engine function, but the checker call stub records at most eight stack arguments, so the ninth word is passed by the rewrite without being machine-checked. Everything else about the function is verified; the gap is documented, not hidden.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of script native handlers in Rust and prove each identical to the original with the differential checker, which compares return values, written memory, stack behavior, and outgoing calls over one thousand trials per function.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Twenty-three of twenty-five handlers verified with zero failures in twenty-three thousand trials. Two were deferred: one is a single trap instruction and the other is a bare jump to its engine function.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The vehicle-attach handler passes nine words to its engine call (three handles and flags plus two by-value vectors). The checker stub that records outgoing calls keeps the callee id plus the first eight stack words, so the ninth word never appears in the call comparison. A rewrite that passed a wrong ninth word would still get a passing verdict on every check.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seven bool-taking handlers build their engine argument inside their own dead incoming-argument stack slot, so the pushed word keeps the context pointer's high bytes with the low byte replaced by the bool. The rewrites reproduce that exact word and the call comparison checks it, but the stack comparison is disabled for those seven because the dead-slot clobber itself cannot be reproduced without inline assembly.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The nine-word rewrite was accepted as verified with the eighth-word-plus gap stated in the lane report: it passes all nine words and every machine-checked comparison passes. The recommended fix is a worker extension that widens call-log entries beyond eight stack words, after which this function should be re-verified with no contract change. Other lanes with handlers forwarding more than eight words should state the same caveat until then.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Read any verified contract whose callee declares nine stack arguments and compare the recorded call log against the pushed words: the log holds the first eight only. The worker source states the eight-word cap where it emits the recorder stub.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first run of the vector-scratch handler failed on the return register: the original reloads it from the context for the return-slot store, so it returns the slot pointer rather than the engine answer. Re-reading the other return handlers before running them caught the same shape in three more and confirmed the fifth genuinely returns the answer. A transposed address typo in one contract was refused at setup, and one run died to machine load with zero failures in its completed trials; all three passed on the second attempt.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-n09">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Native handlers smuggle booleans through their own stack slot</h2>
      <p>Many script native handlers pass a boolean to the engine by overwriting the low byte of their own incoming argument word on the stack and pushing the whole word, so the engine receives the context address with its low byte replaced by the flag. Rewrites must reproduce both the pushed value and the clobbered stack word, and the checker observes both.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original with the differential checker.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Six handlers in the batch coerce a script argument to boolean with a set-byte-on-stack pattern: compare the argument word against zero, set the low byte of the incoming argument slot to 0 or 1, then push that slot. The pushed boolean therefore carries the call context address in its high bytes. A seventh handler spills a float argument over the same slot. The checker's stack comparison covers incoming argument words, so a rewrite that only computes the pushed value still fails on the stack diff.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Safe Rust cannot name its own incoming argument slot without the stack pointer, so the rewrite cannot reproduce the write unassisted. The worker derives the incoming stack address deterministically from the scratch stack base it already reports, and the driver passes that address into a dead word of the call context that the original never reads. Both sides start from identical state, the original ignores the extra word, and the pushed value is independently verified through the outgoing-call comparison.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Other native lanes should expect the same set-byte pattern wherever a handler coerces a boolean, and reuse the incoming-address harness word rather than disabling the stack comparison. Two handlers that pass a pointer to their own stack frame to the engine were deferred instead, because excluding that pointer from the comparison would leave the marshalled data unverified.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run any boolean-coercing native handler under the checker with the stack comparison on: the original shows one stack write the naive rewrite lacks. Resolve the worker's reported stack base plus its fixed offset to the incoming slot address, feed it to the rewrite as input, and confirm the stack and call comparisons both pass over one thousand trials.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first attempt failed most trials on the stack check with no hint of which word differed beyond the count; reading the worker source showed incoming argument words are compared and only the callee frame below them is excluded. A later batch run also died partway when its worker process was lost under machine load, so the driver now restarts the worker and retries instead of crashing.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="production-n03">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Native handlers hide a one-byte stack trick</h2>
      <p>Twenty-one of twenty-five script native handlers in this batch were rewritten in Rust and proven identical over one thousand trials each. The surprise was a compiler quirk in two bool-taking handlers: each overwrites the low byte of its own incoming argument slot on the stack and then pushes the whole word to the engine, so the engine receives the flag mixed with high bytes of a pointer. The value was reproduced exactly and verified through the recorded call arguments.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite a batch of twenty-five script native handlers in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every handler in the batch takes one call-context pointer holding an argument array pointer and a return-slot pointer, forwards between one and nine arguments to a single engine function, and optionally stores the low byte of the answer in the return slot.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three handlers are bare jumps (two are double-jump chains) with no logic at their listed address, and one calls the engine through a function pointer in data, so those four were deferred rather than verified.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two handlers bool-coerce an argument by writing the flag into the low byte of their own dead stack slot and pushing the mixed word; the mixed value is deterministic and was verified exactly, but the write itself cannot be reproduced in safe Rust, so those two contracts skip only the stack comparison.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Verify the twenty-one understood handlers with the scoped stack exception documented in the verdicts, defer the four unsuitable ones with explicit reason codes, and reuse the shared context shape and generator for the remaining native batches.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler from the executable, generate one checker contract and one Rust rewrite per handler from the shared template, build the rewrite crate for the 32-bit target, and run the checker driver for one thousand trials per contract.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first generated contracts used file addresses where the checker expects relative addresses, so the original faulted on every trial until a one-line fix. Two of three parallel checker runs later lost their workers under machine load and the driver crashed on teardown, aborting the batch; a teardown guard was added to the lane driver copy and the sequential re-run passed everything.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-audio"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Rust reader: audio banks and their ADPCM streams</h2><p>A pure-Rust reader now parses and decodes every audio file in the game — archives, bank and streamed containers, wave headers, IMA ADPCM to 16-bit PCM, and the versioned audio configs — and its output matches the reference decoder sample-exact on seventeen channels and streams spanning every container and codec variant. The last unknown block-header word turned out to be an ignorable signed drift marker, confirmed by byte-searching the reference output in the raw file.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Write a clean, dependency-light Rust library for the game's PC audio containers: the audio archives and the bank or stream format inside them, the wave headers, and IMA ADPCM decoding written from scratch, validated sample by sample against vgmstream output. Also parse the versioned audio configuration files as far as their structure can be determined, and report bank and wave counts, sample rates and channel layouts.</p><h3>What was found</h3><ul><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game ships 45 audio archives holding 3,286 entries: 1,869 bank files containing 140,293 short streams, and 1,417 streamed files with 3,045 channels. Thirty sample rates appear, one channel layout reaches seven channels, and all of it parses and decodes with zero failures.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three codecs exist: IMA ADPCM for nearly everything, 16-bit PCM for radio music and some effects, and exactly one Ogg Vorbis stream, which the reader refuses cleanly as unsupported.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The IMA step table matches printings except one entry, found by searching the executable for the table: using the printed value causes plus-or-minus-one drift in loud passages, while the stored value matches the reference decoder bit-exact.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The block channel word once called unknown is a signed drift marker, nonzero in 52 PCM files only. Each channel's seek table stays continuous regardless, so linear playback ignores it — proved by an exact reference match on a file with nonzero markers.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three files defeat the reference decoder, not the reader: on short last blocks it reuses the first block's header size and skips a payload entry, and on one file with lopsided seeks it reads a fixed stride, bleeding one channel's bytes into the other and zeroing a channel from the third block on. Byte searches in the raw file prove both mechanics.</li><li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The per-channel trailers (a short header plus three bytes per data sector) carry seek or state data, but six candidate encodings were tested and rejected, so their contents stay unknown with zero effect on decoding.</li><li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> What the game itself plays for the one file with oscillating block sizes; the reference output there (a channel dead for most of the file) is not plausible as authored audio.</li></ul><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Variant</th><th role="columnheader">Channels checked</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Bank ADPCM effects and speech</td><td role="cell" data-label="Channels checked">3 streams</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">exact</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Bank PCM voice prompt</td><td role="cell" data-label="Channels checked">1 stream</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">exact</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Streamed stereo radio</td><td role="cell" data-label="Channels checked">8 channels</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">exact</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Streamed 3-channel cutscene</td><td role="cell" data-label="Channels checked">3 channels</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">exact</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Streamed PCM with drift markers</td><td role="cell" data-label="Channels checked">2 channels</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">exact</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Short last blocks, lopsided seeks</td><td role="cell" data-label="Channels checked">3 files</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">reference diverges, reader follows seek tables</td></tr></tbody></table><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><ul><li>The reader honours each block's own channel info and seek tables with the wave sample count authoritative, and ignores the drift-marker word; fourteen checksummed anchors in the test suite lock this in.</li><li>The reference decoder stays the oracle for symmetric files only; on the three asymmetric files the seek tables are self-consistent and the reference output is demonstrably wrong, so parity is not claimed there.</li><li>Next lane: trailer contents, the flags word variants, the speech-lookup config layout, and engine observation of the oscillating file.</li></ul><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>Build and unit-test the crate with the host toolchain, then run the game-folder census test with the game directory variable set: it parses all archives, decodes every stream and channel, checks fourteen anchors, and writes a JSON census. Reference WAVs come from the reference command-line tool pointed at extracted entries, compared by checksum over the full PCM.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><ul><li>Hand-built test fixtures kept failing on their own sizes (an 88-byte buffer that needed 92, swapped table offsets) — the tests were wrong, not the reader.</li><li>A compact reformulation of the ADPCM difference formula made matches worse and was reverted to the standard differences.</li><li>The first full census failed on over a hundred strictness checks; each became a documented rule (trailer lengths, count clamping, recorded-but-ignored words) instead of a silent pass.</li><li>An early analysis of the lopsided-seeks file claimed the reference rewound mid-block; a direct byte search of its output in the raw file replaced that with the fixed-stride mechanism.</li><li>One probe failed as file-not-found because the game folder name was mistyped in the probe; the folder itself never moved.</li></ul></article>

      <article class="entry" id="inventory-repair">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Repairing the function inventory: what was not a function</h2>
      <p>The function inventory is repaired and the scare behind the repair turned out to be a measuring error. An independent recursive-descent pass over the plain-code region confirmed nine in ten inventory entries, removed about one in ten false entries, added roughly two and a half thousand real functions the inventory had missed, and showed that the pilot report of total boundary failure came from reading the executable at the wrong file offsets.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A pilot lane had reported that three out of three sampled functions in the mid-size range were not functions at all, casting doubt on the whole inventory of about forty-five thousand entries just as it was about to become the project's work queue. I was asked to rebuild ground truth independently with recursive-descent disassembly from roots that are certainly function entries, check every inventory entry against it, measure the error by size and by provenance, verify on a random sample, and write a corrected inventory with per-function byte ranges.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The descent covered about seventy-two percent of the plain-code bytes and established around thirty-four thousand functions with exact byte ranges, resolving over two thousand jump tables along the way. Against it, the inventory sorted as follows: about thirty-nine thousand entries confirmed with the exact size, around six hundred confirmed with a corrected size, a few hundred thunks and weak gap confirmations kept, and about four and a half thousand rejected. The rejected entries were mostly jump-table case labels mistaken for functions, mid-function over-splits, data and padding, a small number of mid-instruction starts, and a handful of zero-size seed artefacts. Entries where the two analyses agreed were confirmed at over ninety-seven percent; pointer-seeded entries failed at around one in four, which is where nearly all the false entries lived.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The pilot's three cases evaporated. At the correct file offsets all three are clean function entries with standard prologues, and the reported vtable anomaly points at a valid entry too. The pilot had indexed the memory-mapped image with file offsets, shifting every read by three kilobytes, and its byte dumps match the true bytes exactly one page earlier. Its verdicts and enclosing functions are void, though its suggested rejection rules remain sound hygiene.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A random sample of three hundred kept entries passed independent checks: every one is reached by a call or pointer, every path decodes to a clean end, and none sits inside another function. The corrected inventory holds about forty-three thousand functions, of which about thirty-eight thousand count as game functions for scheduling.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The corrected inventory should become the work queue, with progress and schedule recomputed from a game denominator of about thirty-eight thousand. Referenced interior points should not be kept as secondary entries: nearly two thirds of them proved to be jump-table labels when audited. The remaining few hundred weak confirmations and approximate sizes stay flagged until decrypted bytes arrive, and the rejected entries keep their evidence so the unpack work can revisit the ambiguous ones.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The lane folder holds the scripts and data: a descent builder seeded from virtual tables, script handlers, relocated pointers and discovered calls, a classifier with a gap-filling backward stream test, and the corrected inventory, rejection list and headline numbers in machine-readable files. Key counts cross-check exactly against other lanes' published totals. Re-running the builder after the unpack work delivers decrypted bytes should close the remaining coverage gap.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> My first run confirmed the pilot's three bad addresses, which looked like a bug in my own file mapping until raw byte dumps showed clean prologues and exposed the pilot's offset error instead. I also briefly kept referenced interior points as secondary entries before auditing showed most were jump-table labels, and two verification failures turned out to be a noreturn-call padding idiom my checker counted too strictly. A gap-filling script failed once on an indentation error and was rerun with no data lost.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-11"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Second pilot, lane 11: medium functions (250 to 600 bytes)</h2><p>Three of four sampled medium functions were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent to the originals with the differential checker, at about thirteen minutes per verified function; the fourth was deferred for three compounding gaps in the checker.
