      <h2>Second pilot, lane 09: medium functions (250 to 600 bytes)</h2>
      <p>Two of four sampled medium functions were rewritten in Rust and verified bit-identical to the originals over 1200 trials each; the other two were deferred with precise blockers. The main surprise was a seed-bias bug in the checker's random global fill that made one function's deep paths run on 6 percent of trials, found by a coverage audit and fixed in the lane's worker copy.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite four randomly sampled medium game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, recording honest timings including failures. Each rewrite runs against the original from identical starting state over at least 1000 trials with edge values, with outgoing calls intercepted and answered by script.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A main-loop table refresh with nine call sites, including two atomic operating-system calls, passed 1200 of 1200 trials on the second attempt, and a deliberately introduced mutant was caught.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A script proximity tracker built on single-precision vector math passed 1200 of 1200 trials with bit-exact floating point, including not-a-number, infinities, subnormals and signed zeroes, after input shaping and a worker fix described below.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The two remaining functions cannot be verified with the current checker: one executes a heap-resident callback through two register-indirect call sites the checker cannot intercept, and the other is driven throughout by eight register-indirect virtual calls plus thread-local-storage reads.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A coverage audit of the proximity tracker showed only 1 in 200 fresh trials reached its deep logic. Bisecting this exposed a checker bug: the per-trial random fill for globals seeds its generator with the trial number directly, so consecutive trials produce near-identical values and global-driven branches go one way on nearly every trial. Mixing the seed first restored uniform fills and took deep-path coverage to 64 in 200 across every input kind.</p>

      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">Result</th><th role="columnheader">Trials</th><th role="columnheader">Attempts</th></tr></thead>

      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Animation behaviour binder</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">deferred, virtual calls and thread-local state</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials">0</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">0</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Main-loop table refresh</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">verified</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials">1200</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">2</td></tr>

      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Four small checker extensions were added in the lane's own copies and are recommended for folding back: frame-pointer-tolerant call comparison, selective stack-argument comparison, per-callee scripted answers, and a seed-mixing fix for random global fills.</li>
      <li>Coverage audits with a fresh seed should be routine for every verified function, since a passing run can still exercise deep paths on only a few trials.</li>
      <li>Register-indirect call interception, thread-local-storage virtualization, and scripted callee out-parameters are the three checker gaps that blocked the deferred functions, in that order of value.</li>
      <li>Earlier verdicts that used random global fills remain valid as differential results, but their branch coverage wherever globals decide branches should be re-audited.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Copy the checker driver, runtime crate, and worker into a lane folder, build the worker and the rewrite library for 32-bit x86 with panic-abort, write one contract per function describing its calling convention, heap layout, callees, and comparisons, then run the driver for 1200 trials plus a 200-trial coverage audit with a fresh seed and a mutant run. All lane inputs, contracts, verdicts, and scripts stay in the lane's scratch folder.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first rewrite attempt failed on one call argument: a register I read as a data value turned out to be a frame pointer, which the call-log diff showed immediately. The fix took minutes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The thin-coverage finding took longer to chase down, through input shaping, a pinned-global experiment, and a replication of the worker's generator in a standalone script before the seed bias was confirmed. It was worth it: without the audit the verification would have passed while barely testing the interesting logic.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The two deferred functions looked tempting to force through fault-equivalence passes, but that would have verified nothing, so they were recorded as deferred with concrete unblock plans instead.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot-results">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Two pilots, 130 functions: what the rewrite rate really is</h2>
      <p>Thirty lanes rewrote 130 original functions in Rust under a stopwatch and tried to prove each one against the original. Small functions go quickly and mostly verify. Large ones do not verify at all yet, and the reason is the checker, not the rewriting. This entry is the coordinator's summary; each lane's own entry has the detail.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Measure, before committing the whole swarm to it, how long one verified rewrite takes and how often it succeeds. The first pilot used fifty tiny functions chosen because they make no calls. The second used eighty functions sampled at random in five size tiers, with no filtering for difficulty, and the new checker.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <table>
      <thead><tr><th>Tier</th><th>Verified</th><th>Minutes per verified function</th><th>Share of the game's code bytes in this size range</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
      <tr><td>First pilot: tiny, no calls</td><td data-label="Verified">44 of 50</td><td data-label="Minutes per verified function">2 to 10</td><td data-label="Share of the game's code bytes in this size range">about 4%</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Small, no calls (40 to 150 bytes)</td><td data-label="Verified">20 of 24</td><td data-label="Minutes per verified function">2 to 4</td><td rowspan="2" data-label="Share of the game's code bytes in this size range">about 25%</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Small, with calls (60 to 250 bytes)</td><td data-label="Verified">14 of 20</td><td data-label="Minutes per verified function">4 to 8</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Medium (250 to 600 bytes)</td><td data-label="Verified">8 of 16</td><td data-label="Minutes per verified function">13 to 17</td><td data-label="Share of the game's code bytes in this size range">about 20%</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Large (600 to 1,500 bytes)</td><td data-label="Verified">3 of 12</td><td data-label="Minutes per verified function">8 to 15</td><td data-label="Share of the game's code bytes in this size range">about 23%</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Very large (1,500 to 4,000 bytes)</td><td data-label="Verified">0 of 8</td><td data-label="Minutes per verified function">none verified</td><td data-label="Share of the game's code bytes in this size range">about 28%, with the few larger still</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Almost no rewrite was wrong. Across both pilots, failed attempts were nearly all mistakes in the test set-up: a contract naming the wrong global, a driver bug, an input model that was too narrow. Lanes report first-attempt passes for most functions once the contract was right.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Understanding is fast even for big functions. Lanes read and described 500-instruction functions in five to ten minutes. What they could not do was check them.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every deferral above the small tiers traced to the same short list of things the checker cannot yet do: follow calls made through a register or an object's function table, give each callee its own scripted answer, let a scripted callee write its result through a pointer, compare pointers that refer to the same place on both sides, and supply thread-local state. A separate lane measured the whole program against that list: 53% of game functions are checkable as the checker stands, but they hold only 17% of the code bytes. Per-callee answers and call interception together would raise that to 96% of functions.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The honesty test worked everywhere it was run. Each lane planted one subtle mistake in a passing rewrite and the checker caught it, usually within a handful of trials.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Estimated</span> One rewrite covers several functions more often than expected: 5,159 functions fall into 445 groups that are identical apart from addresses, which removes about 4,700 rewrites from the queue.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Production started on the part that works: fifty lanes are rewriting native handlers and small functions now. The checker upgrade runs beside them as its own lane, since it gates half of the code. The schedule estimate published in the chat was built from this table: days for the small and medium functions, with the large ones waiting on the checker.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Each pilot lane's scratch folder holds its results file with per-function timings, its contracts and its rewrite crate. Re-running a lane's driver over its contracts reproduces its verdicts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Three defects were found in the checker itself by lanes using it: random fills for global data were nearly constant because of how the generator was seeded, so tests of functions reading globals were weaker than they looked; a call with more than eight arguments left the stack pointer wrong; and after a trial in which only the rewrite faulted, later trials in the same worker saw corrupted state. None is known to have passed a wrong rewrite, but every verdict issued before the fixes will be re-run under the upgraded checker before it counts.</p>
      <p>One lane reported that all three of its large functions were not functions at all and that the inventory was badly wrong. The inventory repair lane traced that to the reporting lane's own address arithmetic: it had read the file at the wrong position. The inventory's real error rate is being measured separately; the alarming number was an artefact. The coordinator repeated the claim to the project owner before it was checked, which was a mistake.</p>
      <p>Lanes sharing one build output folder overwrote each other's libraries when two crates had the same name, and fifty lanes building at once queued on one lock. Production lanes now build into a folder each. Three times a lane wrote working files into the repository root instead of its scratch folder; they were moved out and nothing was committed.</p>
      <p>Timings are the lanes' own and are rough: several lanes' stated minutes do not add up to their wall-clock time, in both directions. The table uses ranges for that reason.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="rewrite-order">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>The rewrite order: levels, clusters and what the checker can take today</h2>
      <p>Bottom-up rewrite order is computed: every function sits on one of 45 levels, level zero alone holds over fifteen thousand game functions, and just over half of all game functions are checkable with the checker as it stands today. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Work out the order in which the executable's functions should be rewritten, and how many the checker can verify today. That meant building the complete direct call graph from the Ghidra pairs plus a fresh instruction scan, condensing it into strongly connected components, assigning every function a bottom-up level, classifying every game function as checkable now, checkable after a named checker extension, or needing the running game, folding byte-identical duplicates, histogramming sizes, and packing the queue into batches of twenty to forty functions.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p>The union graph has about seventy-three thousand edges over some forty-five thousand functions. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The fresh scan independently re-found nearly ninety-eight percent of the usable Ghidra edges and added about fifteen thousand more, mostly from callers the Ghidra pass had not covered yet.</p>
      <p>Condensation gives about forty-five thousand components, of which only thirty-five hold more than one function, and the longest dependency chain is forty-five levels deep. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The two large mutual recursion clusters hold about a hundred and about sixty functions each, mix several subsystems, and are confirmed by both edge sources, so they are real cycles that must be rewritten as units. Level zero holds over nineteen thousand functions in total, of which fifteen thousand are game code, so rewriting can start wide; the top eleven levels together hold only about a hundred functions.</p>
      <p>Checkability splits as follows. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Category</th><th role="columnheader">Functions</th><th role="columnheader">Share of game bytes</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Checkable by the current checker as it is</td><td role="cell" data-label="Functions">18,905</td><td role="cell" data-label="Share of game bytes">17%</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Checkable after a checker extension</td><td role="cell" data-label="Functions">15,119</td><td role="cell" data-label="Share of game bytes">76%</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Needs the running game</td><td role="cell" data-label="Functions">1,353</td><td role="cell" data-label="Share of game bytes">7%</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Unknown (zero-size entries, no code)</td><td role="cell" data-label="Functions">54</td><td role="cell" data-label="Share of game bytes">0%</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p>The byte shares matter more than the counts: the as-is half is mostly small leaf functions, while the extension bucket holds three quarters of all game bytes. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The three named extensions unlock the middle bucket in this order, each count marginal to the ones before it:</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Extension</th><th role="columnheader">What it adds</th><th role="columnheader">Functions unlocked</th><th role="columnheader">Cumulative checkable</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Per-callee scripted answers</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it adds">a separate scripted answer per callee instead of one shared value</td><td role="cell" data-label="Functions unlocked">9,063</td><td role="cell" data-label="Cumulative checkable">79%</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Register-indirect call interception</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it adds">recording and scripting of calls through registers</td><td role="cell" data-label="Functions unlocked">4,943</td><td role="cell" data-label="Cumulative checkable">93%</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Custom register convention helpers</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it adds">rewrite-side support for non-standard calling conventions</td><td role="cell" data-label="Functions unlocked">1,113</td><td role="cell" data-label="Cumulative checkable">96%</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p>The running-game bucket is almost entirely functions using processor-local storage or structured exception handling, plus a few dozen using operating system traps or timing instructions. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> No game function reads its own code bytes or modifies itself, and none uses locked atomic instructions; atomicity goes through imported operating system functions instead. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      <p>Two findings shape the schedule. First, about ten thousand game functions call into the still-encrypted first megabyte of the code section, so their callees can be stubbed but their calling conventions cannot be read yet. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Second, duplicate folding finds four hundred forty-five groups of byte-identical functions covering over five thousand functions, nearly all tiny template-like bodies, saving about four thousand seven hundred rewrites. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      <p>Sizes are heavily skewed: three quarters of game functions are under one hundred fifty bytes but hold under a fifth of the bytes, while one hundred giants over four thousand bytes hold nearly a tenth. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The queue packs into one thousand one hundred eighty batches of twenty-nine to thirty-one functions each, grouped by subsystem and class and level-adjacent in the call graph. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><p>Dispatch the rewrite queue in level order using the per-function level map, so callees exist before their callers; start with the wide, small level zero.</p></li>
      <li><p>Treat each mutual recursion cluster as one rewrite unit rather than splitting it across lanes.</p></li>
      <li><p>Build the three checker extensions in per-callee, indirect-call, custom-convention order, which reaches ninety-six percent checkable.</p></li>
      <li><p>Fold duplicates before dispatching: each group needs one rewrite, not one per copy.</p></li>
      <li><p>Plan contract authoring for the ten thousand functions calling encrypted callees around inference or a decrypted image, since conventions there cannot be read from bytes.</p></li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Take the function inventory, the Ghidra caller-callee pairs, the virtual table list, and the checker capability notes as inputs. Disassemble every function outside the encrypted range with capstone using the inventory boundaries, collect direct call targets and the instruction feature flags, and union the found edges with the Ghidra pairs. Run an iterative Tarjan pass for components, assign levels by longest path over the condensation, classify each game function against the checker rules, hash masked bytes for duplicates, and pack batches by subsystem, class, and level. The lane reran this pipeline end to end several times; the scripts and their JSON outputs sit together in the lane scratch folder.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The disassembler reports resolved absolute call targets rather than raw relative offsets, and the first scan double-added them, producing a hundred thousand bogus edges that agreed with Ghidra in only two cases. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Comparing five known edges by hand exposed it in minutes.</p>
      <p>Jump tables live inline in the code section here, so the first code-read rule flagged over sixteen hundred innocent functions as self-inspecting. Restricting the rule to pure absolute reads cleared all of them. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      <p>Two smaller traps: some mnemonic names are shared between string instructions and vector instructions and can only be told apart by operand shape, and the tool folds repeat and lock prefixes into the mnemonic text, which hid both string instructions and any locked atomics until the matcher was fixed. A renamed loop variable then shadowed the image base and broke a whole rescan; the per-function error field caught it immediately. The final surprise was genuine: there really are no locked atomic instructions anywhere in the scanned code. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      </article>

      <h2>Second pilot, lane 13: large functions (600 to 1,500 bytes)</h2>
      <p>One of three large functions was rewritten in Rust and verified over one thousand differential trials; the other two were deferred because the checker cannot compare calls that pass pointers to the caller's own stack frame, which turned out to be the main thing separating large functions from the tiny leaves of the first pilot.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite three randomly sampled large game functions in Rust, prove each one identical to the original with the project checker over at least one thousand trials, record honest timings, and confirm on one function that the checker catches a deliberately introduced mistake.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Finding</th><th role="columnheader">Evidence</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>

      <tr role="row"><th role="row"><th role="columnheader">Stack-pointer call arguments</th><td role="cell" data-label="Evidence"><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> read in both the disassembly and the checker's comparison code</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Functions that hand callees pointers to their own temporary storage can never match, because the two sides keep different frame layouts; this blocked both remaining functions</td></tr>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The verified rewrite stands as checked in. Both other functions are recorded as deferred with precise reasons rather than weakly verified with comparisons switched off. The recommended checker improvements, in order of pilot impact, are pointer-aware comparison of outgoing call arguments, interception of register-indirect calls, per-callee scripted answers, and driver input kinds for small-range integers and heap-valued script answers, the first of which was prototyped and tested during this lane.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane's rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows against the shared cargo output folder, generate the contract with the lane's generator script, and run the lane's copy of the checker driver on it; the verdict file records one thousand passing trials. The honesty test script runs one hand-built trial where the correct rewrite passes and the wrong-constant mutant fails on heap writes. The shared worker binary is reused as is and never rebuilt.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first attempt failed because one callee is called from two sites and only the first was patched, so the original ran the real callee and faulted; the fix was one line. Two flag words pushed to a callee carry stale high bytes from unrelated registers, which required reading the checker's stub code to reproduce exactly. The stock mutant run passing looked like a checker failure until analysis showed both multipliers overflow to the same indefinite value on random inputs. Timestamps written to the progress log from memory drifted ahead of the real clock and were corrected against file timestamps; the published timings use the corrected values.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-07"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Second pilot, lane 07: small functions that make calls (60 to 250 bytes, one to three callees)</h2><p>One of five sampled callers verified fully; the other four are written and partially proven but blocked on three checker gaps, with the evidence and the unblock for each recorded.       <article class="entry" id="pilot2-06">

      <h2>Second pilot, lane 06: small functions that make calls (60 to 250 bytes, one to three callees)</h2>
      <p>All five sampled functions were rewritten in Rust and verified identical to the originals: 1000 differential trials each with zero failures, plus 200 extra trials each with full undeclared-write discovery, also clean. One rewrite needed a second attempt; a deliberate mistake in a copy was caught as required.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite five small game functions that make outgoing calls, prove each rewrite behaves identically with the project checker while recording honest per-function timings, and run one honesty test where a subtle mistake must be caught. Deferred functions with stated blockers were an acceptable outcome.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five of five functions verified, covering two deleting destructors, a network send helper, a pool field copy with flag mirroring, and a streaming bounds sweep with floating-point comparisons.</p>

      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Event destructor</td><td role="cell" data-label="Calls made">3</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials, zero failures">1200</td></tr>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Total time was about 24 minutes for five verified functions, under 5 minutes per function. Understanding the code cost the most; each 1000-trial checker run took only seconds.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The one failed attempt was instructive: the original tests only the low byte of a callee answer, and edge values that are nonzero overall but zero in the low byte failed until the rewrite masked the same way. The failure count matched the predicted fraction of such edge values exactly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Two callees sit in the encrypted part of the executable so their bodies are unreadable, but verification did not need them: the call site alone shows the argument shape, cleanup and answer channel the checker observes.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Four small driver extensions written for this lane are proposed for the shared checker: scripted global values including pointers, explicit heap words, null-pointer stack arguments, and thiscall and fastcall rewrite-side call helpers. Three deeper gaps remain for the worker: one scripted answer shared by all callees per trial, no modeled memory effects for stubbed callees, and raw-address call comparison that cannot match stack addresses across codegen.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows without rebuilding the shared worker, then run the lane driver copy once per contract: 1000 trials with the standard checks followed by 200 trials with full-data discovery. Rerun the first contract to confirm the planted mutant still fails on the call comparison.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A relocation-table script double-counted page bases, briefly suggesting game code had no fixup entries and could not work under the checker at all. The passing proofs said otherwise, and the bug was in the script, not the checker: with correct parsing every checked site is relocated normally. The lesson is recorded for the next lane: when a quick script disagrees with a passing machine proof, suspect the script first.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-05"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Second pilot, lane 05: small functions that make calls (60 to 250 bytes, one to three callees)</h2><p>All five sampled functions were rewritten in Rust and verified identical to the originals: 7200 differential trials plus 1200 undeclared-write sweep trials, zero failures, with one deliberately introduced bug caught as required.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Rewrite five small game functions that each call one to three helpers, prove each rewrite behaves identically with the project checker over at least a thousand trials including edge values, and time every step honestly. One passing function also had to survive an honesty test: a subtle planted mistake the checker must catch.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five of five functions verified, most on the first attempt. The rewrites range from about twenty to thirty lines of Rust each and cover a range scan with two helpers, a slot-table append, a filter-node reset, a lookup that forwards copied float data to a pool helper, and a serializer mixing direct and virtual calls.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two checker gaps were closed inside the lane's own copies. First, rewrites can now call helpers that take their object in a register, which the original proofs never exercised. One reset function is verified only on the subset that skips its virtual child release and its allocator path.       <h2>Second pilot, lane 04: small leaf functions (40 to 150 bytes, no calls)</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five of six sampled functions were rewritten in Rust and proven equivalent to the originals over 1200 trials each, at about four minutes per verified function; the sixth was deferred because it needs a live game state the checker cannot provide.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite six randomly sampled small functions in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project's differential checker, and record honest per-function timings including failures. Each function was described as a leaf of 40 to 150 bytes with no calls.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The sample was not quite what the label said: two of the six functions contain register-indirect calls the inventory could not see, and one listed size cuts its function in half mid-instruction. One of the two indirect-call functions was still verifiable with a new technique; the other was deferred.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The slot dispatch function is deferred, not attempted further: its call target chains from per-thread game state that no contract field can set, and testing only its do-nothing path would be a fake pass.</li>
      <li>Three small driver extensions (scripted global fills, scripted stack words, scripted heap words) are proposed for folding back into the checker; without them random inputs cannot align two values or hold a branch split.</li>
      <li>Verdicts should report how many trials ended in faults (see below); until then, a mutant must fail before any pass is trusted.</li>

      <p>Copy the checker driver and runtime into the lane folder, write one contract per function describing its calling convention, inputs, and checks, write each rewrite as a plain Rust export in its own uniquely named crate, build the 32-bit library, and run the driver.       <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first passing run of the gated status check was vacuous: a hand-computed stub word was wrong, so both sides faulted identically on every call-path trial and all trials passed while testing nothing. Only the mutant run exposed it, because the mutant passed too. Fault-against-fault agreement is a real checker behaviour, and the verdict never says it happened.</p>
      <p>Two smaller stumbles: a missing import broke the first rebuild, and two file edits failed on line-ending mismatch before switching to a patch script. Neither cost more than a minute. The shared build folder also made cargo wait on another lane's lock twice, which was harmless.</p>

      <h2>Second pilot, lane 01: small leaf functions (40 to 150 bytes, no calls)</h2>
      <p>Five of six sampled functions were rewritten in Rust and verified behaviour-identical to the originals over 1200 differential trials each with zero failures; the sixth sample turned out not to be a function at all and was deferred with evidence.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite six randomly sampled small leaf functions in idiomatic Rust, prove each one against the original with the project's differential checker (at least 1000 trials including edge values), record honest per-function timings, and run one honesty test where a deliberately broken rewrite must be caught.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five rewrites passed 1200 of 1200 trials each: a sparse record copy, a state-block reset, a voice-slot update with table division, a flag-bit update, and a strided array clear. Every rewrite passed on its first checker run. All five deliberately broken mutants were caught, most within a handful of trials.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two of the six sample entries were wrong. One listed size ended mid-instruction; the true function is slightly longer and the rewrite was verified against the full behaviour. The other range starts with a jump to code elsewhere and continues with the head of a neighbouring method that makes three calls, so there was no leaf function in the range to rewrite.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The divide-by-zero path of the voice-slot function cannot be verified with the current checker. A zero divisor makes the rewrite panic, and the panic terminates the whole checker worker process, so no comparison is produced. A follow-up probe confirmed the original raises a divide-error trap there while the worker survives, meaning the trap codes could never match even with a graceful fault. The verified verdict covers all 255 nonzero divisors; a zero divisor would crash the original in the game too.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Two other lanes' data agree with these readings: a proposed name for the state reset matches a tiny reset helper, and the array clear is called from a constructor, matching a construction-time helper. Nothing contradicted any finding.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Two small driver extensions are proposed for fold-back: bounded small-integer inputs for table indexes, and per-range generated fills (such as nonzero bytes) sent through a request form the worker already accepts. Both are input generation, not weakened comparisons.</li>
      <li>The sampler entry that is not a function should be fixed and resampled; range-by-size slicing should be validated against instruction boundaries.</li>
      <li>Fault-path coverage for operations that panic in Rust needs either a worker that survives rewrite aborts or an explicit documented exclusion; such paths currently cannot verify.</li>
      <li>Bit-guard logic wants input fills biased toward the guard bits: one mutant diverged on only 2 of 100 uniform trials, which slows mutant detection without weakening the passing verdict.</li>

      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Each function has a contract file (calling convention, argument shapes, memory segments, declared globals, checks) and a rewrite export in the lane's rewrite crate, checked by the project's differential worker from identical starting state over 1200 seeded trials.       <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The array clear was first misread as clearing 28 of every 32 bytes; rechecking the store offsets against the loop stride corrected it to the even dwords only, before any checker run.</li>
      <li>One constant's address was first thought to sit in the code section, which would have clashed with the checker's anti-cheat page revocation; recomputing the section ranges showed it is ordinary writable data.</li>
      <li>The compiler's null-dereference lint blocked an intentionally faulting probe, so the probe was rewritten as a volatile load from a computed unmapped address. Two wasted build cycles.</li>
      <li>The checker driver crashed with a traceback when the worker died instead of reporting it; the lane's copy now reports worker death as a verdict error and restarts the worker.</li>
      </ul>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-19"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Second pilot, lane 19: very large functions (1,500 to 4,000 bytes)</h2><p>Neither of the two sampled functions could be verified, and the reasons matter more than the count: very large real functions hit three checker gaps the small proof functions never touched, each one fatal on its own. Both are deferred with the blockers proven from the checker's own source code.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Rewrite two randomly sampled very large game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent with the differential checker, recording honest timings including failures. Each function is roughly five hundred instructions with sixty or more outgoing calls.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first function is a message dispatcher: it parses an incoming message through a helper, then switches on the message id across nine arms, each validating and routing. It makes sixty direct calls plus six indirect ones, touches a dozen global words, and uses no real floating point.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The second function is a copy-style constructor for a pooled world object: it stores a type tag, initializes about two hundred bytes of fields, and queries the source object through virtual calls, with real single-precision float math. Half of its sixty-eight calls are indirect, starting thirty-six instructions in.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three new checker gaps, each independently fatal for the dispatcher, proven by reading the checker worker source against the disassembly:</p><ul><li>The fail path returns an uninitialized stack word. The worker fills the stack with an address-dependent pattern, so no faithful rewrite can reproduce the value.</li><li>The call log compares raw stack addresses. The function passes addresses of its own locals to callees from its first call, and any rewrite frame sits at different addresses.</li><li>Stubbed callees return one value and write nothing, but the parse helper's whole job is filling a struct through two pointers, so all nine dispatch arms are unreachable in testing. Running the real helper instead is impossible because it sits in the encrypted range.</li></ul><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two known gaps also proved decisive: indirect calls cannot be intercepted, so the constructor's virtual-call body would pass only vacuously through fault equivalence; and all stubbed sites share one scripted answer per trial.</p><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Functions verified</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">0 of 2</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Both deferred with proven blockers, zero checker runs</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Work time</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">About 10 minutes</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Mostly reading code and checker semantics, not writing</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Calling-pattern check</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">6 of 6 samples match</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Stack-arg counts predict callee cleanup exactly, a usable contract rule</td></tr></tbody></table><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><p>Both functions are deferred, not attempted blindly: a rewrite that cannot be checked would only produce a fake data point for the schedule estimate. The same sampling confirmed the push-count rule on five more callees.</p><p>Nothing else went wrong. The surprise was how quickly the verdict flipped from a long rewrite job to a short deferral: the first two blockers live in the first dozen instructions of the function, so the ceiling was visible almost immediately.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-18"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Second pilot, lane 18: very large functions (1,500 to 4,000 bytes)</h2><p>Neither of the two very large functions could be verified, and that is the measurement: both spend their lives in virtual calls the checker cannot yet intercept, so the schedule for this size class must include checker extensions first. The deferrals are evidenced, not guessed, including a three-trial run where the original provably faults at its first virtual call.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Rewrite two randomly sampled very large game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite bit-identical to the original with the differential checker, recording honest timings split into understanding, contract, writing, building and checking.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first function is about five hundred instructions: it blends float weights from object fields, calls power and square-root style helpers, then dispatches on a node-type nibble through about two dozen virtual calls across nine exits, returning a true/false status. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The second function is a fragment-instance virtual method of about five hundred instructions that walks a child list doing heavy single-precision matrix arithmetic and ends in one tail virtual call. The table below compares them.</p><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Property</th><th role="columnheader">First function</th><th role="columnheader">Second function</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Size class</th><td role="cell" data-label="First function">about 1,550 bytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Second function">about 2,720 bytes</td></tr><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Calls</th><td role="cell" data-label="First function">25, of which 22 virtual</td><td role="cell" data-label="Second function">4, of which 2 virtual</td></tr><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Globals</th><td role="cell" data-label="First function">reads constant table only</td><td role="cell" data-label="Second function">none</td></tr><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Floating point</th><td role="cell" data-label="First function">SSE plus x87, heavy</td><td role="cell" data-label="Second function">SSE only, very heavy</td></tr><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th><td role="cell" data-label="First function">deferred</td><td role="cell" data-label="Second function">deferred</td></tr></tbody></table><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Four distinct checker gaps block these functions: virtual calls have no interception, one helper takes its arguments on the x87 stack which the contract cannot model, one scripted answer is shared by all call sites per trial, and callees that receive stack addresses can never match under raw-value call comparison. <span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Two of the callees sit in the encrypted part of the executable, so their bodies are unavailable to static reading; The recommended order is: expose the worker's recorder-stub addresses so contracts can plant them where virtual calls will land, add per-callee scripted answers, normalize pointer call arguments as offsets, then add x87-argument callees. The lane also recommends the sampler extend function sizes through the return instruction, since one size ended mid-epilogue.</p><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>Disassemble each function with capstone from the executable on disk, count direct versus register-indirect call sites, and confirm the checker report's interception list covers only direct and import-table calls. For the executed proof, build a trivial rewrite export, run the stock worker with zero-filled heap segments that deterministically skip the first direct call, and observe the original fault at its first virtual call on every trial while the rewrite returns normally.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><p>The oddest moment was a helper call target that disassembled to a two-instruction thunk: it looks wrong until you realise some math helpers are reached through forwarding stubs. Two callee heads disassembled as pure garbage before I checked the section map and placed them inside the encrypted range, which resolved the confusion. Nothing else went wrong; the tooling worked first time throughout.</p></article>

      <h2>Second pilot, lane 17: very large functions (1,500 to 4,000 bytes)</h2>
      <p>Neither of the two very large sample functions could be verified, and the reason is the result: one reads per-thread engine state the checker cannot fabricate, and the other dispatches almost entirely through object vtables the checker cannot intercept. A control run then showed a stub that implements nothing can pass against a faulting original, so the accept gate must require the original to actually run.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite two randomly sampled very large game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, recording honest timings including failures.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">

      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>

Finally run the crashing stub control and confirm its trials pass with no other comparison performed.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first disassembly script was named after a standard library module and crashed on import until renamed. A cargo build waited on another lane's file lock, which cost about half a minute. The most surprising moment was the audio original hanging on a trial where it had faulted twice before, which showed the worker-thread garbage it depends on is not even stable run to run.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-16">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Second pilot, lane 16: large functions (600 to 1,500 bytes)</h2>
      <p>One of three large functions was rewritten in Rust and verified: a table-refresh routine passed 1,300 differential trials with zero failures, and a deliberately introduced bug was caught on the first trial. The other two were deferred with precise blockers, both gaps in the checker rather than failures of understanding.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite three sampled game functions of 600 to 1,500 bytes in idiomatic Rust, prove each one behaves identically to the original with the project's differential checker over at least 1,000 trials including edge values, run one honesty test with a subtle planted bug, and record honest per-function timings including failures.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The middle-sized function, a record-table refresh routine making eleven direct calls to two callees, was verified with two contracts totalling 1,300 trials and no failures. Its behaviour in words: for each of four slots it asks whether a record exists and either copies the sixteen-byte record into a global table row or zeroes the slot, runs three more conditional queries into a second table, then always copies one record out to the caller with the third word forced to zero. All float traffic is bitwise copies with no arithmetic.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The honesty mutant, which stores the third word instead of clearing it, fails quickly through the heap comparison, exactly as designed.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The largest function, a blend-weight and quaternion-blending routine of about 390 instructions with heavy vector float arithmetic, was deferred. Its stack-allocated scratch buffers are filled by callees whose scripted stand-ins have no memory effects, so both sides would read different garbage; its loop bounds come from unconstrained inputs that would hang trials; and one scripted answer per trial cannot serve its four callees.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The smallest function, a probable animation-channel constructor, was deferred. It makes eight register-indirect calls, which the checker cannot intercept, and reads thread-local storage twice, which the checker cannot virtualise. Both are documented checker gaps with no quick fix.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">Size</th><th role="columnheader">Calls</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Blend-weight routine</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">1365 bytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Calls">7, one indirect</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">deferred</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Table refresh</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">1059 bytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Calls">11, all direct</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">verified, 1300 trials</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Channel constructor</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">671 bytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Calls">11, eight indirect</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">deferred</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Two small checker extensions written for this lane are recommended for fold-back: skipping volatile call arguments such as pointers into the callee's own stack frame, and ranged small-integer inputs with heap-relative scripted answers.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The table refresh rewrite is accepted as verified and its crate is ready to integrate.</li>
      <li>The two deferrals stand until the checker grows stub memory effects, below-stack reset, constrained heap inputs, per-callee answers, indirect-call interception and thread-local storage support. The next lane should not retry them on the current checker.</li>
      <li>Trial budgets for table-driven functions should use two contracts: one with pristine globals to force the refresh body, one with random globals to cover the skip path, since a random flag byte almost never takes the interesting branch.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>From the repository root, build the lane's worker copy and rewrite crate for the 32-bit target with the shared cargo output folder, then run the lane's checker driver over its two table-refresh contracts. Expect 1,000 of 1,000 and 300 of 300 passing trials with all comparisons green, verdict files in the lane's verdicts folder, and failing mutant verdicts that name the heap comparison as the first mismatch.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The functions were worked out of order: after recon showed only the table refresh was fully expressible in the checker, it went first so the lane would bank one verification instead of spending the hour on a likely deferral. Timings are recorded honestly regardless of order.</p>
      <p>The first attempt failed only on the lane's own contract: one declared global range was twenty bytes short, and the checker's undeclared-write scan caught it on both sides before any rewrite bug could hide behind it. Widening the range fixed it with no rewrite change.</p>
      <p>The shared scripted-answer limitation meant all four existence queries in one trial had to agree, so mixed present and absent patterns within a single trial went untested. Each slot's both paths are covered across trials and the slots are independent copies of the same code, which made this acceptable, but it is a real coverage hole worth closing with per-callee answers.</p>
      <p>The honesty mutant passed the trials where the mutated word happened to be zero, which is correct behaviour rather than a checker miss: identical behaviour passes, and it failed everywhere the bug was observable.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Second pilot, lane 15: large functions (600 to 1,500 bytes)</h2>
      <p>One of three large functions was rewritten in Rust and verified identical to the original over one thousand differential trials; the other two were deferred because the checker cannot set up the state they need. The pattern is clear: large functions are gated by global pointers and virtual calls the harness cannot yet express, so schedule estimates must include checker extensions, not just rewrite time.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite three randomly sampled large game functions in idiomatic Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the project's differential checker, recording honest timings including failures. Each rewrite runs against the original from identical starting state over at least one thousand trials with edge values; outgoing calls are intercepted and answered by script, so callees are not rewritten.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first function, an object-slot refresh routine of about seven hundred bytes with twenty-three calls to sixteen helpers and no floating point, passed all one thousand trials with zero failures, and a deliberately introduced off-by-one mistake was caught at once. Analysis took minutes; the checker runs took about a minute.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Trial coverage was uneven in a way the pass count hides: the function's table-scan loop body never executed because its table pointer lives in a global the harness fills with unreadable random bytes. Eight of sixteen helpers never fired. The rewrite is proven identical on all harness-reachable behavior, with the deep loop covered by analysis only.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The second function, a float-heavy computation of about eight hundred bytes, is unverifiable with the current checker for two independent reasons: its deep path starts by dereferencing a global pointer the contract cannot aim at valid memory, and its main path passes about ten stack-local addresses as call arguments, which the checker compares by raw value and can never match.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The third function, a task-system virtual method, is blocked by two register-indirect virtual calls the checker cannot intercept. A cross-check with another lane's structure file confirmed it is a vtable slot with exactly the decoded size and call count.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker's shared scripted answer for all callees did not block anything: differential soundness holds with one value per trial, only edge variety suffers. The missing rewrite-side helper for object-style callee calls was added in about ten lines and can be folded back.</p>

      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th><th role="columnheader">Trials</th><th role="columnheader">Minutes</th></tr></thead>

      <ul>
      <li>Count the first function as verified-with-coverage-debt, not fully proven; the pilot schedule should add a coverage-debt category for harness-unreachable code.</li>
      <li>Build three checker extensions before scheduling more large functions, in this order: initialize globals to heap pointers, compare pointer call arguments by pointed-to content, intercept register-indirect calls.</li>
      <li>Fold the ten-line object-call helper back into the shared rewrite runtime.</li>
      <li>Keep per-trial call observations: the coverage histogram, not the pass count, showed which helpers never fired.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>From the repository root, build the lane's rewrite crate for the 32-bit target with panics set to abort, generate the function contract with the lane's generator script (it asserts every call-site opcode and target), then run the lane's checker driver copy for the function contract: the verdict file records the thousand-trial pass and the mutant file records the caught mistake. No rebuild of the shared worker is needed.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One pushed constant looked like an argument to the call beneath it but belonged to the call after; only careful stack accounting caught it, and it would have been the most likely rewrite bug. A scratch constant written by the compiler also turned out to be a real global store, not dead code.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Shell output redirection wrote an unopenable encoding twice before the cause (wide-character redirect) was spotted; later scripts wrote their own output files directly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The all-pass verdict initially felt complete until the coverage histogram showed half the helpers never fired; pass counts alone will overstate pilot progress unless every lane reports reachability.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-14">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Second pilot, lane 14: large functions (600 to 1,500 bytes)</h2>
      <p>None of the three sampled functions could be rewritten, because none of them turned out to be a function: every sampled start address landed in the middle of real code. This is a useful pilot result, not a failure: it caught a sampling defect before it could poison the schedule estimate.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite three randomly sampled large game functions in Rust, prove each one identical to the original with the differential checker, and record honest timings including failures.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two of the three start addresses split a machine instruction in half: one lands on the middle byte of a floating-point load, the other on the second byte of a conditional jump whose landing pad is visible just behind it.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The third start lands on the third of four identical unrolled blocks inside one small function, and its first instruction is a conditional jump that reads processor flags set by the instruction immediately before the start, so it can only be reached by falling through, never by calling.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A scan of the whole code section found no genuine call or jump to any of the three addresses, and the data sections hold no pointers to two of them.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The true enclosing functions were located for two samples: an audio update routine of about 670 bytes with 17 direct calls and heavy floating-point use, and a 273-byte reference-release routine built from four unrolled blocks with four virtual calls.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> A code-pointer table in read-only data genuinely points at the first bad address, matching a vtable slot another lane recorded. Either that slot is never called or the table is not what it was assumed to be; the follow-up is to check the table for a type-info pointer.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>All three samples were deferred with zero rewrite attempts and zero checker trials, because writing a contract for a non-entry address would fabricate a function. The true enclosing functions are recorded for resampling.</li>
      <li>Even at their true starts, the enclosing functions need two checker extensions the project already knew were missing: interception of register-indirect virtual calls, and a separate scripted answer per callee instead of one shared value per trial.</li>
      <li>The sampler should reject any candidate start that splits an instruction, begins with a flag-dependent jump, or has no call, jump or padding boundary leading into it.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the bytes around each sampled start with capstone from the purchased executable on disk, without waiting for the interactive analysis to finish: dump the raw bytes spanning each start, decode the instruction stream from both directions, scan the code section for direct references to each start, and search the mapped image for data pointers to each start. The lane scratch folder keeps the scripts and their outputs.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The naive reference scan first reported two calls targeting the bad addresses, and both turned out to be false positives where the search had landed mid-instruction inside unrelated floating-point code; verifying the bytes at each alleged call site cleared them. The code-pointer table entry was the real surprise and remains unexplained: it is the one piece of evidence pointing the other way, and it survived re-checking against the mapped image rather than the raw section data, which had initially given a wrong location for it.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-08"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Second pilot, lane 08: small functions that make calls (60 to 250 bytes, one to three callees)</h2><p>Three of five sampled functions were rewritten in Rust and proven identical to the originals over thirty-six hundred checker trials with no failures, and the other two were deferred for precise checker gaps rather than guessed at.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Rewrite five randomly sampled small functions that make calls, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the project's differential checker over at least one thousand trials including edge values, and record honest timings including failures.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The three verified functions cover distinct shapes: a physics-side object initializer with two setup calls plus byte packing and a float move, a gated record-linking routine fenced by operating-system wait and release calls and ending in a tail call, and a sweep over four counted object pools that calls an update routine on each flagged slot.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Both deferred functions failed on checker expressiveness, not on understanding. The other passes its call argument in a vector register, which the checker's call log does not record, so a passing result would prove nothing about the argument.</p><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th><th role="columnheader">Trials</th><th role="columnheader">Attempts</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Physics initializer, two calls</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">verified</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials">1200</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">2</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Jump thunk to shared routine</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">deferred</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials">0</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Gated record linking, tail call</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">verified</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials">1200</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Indexed float computation</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">deferred</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials">0</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Four-pool sweep</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">verified</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials">1200</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td></tr></tbody></table><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A deliberately introduced one-bit mistake in the first rewrite was caught by the checker within six trials, confirming the comparisons bite. The checker cannot catch a declared-but-wrong address. Every address after that was derived programmatically and cross-checked before running.</p><p>One rebuild failed with an access-denied error on the output file while another lane's worker was active, then succeeded on retry a few seconds later. Nothing was lost, but shared-output builds remain racy under parallel lanes.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot2-03">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Second pilot, lane 03: small leaf functions (40 to 150 bytes, no calls)</h2>
      <p>Four of six sampled functions were rewritten in Rust and proven identical to the originals over a thousand differential trials each; the other two turned out not to be leaves at all, which is itself a useful scheduling signal.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite six randomly sampled small functions in idiomatic Rust, prove each one behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, and record honest per-function timings, including failures.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Four true leaves passed every trial: a gated readiness flag combining a state word, two flag bits and two float threshold compares; a four-float field setter; an insert-if-absent pair table holding up to a thousand entries; and a conditional linked-list counter.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two samples were mislabelled as having no calls. One makes four register-indirect virtual calls in a search loop; the other chases a pointer chain from a global and ends in a computed tail jump. The checker can intercept only direct calls, and a faithful rewrite would trip its anti-cheat, so both were deferred with documented unblockers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A deliberately introduced one-bit mistake in the first rewrite was caught by the checker within a hundred trials.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>For scheduling, count roughly a third of nominally call-free samples as needing indirect-call support, since static call counts miss virtual calls. Three small driver extensions should be folded back into the checker: scripted stack values, scripted heap words, and scripted heap-pointer values for linked structures. Two worker features would unblock the deferred class: interception of register-indirect call sites, and a way to aim globals at checker-owned memory.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Each function has a JSON contract describing its calling convention, inputs and compared outputs, and a Rust export in the lane crate. The checker runs the original and the rewrite from identical state over a thousand generated inputs, including edge values, and compares return values, written memory, stack adjustment, outgoing calls and faults. The pair-table case aims its object pointer below a small owned heap segment because the real struct is larger than the worker heap.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The linked-list counter failed its first run because the argument sense was read backwards from the branch order; the very first trial exposed it and a one-line fix passed. Rebuilding the rewrite library twice failed on a transient file lock that cleared by itself after half a minute; waiting briefly before rebuilding avoids it.</p>
      </article>

Seed any zero-initialised globals the function reads so trials exercise live logic rather than identical faults.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A first script added the relocation block base twice, producing a quarter-million wrong addresses and a brief false conclusion that a jump table lacked relocations. Dumping the raw blocks showed the tool already returns full addresses and everything was relocated.</p>
      <p>The two pool searches failed their first runs because the rewrites read positions at the wrong offsets of the pointed-to block — documented correctly in the code comment, coded wrong. The return-only failure pattern pointed at a value bug, and the fix passed a thousand trials on both.</p>
      <p>One rebuild waited briefly on the shared build folder lock while another lane built, then succeeded with no action needed.</p>

      <h2>Pilot lane 07: five functions rewritten and timed</h2>
      <p>Five small original functions were rewritten in Rust and each rewrite was compared against the original over one thousand native executions: all five matched exactly. The work also timed each step honestly, including one failed attempt and two tool traps, so the project schedule can be built from real numbers.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite five assigned leaf functions in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with at least one thousand random plus edge-case trials, record the time honestly including failures, and run one honesty test with a deliberately planted bug.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All five rewrites matched their originals on every trial: a byte-string to UTF-16 expander, a small object reset, a float setter, an integer getter, and a random-range float generator with generator state.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The native execution method from the harness lane works for differential checks once extended with heap prefills, so each trial starts from controlled random memory instead of a fixed pattern.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The compiler's thiscall convention matches the originals exactly: the object pointer arrives in the expected register, extra arguments sit on the stack, and the callee cleans them up. This was confirmed by reading the compiled output of the rewrite crate itself.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The honesty test worked: a rewrite copy with one stripped bit flag was caught on 991 of 1028 trials, with only the empty string and short all-ASCII inputs passing.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The random-range function draws from a multiply-add generator state and interpolates between its two bounds; its constant multiplier table entry equals exactly two to the minus twenty-third.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The five rewrites are proposed for integration as written. Two comparison details are recommended for the checker lane: expect a leftover return-address word on the stack after callee-cleaning returns, and compare floating-point results through the 80-bit return register encoding rather than as text. Rebuilding the rewrite binary while trials execute it must be sequenced, never overlapped, because the operating system locks running programs.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>From the lane scratch folder: build the harness fork and the rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows, then run one check script per function. Each script runs its trials with parallel workers, compares written memory byte for byte plus return values and stack discipline, and prints an agree count. The honesty test re-runs the first function's script in mutant mode.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first check of the float setter failed on the check side, not the rewrite: the script expected the wrong stack-pointer advance and missed a constant leftover word the harness leaves behind. Reading the harness trampoline explained both, and the corrected check passed without touching the rewrite. A rebuild also failed once with an access-denied error because trial processes were still executing the old binary; sequencing builds after checks fixed it. Trial throughput was far below the harness lane's solo measurement because the shared host was heavily loaded.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Pilot lane 03: five functions rewritten and timed</h2>
      <p>Four of five small game functions were rewritten in Rust and proved identical to the originals over about a thousand trials each, in forty minutes of work; the fifth was deferred over a genuine floating point corner with the cause fully characterised and a fix scoped.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>The lane was given five leaf functions from the pilot list and asked to rewrite each in Rust, prove identical behaviour against the original with at least a thousand random plus edge-case trials, record honest per-function timings for the project schedule estimate, and run one honesty test showing the comparison catches a deliberate mistake.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Four rewrites pass full differential comparison: a clamped table-slot address function, a flag-byte predicate, a byte conversion, and a five-path linked-record select, each agreeing on every trial.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">What it does</th><th role="columnheader">Trials</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th></tr></thead>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The vector transform writes a fourth output word from uninitialized stack data: nothing stores to the slot it loads, the value never changes across input-varying trials, and it equals the test harness's own stack fill pattern at that slot. It is not a function of the inputs and was excluded from comparison.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The deferred function is bit-exact except when two different NaN payloads meet in one accumulation row. Probing showed single-NaN cases always agree and only payload conflicts diverge; the mechanism is operand-order canonicalization of floating point addition by the toolchain, which changes which NaN payload survives. The fix is pinned instruction order, left for a follow-up.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The honesty test mutated a clamp constant by one in a copy of the slot-address rewrite; exactly one trial in 1019 failed, the boundary input, confirming single-trial sensitivity.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two rewrite bugs were caught by the machine check and fixed: a signed-versus-unsigned comparison, and a pair of swapped branches. Both fixes passed on the first retry.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The uninitialized fourth output word is excluded from that function's contract; no caller can depend on it.</li>
      <li>NaN payload conflicts need a project policy: they are the only float class where portable Rust codegen observably differs from the original, and the observed quieting behaviour comes from emulation, so matching it needs a deliberate decision.</li>
      <li>Input domains belong in the queue record next to each verdict, since one function's wildest inputs read wild memory in the original and are untestable by construction.</li>
      <li>Per-lane test binaries need unique names: the shared build cache silently replaced one lane's binary with another's.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Each rewrite is an exported Rust function with the original calling convention in the lane's scratch crate, with a batch test binary beside it. Drivers run the original through the native execution helper with crafted stack and register inputs, run the same cases through the Rust binary, and compare integers exactly, floats bit-exactly, and pointers by expected relocated address. Random seeds, trial counts, and per-function timings are recorded in the pilot results file in the same folder.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first full test run faulted on every trial because functions with a frame pointer read their stack arguments one word off from frameless ones; the helper's fault record pointed at the exact store and the layout was fixed in minutes. A shared-cache binary collision, a transient link lock, and a publishing-tool timestamp quirk each cost a few minutes and are documented as tool traps. The largest surprise was the NaN finding itself: full-random bit patterns inject signaling NaNs no float literal can express, and without them the operand-order issue would have stayed hidden.</p>
      </article>
