      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">What it does</th><th role="columnheader">Trials agreed</th><th role="columnheader">Attempts</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">First</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it does">returns a game datum address derived from the load base</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials agreed">1010 of 1010</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Second</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it does">returns a second game datum address derived from the load base</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials agreed">1010 of 1010</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Third</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it does">appends one row to three parallel tables and returns the row count</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials agreed">1038 of 1038</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">2</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Fourth</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it does">copies one table entry to an output slot</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials agreed">1018 of 1018</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">2</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Fifth</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it does">stores two arguments into fixed structure slots</td><td role="cell" data-label="Trials agreed">1024 of 1024</td><td role="cell" data-label="Attempts">1</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The comparison is strict: return values, every written word, stack pointer movement, untouched registers, and exact stack artifacts are all asserted per trial. The two simplest functions return relocated addresses, so their rewrites take the load base as an explicit parameter rather than baking in an address.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The table-append function re-reads its row count before every store, which matters when a wraparound count makes an early store land on the count slot itself. The first rewrite read the count once and failed 28 trials; the fixed rewrite matches on all of them including dedicated aliasing trials.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The table-copy function reads from uninitialised-image memory that is zero in a fresh process, so each trial sets the entry under test to a known value first. Its byte shuffle provably reproduces its input for every possible word, and the rewrite expresses the net copy directly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A deliberately planted one-bit mistake in a copy of the first rewrite was caught on all 1010 honesty-test trials.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Lane time was about 52 minutes for five verified functions, roughly 10 minutes per function including write-up, or about 8 minutes excluding it. The comparison runs were the largest cost at 18 minutes; single-shot trials cost a fraction of a second each under load.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Rewrites that need a game address take it as an explicit parameter (load base or table pointer) instead of baking in a value. This worked for three of the five functions and keeps the Rust portable.</li>
      <li>Wraparound counts and indices stay in every future corpus: the one genuine bug this lane found only triggers on a wraparound input.</li>
      <li>The checker should record memory diffs on faults too, so faults after partial writes become comparable; this lane had to exclude that case and cover the same code path with mapped trials instead.</li>
      <li>A persistent checker worker that maps the image once would cut the largest time cost, the per-trial process setup, to nearly nothing.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane's extended 32-bit harness and the rewrites crate for the 32-bit Windows target, then run the comparison driver, which executes both sides over edge values plus a thousand seeded-random trials per function and asserts identical observations. A separate script confirms the built library exports all five symbols with the expected callee stack cleanup. All scripts, seeds, and expected trial counts are recorded with the lane's scratch outputs.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A first probe of the relocation table double-added the page base and wrongly concluded the absolute addresses were unrelocated. The running functions contradicted it immediately, and a corrected probe settled every site. Lesson kept: a cheap runtime check beats re-reading library docs.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A first dump of the copied table read past the end of the file-backed data and returned bytes belonging to a later section. The table actually lives in zero-filled memory, which changed the test design: every trial now sets the entry under test explicitly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One driver assertion wrongly claimed a register holds the result at return; the register actually carries the result mid-function but is saved and restored. It failed all 1018 trials while the rewrite matched on every stored word, which made the driver bug obvious.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="merge-structures">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Merging the class layouts into one set of Rust types</h2>
      <p>All class layouts recovered so far are now one consistent set: about thirty eight hundred classes merged from the family lanes, the script native lanes, the RTTI hierarchy and the public headers, with ten thousand resolved conflicts, thirteen hundred open ones, and a draft Rust crate of three hundred forty layout structs that builds for both thirty two and sixty four bit targets.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Combine every recovered class layout into a single set of structure definitions, resolving conflicts explicitly, and generate Rust types with compile time size and offset checks.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> every expected source file was present: all fifteen family layouts, all twenty two native field lists, the RTTI hierarchy and the public header names. Nothing is waiting on a missing lane.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the merged set holds about thirty eight hundred classes and about eleven thousand fields after deduplication, with roughly three thousand high confidence fields and a similar number at medium confidence. About three thousand classes now carry base class links, mostly from RTTI.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the draft crate holds three hundred forty structs covering about fifty six hundred fields, with explicit padding for unknown ranges and pointer fields that stay four bytes wide on sixty four bit hosts. It builds cleanly for both targets, and a deliberately corrupted assertion was shown to fail the build, so the checks are live.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the largest gaps: the player object has only a handful of fields, the top level game and world objects have no records at all, physics instances are thin, and vehicle layouts are rich but about half low confidence.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Inherited fields are recorded once, on the owning class. A first rule that moved fields by size comparison was tried and rejected because it pulled derived only members into their bases; the shipped rule moves a field only when two independent child subtrees agree on it, or drops it as a duplicate with its evidence transferred to the owner.</li>
      <li>Sizes from the lanes are lower bounds, so each Rust struct asserts its size rounded up to four byte alignment and is documented as a prefix of the true layout.</li>
      <li>About seventy observations turned out to be global variables rather than struct fields and were split into a separate globals file for a later lane.</li>
      <li>Recommended next analysis: allocator and pool stride work for true sizes, a dedicated pass for the game and world objects, and targeted review of the twenty high confidence kind conflicts listed in the conflicts file.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the merge script in the lane scratch folder to regenerate the merged structures, conflicts, globals and moves files, then the generator script for the crate, then build the crate for both the thirty two bit and sixty four bit Windows targets. The merge log records each decision class with counts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Each lane used its own schema for sizes, bases and fields, including one off wrappers and word widths such as dword and vec3, so the first merge attempt miscounted several hundred fields until every spelling was normalised. Absolute memory addresses disguised as field offsets inflated some layouts to tens of megabytes before the globals split caught them. The first base attribution rule looked principled but was circular, because base sizes already contained misattributed bytes; spotting train only and ped only members landing in their bases is what exposed it. The Rust generator initially produced over a thousand assertion failures from implicit padding before alignment aware typing fixed them.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="merge-names">

      <h2>Merging the names: what 22 native lanes agree on</h2>
      <p>All recovered function names are now one table: about ninety-six thousand proposals merged into under twenty-two thousand symbol records, and meaningful names rose from under three thousand to just under ten thousand. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The strongest result is agreement, not volume: every native lane independently found the same few handle-to-object lookup helpers, and the merge confirms them with up to twenty-two supporting lanes and hundreds of supporting script natives each.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Merge every function name the project had recovered into one table with one naming convention, resolving conflicts between lanes, keeping rejected alternatives, and counting named functions before and after by confidence, by subsystem, and inside the encrypted range. Placeholders such as class-plus-slot-number were not to count as names, and no name was to be invented beyond what the evidence supports.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The merge consumed proposal files from all twenty-two native lanes plus the native handler table, the vtable inventory, fifteen class-structure lanes, the script interpreter lane, the startup lane, the library lane, and mechanically extracted report mentions.</p>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The agreed lookups include the pool handle lookup, the player index lookup, the script handle to index conversion, the model info hash lookup, the current script thread accessor, and the local player ped getter, each with between six and twenty-two supporting lanes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of the remaining conflicts, ninety-one are genuine disagreements with a winner picked by rule, twenty-three are handler names beating descriptive proposals, seventeen are disputed shared stubs with no winner, and ten are lanes contradicting themselves.       <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>One convention: <code>Class::Method</code> for methods, bare public names for native handlers, <code>NativeImpl_X</code> for one-to-one engine callees, subsystem-prefixed CamelCase for shared helpers, exact spelling for library and CRT symbols.</li>
      <li>Names agree fuzzily on shared word tokens, so differently spelled proposals for the same helper count as agreement; the winner is the spelling with the most supporting natives.</li>
      <li>Guesses about encrypted bodies stay low confidence or placeholders; destructor claims against unreadable slot targets were demoted to placeholders.</li>
      <li>Colliding names for different functions take numeric suffixes after a byte comparison proved no pair identical.</li>
      <li>Recommended next: feed the missed functions to the work queue, and revisit the disputed shared stubs once decrypted bytes are available.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Collect the proposal files from every lane, normalise addresses and confidence spellings, group proposals by address, then group names by shared word tokens. Pick winners by supporting native count, apply the confidence caps, check every address against the function inventory, and compare the bytes of any two functions that end up with the same name. The merge script repeats all of this in one run.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One class lane labelled the same encrypted stub as the deleting destructor of dozens of classes; taken literally this produced over a thousand bogus conflicts, and the fix was to demote all such opaque claims to placeholders. A camel-case word splitter briefly merged two competing constructor claims because they shared a three-letter prefix; the fix requires the shared word to appear in a supporting native name. A shell quoting glitch once reported thousands of lost names; a clean rerun from a file verified the true number was two, both shared stubs correctly demoted. The billiards mini-game natives kept matching the pool-lookup search and had to be excluded by hand-written filter.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="replacement-loader">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Replacement loader built and tested without the game</h2>
      <p>The loader that will live inside the running game and swap original functions for Rust rewrites is built, and every part of it passes its tests without the game ever launching. The proxy library forwards the full set of system library exports, the hook engine replaces functions behind individual on/off switches, and a watched control file drives toggling, bulk operations and bisecting. What remains is running it against the real game, which only the owner can do.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Build the 32-bit replacement loader as Rust crates: a proxy library that stands in for a system library the game already loads, a hook engine written from scratch (function-start hooks with trampolines, virtual table slot replacement, import table slot replacement), a registry of replacements with run-time switches driven by a watched control file, logging with timestamps, a crash handler recording which replacements were active, and a safe mode. Prove it all with unit tests that run without the game, including a small 32-bit test program with several kinds of functions hooked under concurrent calls from several threads.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The proxy library forwards every export of the system library it stands in for, with names and ordinals matching exactly, and the forwarding table is generated from the real library at build time rather than hand-written. The library itself imports only core system libraries, so it cannot load itself in a loop.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The hook engine handles the calling conventions the game uses, including class methods, through small generated adapter stubs. Hooks install, call through to the original, toggle on and off, and remove cleanly, including while four threads call the hooked function and the main thread toggles a hundred times. Creating a hook on an unsuitable target (too short, undecodable, unreadable, out of range) returns a clean error and touches nothing.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The readiness gate works as designed: in the test program, which has no game code in it, the loader waits, times out, stays fully disabled, and logs the whole sequence. The log from that run shows startup, the readiness checks, the timeout, and a clean shutdown with all hooks off.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Check group</th><th role="columnheader">Checks</th><th role="columnheader">Result</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Decoder and planner unit tests</td><td role="cell" data-label="Checks">12</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">all pass</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Control file and bisect unit tests</td><td role="cell" data-label="Checks">4</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">all pass</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Live 32-bit hook tests</td><td role="cell" data-label="Checks">58</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">all pass</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Proxy export fidelity</td><td role="cell" data-label="Checks">193 exports compared</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">all match</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Compiler lints</td><td role="cell" data-label="Checks">all crates, both targets</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">zero warnings</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The design is ready for live testing against the game, starting with the proxy alone and adding one trivial hook at a time.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Whether the game's start-up protection objects to an extra module in the process or to patched code. Nothing in the static analysis answers this; it is the first thing live testing must establish.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Exports for the proxy are declared through the linker's directive section, the same mechanism the C compiler uses. A separate definition file and command-line export flags were tried and cannot resolve the generated symbols; this is documented in the build script so nobody rediscovers it.</li>
      <li>No third-party hook library is used. The engine is hand-written, which keeps the dependency list empty and the proxy's own imports limited to core system libraries.</li>
      <li>The hook table ships empty. No game target is registered until its live address and expected bytes are confirmed with the game running.</li>
      <li>Live testing follows a fixed eight-step order: proxy alone, coexistence with the community loader, timing calibration, first trivial hook, toggle mechanics, debugger etiquette, protection reaction, and a memory snapshot diff. Each step stops at the first surprise.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the workspace for the 32-bit Windows target and run the host unit tests, then run the 32-bit test program with the path to the freshly built proxy library as its argument. The program prints one line per check and a final pass and fail count with a matching exit code. Comparing the proxy library's export table against the system library's export table confirms the forwarding is complete. All commands and the eight live-test steps are written up in the loader manual kept with the lane's work.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The proxy refused to link for a long time: the linker reported every generated stub as unresolved even though the symbols were provably present in the object files. A minimal probe showed even plain Rust symbols failed the same way, which pointed at the export mechanism rather than the code. Switching to directive-section exports fixed it on the first try.</li>
      <li>The first version of the class-method adapter passed the wrong second argument to the replacement function; a live capture showed it receiving a code address instead of the test value. The stub was rewritten to rebuild the argument frame properly, and the test now asserts the values end to end.</li>
      <li>A caller-side adapter turned out to be callee-pops, so calling it with the wrong prototype corrupted the stack silently and crashed later. The prototypes were fixed and a register-preservation check was added that would catch any repeat.</li>
      <li>One confusing hour came from a self-inflicted cause: a probe build script left in a non-empty state made cached linker flags look like a build-tool bug. Reading the file on disk settled it immediately.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-vehicle-ped-meta">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: vehicle, ped and weapon extra data inside resources</h2>
      <p>The gameplay data attached to models lives in skeleton bone names, and a new crate now reads it: every vehicle part, ped joint and weapon mount across all three titles parses with zero failures.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the extra data inside model resources: vehicle layout (seats, doors, wheels, lights), ped components and variations, and weapon attachment points, reusing the model, archive and resource crates and validating against the plain-text data files.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> vehicles name one skeleton bone per functional part, with the bone position as the part location; 211 vehicles use 140 distinct bone names, all classified. Seat, wheel, door, light, extra and siren counts were measured per vehicle, and seat positions mirror across the car to half a millimetre on all but two genuinely asymmetric vehicles.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> every ped shares an 80-bone animation rig, while story characters extend it with articulated thumbs and joint-based faces. Ped body parts are dictionary entries counted per model; the playable characters instead ship loose per-part drawables with numbered texture variants.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> firearms name grip, muzzle, ejector and magazine bones; melee weapons and props carry a single root bone. All 26 firearms and every other weapon file parsed.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> every vehicle, ped and weapon named in the text definitions resolves to a model file, except cutscene characters which live in the cutscene archives. Seat counts exist nowhere in text: the bones are the sole source.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> vehicle shape (car, bike, boat, helicopter) can be guessed from bone sets alone, with helicopters identified by rotor bones since they also carry landing-gear wheels.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> the dictionary hash algorithm, two small companion formats, and what two ped component slots mean.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The new crate exposes layouts, rigs and mounts over the existing model reader and is ready for review. The model reader should adopt the shared resource container next so the two container copies become one. Texture variants and cutscene models belong to their own lanes.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane crate and run its tests with the game folder exported; the integration tests open all fifteen model archives, parse every fragment, drawable and dictionary, and print the full census. A summary example prints one file's layout for inspection without writing anything.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The skeleton pointer sits four bytes earlier than first assumed, which silently yielded empty bone lists until the model source was re-read. Boat propellers were first mistaken for helicopter rotors, and helicopters were then found to have landing-gear wheel bones, so the shape guess needed two fixes. A one-letter typo in a misc bone and an underscore-less extra name were kept as explicit spellings rather than normalised away.</p>
      </article>

The reader had to depend on the archive and resource container crates from earlier lanes instead of reimplementing them.</p>

Strict number parsing was kept for the single trailing-comma value rather than guessing how the game reads it. The animation lane owns the referenced animation files next, and the audio lane owns the unresolved audio names.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Open the three animation archives for cutscenes with the archive crate, read each description entry, and parse the text with the new reader. The integration test does this end to end when pointed at a game install and pins every count above, and the catalog example prints the per-cutscene data as JSON. Unit tests use small hand-built fixtures only.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The payload padding was confusing at first: files are padded to a block boundary with zeros and uninitialised-memory fill, which looked like a binary trailer until the last-text-line rule made it fall into place. The shell also misreported successful commands as failed because the build tool writes progress to its error stream, so results were taken from the tool output lines instead. Most usefully, the integration test caught four data quirks the survey scripts had missed, because the survey never type-checked rows; the reader now pins all of them.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="format-animation">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: animation dictionaries and clips (WAD)</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every animation dictionary in the game now parses: a new Rust crate reads all 1,701 animation files, all 22,166 clips inside them, and over a million animation channels with zero failures, and checks the three rules the format follows.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the animation dictionary format: the dictionary of clips, each clip's header, the channel and codec types used for rotations and other tracks, and decoding clips to per-frame bone transforms, reusing the archive and resource crates from sibling lanes.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Each dictionary is a standard resource of the generic kind holding a hash table of clips. Clip names hash with the Jenkins function, durations always equal one less than the frame count divided by thirty, and static rotations are unit quaternions. All three rules hold for every clip and every channel in the game.</p>

      <p>Build the crate in the lane scratch folder, run its unit tests on hand-built bytes, then set the game folder variable and run the integration test, which walks all six animation archives and re-checks every number above. A summary example prints one dictionary's clips, codec mix, and validation results without writing anything.</p>

      <p>The clip tables and the file-level table look alike but hold different object shapes, which silently emptied the first codec census until full pointer chains were dumped by hand.       <h2>Pilot lane 10: five functions rewritten and timed</h2>
      <p>Three of five pilot functions were rewritten in Rust and proved bit-identical to the originals over about a thousand native trials each; the other two were deferred with a concrete blocker, and the pilot surfaced a gap in the leaf-selection filter. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span></p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite the last five functions of the pilot fifty in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original by native execution, time every step honestly, and run one honesty test with a deliberate mistake to confirm the comparison can catch errors.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p>The five functions and their outcomes:</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Function</th><th role="columnheader">What it does</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Bucket mapper</td><td data-label="What it does" role="cell">maps a float sample to one of eight buckets</td><td data-label="Outcome" role="cell">verified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Float tracker</td><td data-label="What it does" role="cell">updates a timestamped smoothing state with init, predict and clamp paths</td><td data-label="Outcome" role="cell">verified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree on the second attempt</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Slot store and slot copy</td><td data-label="What it does" role="cell">write through a table-selected offset into an object</td><td data-label="Outcome" role="cell">deferred: the table is runtime-initialised global data</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Small clearer</td><td data-label="What it does" role="cell">zeroes twelve bytes and returns the object</td><td data-label="Outcome" role="cell">verified, 1020 of 1020 trials agree</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The deferred pair reads its offset table from writable global data whose file image is unrelated text, so the game must fill the table in at run time. A rewrite can only take that table as a parameter until runtime bytes exist, and running the original against file bytes would only exercise wild offsets. The leaf-selection filter missed these because it only screens plain absolute reads, not indexed ones; the candidate pool should be re-screened.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two subtleties needed exact handling: the bucket mapper's float-to-integer step returns a special indefinite value for out-of-range inputs where Rust saturates, and the tracker's comparisons use ordered float semantics that differ from min and max on NaN. Both are covered by targeted edge trials plus uniform random bit patterns.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The honesty test confirmed the comparison catches a plausible mistake: a mutant that trusted Rust's saturating float-to-integer cast failed 174 of 1020 identical trials.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Ship the three verified rewrites; keep the two table-dependent rewrites parameterised over the table and marked unverified until runtime bytes or a table-patching runner exist.</li>
      <li>Re-screen the leaf pool for indexed absolute reads of writable data before assigning more pilot functions.</li>
      <li>Budget pilot comparisons at a few trials per second per machine with single-shot runners; batching would change this substantially.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane's twin crate for 32-bit x86, then run its parallel driver: it feeds identical edge and random inputs to the original through the native runner and to the Rust twin, and compares return values bit-exactly, floating-point results bit-exactly, written memory byte-exactly, and the stack pointer after return. Machine records of every trial batch are kept with the lane's data files.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Three unaligned-pointer trials for the small clearer first appeared to fail, but the original was correct: a twelve-byte zero at an unaligned address spans four partial double-words, and the driver's comparison had assumed aligned writes. The driver was fixed to compare byte-exact images and the trials re-run. The tracker's first attempt missed ten trials because the original's floating-point return quiets signalling NaNs while the rewrite passed them through; the rewrite now quiets at return and keeps raw bits in the store. The candidate record for the bucket mapper also lists a register input that its own code zeroes before reading; the rewrite treats it as clobbered, not input.</p>

      <h2>Pilot lane 08: five functions rewritten and timed</h2>
      <p>Five small original functions were rewritten in Rust and each rewrite agreed with the original on all 1000 comparison trials, in about 34 minutes of wall time. The comparison harness caught three genuine mistakes in the first drafts, and a deliberate off-by-one mutant failed all 200 of its trials, so the passing results can be trusted.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite five assigned leaf functions in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original over at least 1000 trials with random and edge-case inputs, and record honest per-function timings for the project schedule estimate, including failures. One extra check was required: introduce a subtle mistake into a copy of a passing rewrite and confirm the comparison catches it.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All five rewrites pass 1000 out of 1000 trials with zero stack-cleanup mismatches. The five functions, in plain words, are:</p>

      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Total wall time was about 34 minutes, or about 7 minutes per verified function. The largest share was running the comparisons: each single-shot trial takes about 0.4 seconds, so the 5000 graded trials took about 15 minutes even with 14 parallel workers. The honesty test failed all 200 trials as intended, with the exact signature of the planted slip.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three first drafts were wrong in instructive ways: one destination layout was read as contiguous when it is strided, one floating-point comparison was taken in the wrong sense, and one function returns an address that shifts when the program image is relocated, so that comparison has to account for the loader offset. The harness caught all three before any result was claimed.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The native-execution comparison method works for this class of function and should be kept: run the original in a relocated mapping, call the rewrite through its real calling convention with the same inputs, and compare return values, stack cleanup and written memory exactly. Three recommendations follow from the problems hit: give every lane binary a unique name because the shared build cache is one namespace; declare functions that return addresses in their queue contracts so the relocation offset is handled systematically rather than per-driver; and build the persistent batched checker worker from the harness design, which would cut a 1000-trial check from minutes to seconds.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the lane rewrite crate for the 32-bit Windows target with no network access, freeze a copy of the comparison binary in the lane folder, and run the lane differential driver with the project Python environment. The driver needs the runfn helper from the emulator-harness lane and the original executable, both used read-only. It generates edge values plus seeded random inputs, runs both sides, and reports agreement counts, stack-cleanup mismatches and timing per function.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Mid-run, the comparison binary started failing every trial with an unfamiliar error message. Another lane had built a different program under the same file name into the shared build cache, silently replacing the binary. Renaming to a lane-unique name and running from a frozen copy in the lane folder fixed it, at a cost of a few minutes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A relocation-table query wrongly reported that the table-base constant in the range-gate function is not relocated, because the parsing library already returns full addresses and the query added the page base a second time. The live runs contradicted the query within the hour: every result differed by exactly the loader offset, and a corrected query confirmed the relocation entry. Dynamic evidence overruled the bad query.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The strided copy looks like it moves the populated lanes of a four-wide structure while skipping padding slots, but which structure is unknown from the function alone.</p>

      <h2>Rust reader: particle and visual effect definitions</h2>
      <p>The game keeps all of its particle and visual effect definitions in five binary packages plus text rule tables and small emitter files, and a new Rust crate now reads all of them: every package parses, most entries resolve to plain names, and no open-source reader existed to compare against, so the binary layout was worked out first-hand from the files.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the particle effect resources and effect rule files: emitters, effect rules, particle rules, keyframed properties, and referenced textures and models, reporting the structure as far as it can be established with counts of effects and emitters.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The effect data is five binary packages (three for the base game, one per episode), ten text rule files, and eight small emitter and renderer files. Nothing particle-related lives inside any of the 303 game archives.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Each binary package holds five banks, and each bank is a dictionary of name hashes pointing at records. Across the five packages there are 3,572 bank entries, and 2,765 of them resolve to plain readable names stored in the same file.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One bank in every package is the emitter bank: its two record classes split in exactly the count of the two particle type tags found in the same file, giving 998 sprite emitters and 151 model emitters in total.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The text rule files share one simple shape (a version line, comment headers, and named tables of fixed-width rows): 23 tables and 929 rows across the ten files, all parsed by one generic reader. The emitter files name their engine types and properties as readable strings.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Bank keys are the Jenkins one-at-a-time hash of the entry name, the same function the archive format uses for entry names.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The inside of each record (emitter parameters, keyframed properties, texture and model references) is not decoded yet, and four of the five bank roles are still guesses. About eight hundred entry hashes match no name in their own file.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Package</th><th role="columnheader">Bank entries</th><th role="columnheader">Entries with names</th></tr></thead>

      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate and run its tests with the game folder pointed at by the usual environment variable: unit tests use hand-built fixtures, and the integration tests parse all five packages, all ten rule files, all eight emitter files, and scan every archive for particle entries. Two example programs print a one-file summary and a JSON census of counts and shapes.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The particle type tags at first looked like they sat inside the emitter records, because their counts matched the emitter classes exactly; a wider search showed the tags live elsewhere in the file, so the match means a one-to-one reference, not inline storage. The public wiki page for the package format and a forum thread about particle modding both failed to load, and the open-source archive tools name only the package type ids with no reader, so there was no prior layout to check against. A first census script printed absolute install paths into its output and was fixed to emit paths relative to the game folder.</p>

The functions were a four-value store with flag bits, a table-lookup byte splice, a logarithm-like float helper, a two-instruction object initialiser, and an angle wrapping routine.</p>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The deferred function reads a writable global table through indexed addressing, which the leaf-selection filter does not flag; the file bytes at that table are game text, so its real contents are runtime state.       <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first logarithm rewrite failed half its trials because the table index was misread as the input sign bit when it actually always selects the zero entry; re-reading the register flow fixed it. The angle rewrite first failed one trial because a hand-written edge value was a signaling NaN mislabeled as quiet, which led to the out-of-contract rule above. The honesty-test constant first chosen as wrong turned out to round to the correct value and had to be replaced with one genuinely one bit off. Build times were dominated by waiting on a shared build cache locked by other lanes.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="natives-02">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Native handlers ATTACH_PED_TO_CAR to CLEAR_ROOM_FOR_OBJECT: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 handlers in this batch were disassembled and matched against the public native database and the decompiled mission scripts. Nearly every handler is a thin wrapper that unpacks script arguments and calls one engine function, and the engine functions resolve script handles through a single shared pool lookup. Four public param counts are wrong, one documented return value never reaches scripts, and the shared pool lookup sits in the encrypted part of the executable so it could only be observed, not read.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover engine names and meanings from a batch of 140 script native handlers, propose names for the functions each handler calls, record object fields the handlers touch, and note stubs, shared handlers and encrypted code.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every handler receives one pointer to a call context. Slot zero of that context points at the return-value slot and the third slot points at the argument array. No handler in this batch reads anything else from the context, and none writes back into the argument array. Twenty-five handlers return a value; the rest are void at the script level.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Most handlers share one shape: read the arguments, call a single engine function, store the result if there is one. Ten handlers are a bare jump to the engine function, three are jump chains ending in a few inline instructions that flip a global flag, and two attach handlers pass through a shared second-stage unpacker. The breakpoint native is a lone trap instruction and is never called by shipped scripts.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Forty-three engine functions resolve script handles through one shared lookup routine, always with the pool pointer in the same register and the handle on the stack. The same routine serves the ped, vehicle and object pools. It lives in the encrypted first megabyte of the code section, so its internals stay unknown; only its call pattern is established.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The observed argument counts agree with the public database for all but four natives. The travel-distance native reads six arguments, not seven; the mission-entity check reads three, not zero; the ceiling function reads one, not two; and the event-precedence clear reads two, not zero. The decompiled scripts agree with the binary in each case.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The camera-sequence progress handler calls its engine function but never stores the result, so whatever the engine computes never reaches scripts. No shipped script calls that native. Separately, three decision-maker natives share one identical handler, and the two cell-camera visibility natives share one engine function.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Field meanings proposed from single-purpose wrappers include the two car colour bytes, the last-damage bone and last-weapon-damage fields (the latter at the same offset on peds, vehicles and objects, so it sits on a shared base class), ped flag words for blocked animations and cover behaviour, per-bit player damage flags, and a stat-id range that decides which stats can carry a string.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Engine wrapper functions are proposed for naming after their native, with the shared pool lookup, the second-stage unpackers and the pool and manager globals proposed as cross-lane shared names. The four wrong public param counts and the dropped progress return should be fed back to the native documentation. The encrypted pool lookup needs the decrypted executable before anyone can go further.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone, follow jumps to the end of each chain, record argument-array reads, direct calls and return-slot writes, and compare the highest argument index against the public param counts. Then disassemble one level down from each engine function and record which pool or manager global it loads before resolving handles. The per-native records, proposed names and proposed fields ship as JSON alongside the lane report.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The disassembler prints small numbers without a base prefix, so an early version of the analysis script misread offsets and found no arguments at all until the parser was fixed. A register-tracking bug then tagged the wrong values until stack loads were excluded from propagation. The shared pool lookup initially decoded to two plausible instructions before its bytes were recognised as ciphertext, and those two phantom instructions were thrown out. A script-usage scan over the decompiled missions took far longer than planned because of per-native regex passes.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="checker">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>The checker: proving rewrites match the original</h2>
      <p>The project now has a working equivalence checker: a tool that runs an original game function and its Rust rewrite side by side from identical starting state and compares everything observable. It was proven on twenty small functions of mixed kinds, where every correct rewrite passed and every deliberately broken one failed.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Build the tool that decides whether a Rust rewrite behaves the same as the original function: run both from identical state, compare return values, written memory, stack-pointer movement, outgoing calls and crashes, with generated inputs, scripted callee answers, crash and hang handling, and protection against rewrites that cheat by calling the original. Then prove it on twenty functions and show it catches subtly wrong versions of each.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker works end to end. Twenty functions were proven: six plain arithmetic routines, four pointer-writing constructors and setters, three methods reading object fields, two global-variable readers, three functions calling other functions through intercepted call sites, and two returning floating-point values. Each ran two hundred generated inputs against its rewrite with zero failures, and each of twenty mutants (off-by-one constants, swapped arguments, wrong operators, missed writes, wrong signs, a value returned in the wrong register part) failed as required.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Cheating rewrites are caught: a rewrite that reads the original code or calls the original function is reported as cheating, because the original code pages are made inaccessible while the rewrite runs.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Calls into system and library routines are intercepted: a wrapper that calls through the import table was checked over fifty trials with the call recorded and a scripted answer returned to both sides.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The checker caught four genuine mistakes during its own construction, including a wrong return value in one of the proof rewrites and three comparison rules that were too strict (a callee's own stack frame, scratch registers at call sites, and a misaligned global range in a contract).</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Throughput is a few milliseconds per trial for simple functions, rising to around a tenth of a second when every writable data section is scanned for undeclared writes. The full twenty-function proof runs in a few minutes. The host slows noticeably under sustained load, so every verdict records its own timing.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The verdict file format matches what the work-queue acceptance tool expects, and all twenty verdicts pass its validator. Recommended next steps: per-callee scripted answers for functions calling several routines, interception of register-indirect calls, a faster undeclared-write scan, and one worker process per processor core.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the 32-bit worker and the rewrite library with the project's Rust toolchain, then run the Python driver over the twenty example contracts in the lane scratch folder. It produces one verdict file per function plus a summary with throughput. A second script demonstrates the cheat detection and the import-table interception.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two candidate functions taken from the earlier function survey turned out to be mid-function fragments rather than real entries and had to be replaced after disassembly showed they started with register restores. A shared build cache made one rebuild fail with an access error until a stray worker process exited. The queue tooling renamed one of its address helpers mid-task, which broke the validation snippet until it was pointed at the new name; the verdict format itself was unchanged.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Rust reader: save game files</h2>
      <p>The save game container now has a clean Rust reader, and the executable confirms the public documentation where it matters most: all 32 documented data block names sit in the binary as one contiguous table in exactly the documented order. No save files exist on this machine, so the framing itself is verified against documentation and executable strings only, never against a real save.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a reviewable Rust reader for the save game format covering the container: file header, block table, block names, sizes and checksums. Work from public documentation and the executable's own strings, check whether the owner has any save files, and build on the archive and resource crates finished by earlier lanes instead of reimplementing their magics.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The executable holds all 32 documented block names as one contiguous table in exactly the documented order, from the simple-variables block to the vehicles block. The last thirteen entries carry a not-defined prefix whose meaning is unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The binary references sixteen slot file names, one more than the fifteen the public wiki documents.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The save version for this build is 57, read from the game's own version data file, and the executable looks up that version stamp by name.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two earlier suspicions were wrong, and the string context proves it: the NTRU and ECC error lines belong to a TLS networking stack, not to save encryption, and the checksum match and mismatch lines sit next to a network damage tracker, not save code. The documented save container is plaintext with an additive checksum the game reportedly ignores.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> This machine holds no save files: the current documents save folder and the legacy application-data save folder do not exist, and a full recursive walk of the installed game found no slot files.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> No archive key handling is needed for saves. The reader still depends on the archive and resource crates by path so its payload sniffer reuses their header detectors instead of duplicating them.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>

      <li>The parser is strict about block framing but lenient about the trailer, since the order and presence of the checksum and end block are unconfirmed. The first lane with a real save should run the bundled summary tool over it and correct the specification.</li>
      <li>Both sibling crates were reviewed as a downstream user: no correctness bugs found, two minor unbounded-allocation notes filed for their owners.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate and run its 22 unit tests on hand-built fixtures plus the integration test, which scans the game folder and the standard user save locations when given the game directory and otherwise skips. String findings come from read-only scans of the executable for the documented block names, slot names, version-stamp references and checksum and crypto vocabulary, checking the surrounding text of every hit. The summary example prints a block table and checksum verdict for any file it is given and never writes.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The wiki page is too long for a single fetch, so its container sections were pulled one at a time through the wiki programming interface. The build tool reports failure through the shell even when its own result lines say success, so every pass above was confirmed from those lines rather than the exit code. A machine-wide filename sweep for saves in odd places is slow; the documented locations plus the game-folder walk already cover every place saves are known to live.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="format-data-files">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: plain-text gameplay data files</h2>
      <p>A zero-dependency Rust crate now reads every plain-text gameplay data file the game ships: vehicle handling, vehicle and ped definitions, colours, population groups, personalities, weapons, time cycle tables, water, materials, load lists and interface tables. All 175 in-scope files parse with no file-level failures.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean reader for the game's plain-text data tables, with a typed parser per file, record counts for every file, and a report of every line that fails. Handling data, vehicles, peds, weapons and time cycle had priority.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seven line-grammar families cover the corpus: semicolon tables, hash sections closed by end markers, slash-commented tables, keyword rule lines, load directives, bracket sections, and small XML files. Text encoding is Windows-1252 rather than plain ASCII.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Priority tables parsed in full, base game plus both episodes: hundreds of handling rows across car, boat, bike, flying and animation-group sub-tables; over a hundred vehicle definitions and several hundred ped definitions; dozens of weapons; nine weather blocks with eleven time slots each; hundreds of water quads and population rows.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Several files that look like text are binary grids and were set aside as out of scope for a text reader. Two supposed settings files contain only commented-out lines and no active data.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The shipped files contain real typos: missing and doubled commas, one dotted number where a comma belongs, truncated rows, paren notes without comment markers, and episode files missing their final end marker. The parser heals the unambiguous cases, collects the rest as reported row errors, and never guesses values.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Episode data files hold only new or changed rows, so they act as partial overrides of the base files; the exact merge rule is unknown.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Trailing value blocks in the time cycle tables, parts of the object and material rows, and the meaning of a placeholder marker in the material conversion table remain undocumented.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Keep one router function that maps file names to typed parsers, with a structural fallback scan for files without a typed parser yet, so later tools drive the whole corpus through one call.</li>
      <li>Type the remaining forty-odd scan-only files next, starting with vehicle extras, animation and melee tables, clothing and furniture rules, and scenario files.</li>
      <li>Resolve the unknown trailing values against engine behaviour rather than guessing from values alone.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate and run its test suite with the game directory exported: unit tests use hand-built inputs, and the integration test walks the data folders, parses each file, and writes a JSON report of counts and errors when a report path is exported. An example binary prints a summary of a single file for manual inspection.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The handling file's own header comments disagree with its data: the description block names six traction columns while every row carries five, and the column ruler shows a handbrake column the descriptions never name. Both were resolved in favour of the data. The material conversion file uses a double-hash token as data in one column, so comment stripping had to be restricted to line starts for that file. Two object rows stop mid-record with no way to recover the missing values; they are reported as errors rather than padded.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-audio-config">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: audio configuration and metadata tables</h2>
      <p>The game's audio metadata is fully mapped and a zero-dependency Rust reader now parses every object of every shipped file: five versioned table kinds plus the speech lookup, about thirty-two thousand objects in total, with per-type field layouts verified by exact byte consumption.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the versioned audio metadata files that drive the audio engine: the container header, name and hash tables, the object table, and each object type's fields as far as determinable, with confidence levels. No game data in the crate, permissive licences only, platform-independent parsing, tests on hand-built bytes plus a real-data test gated on an environment variable.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The versioned files share one container: a version number, a packed object blob, an archive-name table, an object directory, and two relocation tables for hashed references. Every shipped file ends exactly after the relocation tables, and every object range lands inside the blob.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Object types decoded per file kind: one category type, fifteen curve kinds, seven effect kinds, twenty-three sound-graph node kinds, and twenty-six game-object kinds covering collisions, emitters, radio scheduling, interiors, vehicles, zones, weapons and more. Speech files use a separate unversioned layout of voices, contexts and bank names, all cross-references checked.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The field schemas were checked by decoding all thirty-two thousand objects and requiring each schema to consume its object's bytes exactly. All but one object pass; the exception is a single debug curve object with twelve unexplained trailing bytes, which the reader preserves rather than failing.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two corrections to public documentation came out of the verification. The sound node that prints a variable value stores a counted string, not the fixed fifteen bytes the reference tool assumes; one shipped object uses a shorter label, which proves it. And the supposed sixteen-byte file header from an earlier probe does not exist: those words are the start of the object blob.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Seven game-object kinds keep unknown bodies. Five have fixed sizes, so their layouts are at least bounded; scripted reports look like a count plus seven-byte entries, and train stations look like a struct plus a counted name. Speech voices and contexts are anonymous hashes with no public name list.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The crate decodes leniently: bytes a schema does not describe are returned as trailing bytes on the object, never an error, so partial knowledge stays usable and explicit.</li>
      <li>No dependency on the archive or resource crates: these files are loose and uncompressed, and the archive crate's hash normalisation differs from the audio hash, so the reader carries its own twelve-line hash function.</li>
      <li>Next work is the unknown fixed-size game objects, the XML sidecars for wave slots and archive maps, and a name list to resolve speech hashes.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build and test the crate named lf-audio-config in the lane scratch area with the standard build and test commands; set the game-directory environment variable to also parse and fully decode all twenty-one shipped metadata files and check the locked census totals. The manual example prints a per-file summary of names, counts and type histograms without writing anything.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first container reading put the name table right after a sixteen-byte header, which fit the offsets of small files but misaligned everything else; the reference tool's model of a blob size followed by packed objects resolved it and then verified byte-exact on all files. A hand-guessed hash test vector was wrong and was replaced with a machine-computed value. The shared build lock and PowerShell's habit of failing on tool stderr noise each cost a few retries and are worth knowing about rather than fighting.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="structures-render">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Class layouts: render phases, draw commands and other rendering classes</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Draw commands turned out to be small self-describing records with a shared six-slot interface, while the core graphics resource classes sit almost entirely in the encrypted part of the binary and yielded no layouts. Of 174 classes, 130 got a size and 1,653 fields were recovered in total.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the render family: draw commands, render phases, particle, drawable, sky and core graphics classes. For each class: which virtual slots it overrides or inherits, what its constructor and destructor initialize, its object size and how that size was found, its fields with confidence levels, and which other classes it relates to. Then describe the family as a whole and recommend a rewrite order.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every draw command shares one base layout: a virtual table pointer plus a four-byte sequence number, eight bytes in total. Each command constructor stamps the base table, mixes a global counter into the sequence field, stamps its own table, then initializes its parameters. All 49 command tables have exactly six slots.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Slot</th><th role="columnheader">Meaning</th><th role="columnheader">Evidence</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">0</td><td role="cell" data-label="Meaning">deleting destructor</td><td role="cell" data-label="Evidence">pattern matches in 43 of 49 classes</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">1</td><td role="cell" data-label="Meaning">per-command execute function</td><td role="cell" data-label="Evidence">real code in every measured subclass</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">2</td><td role="cell" data-label="Meaning">returns the object size</td><td role="cell" data-label="Evidence">constant matches measured size in all 31 readable cases</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">3 to 4</td><td role="cell" data-label="Meaning">unknown, never usefully overridden</td><td role="cell" data-label="Evidence">47 of 48 subclasses share the base version</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">5</td><td role="cell" data-label="Meaning">per-command id number</td><td role="cell" data-label="Evidence">unique small integer per class, one collision</td></tr>

      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Command sizes run from 12 bytes for the smallest state commands up to about a thousand bytes for the phone camera and player commands. Fourteen sizes carry high confidence and 27 medium confidence; the rest are lower bounds or unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The render phase base class is large, about 2,300 bytes, with 15 virtual slots. One slot is overridden by all 24 phases and looks like the main per-phase render function. Notably, slot zero is not a deleting destructor: it touches no object memory at all, so phases are probably never destroyed through the base interface.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The particle and sky classes were mostly readable, with sensible sizes from 12 bytes to about 1,700 bytes. Two particle classes each embed three keyframe objects, confirmed by table stores at three member offsets. The sky and procedural texture classes were the most readable group at ninety-one percent.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The core graphics resource layer gave up nothing: ninety-eight percent of its virtual functions and ninety-four percent of the shader and model layer sit in the encrypted range, and no constructor for them appears in readable code. Override tables were still recorded since they need no code. No public headers were found for any class in this family.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The per-command id numbers look like draw-list type tags, and the per-phase main slot looks like the render entry point, but both names are guesses from position and override patterns, not from symbols.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Two measurements conflict and need manual review: the keyframe class measures 52 bytes from its own constructors but sits at a 40-byte stride where embedded, and two small shader variable subclasses measure smaller than their base. Also unknown: the roles of the never-overridden command slots, most phase slots, all core resource class internals, and pool element sizes.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Recommended rewrite order: draw commands and sky and procedural classes first (highest confidence), then particles once the keyframe size conflict is resolved, then render phases (interface mapped, some slots encrypted), and the core resource layer last since it is blocked on the encrypted range and must not be guessed. Sizes carry explicit confidence levels so later workers know what is solid and what is a lower bound.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Search the readable code for each class table address to find constructors, disassemble the hits while tracking the object pointer through register copies, merge field accesses across each class's own methods, and cross-check sizes against allocation constants and the size slot. The lane data file holds one record per class with slots, constructors, fields, sizes and relationships.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>A wrong attribute name in the disassembler bindings silently emptied every result until a standalone test exposed it; errors hidden inside broad exception handlers cost the most time.</li>
      <li>Two register-tracking bugs misattributed foreign memory accesses to the object and inflated some sizes badly; both were fixed and all numbers re-derived.</li>
      <li>Constructors that build embedded member objects were first mistaken for constructors of the member class; only table stores at offset zero now count as constructor evidence.</li>
      <li>A truncated shell pipe killed a script halfway through writing its output file; the file was rebuilt from the intermediate data and re-verified.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

The main root carries 21 virtual slots; a mid-level response branch adds one slot; two leaf classes add their own slot directly under the root; the handler, scanner, factory and group classes form four small separate hierarchies with 84, 4, 2 and 1 slots.</p>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Slot zero of every class is the scalar deleting destructor; the shape was confirmed for every readable target. Three classes merge the deleting step into a single destructor body instead.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 55 classes override the first virtual slot after the destructor with a stub returning a per-class constant, and 49 do the same for the second slot. <span class="evidence">Inferred</span> These two numbers are most likely an event type identity and a category or response code. The full per-class table is in the lane data file.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Base layouts are small: the root holds one integer and one flag byte above its table pointer, and the response branch adds one flag and two integers with fixed initial values. Richer leaves include a damage event that embeds a ped damage-response object and carries refcounted entity pointers, a gunshot event with a triple of floating-point fields, an event group holding an inline queue of eight fixed entries, and a scanner of at least 296 bytes with several embedded members.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Events are normally built as short-lived stack values or through a custom pool allocator that takes no size argument, which is why almost no exact sizes could be recovered. The one exception is the global event group, built once as a singleton through the normal allocator at 76 bytes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Two size hints from an older public build (handler and scanner pads) sit just above the observed field extents here, which is consistent with those sizes still holding, but they remain unverified for this build.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Suggested rewrite order: the two base classes first (layouts, destructor shape, identity-stub convention), then the event group container, then leaf events parents-before-children, then the factory, and the scanner and handler dispatch loop last since they depend on every event type. The handler's per-event methods can likely be mapped to event types using the new identity table. The 24 classes without a standalone constructor and the pool allocator behind heap events are explicit follow-up work.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Join the batch classes to the recovered virtual tables by their object-locator entries. Scan the unencrypted code for each table address as an immediate value, keeping only hits backed by a relocation entry. Treat a function as a constructor only if disassembly shows it storing that table at the object's start; treat slot-zero targets as deleting destructors only if they show the flags-check, delete and return-this shape. Find allocation sites by scanning for direct calls to each constructor and matching the strict push-size, call, move-to-this pattern in the disassembled caller. Collect field accesses across each class's own methods and roll base-class fields into each descendant for cumulative layouts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first run reported ten constructors for a task event class; manual reading showed nine were large functions building the event as a stack temporary. Constructor attribution was then restricted to functions storing the table at the object's start, which cut the total to the 63 real ones. A second bug classified dozens of handler dispatch methods as deleting destructors because they also call constructors; requiring the exact destructor ending fixed it. An early size heuristic that accepted any nearby constant produced impossible odd sizes, so it was replaced with a strict allocator-call pattern, which left exactly one size standing. The darkest class keeps only one analysable method with its destructor encrypted, and both New-York factory and scanner variants show almost nothing readable.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Class layouts: audio classes</h2>
      <p>All 78 audio classes now have recovered object layouts and virtual interfaces: every vtable slot is labelled overridden or inherited, nearly every class has its constructor and destructor identified, and most have a measured size. The sound-node family shares one base implementation with a single behaviour slot per node, while the game-side emitters range from under a hundred bytes to around twenty eight kilobytes.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the audio class family: per-slot override analysis, constructors and destructors, object sizes, field lists with proposed meanings, and relationships between classes, working only on unencrypted code.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The batch holds 78 classes in 9 single-inheritance families plus two orphans, with 646 vtable slots in total. About 28 percent of slot targets fall in the opaque range and were not analysed; the remaining 257 distinct code targets were all disassembled across 474 functions with no failures.</p>
      <ul>
      <li>Sound nodes: one base of ten slots with 24 subclasses. The base implements most slots once and every subclass overrides the same behaviour slot plus its destructor. Six node sizes are confirmed by two independent methods.</li>
      <li>Effects: a base of seven slots with seven subclasses that reimplement nearly every slot each, plus six small platform backends with three slots each.</li>
      <li>Voices: a base of twelve slots with four backends that override everything except one shared default slot. The backends look like they share one creation helper.</li>
      <li>Game emitters: a tiny root (a vtable pointer plus one id word) with nineteen per-type emitters. Most emitters override one key behaviour slot; eight of them point it at a shared default, effectively disabling it.</li>
      <li>Radio: a seventeen-slot interface whose base holds no state; both children override most slots with small bodies that delegate through a single pointer field.</li>
      <li>Odd cases: one sound base puts its deleting destructor in slot five instead of slot zero; one attribute class belongs to the 2d-effect family rather than the audio tree and shares its deleting code with a sibling class; four classes and one vtable-less root have fully opaque construction.</li>
      </ul>

      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The opaque-range slot fillers shared by hundreds of tables are pure-call or deleted-function defaults, judged from fan-in alone. Several large emitters embed whole radio or speech objects as members.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite in this order: the tiny roots first, then the sound base once plus one behaviour slot per node, then effects, voices, radio, the thin emitters, and the big partly-opaque emitters last. Per-class layouts, sizes and confidence levels are stored as machine-readable data for later lanes.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane script from the repository root with the project Python environment. It scans the executable for vtable addresses confirmed by relocations, disassembles the owning and called functions, attributes each to its class through the class hierarchy, and writes one record per class. Runtime is a few minutes. Hand-read dumps of the destructor patterns and the root constructor confirmed the automatic classification.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Early runs attributed derived-class destructors to the base class because link-time optimisation inlines base destructors into derived ones; the fix was to attribute multi-vtable functions to the most-derived class. Identical destructors are folded across sibling classes by the linker, so one code body can serve several classes. A variable in the script briefly shadowed the disassembler handle and silently emptied 54 analyses; error capture was added and the final run has zero failures. One shared helper resisted automatic attribution for a while and was verified by hand instead. Two data labels in the machine output name a base class where the most-derived class is meant; the written report corrects them.</p>
