      <article class="entry" id="pilot-09">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Pilot lane 09: five functions rewritten and timed</h2>
      <p>All five assigned small functions were rewritten in Rust and verified against the originals: every one of more than sixteen thousand comparison trials agreed, and each rewrite passed on its first attempt.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Rewrite five small leaf functions in Rust, prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original over at least a thousand random plus edge-case trials, run one honesty test with a deliberately introduced bug, and record honest timings for the project schedule estimate.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five of five functions verified, with full agreement across two independent random seeds: two simple setter routines, a bounded string copy with padding, a status-bit lookup through a pointer chain, and a five-argument initialiser that returns its object.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The largest of the five, at over a hundred instructions with several alignment-dependent paths, turned out to be the standard bounded string copy routine, confirmed three independent ways including its debug symbol name.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One function reads a game data table that lives in writable memory, contrary to the pilot brief that the chosen functions touch no global data. The rewrite takes the relocated table address as a parameter instead, and the test crafted table entries in a private copy of the image.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The honesty test worked: a copy-paste bug (storing one argument twice) was caught in all but the handful of trials where both arguments happened to be identical.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Total hands-on time was about eight minutes for five functions, or under two minutes per verified function. About three of those minutes built a reusable batched checker; the marginal cost per function was under a minute.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Batched in-process comparison is the way to check rewrites: mapping the executable once and calling both sides thousands of times in one process checked each function in under a second, against several minutes per function for the earlier one-process-per-trial loop. The under-a-minute marginal figure is a floor for trivial leaves, not a project average: these were simplest-case functions, one was a standard routine, and none needed a second attempt. Harder functions with calls, globals, or ambiguous signatures will take longer.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>The lane folder holds the Rust crate with the five rewrites and the batched checker, a machine-readable results file with timings and trial counts, and the disassembly scripts. Rebuilding the crate for the 32-bit target and running the checker once per function repeats the full comparison in a few seconds each.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Three small build failures slowed the checker, all in throwaway comparison code and none in a rewrite: two borrow-checker complaints about generating random numbers inside argument lists, and a format string with one argument too few. A prebuilt one-shot helper initially looked like the faster path, but its per-trial process cost would have eaten the whole time budget, so the first half of the session went into the batched checker instead; that bet paid off. One shell oddity: a passing run reported a failure exit code because the shell treats any program warning text as an error, which cost a few minutes to confirm as harmless.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Native handlers SET_RADAR_SCALE to SET_VIEWPORT_MIRRORED: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 script natives in this batch turned out to be thin wrappers: almost every handler just forwards its script arguments to one engine function, which means each engine function can be named straight from the native's public documentation.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the handlers of 140 natives, from SET_RADAR_SCALE to SET_VIEWPORT_MIRRORED, work out the script call context layout, and propose names for the engine functions and object fields each handler touches, using the public native documentation and the public decompiled mission scripts as the source of meaning.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context layout: handlers receive one pointer, and the script argument array hangs off it at a fixed offset, one 32-bit slot per argument. Two neighbouring slots are never touched by any handler in this batch, and since no native here returns a value, the return slot stays unknown.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 135 of the 138 readable handlers call exactly one engine function. Two day-shift natives share a five-call tail, and one pool-physics native branches on its argument. Two natives share an unreadable stub handler with 44 other debug and stripped natives.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three argument marshalling idioms: integers pushed directly, booleans normalised through a compare and set instruction that overwrites the saved context pointer on the stack, floats moved through vector registers into reserved stack slots.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> No handler resolves a script handle itself. Handle to pointer lookup always happens one level down inside the engine function, through a shared pool lookup reached with the pool in one register and the handle on the stack, seen at vehicle and ped call sites.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The public documentation is wrong about SET_TIME_ONE_DAY_BACK: it claims the native does nothing, but the handler holds a complete day-decrement path with month rollover and weekday update, and the shipped main script calls it.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The public database lacks signatures for seven natives; handler evidence fixes their argument counts, including two for the vehicle alarm duration and four or five for the trip-skip family. Script call sites confirm the alarm duration is passed in milliseconds.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two vehicle natives write the same two-byte alarm field, and the clock date globals were confirmed by disassembling the day shift in both directions. Two presence-template natives call into the encrypted code region, so that worker stays unnamed beyond its template id argument.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> 139 engine functions proposed for naming, most with high confidence since each maps one to one onto a documented native; area prefixes such as vehicle or ped come from code region and documented meaning.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Nine structure fields proposed, strongest the vehicle alarm time and the clock date globals; the rest are medium or low confidence single-sighting proposals.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Later lanes should expect handler, setter, then pool lookup, not handler straight to lookup, and a lane with value-returning natives still needs to pin down the return slot.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each listed handler with Capstone from the executable, tag the context pointer and argument array with a small abstract interpreter, compare argument counts against the public native database, and grep the public decompiled mission scripts for call sites. Targeted disassembly of a dozen engine callees confirms the pool lookup pattern and the clock arithmetic. The encrypted prefix of the code section is never disassembled.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The boolean idiom initially looked like handlers passing their own context pointer to the engine; it is actually a normalised zero or one written over the saved pointer slot. One door-state native shows both four and six argument call sites in the decompiled scripts while the handler reads six, so its signature either grew between builds or the decompiler merged two same-named natives. Ten sampled natives are never called in the shipped scripts at all.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Native handlers GET_CHAR_MELEE_ACTION_FLAG1 to GET_LEVEL_DESIGN_COORDS_FOR_OBJECT: what they reveal</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 140 native handlers in this batch were disassembled, and every one follows the same shape: a tiny wrapper that reads script arguments from a call context and forwards them to a single engine function. That engine function is where the meaning lives, and it names ten character flag bits, the money field, the driver seat, extra car colours, and the shared routines that turn script handles into object pointers.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Work through a batch of 140 script native handlers, recover the call context layout they share, describe what each handler does at the engine level, propose names for the engine functions they call and meanings for the object fields they read, and cross-check everything against the public native documentation and the public decompiled mission scripts.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context holds a return-slot pointer, an argument-array pointer, and a small pool of temporary vector slots with a cursor and a back-pointer table. Handlers that take a position copy it into a temporary slot and hand the engine a pointer to the copy; one unused-looking field between the return and argument pointers was never read by anything in this batch, so its meaning stays unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Handler shapes fall into a few buckets: most write the return slot, about half use out-parameters only, three are trampolines that forward the whole context to a shared dispatcher, and two console-related getters are stubs that return a constant without calling anything. One handler is shared by two natives, and eight engine functions are unconditional jumps, five of them into code that is encrypted on disk.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nearly every character, vehicle and object getter funnels through one shared handle-to-pointer routine, with a separate routine converting pointers back to handles; group and network lookups have their own shared helpers. The pools are selected by globals, one each for characters, dummy characters, vehicles, objects and interiors.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Ten single-bit character flags were pinned to exact words and bit positions, covering melee action flags, execution and stun readiness, movement animation blocking, leaving boats and water, cowering, ducking when aimed at, and walking alongside the leader. Also recovered: the character money field, model index chain, body-part damage array, weapon manager location, the vehicle driver seat and extra colours, and the engine sub-object used for engine health.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 140 natives are documented in the public native database, and 97 of them are called by the public decompiled mission scripts, with the game timer and integer stats the most used. The console getters, scores, and several restart-node getters are never called, which strengthens the read that the console getters are debug leftovers.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Proposed names were recorded for every per-native engine function plus the shared helpers, with confidence levels and supporting natives, for the coordinator to merge into the function inventory.</li>
      <li>Proposed field meanings were recorded for the character, vehicle, object and network-object classes found above.</li>
      <li>The shared handle-lookup routines and pool selector globals should be published to the other native lanes as anchors, since every batch will re-derive the same few addresses.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone in 32-bit mode, following branches until each path returns, then disassemble the head of each direct callee. Read argument indices from array accesses off the context argument pointer, return behaviour from stores through the context return pointer, and pool usage from the register setup before each lookup call. Compare arities against the public native database and call counts against the public decompiled scripts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two surprises needed untangling. A getter named for groups turned out to read a per-character flag bit, not group state. And disassembly that runs past tiny jump-ending functions silently attributes a neighbouring function's calls to the wrong native; the fix was to stop at padding bytes rather than trusting inventory sizes, which proved unreliable for small functions. One shared sub-call target is not aligned with any known function start and is left as unknown for a follow-up lane.</p>

      <h2>Native handlers FINISH_WIDGET_COMBO to GET_CHAR_MELEE_ACTION_FLAG0: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 handlers in this batch were disassembled, and the script-native call context layout is now settled: a return-slot pointer, an argument-array pointer and a small vector-temporary area. Nearly every handler is a thin wrapper around exactly one engine function, and every handle-taking engine function funnels through one shared pool lookup. Two natives turned out to be hardcoded stubs.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover names and meanings for the engine code behind 140 script natives, from FINISH_WIDGET_COMBO to GET_CHAR_MELEE_ACTION_FLAG0: disassemble each handler, work out the call-context layout, describe what each handler does, and propose names for the engine functions and object fields it touches.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context holds a return-slot pointer, an argument-array pointer and a vector-temporary area with a count and a writeback table. Scalar out-parameters are passed straight through as script-memory pointers; only three-float vectors are copied into temporaries. A fourth context field is never read by any handler in the whole table, so it is write-only or unused.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of the 140 handlers, 131 call exactly one engine function, 8 are a single tail jump, and one (the floor helper) is fully inline arithmetic. Four blip natives share one handler because they all return the same blip field.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All ped, vehicle and object engine functions resolve script handles through one shared pool lookup, told apart by which pool object is passed in. The lookup body sits in the encrypted part of the executable so only its convention could be recovered. The blip and player lookups are in plain code and were recovered completely, including pool capacities and handle validation.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Position and orientation getters all read from an entity matrix with right, forward, up and position rows. Health and speed come from shared virtual calls used identically by peds and vehicles. Blip records yielded a dozen field meanings, and ped and vehicle structures yielded flag bits for in-vehicle state, melee, cover, fleeing and sirens.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two natives are stubs that ignore their arguments and always return the same constant. One widget native and one cellphone native call into the encrypted region, so their behaviour is unknown. The weather natives and one weapon path also depend on encrypted helpers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The extracted-displacement native scales its result by the frame-time value while the extracted-velocity twin does not, making displacement frame-rate dependent by construction. The blip-rotation native returns floored integer degrees. Position freezing skips one vehicle category, and ped position and heading silently substitute the vehicle when the ped is inside one.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Proposed names were recorded for every engine function in the batch plus the shared helpers, five virtual slots and the key pools, tables and globals, each with a confidence and the supporting natives. Low-confidence helper bodies and the encrypted callees were left for later lanes with the runtime-decrypted image. The rewrite should preserve the observed quirks: the stubs, the shared blip handler, the in-vehicle substitution and the frame-time scaling.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler address from the coordinator batch list with capstone directly from the executable, following direct jumps and stopping at returns; record direct calls, absolute data references and reads through the context pointer. Then disassemble each engine target the same way, track the entity pointer returned by the pool lookup, and note which offsets are read or written. Cross-check signatures against the public native database and call shapes against the public decompiled mission scripts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first analyser build silently merged engine code into handlers that tail-jump, because it followed every direct jump; far jumps are now treated as tail calls. A crash in the register-name helper of the installed disassembler library was worked around with a local register table. One engine function past the end of the cellphone native was briefly misattributed to it before the chained jump was noticed.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-textures">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: texture dictionaries (WTD)</h2>
      <p>Every loose texture dictionary in the game now parses with a new pure Rust reader, and every texture in them decodes to plain pixels: 205 files, 2,286 textures, zero parse failures.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the texture dictionary format: the dictionary structure, the texture records, decoding of every pixel format found in the game to RGBA8, and an in-memory DDS export for inspection in tests. Report the format and size distribution across every reachable dictionary.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 205 loose dictionaries share one container design: a small header naming the resource type, then a single compressed payload that expands into a structures segment and a pixel-data segment. Each dictionary holds a hash table and a pointer list over texture records carrying name, dimensions, mip count, format code, stride and a data pointer.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Exactly five pixel formats appear, with this distribution:</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Format</th><th role="columnheader">Textures</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">DXT5</td><td role="cell" data-label="Textures">1389</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">DXT1</td><td role="cell" data-label="Textures">862</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">DXT3</td><td role="cell" data-label="Textures">18</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">A8R8G8B8 uncompressed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Textures">16</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">L8 uncompressed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Textures">1</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three layout rules were pinned down that public documentation did not state: stride times height always equals the top mip level size including compressed formats, the name hash is computed over the short title rather than the stored name, and every dimension is a multiple of four though many are not powers of two. Most textures carry a single mip level; the deepest has eight. One dictionary is empty.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The new decoders were cross-checked against an independent image decoder on real textures: four of five formats match byte for byte, and the fifth differs only by one brightness step in one colour channel on some texels, a known rounding-convention difference.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The crate keeps unknown fields as raw values rather than guessing meanings, and sizes mip data with block rounding, which is the principled rule even though shipped files never expose the difference. Dictionaries inside encrypted archives stay out of reach until the archive work lands; the next texture step is to run this reader over those once extraction exists, since map and vehicle textures will extend the distribution. Cube and volume textures were not observed and stay unsupported until one is found.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate and run its unit tests, which use only hand-built byte vectors. With the game directory in an environment variable, the integration test parses every loose dictionary, checks the stride and hash rules, decodes the top mip level of each texture and builds a DDS in memory; it reports exact counts and fails on any error. A worked example program prints a one-file summary to standard output.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The public wiki page for this format is a stub with no layout, so the field order came from reading an open-source parser, then confirming every field against real files. A first guess at the hash input matched nothing until the short-title form was tried. Two words first read as padding turned out to be capacity counts. One calibration script reused a single output file without an overwrite flag and silently re-read stale bytes, briefly suggesting large decoder differences that vanished on re-run. Every format lane named its example program the same thing, so a test run silently executed another lane's binary until the example was renamed.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Rust reader: navigation meshes and vehicle paths</h2>
      <p>A new Rust crate now reads every pedestrian navmesh and every compiled vehicle path file in the game, and it corrected two public format notes along the way: the vehicle link table is owned by a partition rule rather than a per-node count, and its length byte comes first rather than second.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the pedestrian navigation meshes and the vehicle path node files, verify the public prose documentation against the real files, and validate adjacency in both directions.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The navmesh documentation held up for the parts it covers: the resource container, the sixty by sixty tile grid, the vertex and index arrays, and the polygon first-index rule checked out on all ten thousand plus tiles.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Navmesh files parsed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">10,839 of 10,839</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Every tile and boat mesh opens with zero failures</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Walkable polygons</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">About 5.65 million</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Three meshes per map plus a small test set</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Path node files parsed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">192 of 192</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Three maps times sixty-four squares, zero failures</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Road nodes and links</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">About 95 thousand nodes, 160 thousand links</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Every link target exists and the graph is fully symmetric</td></tr>

      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The vehicle path notes needed two corrections. A node's links run from its own start marker to the next node's start marker, which partitions the link table exactly; the documented per-node count field does not match this and must not be used as one. The link length byte sits before the flag byte, not after it, which geometry settles decisively.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Polygon adjacency in the navmesh is still not decoded. The obvious small fields inside each polygon record were tested as neighbour references and are asymmetric in every tile, so they are something else. A per-corner side table with none-markers is the prime remaining candidate, as is the unexamined trailing region of each tile. The per-tile height base and any cover points are likewise still unknown.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The crate exposes what is verified and keeps the rest as documented raw bytes rather than guessing. The next lane should attack the per-corner side table first, then fit height bases from road node heights and search the trailing region for the matching field.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate and run its tests with the game folder exported: the integration suite opens the path and navmesh archives with a key it locates at run time in the owner's executable, parses every member, and re-checks all counts and the adjacency claims. Without that variable the suite skips cleanly.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The link table looked deeply broken at first: ownership windows overlapped heavily and a few nodes appeared to read past the end of the table. Both symptoms vanished once the count field was recognised as wrong and ownership was read as a partition instead. A late refactor of the edge-region accessor was covered by unit tests but did not get a second full integration run, so the suite should be re-run once after integration.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="script-interpreter">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>The script interpreter, mapped end to end</h2>
      <p>The whole script virtual machine interpreter is now mapped: every opcode handler, the thread layout, the functions around it, and the first behavioural test of original engine code on this project, which ran a tiny synthetic program and left the right answer on the script stack.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Map the script virtual machine interpreter precisely: find its opcode dispatch, enumerate every opcode with its stack effect and operand bytes, describe the thread context as the interpreter uses it, identify the surrounding functions, and if possible run the original interpreter in isolation on a synthetic program.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The interpreter is a single function that fetches one opcode byte and dispatches through a jump table of 78 entries, one per named opcode.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> High byte values are not looked up: each pushes its own value minus a constant, giving small integers directly. Only two byte values are invalid and abort the thread.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 78 handlers were read individually. Their behaviour matches the public instruction names in every case, with five quirks a rewrite must copy, including division by zero leaving the dividend in place and a supposedly unsigned push that sign-extends.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Native calls are bound when a script loads, not looked up while it runs: the loader overwrites each native hash in the code with the handler address, writing zero for unknown hashes, and the interpreter simply calls whatever address it finds.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The thread layout derived from the handlers agrees with the layout published by the open-source script debugger on every field, with no disagreements, including the five thread states and the order of the five virtual functions.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Eighty-two related functions were identified with roles, including the per-frame scheduler, thread reset, kill and spawn, the program and native tables, the loader, the native binder, and the game-specific thread overrides.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The original interpreter bytes executed a synthetic program (push two numbers, add) and produced the correct stack, plus both error paths. The per-instruction budget, the saved instruction pointer and the restored globals all behaved as the static analysis predicted.</li>
      </ul>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Named opcodes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">78</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">one handler each in the dispatch table</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row">Push-immediate byte values</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">176</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">each pushes a small integer with no operand bytes</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Invalid byte values</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">2</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">both abort the thread with the same error</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Related functions identified</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">82</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">scheduler, lifecycle, tables, loader and overrides</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row">Behavioural tests passed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">3</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">arithmetic plus both error paths on real interpreter bytes</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>A Rust rewrite should implement the loader-time native binder rather than any run-time hash lookup, reproduce the five arithmetic quirks exactly, and take the text-formatting helper and the log sink as engine-provided hooks, since both live in the encrypted part of the executable and cannot be studied statically. The three behavioural tests are the seed vectors for the rewrite's test suite. Two small corrections for earlier survey notes: the script file extension string does appear in the executable, and opcode zero is invalid rather than a no-op.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the interpreter function with a standard x86 disassembler and follow the single computed jump to the opcode table; each entry leads to one handler whose stack traffic can be read directly. The instruction-length helper next to it confirms every operand size independently. The behavioural test maps the interpreter's code pages into a scratch process with relocation fixups, builds a synthetic thread, program and bytecode program on a scratch heap, calls the interpreter entry point with a small instruction budget, and reads back the thread state and stack words.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The Python emulator crashes on this machine even for two trivial instructions, so the planned unicorn demo was rebuilt as a small native runner instead, which took several iterations of mapping and relocation work. The native call path looked impossible at first: the handler calls the operand with no lookup in sight, until the loader's binding pass explained that the operand is already a handler address by run time. A block of composer-data code just past the interpreter was briefly mistaken for script thread management until its virtual table gave it away.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Class layouts: user interface, front end, HUD, replay editor and web browser classes</h2>
      <p>The interface family is now mapped: 78 classes, almost all of their virtual functions identified, and two surprises — every interface object carries a virtual function that returns a hash of its own class name, and the deleting destructor sits in the third slot instead of the first. About two in five virtual functions are trivial field getters and setters, so a large share of the rewrite is mechanical.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the user interface, front end, HUD, replay editor and web browser classes: for each class, its virtual function table with overridden versus inherited slots, its constructors and destructors, its object size, its fields with confidence ratings, and its relationships to other classes, plus a family-wide inheritance tree, shared interface description, and rewrite order.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 78 classes were processed, covering 6,399 virtual function slots, of which 93 percent point at readable code and 7 percent into the encrypted range. 76 classes have at least one constructor or destructor in readable code. Two do not: one class has no virtual table at all, and one task-related class whose base lives in another lane's batch.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The interface framework is one large single-inheritance tree. A layout root with 115 virtual functions sits at the top, a panel class adds 8 more, and around 45 widgets, menus and video editor screens hang below it, most adding nothing and differing only in which functions they override. The widest tables belong to text, layout and video clip classes with up to 149 slots. Separate small families cover the HTML browser nodes, the replay editor overlay widgets, and the play statistics classes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Slot zero of every interface table is a small stub that hashes the class's own name string; the stored name was read back and matches the owning class in 47 of 51 cases, with 4 classes inheriting another class's stub. Slot one is a shared boolean setter, and slot two is the scalar deleting destructor. No vector deleting destructor appears in any table in the batch.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 42 percent of all slots are trivial accessors: 1,734 getters and 929 setters, including paired float getters that look like rectangle coordinates and dense boolean flag accessors. Only about 5 percent of slots are true unknowns. Roughly ten slots in the root table look like pure virtuals: the base entry is an encrypted stub and many subclasses override it with readable implementations, so the behaviour is recoverable from the overrides.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Object sizes were recovered from allocation sites for 14 classes, including three cases with three agreeing callers each; the rest are lower bounds from the furthest field observed, with the weakest cases flagged as unknown. The panel base is about 480 bytes, the basic video clip about 768, and its montage subclass about 796. Constructor chains into base classes were confirmed throughout.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The HTML node classes have single-entry virtual tables holding only the destructor, confirmed by reading the raw table memory, so their behaviour must live in non-virtual functions. The replay widget root is abstract with two pure virtuals. The statistics classes have five slots each. One upload class has no virtual table and needs string-based discovery instead.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The recommended rewrite order starts with the tiny statistics and font classes, then the HTML nodes, then the replay widgets, then the shared interface root with its accessors and hot override slots, then the panel class, then the leaf widgets, and finally the wide text, layout and clip classes. Deferred to other lanes: the upload class, two task and network stragglers that landed in this batch, one suspicious size bound, and the slot-order puzzle below.</p>
      <ul>
      <li>Rewrite the roughly ten pure virtuals from their readable overrides, not from the encrypted base stubs.</li>
      <li>Analyse each shared implementation once: thousands of slots collapse to dozens of unique functions.</li>
      <li>Mine the captured constructor string references for real field names before writing headers.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>All work was done with a Python script using capstone on the readable code range only, driven by the RTTI class and virtual table inventories from earlier lanes. The script scans readable code for each table's address to find constructors and destructors, tracks the object pointer through each function to collect field accesses with widths and read/write direction, classifies each virtual function by shape, and votes object sizes from allocation call patterns. Per-class records with fields, slots and constructors are stored as structured data alongside the lane report.</p>

      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Measure</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">Meaning</th></tr></thead>

      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The virtual table head contradicts the usual compiler order: the deleting destructor is in the third slot, preceded by the class-name hash stub and a boolean setter. The table boundaries were verified against the runtime type records on both ends, so the order is real, but the cause is unknown. A later lane should find a virtual delete call site and read which slot index it actually calls.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two tool bugs were caught by hand-checking against raw reads: a capstone API guard that silently disabled all analysis on the first run, and an allocation-size matcher that picked the furthest rather than the nearest candidate, which was fixed after a hand-read caller showed the true size. Three size votes that contradicted base-class sizes or field reach were rejected rather than reported.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One benchmark class produced an implausibly large size bound from a single far field access, almost certainly a tracking artefact, and is flagged as unknown.       <article class="entry" id="structures-tasks-b">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Class layouts: AI task classes, second half (CTaskSimple* and other CTask*)</h2>
      <p>All 137 classes in the second task batch now have recovered layouts: the shared virtual interface is mapped slot by slot, over a hundred destructors are identified, 99 task-type IDs are read out, and 1,320 field observations are recorded with confidence grades. The main caveat is that every object size is a lower bound, because tasks come from a pool allocator that takes no size argument.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover object layouts and virtual interfaces for the AI task family, second half: the CTaskSimple leaf classes plus the CTask root, the move interface, and the small task scaffold classes. For each class: which virtual slots it overrides, its constructors and destructors, its size, its fields, and its relationships to other classes, all from the unencrypted code only.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The family shares one virtual interface: the root has 17 slots, the simple-task base extends it to 20, and most leaves keep 20. Slot zero holds the deleting destructor in nearly every class, one slot is overridden by almost all leaves with a small integer constant that acts as a task-type ID (99 recovered), and one slot keeps a single shared implementation inherited by the whole family. Two slots are never overridden by any class.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Fifteen movement classes use multiple inheritance: each carries a second 13-slot table for the move interface, embedded one fifth of the way into the object, with a float and a flags word beside it. The animation-driven NaturalMotion leaves have the widest tables at 29 slots and the largest method bodies.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Constructors were found for nearly every class by searching plain code for each class table address. Destructor identification is strong: over a hundred real destructors confirmed through the deleting-destructor call pattern. Field recovery totals 1,320 observations, about a quarter high confidence, a third medium, the rest single sightings kept as guesses.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Tasks are pool allocated: every construction site draws memory from a pool with no size argument, then calls the constructor with its parameters. An early attempt to read sizes from nearby constants failed because those constants turned out to be constructor arguments, such as pause durations. All sizes are therefore lower bounds from observed fields, ranging from tiny flag tasks to path and animation tasks of a few hundred bytes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The recommended rewrite order is the root and move interface first, then the simple-task base and scaffold, then trivial leaves, then the animation and pathfinding subtrees, with the NaturalMotion family last as the largest piece.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Three classes stay opaque: two keep all their own code in the encrypted range, and one intermediate base class has no virtual table in the recovered data at all, so its layout needs a recheck of its records.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Accept the 99 task-type IDs and the slot map as the family's interface contract for rewrites.</li>
      <li>Treat all sizes as lower bounds until task pool element sizes are measured.</li>
      <li>Recover constructor signatures next, since argument values are visible at the pool call sites.</li>
      <li>Defer the two encrypted classes and re-examine the base class missing its table before laying out its children.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable headers and relocation table, join the batch class list with the RTTI virtual tables, and scan plain code for each table address as a relocated immediate to find constructors and destructors. Disassemble each method, track the object pointer through register copies, and record every field access with width and direction. Classify virtual slot targets by shape: constant stubs, getters, jump thunks, destructor fragments, or general code. Compare each slot against the base class tables to mark overrides, and aggregate field sightings across each class's own methods with confidence by sighting count.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first build double-added the image base to relocation entries and produced tens of thousands of bogus cross-references; the fix was one line. A sizing heuristic then mistook constructor arguments for allocation sizes until caller-window dumps showed several different values reaching the same constructor. About a quarter of the first constructor candidates turned out to be neighbouring functions or type checks rather than stores, and were reclassified. Tiny adjacent destructors share bytes, so their records needed filtering to each class's own table.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="structures-tasks-a">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Class layouts: AI task classes, first half (CTaskComplex*)</h2>
      <p>All 197 complex task classes now have recovered layouts: every class has at least one identified constructor or destructor, the shared deleting-destructor protocol is confirmed, and all class-specific code was found outside the encrypted range.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover object layouts and virtual interfaces for the first half of the AI task class family: per-slot override analysis, constructors and destructors, object sizes, field lists with confidence, relationships, plus a family-wide interface summary and rewrite order.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The family is flat: one root with mostly direct children, plus small nests for movement, combat subtasks, scenarios, vehicle subtasks, condition waits and wandering. Tables hold 21 to 26 slots.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Slot zero is the scalar deleting destructor in nearly every class: destroy the object, then return it to a pool when a flag is set. About one in seven classes inlines the pool arithmetic; the rest call a shared pool helper.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Over 460 constructor and destructor functions were identified by the order of base calls versus vtable stores. Optimizer output complicated this: many constructors pass the object pointer in registers other than the usual one, and some destructors are fully inlined into their deleting wrappers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The movement subgroup carries a second 13-slot interface at a fixed object offset, with a distinct table per class. Six factory-style functions each construct several task types.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> About a third of all vtable slots point into the encrypted range, but these are only a few dozen shared stubs, not class-specific code. Every overriding function examined is readable. The one family-critical encrypted dependency is the shared pool-free helper used by task destruction.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The root class adds one pointer-sized field past its base, most likely the subtask pointer. One virtual slot returns a per-class constant in the few classes that reduce it to a stub, which reads like a task-type identifier.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Most virtual slot meanings beyond the destructor, exact object sizes for the majority of classes (current figures are lower bounds; pool element sizes would settle them), and one odd unaligned secondary-table entry.</p>

      <li>Field tracking for the next lane must follow object pointers in registers other than the standard one, or layouts for optimizer-output functions stay partial.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Scan the readable code for each class vtable address as an immediate, keeping only hits backed by a relocation entry; attribute each hit to its function via exported function bounds; disassemble with capstone; classify constructors versus destructors by whether the base call precedes the vtable store; confirm deleting destructors by the destroy, flag-test, pool-free shape; collect field offsets from object-pointer accesses in each class's own methods. Scripts and JSON data sit with the lane's scratch outputs.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first scan found almost nothing because of a relocation bug that added the image base twice; fixing it raised the hit count from 4 to over 500. A first classifier mistook branching constructors for deleting destructors until a real deleting destructor was read. The longest wrong turn was misreading deleting destructors as clone methods for about an hour; the call target is the plain destructor and the order is destroy-then-free, which settled it.</p>

      <h2>Class layouts: physics, collision, fragments and cloth</h2>
      <p>All 92 physics classes now have recovered object layouts and virtual interfaces: 89 virtual tables with 2,039 slots were classified slot by slot, constructors were found for 74 classes, 1,864 field evidences were harvested, and sizes were estimated for 88 classes. The headline patterns are a near-universal deleting destructor in slot zero, pure-virtual placeholders kept in the encrypted prefix, a strange slot aliasing trick in the bound family, and ten factory functions that build sibling classes together.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the physics, collision, fragment and cloth class family: for each class say which virtual slots it overrides, inherits or introduces and what each function does in a phrase; find constructors and destructors by searching readable code for vtable stores; estimate object sizes from allocation sites or field extents; list fields with widths, kinds and confidence; record relationships; then describe the family tree, the shared base interfaces, the encrypted fraction and a rewrite order.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Slot zero is the scalar deleting destructor in practically every table: 76 of 89 were confirmed by reading the function shape (flag test, vtable downgrade to the base table, free through the engine allocator, callee-cleaned return), 9 more match the shape closely, 2 are encrypted and 4 stay unknown. Slot one is usually not the vector deleting destructor here; only 8 classes show one, while 21 keep a pure placeholder and the rest hold ordinary virtuals.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> About a quarter of all slot entries point into the encrypted prefix, but they collapse to only 31 unique targets, most of them shared stubs. The most-used stub fills exactly the slots that derived classes override with real code, so it reads as the pure-virtual placeholder. Base interfaces that look heavily encrypted are really heavily pure; the meanings come from the readable overrides.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The bound family aliases one virtual slot onto another through a tiny tail-call thunk: slot one re-dispatches to slot forty-eight through the object's own table, and thirteen of fifteen derived bound types inherit the thunk unchanged. The material manager does the same for two of its slots. The reason for the duplication is not known.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Ten factory functions construct unrelated sibling classes: one builds the collision dispatcher together with all five narrow-phase algorithms, one builds capsule, sphere and surface bounds, one builds three broadphase strategies, three build the rope triple, two pair narrow-phase helpers with the manifold result, one initialises two fragment singletons, and one builds the three water classes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The fragment instance class shows textbook multiple inheritance: its constructors store the breakable-instance table, then their own table, then a second table at offset eighty for the streamable reference, and secondary-interface methods adjust the object pointer back by eighty.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The recommended rewrite order is: the bound root contract first, then capsule, sphere, composite, polyhedron, box and the mesh chain; the instance chain with the fragment multiple inheritance; the self-contained collider; the joint contract with its three derived types; the broadphase strategies; the narrow phase validated against upstream Bullet headers; and finally archetypes, materials, rope, simulator, fragment managers and water, with the opaque allocator last. Field records carry high, medium or low confidence so later tools can weight them, and anything seen only once is marked a guess.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane analyzer script from the repository root with the project Python environment; it reads the game executable together with the RTTI tables, the function inventory and the call graph export, and rewrites the structures and statistics files in the lane scratch folder in about two minutes. It only disassembles the readable code range and keeps only vtable references backed by a relocation entry. Full per-class records, including every slot description, constructor, field and relationship, are in the lane data file.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A script variable reused the name of the disassembly engine object and silently zeroed every result, because all detail accessors were wrapped in exception handlers; it took a full empty run to notice, and the fix was a rename. An early factory rule wrongly flagged constructors with inlined base-class initialisation as factories; the fix was to treat base-plus-derived stores as one constructor and only call unrelated sibling stores a factory. The slot-one findings were genuinely surprising: the expected vector deleting destructor is mostly absent, and the slot aliasing thunk has no confirmed explanation yet. Size estimation from allocation sites needed a field-extent cross-check before it could be trusted, and a few sizes remain suspect even now.</p>

      <h2>Class layouts: online service, session and leaderboard classes (rage::rl*, rage::sn*)</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The online family is 2,009 classes, of which 1,924 are four leaderboard templates stamped out 481 times each; the two workhorse templates share a single byte-identical virtual table across all copies, and every session task inherits an eleven-slot base interface whose table the earlier table recovery had missed.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the online service, session and leaderboard classes: for each class the virtual table slot meanings, constructor and destructor behaviour, object size, field list with confidence, and relationships, plus a family tree, a shared-interface description, the encrypted-code fraction, and a rewrite order. Template copies were to be grouped, not analysed one by one.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The batch splits into four leaderboard templates of 481 classes each plus 85 other classes. The leaderboard template carries a four-slot table identical in all copies: a deleting destructor, a getter returning the embedded info object, and a bounds-checked row accessor with a stride of 312 bytes. The leaderboard-info template has a seventeen-slot table that is different for every board but follows one pattern: a destructor, a per-board stub returning a schema descriptor pointer, shared getters in a handful of variants, and a stub returning a fixed constant. The leaderboard-update template has a three-slot table of plain field getters with no destructor at all.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The session tasks share an eleven-slot base interface: destructor, a shared constant getter, two state methods touching a started flag and a state word, three opaque base slots, a per-task worker, a forwarder that calls the worker with a default argument, one more opaque slot, and a per-task stub returning a static descriptor pointer. Two tasks add a twelfth slot. The base table itself was found by reading raw memory after destructors kept storing an address no table list knew. Six fire-and-forget wrappers override nothing and add no fields.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Session events form a two-slot hierarchy whose second slot is always inherited; most derived first slots just return a per-event static descriptor. Thirty-seven tiny descriptor classes have a single destructor slot each. Task objects are large, from roughly 160 bytes to roughly six thousand, while events with genuine constructors range from about a hundred to about six hundred bytes. About one slot target in five points into the encrypted first megabyte and could not be read; the base leaderboard tables and the notifier are fully opaque.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Rewrite first the leaderboard trio, which is fully readable and identical across copies, then the task interface and tasks, then events; leave the encrypted base classes and the interface-only classes for later.</li>
      <li>Treat all object sizes as lower bounds, not exact sizes; no allocation-site constants were recovered.</li>
      <li>Parse the per-board schema descriptor blobs and the base task slot functions next; both are readable and were left untouched for lack of time.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Load the batch list and the recovered table list, scan the unencrypted code for each table address as a four-byte value using a sliding window, map each hit to its containing function with the function inventory, and disassemble the slot targets and the referencing functions. Shared slot targets are identified by counting matches across tables, and base tables are compared slot by slot for override status. The per-class records live in the structures data file with one entry per class.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first scan stepped through the code four bytes at a time and missed most constructor references, because immediate values are not aligned; only a byte-by-byte scan found them. Early field lists contained absurd offsets in the tens of kilobytes until three fixes landed: registers reused as scratch had to be untracked, functions building many objects had to be excluded from field evidence, and disassembly running past a tiny stub into the next function had to be cut off. One record initially suggested a leaderboard info class inherits from two bases at once; the slot evidence supports the interface half of that claim but the declaration half is still unresolved.</p>

      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Class layouts: entities, vehicles, peds, objects and model information</h2>
      <p>All 85 classes in the entity family now have recovered layouts: 7 exact sizes, 3 more at medium confidence, lower bounds for 69, and 6 left unknown because their code sits entirely in the still-encrypted part of the executable. The headline numbers are a 112-byte entity root, exact model-info sizes from 96 to 352 bytes, a 4864-byte vehicle base, and vehicles and peds that run to several kilobytes each.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the entity family: the entity, vehicle, ped, object and model-info classes. For each class that meant its virtual table with per-slot meanings, its constructors and destructors, its size, its fields with widths and likely kinds, and its relationships to other classes, plus a family-wide inheritance tree and a recommended rewrite order.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every constructor and destructor was found by searching the unencrypted code for the class's virtual table address, and every one of the 160 matches was confirmed by the relocation table, so none are coincidental byte matches.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seven sizes are exact: the six model-info classes plus the vehicle base. The model-info sizes came from array destruction code, where the per-element stride is the class size, and the vehicle size came from its constructor's initialisation range together with the fact that every vehicle subclass starts its own fields at the same offset, storing a small type number there.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The constructor call chains match the inheritance tree: each vehicle constructor calls the vehicle base constructor, which calls the physics constructor, and so on down to the entity root. Objects, peds and vehicles each embed audio tracker objects at fixed offsets, found by virtual table stores at non-zero offsets.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The entity root is small and stable: its measured size exactly matches the size recorded in public headers for an older build. The physics class looks slightly larger than in that older build. Vehicles and peds are much larger than their ancestors, with constructors that initialise dozens of fields including recognisable floating point constants.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> About a third of the family's virtual functions sit in the encrypted range, including all of the network event and network array classes, which could not be analysed at all. Five further classes have no constructor or destructor in the visible code.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The destructor layout is slightly unusual: the entity spine appears to keep its deleting destructor in the second slot rather than the first, while the model-info classes use the first slot. Some high-offset field evidence in the largest vehicles may be shared between classes by the linker's identical-code folding, so those size bounds are marked low confidence.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite in this order: model-info classes and the entity root first, then the physics spine, then buildings and objects with the world scanners, then the vehicle base and its factory, then peds with their intelligence, then the vehicle subclasses smallest first, and the fully encrypted network classes last. Field names taken from public headers for an older build are kept clearly labelled as such and treated as unverified here.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Take the virtual table addresses from the RTTI recovery, search the unencrypted code section for each address as a four-byte value, and keep only matches confirmed by a relocation entry. Disassemble the containing functions, track the object pointer through register copies while discarding registers that get overwritten, and record every access through it with width and direction. Compare each virtual table slot by slot against its base class table to separate inherited, overridden and new slots, and classify small slot bodies by shape. Sizes fall out of array strides, constructor ranges, and subclass field starts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two bugs wasted the first analysis pass: a register-name mapping that never matched, which silently produced zero fields for every class, and object-pointer tracking that never forgot, which attributed accesses through member pointers to the object itself and inflated some classes to four times their real size. Both were caught by comparing against the older-build sizes and fixed with stricter tracking. A planned size source, heap allocation sites, found nothing at all: none of these constructors are called directly from visible code, so all size evidence comes from strides, constructors and field touches instead.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="natives-22"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Native handlers TASK_TIRED to WRITE_LOBBY_PREFERENCE: what they reveal</h2><p>Ninety-four script-native handlers were disassembled and every one is now understood: most are thin wrappers that turn script handles into engine object pointers through shared pool lookups, while a few inline helpers, tail jumps and shared particle-effect unpackers cover the rest. The work produced proposed names for over eighty engine functions, twenty object fields, and several surprises, including natives that return values their documentation omits and one whose parameter the engine ignores.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Disassemble the handlers of the ninety-four natives from TASK_TIRED to WRITE_LOBBY_PREFERENCE, recover the call-context layout, describe what each handler does at the engine level, and propose names for the engine functions and object fields they touch, with confidence levels.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every handler receives a single context pointer holding a return-slot pointer and an argument-array pointer; no handler checks an argument count. Handlers fall into five shapes: thin wrappers, tail jumps into context-taking engine functions, fully inline helpers, shared particle-effect unpackers, and one handler in the encrypted range that was skipped.</p><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Finding</th><th role="columnheader">Detail</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Pool lookups</th><td role="cell" data-label="Detail">One shared routine resolves all ped, vehicle and object handles; the pool is selected by a global pointer. Player indices go through a separate player-struct resolver.</td></tr><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Task ids</th><td role="cell" data-label="Detail">Each task native funnels into one task-assign routine with a numeric task id; the unwarped step is a hard-coded constant.</td></tr><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Deobfuscation</th><td role="cell" data-label="Detail">The string deobfuscator XORs with a four-byte repeating key into a static buffer, capped at sixty-four characters.</td></tr><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Ignored parameter</th><td role="cell" data-label="Detail">The ducking-toggle native reads two arguments but its engine function never looks at the second one; The pool lookup, task allocator, particle spawn core and several network implementations sit in the encrypted first megabyte and need the decrypted view; the teleport native's fifth parameter cannot be resolved from shipped scripts and needs a live test.</p><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone using section-aware address mapping, stopping at returns and unconditional jumps while keeping code reachable from forward branches; dump the first hundred or so instructions of each direct callee; read argument indices, boolean normalisation, by-value vector construction and return-slot writes from the instruction stream; and cross-check parameter lists against the public native database and call sites in the public decompiled mission scripts.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><p>The first extraction pass stopped at the first return instruction, which silently dropped code after conditional branches in the wait natives and bled neighbouring handlers into tail-jump stubs. Fixing the disassembler to respect branch targets and unconditional jumps changed several call attributions. Argument-index tracking also needed two iterations before register reuse stopped misclassifying reads. Both traps are worth knowing for the remaining native batches.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="natives-16"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Native handlers SET_CAR_PROOFS to SET_DECISION_MAKER_ATTRIBUTE_STANDING_STYLE: what they reveal</h2><p>All 140 script natives in this batch follow one uniform design: each handler reads its arguments from a call context and forwards them to a single engine function, and almost all of those engine functions resolve the script handle to a game object through one shared lookup routine with separate pools for characters and vehicles.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Disassemble the handler behind each of the 140 natives from SET_CAR_PROOFS to SET_DECISION_MAKER_ATTRIBUTE_STANDING_STYLE, work out the call context layout, describe what each handler does at the engine level, and propose names for the engine functions called and meanings for the object fields touched, using the public native documentation and the public decompiled mission scripts as the source of meaning.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context carries a pointer to the argument array eight bytes in; every handler in the batch reads all of its arguments through it. Boolean arguments are normalised to zero or one and floats travel through vector registers, both with recognisable instruction idioms.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of 137 distinct handlers, 136 were disassembled and each calls exactly one engine function, all different. Four natives share one handler that sits in the encrypted part of the executable and was skipped.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One shared lookup routine resolves script handles to object pointers for 114 of the 136 engine functions, taking a pool pointer plus a handle. The pool used splits exactly by native family: character natives use one pool, vehicle natives another. Two natives that take two handles look up twice, including one that consults both pools, which confirms the split.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Character behaviour flags live in a run of flag words on the character object, with 47 single-bit assignments mapped to named natives and no two natives sharing a bit. Damage immunity flags sit at the same field with identical bits on both characters and vehicles, so that field belongs to a shared base class, with two relationship-based damage modes that actively clear each other.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The nine decision-maker attribute setters share one code shape: convert the handle to an index, range-check it against 54 slots, lazily create a manager object, then write one field. Six attributes pack as bit ranges into one word and three are single bytes or bits, all mapped.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All six coordinate setters route to one teleport function, differing only in flag constants. The money native sends its amount to a helper and sets only a flag bit inline. Health setting clamps to a maximum and consults the streaming system rather than storing blindly.</p><p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Handler argument counts match the public native database for every disassembled handler except two where the public entries list no parameters at all, so those two public entries look incomplete. About one native in seven is never called by the shipped mission scripts, mostly multiplayer or edge-case natives, but all still have real engine bodies.</p><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Finding</th><th role="columnheader">Count</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Natives analysed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">140</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Full batch covered, four via the shared encrypted stub</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Engine functions named</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">148</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">136 unique callees plus 12 shared helpers</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Object fields proposed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">55</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Flag bits, scalars and decision-maker fields with supporting natives</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Script call sites read</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">32,650</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Public decompiled scripts confirm live usage of 121 natives</td></tr></tbody></table><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><p>The shared handle lookup is the highest-value target for other lanes: every batch will route through it, and its pool argument identifies the object class of any native. Each was fixed by re-reading the bytes more carefully, and the fixes are recorded so the next lane does not repeat them. The core entity classes are also absent from the project's RTTI table, so object classes are named by pool rather than by verified class name.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="natives-15"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Native handlers RETUNE_RADIO_TO_STATION_INDEX to SET_CAR_ON_GROUND_PROPERLY: what they reveal</h2><p>All 131 readable handlers in this batch of 140 script natives were decoded, and they share one simple calling convention: each handler receives a single context pointer holding a return slot and an argument array.       <h2>Native handlers LOCATE_OBJECT_3D to NETWORK_SET_HEALTH_RETICULE_OPTION: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 handlers in this batch are thin forwarding shims: they marshal script arguments, call one engine function, and store the result.       <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the handler of each native from LOCATE_OBJECT_3D to NETWORK_SET_HEALTH_RETICULE_OPTION, recover the call-context layout, describe what each handler does at engine level, propose names for the engine functions each handler calls, record any object fields touched, and flag stubs, shared handlers, and encrypted code.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context is a small struct: offset zero holds the return-slot pointer, offset eight holds the argument-array pointer, offset twelve is a scratch-slot counter and offset sixteen starts sixteen-byte scratch slots. The word at offset four is never touched by any handler in this batch, so its purpose stays unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Handler shapes are uniform. About three quarters return a boolean or integer through two fixed instruction patterns, the rest return nothing, nine are pure tail jumps, and none is a stub: every handler reaches engine code.       <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three handlers are shared. One serves eight platform and version-check natives, one serves eleven natives including version checks and copy-protection spot checks, and one is shared by the link-connected and rendezvous-success natives, which looks like a copy and paste alias.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Six handlers reach engine code that is still encrypted on disk, including both shared platform-check handlers.       <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The shared helpers, seen by reading one call past the handlers: a script-handle to entity-pointer lookup used identically by the object, car and character mark-as-no-longer-needed paths with a per-type pool global; a player-index to player-pointer lookup; and a zero-argument gang-manager getter. Seven documentation gaps were found against the public native database, including one native with no entry at all and several where the handler reads more arguments than documented.</p>

      <h2>Native handlers HAS_CAR_BEEN_DAMAGED_BY_WEAPON to IS_CHAR_IN_ANY_HELI: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 139 readable handlers in this batch of 140 script natives were traced from handler to engine code, yielding 229 proposed engine function names and 62 proposed object fields.       <h3>What was asked</h3>

      <h3>What was found</h3>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nearly half the engine functions resolve script handles through one shared pool lookup, called with the pool and the handle, returning an object pointer or nothing.
