      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Pool lookups through the shared getter</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">66 engine functions</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">one calling convention for all handle resolution in the batch</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Public doc arg-count gaps filled</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">7</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">six natives with missing counts plus one wrong count</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The shared pool lookup and the three pool identities should be cross-checked against the other native batches; disagreement would mean a pool or variant split.</li>
      <li>The natives that bottom out in encrypted code need a decrypted-memory read before they can be named with confidence.</li>
      <li>The argument-count corrections should be fed back to the native database data.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler from the batch list with capstone directly from the executable, follow each direct call to its engine function, and note the pool global loaded before each shared-lookup call. Compare observed argument reads against the public sanny database entry for each native, and check call counts in the decompiled mission script collection. All per-native records, proposed names and fields are stored as JSON alongside the lane report.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two handlers pass the raw call context plus a function pointer to a generic adapter, so the first disassembly pass attributed the wrong function to them; reading the adapter showed the real engine function hiding in a pushed argument. Argument counting also first tripped over the context dereference itself, which looks like an argument read; tracking which register holds the argument array fixed it. The death-or-arrest native looked like a stub until its two update calls were noticed, and two handlers turned out to skip the null check every other pool user performs, meaning an invalid handle would crash there.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-script-sco">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: compiled scripts (SCO) and a disassembler</h2>
      <p>A new Rust crate loads every shipped compiled script and disassembles it: all 941 scripts parse and fully decode with zero failures, and native calls resolve to names through the engine native table.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the compiled script format with a disassembler: header, code, statics, globals, native calls and encryption, verified against the real game files, with native names loaded from a data file at run time rather than embedded.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All but one shipped script share a single encrypted container version; the exception is an unencrypted leftover from an older container version that decodes with the same instruction set.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The corpus holds about fourteen and a half million instructions with roughly seven hundred thousand native calls to about twenty four hundred distinct natives, of which over ninety nine percent resolve to names.</p>
      <ul>
      <li>Most called natives are injury and death checks, debug print helpers, the game timer and the wait helper, matching an independent count made from the older decompiled reference set.</li>
      <li>Five fixed opcodes never appear in any script, including the two exception opcodes, and small-constant pushes above thirty one are never used.</li>
      <li>Only six scripts declare a globals segment, in per-episode pairs.</li>
      <li>The header signature word is one constant per episode, not zero-everywhere as the public wiki suggests.</li>
      <li>Nineteen called native hashes are not registered in this build; eight of them sit in the stale leftover script and the rest look like dead code paths.</li>
      </ul>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two scripts disassembled with this crate match an independent open-source disassembler instruction for instruction.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The crate is ready for review and integration: it parses from byte slices with explicit little-endian reads, returns typed errors instead of panicking, keeps the decryption key in memory only, and carries unit tests plus a game-data integration test. Next steps are attributing the unregistered native calls to live or dead code paths and mapping carved scripts back to archive file names once the keyed archive reader lands.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build and test the crate in the usual way, then run the integration test with the game folder environment variable set to parse and disassemble all scripts, optionally writing the per-script statistics file. The example binary summarizes a single script file to standard output and never writes game content anywhere.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The most confusing source was an instruction-set document inside an otherwise reliable open-source tool repository: it describes a newer script target, not this game's, while the repository's code for this game's target is correct. The crate follows the code.</p>
      <p>The first corpus run silently missed the leftover script because the test only scanned for the current container version; reading that archive's entry directly exposed the older magic. A debug-mode key search took minutes where a release build takes seconds, and a shell default wrote reference output in an unexpected encoding that broke the first comparison.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="structures-misc-a"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Class layouts: remaining game classes, first half by name</h2><p>Layouts were recovered for the first half of the remaining game classes: about two thirds of their code sits in the encrypted part of the executable and could not be analysed, but virtual interfaces, constructor patterns and size estimates were recovered for the rest, including an odd case where derived destructors store the base class table address.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Recover object layouts and virtual interfaces for 137 classes: per-slot virtual tables, constructors and destructors, object sizes, field offsets and kinds, and relationships, working only on the unencrypted code with a relocatable-reference search.</p><h3>What was found</h3><ul><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 137 classes hold 2,072 virtual slots; 64 percent point into the encrypted range and were not analysed.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 61 constructors, 13 deleting destructors and 49 factory-style creator functions were identified; 470 field observations were recorded, most of them low confidence single sightings.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the render-command family (14 tiny classes) is allocated 12 or 16 bytes at a time through a shared allocator, which pins their sizes.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the eight effect classes derived from the 2d-effect base get their sizes (16 to 168 bytes) from array-destructor stride measurements, since their own code is encrypted.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the network-event and entity-parse families are fully encrypted with no references in readable code, so nothing beyond table shape is known about them.</li><li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> a large dispatcher routine referencing seven task-descriptor tables is a task factory, not a destructor as first labelled.</li><li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> why the derived effect destructors store the base class table address rather than their own.</li></ul><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><p>Rewrite in this order: the tiny render commands first, then shader effects and cutscene events, then task descriptors once their bases land, then headers-only for the effect family, and the encrypted network and parse families last. Sizes from destructor strides outrank sizes from field offsets where they disagree.</p><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>Scan the executable relocation table for code sites whose stored value equals a class table address, decode each site instruction, and classify the containing function by whether it stores the table through the object pointer, an alias, a fresh allocation, or a global. Slot override analysis needs no disassembly: compare each slot target with the base class tables.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><p>An early decoder took the first instruction covering a reference site and misclassified several creators; verifying each decode against the relocation value fixed it. A destructor heuristic misfired on the task factory until its body was read. Allocation-size guesses below four bytes turned out to be argument noise and were discarded.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="structures-core">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Class layouts: core engine classes: files, resources, parsing, containers, system, script</h2>
      <p>Most of the core engine's virtual functions live in the encrypted first megabyte of the code section and cannot be recovered statically: only about one slot in six was readable, and half the classes yielded no layout evidence at all. The script threads, paged-resource dictionaries, tokenizers, time manager and container templates did yield real layouts, including a uniform dictionary shape shared by eight classes and an empty tokenizer subclass.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of 114 core engine classes covering files, resources, parsing, containers, system and script code: per-slot override analysis, constructors and destructors, object sizes, field lists with confidence, and relationships, working only on the unencrypted code with capstone.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of 1,308 vtable slots across 103 tables, 224 were readable and 1,084 point into the encrypted region. Relocation-backed cross references found 294 vtable uses in plain code, which validated down to 20 constructors, 32 destructors and 14 scalar deleting destructors across 35 classes, plus 231 fields (67 high, 34 medium, 130 low confidence).</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Family</th><th role="columnheader">Classes</th><th role="columnheader">Readable slots</th><th role="columnheader">Outcome</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Paged resources</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">13</td><td role="cell" data-label="Readable slots">about three in five</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">dictionary layout recovered, uniform across eight classes</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Script</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">10</td><td role="cell" data-label="Readable slots">about one in four</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">script thread and game thread fully readable</td></tr>

      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">System allocators</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">11</td><td role="cell" data-label="Readable slots">few</td><td role="cell" data-label="Outcome">time manager readable, allocators opaque</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Slot zero is the destructor on every readable interface, and destructors appear in three shapes: a plain body that resets the virtual table and tail-calls the base destructor, a scalar deleting destructor guarded by a flag argument that frees the object, and base destructors inlined into derived ones by link-time code generation.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The concrete tokenizer subclass overrides nothing: all 41 of its virtual slots are inherited unchanged, so it shares its parent's layout exactly. The eight paged-dictionary classes share one 32-byte layout shape with a count and an entries pointer. The script thread's destructor initializes a long field list, and the game thread extends it with flags and two more words.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The root base class holds a small handful of fields plus an embedded subobject about ninety-six bytes in, which is surprising for a root class and needs review. The paged-resource base has a single word after its table pointer, matching the one public stub member recorded for it.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Object sizes could only be bounded from below by the highest observed field; allocation sites were unusable because the allocator helpers sit in the encrypted region and objects appear pool-allocated. Member construction edges and creator relationships were not recovered.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite in this order: the standard exception types and holder templates first (fully readable), then the root base, the paged base and dictionaries, then the script threads and the time manager, then the tokenizers and loader, and the opaque families (file devices, parsing, memory allocators, shader params) last as one blocked group needing a decrypted binary or dynamic analysis. Layouts recovered here ship with per-field confidence and must be rechecked once the encrypted region is readable.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Find every virtual table address stored into an object by scanning the relocation table for code locations whose value equals a known table address, map each site to its function with the function inventory, and disassemble with capstone while tracking which registers hold the object pointer. Attribute a function to a class only if its first table store (destructor) or last table store (constructor) is that class's table and every other store at offset zero names a strict base class; anything else is inlining or a factory. Classify readable slot bodies by shape: table store means destructor, single load means getter, calls only means forwarder.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two silent bugs wasted the first runs: wrong capstone operand-type constants dropped every memory access, and adding the relocation block base twice (the library already returns full addresses) hid all but two of the table references. The disassembler also ran past function ends into neighbours until it learned to stop at padding and known entries. The stranger findings are that the root base class seems to embed a subobject of its own kind, that dozens of functions mention one template's table without ever storing it, and that the whole file-device and parsing trees are dark while their close cousins are readable.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="structures-animation">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Class layouts: animation, motion tree and Euphoria</h2>
      <p>All 148 animation, motion tree and Euphoria classes now have recovered object layouts: constructors, destructors, field maps and size estimates derived from the unencrypted code, with the worst gaps flagged rather than guessed.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the animation family: which virtual slots each class overrides, which functions construct and destroy it, how big it is, what lives at each field offset, and how the classes relate. Work only on the unencrypted code.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every class in the batch was matched to its runtime type record, yielding 149 virtual tables. Scanning the unencrypted code for references to those tables found 466 use sites in 313 functions, of which 309 were confirmed to store a table address into an object under construction. In total 319 constructors and 78 destructors were classified, 38 storing functions stayed ambiguous, and 2291 field records were extracted.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The family splits into clean sub-hierarchies: eighteen behaviour classes share one eight-slot base, thirteen animation channel codecs share a 21-slot base, sixteen motion tree nodes share a 14-slot base with three nodes adding a fifteenth slot, and the effector, creature component, frame filter and request families each share uniform table sizes. Slot zero is the destructor in every family checked, and deleting destructors appear in both scalar and vector forms.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Only six percent of distinct virtual function bodies live in the encrypted range, but they cluster in base-class tables: shared core implementations are encrypted far more often than per-type overrides. Two classes are fully opaque (one network event with all 24 slots encrypted, one joint data class), and seven classes show no construction code at all in the visible range.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Several slots returned small constants or per-class static descriptors when examined: motion tree nodes expose a descriptor whose first field is a per-class numeric id, channel codecs return small type numbers, and effectors expose pointer and float getters consistent with target handles and weights. Meanings for most other slots remain unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Object sizes range from a few bytes for empty shells and simple requests up to around eight hundred bytes for behaviour objects and several kilobytes for frame buffers. About thirty sizes are confirmed by allocation sites; the rest are lower bounds from the highest field touched. Base-class sizes that exceed their smallest derived class are flagged as overestimates caused by inlined construction.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Layouts are recorded per class with per-field confidence and evidence, in a machine-readable structures file for later rewrite work. The recommended rewrite order is channel codecs first, then frame degrees of freedom and filters, then motion tree nodes and requests, then the game animation layer, then effectors and creature components, then the ART framework and behaviour objects, and finally the composers and physics glue, which hold the most encrypted code. Public header collections were checked and contain no usable layouts for this family, so everything rests on the binary evidence.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Join the batch class list to the RTTI class and table inventories by mangled name. Collect every relocated position in the unencrypted code whose stored value equals one of the family table addresses. Map each to its containing function from the unified function inventory, disassemble with capstone, and track the object pointer starting from the thiscall register while also promoting any register that receives a table store. Classify each virtual slot body by its opening instructions, merge field accesses across each class's own methods, and estimate sizes from the highest offset touched, cross-checked against allocation-size constants.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>A relocation bug initially found one table reference instead of 466: the page base was added to a value that already included it. Checking the library's actual semantics fixed it.</li>
      <li>A capstone bug made every constant-returning function appear to return 19: reading the immediate field of a register operand yields the register id. Spot-checking raw bytes caught it, and the corrected values (type ids, sizes, descriptor pointers) proved far more useful.</li>
      <li>Optimised code often passes the object in registers other than the usual thiscall register, which first hid a third of the constructors. Treating any register that receives a table store as the object pointer recovered them.</li>
      <li>Derived constructors inline their base construction, so base-class field sets are polluted with derived-class offsets. Suspect sizes are flagged in the data rather than silently reported.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

The shared debug stub address in the encrypted range also needed care: several natives resolve there and yield no code at all, which is a normal outcome, not a tool failure.</p>

      <h2>Native handlers SET_MULTIPLAYER_HUD_TIME to SET_RADAR_AS_INTERIOR_THIS_FRAME: what they reveal</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 140 handlers in this batch were disassembled. Nearly every one is a thin wrapper that unpacks script arguments and calls a single engine function, which made it possible to propose names for 193 engine functions and 125 object fields and globals, most at high confidence.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Work through a batch of 140 script natives, disassemble each handler, recover the engine functions each one calls and the object fields each one touches, and propose names for them based on the natives' publicly documented meanings.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The script call context layout is now pinned down: the first slot points at the return-value slot and the third slot points at the argument array. The middle slot is never read by any handler seen so far and stays unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three shared lookups do most of the work: a pool lookup turning script handles into object, ped and vehicle pointers, a player-index lookup, and a network-id lookup. The pool lookup's algorithm was confirmed from a handler that inlines the whole thing.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Objects and peds share base-class fields at identical offsets, including the alpha value and the invincibility flag. Ped behaviour flags sit in four flag words, and this batch pinned down the exact bit for about twenty of them, from evasive dives to weapon animation blending.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Several natives use inverted logic: motion blur, the four ped pathing options and player targetting all store the opposite of the script argument. The object-proofs native writes its five arguments to bits in shuffled order and always clears one extra bit.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three natives cannot be analysed statically: one handler and two engine targets sit in the encrypted part of the executable. The natural-motion message table has live names only on even slots, which script authors must already know.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> One object native scales its spin by the last frame time, and two natives stamp events with a millisecond game clock, so those behaviours depend on frame timing.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Proposed names use plain engine vocabulary (pool lookup, player info, damage flags) with a confidence grade each, so later lanes can adopt, adjust or reject them. The encrypted callees keep low-confidence shape-based names until runtime analysis can see them. The next lane in this series should check the odd message-table slots against actual script calls.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone straight from the executable, follow its single call one level deeper, and record pool lookups, flag bit operations and global stores. Cross-check argument counts against the public native database and usage examples against the public decompiled mission scripts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The console output redirect wrote UTF-16 on one run and a careless conversion step then truncated the file, so that analysis step had to be re-run. A histogram script initially misread argument slots because capstone prints small offsets without a hex prefix; the affected numbers were re-derived rather than trusted.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="natives-14">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Native handlers PRINT_WITH_5_NUMBERS_NOW to RETUNE_RADIO_DOWN: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 script natives in this batch were traced from handler to engine code. The call context layout is now settled, every handler shape is catalogued, the shared pool lookup and the script-handle manager with its per-kind type ids fell out of the data, and nine natives turned out to take arguments the public database does not list. Five natives share one handler that sits in the encrypted range and could not be analysed.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the handler of each native in the batch, work out the call context layout, describe what each handler does at engine level, propose names for the engine functions it calls and meanings for the object fields it touches, and aggregate everything into shared tables.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every handler receives a single pointer to a call context. Offset 8 holds the argument array, offset 0 points at the return slot. Booleans arrive as integers and are narrowed inside the handler, floats travel through vector registers, and three-dimensional positions are assembled on the stack and passed by pointer.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of the unique handlers, 108 simply forward their arguments to one engine function, 27 are bare tail jumps, and one shared handler is encrypted. Nine natives return a value. No decrypted handler is an empty stub.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All ped, vehicle and object lookups funnel through one shared pool routine called with the pool object and the script handle. Ped, vehicle and object pools each have their own global. A script-handle manager tracks what each script owns, with a distinct type number per kind of thing: peds, groups, fires, blips, textures, models, animations and more.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Some natives take their handle by reference and clear the script variable, confirmed both in the handler code and at every call site in the shipped mission scripts. Two removals that sound alike differ exactly in this: one takes the handle, the other takes a pointer to it.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The statistics system stores float stats and integer stats in two arrays selected by id range, with a few special ids computed on the fly. Mission-passed registration adds one stat into another, zeroes the first, and stamps the game time.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nine natives read input arguments the public native database does not list, including one that reads seventeen. None of the nine is called by the shipped scripts, which explains why the database never got corrected. The handler code is authoritative.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Two natives that register race bests share one handler and therefore do exactly the same thing. One multiplayer registration native ignores its first argument. The weapon pickup regen-time reset takes a pickup handle while its three siblings take nothing. The client and host broadcast registrations disagree by four bytes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Five natives share a handler inside the encrypted first megabyte, so nothing can be said about them yet. The same encrypted address is also called as an engine function from the multiplayer kill path, so it is not simply dead code.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Handler disassembly is authoritative for argument counts; the public database loses where they disagree.</li>
      <li>The pool routine, pool globals, player info accessor and handle-manager type ids should be cross-checked against the other native batches, which will have found the same functions.</li>
      <li>The five encrypted-handler natives go back in the queue for re-analysis after decryption.</li>
      <li>One shared lookup used by both a weapon-stat reset and a pickup regen-time reset needs a confirming sighting from another batch before its name is trusted.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone in 32-bit mode, following branches until each path returns. The first two loads give the context layout: the stack argument is the context, context plus 8 is the argument array. Record every slot read, every direct call and jump, and any store through context plus 0. Then disassemble each call target the same way and match its shape against the native's documented behaviour and its call sites in the public decompiled mission scripts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The shared handler at the low address initially disassembled to plausible-looking garbage, including privileged instructions, before it was recognised as encrypted bytes. The first version of the observer script also counted the argument-array load itself as a phantom third argument on every one-argument handler; restricting the scan to the handler's own bytes fixed it. The public database counts return slots inconsistently, so mismatch detection had to allow both conventions and only flag genuine disagreements.</p>

      <h2>Native handlers IS_PED_IN_GROUP to LOCATE_OBJECT_2D: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 handlers in this batch were disassembled, and all but one yielded their engine meaning: each handler is a thin wrapper that unpacks script arguments, resolves handles through object pools, and calls one engine function. The work produced proposed names for over two hundred engine functions and fifty structure fields, plus a map of task ids, player states, and model type codes.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Analyse the batch of script natives from IS_PED_IN_GROUP to LOCATE_OBJECT_2D: disassemble each handler, compare it against the public native databases and decompiled mission scripts, describe what it does at engine level, and propose names for the engine functions it calls and meanings for the object fields it touches.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Handlers take a single call-context pointer holding a return slot pointer and an argument array pointer; bool arguments are normalised in the handler and outputs are written through direct pointers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One shared pool routine turns script handles into object pointers for the ped, vehicle, object, and room pools; it lives in the encrypted range, so its role was characterised from about fifty call sites rather than its body.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Ped task chains were decoded: each node carries a task id, flags, and a next link. Observed ids include aiming, car-bomb placement, climbing, jacking, arrest, and a retreat check that requires two ids at once.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Player state is a small enum (ready, playing, dead); model types distinguish peds from vehicles with per-class subtype codes; entity type bits distinguish vehicles, peds, and objects; the screen fade controller uses two channels with a four-state enum.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seven natives are stubs. One player query always returns false despite doing a lookup; four online and platform queries share one handler that calls a shared stub; the recording and replay-system queries call similar stubs. Public databases already document most of these as always false.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Several public database entries disagree with the code: one vehicle-network query takes two arguments where none are listed, one path-loading call takes a rectangle rather than a point plus radius, and one text-streaming check passes two arguments rather than three.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Proposed engine names and field meanings were recorded with confidence levels in the lane data files for the coordinator to merge. The shared-stub constant claims and one suspicious near-null read in the wanted-level path should be rechecked once decrypted bytes are available. Later lanes can reuse the pool, task, player-state, and model-type findings directly, since the same few routines serve every native.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each listed handler from the game executable with capstone, never touching the encrypted first megabyte; read each direct callee the same way; cross-check argument shapes against the public native database and call sites in the decompiled mission scripts; aggregate shared callees and repeated field accesses into the proposed-name tables.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>An early script followed a tail jump into the encrypted range and printed garbage disassembly; a guard was added and all dumps were regenerated, so no encrypted bytes were analysed. The file search tool silently skipped the mission-script cache because the path is git-ignored, which cost one round trip before switching to a direct search. Two bike-class checks read different offsets four bytes apart, and one stuck-vehicle flag looks dead; both are recorded as observed rather than resolved.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Class layouts: game-level network classes (CNet*, CNetwork*, net object and sync classes)</h2>
      <p>Nearly all of the game-level network code sits in the encrypted first megabyte of the program, so only three of the 103 classes yielded object layouts, but those three include a fully recovered interpolator layout, a verified destructor pattern for five replicated tasks, and the array manager start-up sequence.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of 103 game-level network classes: replicated-entity wrappers, replicated tasks, interpolators, the array and event managers, sync-data classes and wire-message descriptors. For each class: which virtual slots it overrides, its constructor and destructor behaviour, its size, its fields, and what it relates to.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of 1,787 virtual slots across the family, 98.8 percent point into the encrypted range and cannot be analysed statically. A whole-program scan for references to the family tables found only 16 in readable code, covering 9 classes. The family shares a small set of default slot implementations, which explains why unrelated tables look similar.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One interpolator class was recovered almost completely: an entity pointer, three heading floats, three blend handles and a flag byte, with a base-class dirty flag shared by its siblings. Its constructor, update, re-seed and state-push functions were all read.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five replicated animation tasks share a textbook destructor (store table, call base destructor, conditional delete) and a task-id getter that reuses the matching offline task implementation, so clone tasks keep offline numeric ids. Task-info factory functions build these tasks by allocate, base-construct and re-target steps, and a large dispatch factory builds them by type id.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The array manager constructs itself on a global instance and sets up 31 message buffers; its city-specific subclass retargets that instance and sweeps a 960-entry global array of replicated data. All 28 message descriptors share a single inherited slot implementation, and one descriptor init revealed its message size.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two hierarchy surprises: the helicopter and plane network classes derive from the automobile class rather than directly from the vehicle class, and the physical-entity network root is a non-polymorphic data class whose children add the virtual table pointer.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Slot zero is the deleting destructor across the family by compiler convention, and slot four of clone tasks is the task-type id, but most slot meanings in the entity, event and sync-data trees stay unknown until the encrypted range can be read.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite in this order: the recovered interpolator plus its base, then the animation clone tasks, then the array managers, then the descriptors, and everything else only after the encrypted range is decrypted through dynamic analysis of the start-up decrypt routine. No public-header cross-check was possible because the public sources contain none of these classes.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Scan the readable code for each class table address as a four-byte value, keep only hits that carry a relocation entry, map each hit to its containing function from the function inventory, and disassemble those functions plus the readable virtual slots with flow-sensitive tracking of which registers still hold the object pointer. The lane data file records one layout record per class with per-slot status, constructors, fields and confidences.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>An early register-tracking pass wrongly attributed entity accesses to the object, including one implausibly large offset, and an early heuristic mislabelled a boolean predicate as a destructor; both were corrected by re-checking every description against full disassembly. The relocation check initially reproduced the known double-add trap before all 16 hits verified. One inventory function turned out to be two real functions merged together.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Native handlers TAKE_CAR_OUT_OF_PARKED_CARS_BUDGET to TASK_SWIM_TO_COORD: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 handlers in this batch were disassembled and matched against the public native database and the shipped mission scripts. Nearly every handler is a thin straight-line wrapper that forwards script arguments to one small engine function, and the engine functions share a tiny set of pool-lookup and task-assignment helpers. Seven undocumented natives had their true argument counts measured, and two car-mission natives read one more argument than any mission passes.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each native handler in the batch, recover the call-context layout, compare handler behaviour with the publicly documented parameters, propose names for the engine functions each handler calls, record object fields touched, and aggregate shared helpers across the batch.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context is a pointer to three slots: a return-slot pointer, an unread slot, and an argument-array pointer holding 32-bit argument slots. No handler checks the argument count.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Handler shapes: 135 thin wrappers calling one engine function each, 3 handlers that pass through a shared argument-unpacking adapter, 1 handler that only clears the script route-point counter, and 1 debug native routed to the shared encrypted stub.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 128 of 140 handlers take exactly the documented number of arguments. Seven natives with no documented parameters were measured: most take one to three integer arguments, one takes eight arguments including two flags, one takes a position vector, and one fifteen-argument variant goes through the adapter.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two ped-target car-mission natives read a ninth script argument as a flag, but missions pass eight. The engine supports a parameter the public docs omit and no shipped mission uses.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Only four natives return values: one float math function and three shimmy movement queries returning true or false. All other natives in the batch return nothing.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The engine functions converge on three shared helpers: a handle-to-pointer pool lookup selected by a pool register, a task-setup allocator, and a task-assignment routine taking handle, task and slot. The pool helpers sit in the encrypted code range so their names rest on call-position evidence.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One vehicle flag byte toggled by the parked-cars-budget native, and the script route-point counter incremented by route extension and cleared by route flush, were pinned down. The tangent native takes degrees: its engine code multiplies by the exact pi-over-180 constant.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Fourteen natives are never called by any shipped mission, including all of the newly measured undocumented ones and a fully wired spaceship movement native.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Proposed names were recorded for every engine function in the batch: per-native engine glue named after its native at high confidence, shared helpers named by role at medium confidence, and a few frequently called unknowns left unnamed with call counts. The next lane should confirm the pool-helper names against decrypted code or runtime observation, and check every ped-target car-mission call site for a nine-argument caller.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with a direct x86 decoder, following jumps until return; extract direct call targets and argument-slot accesses; join native names against the cached public native database for documented parameters; count handler argument slots against documented inputs; scan each engine callee for its own call targets and tally the shared ones; search the decompiled mission scripts for each native name with word-boundary matching and depth-counted argument lists.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>An early argument-count pass double-counted one slot because the instruction that loads the argument-array pointer itself looks like an argument read; every handler appeared to take three arguments. Re-running the count with that instruction excluded made all documented natives match exactly, which is what exposed the two genuine nine-argument readers. The two most-called helpers initially decoded as garbage until recognised as residents of the encrypted code range, so they were characterised by position and frequency instead of disassembly.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Native handlers ABORT_ALL_GARAGE_ACTIVITY to ATTACH_PARACHUTE_MODEL_TO_PLAYER: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 natives in the first batch now have analysed handlers, and the analysis pinned down how script natives talk to the engine: a single call-context object, two return conventions, five shared argument unpackers, and one universal handle-to-pointer lookup used through three per-type pools. The lookup itself sits in the encrypted part of the executable, so its algorithm stays unknown for now.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the handler of each native in the batch, recover the call-context layout, describe what each handler does at engine level, propose names for the engine functions it calls and meanings for any fields it touches, and aggregate the evidence across the batch.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context holds a return-slot pointer and an argument-array pointer; one handler also reads and bumps a likely argument count. Most handlers unpack script arguments and call one engine function; a few pass the context to shared unpackers that build vector temporaries; zero-argument natives jump straight to their engine function.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Results come back two ways: through the context return slot, or through an extra pointer argument the engine writes through. The public signature database does not record outputs reliably, so handler evidence had to decide each case.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Thirty-five engine functions resolve script handles through a single shared lookup with per-type pools for characters, vehicles and objects, plus one interior lookup. Field reads pin a matrix pointer and a sub-object pointer on the common entity base, and an armour value with its clamp source on characters.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seven natives have no documented signature at all; handler reads supply their argument counts. Two natives share an encrypted stub handler and were skipped. All widget natives funnel into encrypted code whose behaviour is unknown.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Proposed names were recorded for every reached engine function with confidence levels, strongest where several natives corroborate one callee. The pool lookup signature and the three pool identities should be cross-checked against the other native batches and then promoted to shared definitions. The encrypted lookup algorithm and widget worker wait on decrypted bytes.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler from the executable with capstone until it returns, track which context offsets and argument slots it reads, and read one level into each engine callee to find pool lookups and field accesses. Compare arities against the public native database and spot-check call sites in the public decompiled mission scripts.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>An early scan ran past the end of small functions and wrongly attributed a neighbouring function's pool call to three natives; fixing the stop condition removed the false attributions. An early register tracker also misclassified one context load as an argument read and had to be reordered. Both bugs are fixed in the final data. The argument-count offset rests on a single handler and should be treated as a hint, not a fact.</p>
      </article>

      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Group</th><th role="columnheader">Classes</th><th role="columnheader">Interface</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Render callbacks</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">47</td><td role="cell" data-label="Interface">Six slots: deleting destructor, invoke, argument-size constant, two shared stubs, arity tag constant</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">Viewports</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">9</td><td role="cell" data-label="Interface">Thirteen to fifteen slots; only the first three hold real code, the rest are shared stubs</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Lighting and shader</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">13</td><td role="cell" data-label="Interface">Seven-slot shader classes each paired with a two-slot variable-cache companion</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">Collision</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">9</td><td role="cell" data-label="Interface">Two-slot detector interface with a shared embedded solver object</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Events, tasks, attributes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">11</td><td role="cell" data-label="Interface">Mostly encrypted; the four event classes are fully opaque for now</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Strays</td><td role="cell" data-label="Classes">48</td><td role="cell" data-label="Interface">System interfaces, math types, streaming, drawables, loggers and singletons</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The callback tag slot returns one constant per arity: no-argument, then one through six arguments each step the value by exactly one, and the global-variable setters share their own tag. The size slot likewise returns the argument block size. This is the family's dispatch key.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Field recovery found about 1,360 field accesses, of which roughly 190 are high confidence (seen in three or more methods) and 260 medium. Sizes are lower bounds from the highest field seen; several agree with allocation sites, including one stream reader of about 128 kilobytes with a large embedded buffer and one fog controller matching its allocation size exactly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Eighteen classes yielded no fields at all: the four event classes, the Direct3D wrapper, system interfaces, plain math types and small stubs whose code is encrypted or trivial.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Rewrite order: system interfaces and plain types first, then base classes before their derivatives (variable caches, shader classes, the viewport tree, the stream reader), then the callback family once its external base is done. Event classes and the Direct3D wrapper wait for decryption.</li>
      <li>Sizes derived from a single far-offset access should not be trusted; two such sizes in this batch are flagged unreliable in the data.</li>
      <li>Constructor candidacy should require relocation-table confirmation, after one template matched thirty false candidates through byte collisions.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Load the batch list, the RTTI vtable recovery and the unified function inventory; search unencrypted code for each table address as an immediate and map hits to enclosing functions; disassemble constructors, destructors and overriding virtuals with capstone while following register copies of the object pointer; compare each slot target with the same slot of each direct base. Per-class records live in the lane data file with slot verdicts, constructors, fields, sizes and relationships.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first field pass missed most constructor stores because compiled constructors copy the object pointer into another register before use; adding that tracking more than doubled the field count. The same tracking first produced nonsense sizes by following stale registers, fixed by dropping the tracking on address arithmetic and ignoring negative offsets. An allocation-size heuristic based on nearby pushes proved noisy and only corroborates sizes rather than establishing them.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="structures-cameras">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Class layouts: camera classes (CCam*)</h2>
      <p>All 156 camera classes fall into two flat families with no deeper inheritance: 43 gameplay camera classes sharing an eleven-slot virtual interface, and 113 script-instruction classes sharing a three-slot interface where every subclass implements its own execute step. Object sizes were recovered exactly for the instruction family from factory code, while gameplay camera sizes remain estimates.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Recover the object layouts and virtual interfaces of the camera class family: per-slot override tables, constructors and destructors, object sizes, field lists with confidence levels, and relationships between classes, working only on unencrypted code.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The family splits into two single-inheritance groups. The gameplay camera group has a common root with 42 direct children and eleven virtual slots each. The script instruction group has its own root with 112 direct children and three virtual slots each. No public headers exist for any of these classes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The shared destructor pattern was read directly: slot zero is a deleting destructor that destroys the object, tests a flag, and frees the memory, using a custom allocator for gameplay cameras and the standard delete for script instructions.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every script instruction class is built by a small factory that allocates an exact size, zeroes a flag byte, copies its parameters, and installs the virtual table. All 112 subclass sizes were recovered exactly, ranging from 8 to 48 bytes, most commonly 12 or 16. One instruction's execute step was read in full: it resolves a camera id through a lookup and stores its value into the camera.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The camera root builds two embedded helper objects and initialises a flag block near the end of its own storage, putting its minimum size at 320 bytes. Fourteen thin subclasses add no fields at all.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Most un-overridden slots point at one shared stub in the encrypted region, best explained as identical tiny return bodies folded together by the linker. One slot per gameplay camera is overridden with code that sits entirely inside the encrypted range, so those overrides cannot be recovered yet.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> About seventy percent of gameplay camera slot targets and one third of instruction slot targets point into the encrypted region, but nearly all of those are shared stubs rather than per-class code.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite in this order: the instruction base and its execute protocol first, then instruction subclasses grouped by which camera setting they write, then the camera root with its two embedded objects, then the fourteen trivial leaf cameras, with the large gameplay, follow, replay and transition cameras last. The encrypted slot overrides should stay pure-virtual stubs until decrypted code is available.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Search clear code for each virtual table address using the relocation table to find constructors, destructors and factories; compare each child table slot by slot against its base; scan the owning functions for object-pointer field accesses with register-alias tracking; read factory allocation constants for exact sizes. All per-class records are stored as structured data for later tooling.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>A first field scan produced absurd thousand-byte offsets because registers were never removed from tracking after reuse; adding invalidation on overwrite and on calls fixed it. A debug script once printed ciphertext decoded as nonsense instructions; it was recognised at once and none of it was kept. The function inventory is missing the camera root destructor and the allocator delete function, and the call graph yielded almost no constructor callers, so gameplay camera sizes stay low-confidence estimates from the highest touched field.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="natives-17">

      <h2>Native handlers SET_DECISION_MAKER_ATTRIBUTE_TARGET_INJURED_REACTION to SET_MULTIPLAYER_HUD_CASH: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 140 script native handlers in this batch are readable, unshared, and almost all are thin wrappers: each converts its script arguments and calls exactly one engine function. The work recovered the exact native call context layout, true argument counts for four natives the public database lists as taking no parameters, and two further documentation errors, and it identified the shared engine helpers behind whole native families.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the handler of each of 140 named script natives, from SET_DECISION_MAKER_ATTRIBUTE_TARGET_INJURED_REACTION to SET_MULTIPLAYER_HUD_CASH, and for each one describe what it does at engine level: which objects it looks up, which functions it calls, which fields it reads or writes. Work out the call context layout handlers receive, propose names for the engine functions they call with confidence levels, record directly touched fields, and flag stubs, shared handlers, and handlers in the encrypted range. Aggregate shared helpers and surprises across the batch.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The call context layout, from 135 batch handlers plus probes of value-returning handlers outside the batch: the context's first slot holds a pointer to the return-value slot, and its third slot holds a pointer to the argument array of 32-bit words. The middle slot is never read by any of the 146 handlers examined, so its meaning stays unknown. Handlers convert script words to C++ types at the call boundary in directly readable ways: booleans are normalised with a compare instruction, floats travel through SSE registers, and integers, handles and pointers are pushed as words.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Handler shapes across the batch:</p>
      <ul>
      <li>136 handlers call exactly one engine function each; 4 call nothing and store globals directly (three mobile-phone setters writing position, rotation and scale triples, and a flag setter).</li>
      <li>No handler lies in the encrypted range, no handler is shared with another native, and none is a stub: even the smallest does real work.</li>
      <li>No handler resolves script handles itself. Handle-to-object resolution happens one level down, inside the engine functions.</li>
      <li>Two zero-argument hint natives allocate camera-script-instruction objects whose classes match known camera queue instruction types, and submit them through one shared dispatch routine.</li>
      <li>One priority native ignores its arguments and runs shared code that writes one of two values to a global priority word depending on a flag.</li>
      </ul>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Six public documentation corrections came out of comparing documented parameter counts against the words each handler actually reads:</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Native</th><th role="columnheader">Documented</th><th role="columnheader">Handler actually reads</th></tr></thead>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Shared engine helpers found one level below the handlers: a single encrypted helper called by 29 engine functions across vehicle, ped, object, player and group natives (always as a method on a global object with one handle argument); a decision-maker lookup, initialiser and sub-object accessor shared by all four decision-maker attribute setters; a player table getter indexing a 32-entry table; a stats setter core writing a global float array; a bounded wide-string copy used by menu and text code; and an encrypted allocator with the classic push-size, call, null-check shape.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The encrypted helper with 29 callers is most plausibly the shared script-handle resolver, but its body is unreadable so no name is proposed for it; its fan-in and call pattern are recorded for the unpack lane instead.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Usage in the public decompiled mission scripts: 87 of the 140 natives are called at least once, 53 never. The most used are the float stat setter, the extra car colours setter, and the game camera heading setter. Unused natives cluster in multiplayer, episode-specific extras, and camera debug setters, consistent with the reference scripts coming from an older build.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Each unique engine function behind a native gets a schematic proposal naming the native it implements, at medium confidence; shared functions get behaviour-derived names with confidence from fan-in and body evidence.</li>
      <li>A documented parameter count of zero in the public database should be treated as unknown, not as zero arguments: four natives in this batch prove it.</li>
      <li>Later lanes should merge evidence for the three encrypted helpers (the shared resolver, the allocator, and the priority-path helper) across all native batches rather than proposing names alone.</li>
      <li>The wide-string copy helper is a utility, not game logic, and a candidate for exclusion from game-code counts.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each listed handler from the executable with capstone using recursive descent that follows internal jumps, stopping at returns; record direct call targets, argument-array index uses by type (compare for boolean, SSE move for float, push for word), and absolute global references. Resolve one level of callees the same way, join documented parameters from the public native database and call counts from the decompiled script reference set, and compare the highest argument index each handler reads against the documented count. The machine-readable per-native records, proposed function names, and proposed fields ship with the lane's data files.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The task brief expected handle lookups at handler level, but handlers turned out to be pure forwarders and the interesting sharing sits one level down, half of it in the encrypted range. The deliverables follow what is actually there.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A first version of the argument-count checker skipped every use of one displacement to avoid the context-pointer load itself, which also skipped a real argument slot and fabricated 22 mismatches. After excluding only the identified load instructions the genuine mismatch count is the six reported above.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The middle context slot stayed unknown after 146 handlers, and no frame-time dependence was seen in any batch handler. Both may live deeper than the one level of callees examined here.</p>

      <h2>Native handlers DISPLAY_GRIME_THIS_FRAME to FINISH_STREAMING_REQUEST_LIST: what they reveal</h2>
      <p>All 136 readable handlers in this batch of 140 script natives follow one pattern: each marshals its script arguments and calls exactly one engine function, and the shared helpers they converge on expose the handle-to-pointer pool lookup, the player table, and the layouts of the fire, text-slot and sprite draw-list tables.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Disassemble the handlers of 140 script natives, from DISPLAY_GRIME_THIS_FRAME to FINISH_STREAMING_REQUEST_LIST, using only the executable on disk. For each one, recover the argument and return-value handling, describe what it does at engine level, propose names for the functions it calls, record any object fields it touches, and aggregate the shared lookups and tables across the batch.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every handler receives a single call-context pointer holding a return-slot pointer, an argument count, and an argument-array pointer. Integer and handle arguments are passed through directly, boolean arguments are normalised to zero or one, and floating-point arguments travel through vector registers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of the 140 natives, 136 handlers were fully disassembled: most forward to one engine function each, nine jump straight to tiny bodies that only set or clear global flags, and four handlers sit in the encrypted part of the executable and were skipped. No two natives in this batch share a readable handler.</p>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Concrete object fields recovered include the vehicle hydraulics flag, the vehicle explode operations in the virtual table, the train direction value, the ped helmet flag, the object physics pointer and model index, and an entity flags word shared by the attractor and GPS natives.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>

      <li>Three low-level callees were identified as static C runtime functions rather than game code, so no game names were proposed for them.</li>

      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Disassemble each handler address from the batch list with capstone directly from the executable, stopping at the first return, tail jump or padding; follow single-jump trampolines; record direct call targets, argument-slot reads, return-slot writes and global accesses; then disassemble each called engine function the same way and join the results with the public native database entries and the public decompiled mission scripts. Analysis scripts and machine-readable results live with the lane report.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Linear disassembly initially ran past tail jumps into neighbouring functions and mis-attributed their calls; bounding each decode at the first return, tail jump or padding fixed it. An early version of the argument tracker counted a phantom argument in every handler because the argument-array load read itself; skipping that load fixed the counts. The encrypted pool-lookup body was briefly decoded before its address range was recognised; those bytes were discarded and only the call pattern is reported.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="rust-workspace"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Rust workspace scaffold: eighteen crates, CI, and a layout convention</h2><p>The project now has a buildable Rust workspace ready for review: eighteen empty but compiling crates, one crate per engine subsystem, shared compile-time layout checks, and a three-runner CI workflow. Everything builds and tests pass on all three Windows targets with zero third-party dependencies.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Scaffold the Cargo workspace and continuous integration so the coordinator can copy it into the repository: a core crate for shared types, one crate per engine subsystem, a format-reader area, a trait-only platform layer, the 32-bit replacement DLL crate, a place for the checker, pinned toolchain, shared lints, licence policy, and cheap CI on public runners. The key design question was how to separate code that mirrors the original 32-bit memory layout from code that is free to be idiomatic.</p><h3>What was found</h3><ul><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The full workspace builds cleanly for all three Windows targets with formatting and clippy checks passing and warnings denied.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Tests pass on every target: three unit tests plus two documentation tests, including 32-bit and 64-bit Intel binaries running under emulation on the ARM64 host.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The layout assertion macros work in both directions: correct layouts compile, and a deliberately wrong size fails the build with an error naming the type.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Windows binaries link the C runtime statically and need no redistributable install, confirming the earlier toolchain finding.</li><li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The 32-bit DLL exports its version symbol and the workspace unsafe rule behaves as designed: the export needs an explicit justification comment to compile.</li><li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Cold builds take a few seconds now; build times will grow with real code and the first dependencies.</li><li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The CI workflow has never run anywhere yet. Its first run on all three runners still has to be watched before it is trusted.</li></ul><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><p>Each subsystem crate gets a layout module for fixed 32-bit memory types, kept apart from portable code by three rules: C representation, 32-bit pointer wrappers instead of real pointers, and compile-time size and offset checks on every type. Conversion to 64-bit portable types happens at that module boundary in a later phase. Recommended next steps are to review and land the scaffold, confirm the placeholder licence, decide where the layout convention document should live, and watch the first CI run.</p><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>From the lane scratch folder, a generator script produces the whole scaffold so it can be rebuilt from scratch. Verification is the standard sequence: format check, clippy with warnings denied, then build and test the workspace for each of the three Windows targets. A small check script confirms the DLL export and the static runtime imports, and a temporary crate with a wrong size proves the assertions bite. No game files are involved at any step.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><p>Two things bit during verification. First, Cargo reads its configuration from the current directory, not from the manifest path argument, so early builds silently missed the static runtime flags until the commands ran from inside the workspace. Second, the current Rust edition treats the no-mangle marker as unsafe, so the DLL export tripped the new unsafe rule; the fix is now the documented example of that rule. A clippy float-comparison warning in a test also suggests maths code will need epsilon comparisons throughout.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-shaders">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: the shader container (FXC)</h2>
      <p>The game ships its compiled shaders in a small container format that is now fully mapped: every one of the 612 files parses end to end with nothing left unexplained, and a new dependency-free Rust crate reads them all.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the compiled shader container: its header, the vertex and pixel programs with their Direct3D 9 bytecode, the technique and pass tables, the parameter tables with names, types, registers, defaults and annotations, and the vertex declaration sidecars. Parse every shader file, count programs and shader model versions, list parameters and techniques, and check the bytecode by walking each program to its end marker.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All 612 shader files (102 shaders in 6 graphics-card variant folders) parse with zero errors and zero leftover bytes, using two independent implementations.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The files hold just over ten thousand shader programs, split roughly evenly between vertex and pixel programs, and every one targets the same shader model generation with no older programs anywhere.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Past the programs sit two parameter groups (engine-wide shared values, then per-material values) with typed entries, tool annotations such as interface ranges, and default values; then a technique table naming up to two dozen rendering setups per file, each pass pairing one vertex and one pixel program with render states.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two details needed care: the pixel count is stored as one more than the programs that follow, and techniques number pixel programs starting from one, not zero. Both rules are confirmed by the fact that every pass in every file lands in range only with this reading.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Sidecars check out: each shader has a matching vertex declaration file, and all material preset files parse. Surprisingly, none of the preset names match any container parameter name, so presets must resolve through a different engine path.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Parameter type codes map to integers, scalars, short vectors, textures with sampler settings, switches, and matrices; render-state numbers are engine-specific codes rather than raw Direct3D values. Both are exposed as raw numbers with full censuses so no later tool depends on the guess.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> A few mechanics remain unexplained: the count-plus-one pixel header, a permanently zero index byte, the exact state-code meanings, and the vertex declaration bit assignments. All need a running game to confirm, not more static reading.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The new crate, lf-shaderpack, is recommended as the project reader for this format: it parses from borrowed bytes with explicit little-endian reads, returns errors instead of panicking on malformed input, carries no dependencies and no unsafe code, and documents the format including its unknowns. Its natural next use is feeding the existing shader translation pipeline: each program yields its bytecode plus its stage, techniques give the vertex and pixel pairings, and the parameter tables give every name, register and default the translated shaders must expose.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate in the scratch folder with the normal build command, run the test suite with the game folder environment variable set, and run the summary example against any single shader file. The unit tests use only hand-built fixtures; the integration tests read the real game data read-only and pin the expected file and program counts so a data change fails loudly.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The technique table resisted the first three readings: passes turned out to carry a variable-length render-state block that initially looked like extra passes or extra techniques, and only the pixel-index numbering rule made the whole corpus line up. An earlier lane report also had the container magic slightly wrong by one letter, and its program totals double-counted interior matches from a raw scan; both are corrected in the new format specification.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Rust reader: collision bounds (WBN and bounds inside other resources)</h2>
      <p>A clean Rust reader now parses every shipped collision file, all 1079 of them, with zero failures, and confirms that all sixteen million collision vertices sit inside their stated bounding boxes.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the game's collision bounds: the bound types, their headers, vertex quantisation, polygon records, material indices, the tree node layout, and composite children with transforms, plus the minimal resource-container reading needed to reach them. Validate the geometry by checking every vertex against its bounding box.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game ships 1079 collision files in its map archives: 732 single-bound files and 347 bound dictionaries, holding 9102 bounds between them. Every file uses the same resource container and compression, and none uses the graphics segment.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Bound kind</th><th role="columnheader">Count</th><th role="columnheader">Notes</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Sphere</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">92</td><td role="cell" data-label="Notes">Radius tail matches the header radius</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Capsule</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">15</td><td role="cell" data-label="Notes">Header radius always equals cylinder radius plus half the length</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Box</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">1799</td><td role="cell" data-label="Notes">Always exactly 8 vertices and 6 quad faces</td></tr>
