      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Mesh totals: 8030 meshes, about sixteen million vertices, about fifteen and a half million polygons, of which roughly two thirds are quads. Every vertex index is in range, every face normal is unit length, every neighbour reference is valid or empty, and every vertex lies inside its bound's stated bounding box. Material indices run from zero to 117.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Four engine bound kinds with known class names have zero shipped instances, and three kind values have no confirmed meaning at all. The public wiki's large bounds-data table does not describe these files; the open-source readers' field offsets and formulas all checked out, except one mislabelled flag byte and one doubtful field name.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The BVH search tree is most likely built when the file loads, since nothing tree-shaped exists on disk. <span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The trailing header bytes, one header float, the capsule's zero vectors, two auxiliary pointers, the dictionary hash algorithm, and the purpose of the second vertex array remain uninterpreted.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The reader is written as an independent implementation in a new crate with hand-built test fixtures, a corpus test gated on an environment variable, and a one-file summary example. The container reading inside it is marked as temporary until the shared container crate lands. Bounds embedded in fragment files were left for a follow-up once that container is mapped.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the crate's unit tests for the fixtures, then run the corpus test with the game directory variable set: it lists the map archives, locates the archive key in the owner's executable at run time, parses each collision entry in memory, and prints the counts, the kind histogram, and the validation report. The example binary prints the same summary for a single extracted file.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>An early read of the survey output seemed to show boxes without mesh data; the raw dumps showed the opposite, and every box turned out to be a full eight-vertex mesh. The field the references call shrunk vertices differs from the main vertices by a large constant shift on sampled bounds rather than a small inset, so the name is probably wrong. The test compressor defaults to a different header level than the game writes, which broke the first fixtures until they were set to match.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-text-gxt">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: localisation text (GXT) and fonts</h2>
      <p>The game keeps every localised string in one binary file per language, keyed by hashed labels, and this lane shipped a clean Rust crate that reads all of them plus the font and menu description files.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write an original Rust reader for the localisation text format (table list, hashed-label key tables, string data with its encoding), implement label lookup with the label hash function, and document and parse the font metrics and plain-text front-end files such as menu, HUD and colour descriptions.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nineteen text files ship: seven base languages plus six per episode pack. Every file uses the same container version with sixteen-bit text units.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The base files hold about five hundred tables and sixty thousand strings each; the episode packs hold roughly one hundred and sixty and one hundred and forty tables with twenty-four and nineteen thousand strings.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Labels hash with the Jenkins one-at-a-time function after folding upper-case to lower-case. Nearly all menu labels resolve, and three sample labels decode to their expected words end to end.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Text units are font glyph codes, not Unicode. Western languages use a single low page, Russian adds a second page, and Japanese spans many pages.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Font files describe three or four fonts each with glyph maps, width tables and spacing; the Japanese font adds two extra width sections and signed width adjustments.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Menu, HUD layout, colour palette, radio strip and frontend layout files all parse, including two different radio file shapes and several comment and spacing quirks.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The public wiki transcription of the hash function only behaves correctly with unsigned-byte semantics; read the naive way it corrupts labels containing digits.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> How the renderer picks a font for each glyph page, and whether three unresolvable menu labels are dead references or conditional content.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The crate parses every shipped file without error and is ready for review and integration. Later work should resolve glyph pages against the font texture dictionaries with the textures lane, and the wiki hash transcription deserves a correction.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate in the lane scratch folder with the host toolchain, run the unit tests, then set the game directory variable and run the integration tests, which parse all nineteen text files and every font and front-end file and check label lookups.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The documented hash scored zero matches at first because standard CRC variants are not what this game uses, and the first correct-looking transcription scored only a third because of a signed-versus-unsigned subtlety in its case handling. Integration testing then surfaced five genuine file quirks in a row, including non-text comment bytes, negative font widths and a second radio file shape, each fixed in the parser as found.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="pilot-candidates">

      <h2>Pilot candidates: 300 emulator-ready leaf functions, and a broken emulator</h2>
      <p>The pilot set is chosen: 300 small leaf functions verified by static analysis, with the first 50 ranked for rewriting. But no dynamic test could be run, because the CPU emulator fails on this machine even for two instructions.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Pick the first functions to rewrite in Rust for the pilot: call-free leaf functions that are easy to check in a CPU emulator, ranked by caller count and recognisable purpose, grouped into families, with known algorithms identified and the top 50 recommended in order.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> From the 45 thousand functions in the independent lane list, after removing library ranges, functions with calls, switch tables and oversized entries, about ten thousand call-free pre-candidates remained. Capstone verification kept 5,510 leaves: 4,033 straight-line and 1,477 with branches but no indirect jumps, no calls, no global writes, and reads of constant data only.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A new stack-balance check dropped a further 1,208 supposed functions. Samples show they are shared epilogue fragments and switch-case tails the function list over-split, not real entries. The final verified pool is 4,302 functions.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The emulator does not work on this host. Running even two trivial instructions fails with a Windows error, and the emulator lane's own minimal test fails the same way, so its earlier passing results could not have been produced on this machine. Mapping memory and reading registers work; only execution fails.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The finished Ghidra export lists about 31 thousand functions against the lane list's 45 thousand, with 28 thousand shared entries. Over nine hundred Ghidra-only entries sit inside the encrypted first megabyte and are ciphertext decoded as code. Caller counts agree exactly on about three quarters of a two thousand function sample.</p>

      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Ship the statically verified 300 with signatures, caller counts, families and purpose guesses, and mark test vectors as missing rather than faking them. Begin rewrites with the two trivial calibration accessors, then the high-caller hash and float helpers.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the selection script with the project Python environment to rebuild the 5,510 verified candidates and the Ghidra comparison, then the finalise script for the stack-balance proof and the pilot ranking. Run the emulator lane's own minimal test to confirm emulation fails on this host. All scripts and data files live in this lane's scratch folder.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The emulator's memory-protect call cannot split the middle of a mapped region and fails with a misleading out-of-memory error; executable stubs needed their own memory mapping. A crash-reporting helper printed a fake fatal exception during mapping and then execution continued normally, which cost one debugging round trip. One constant in my own algorithm table evaluated to zero and briefly tagged hundreds of functions as a floating point match; it was filtered and is documented in the report.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="work-queue">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>The work queue that hands out functions easiest first</h2>
      <p>The rewrite phase now has its dispatcher: a small set of Python tools backed by one SQLite database that orders every game function by difficulty, claims them atomically so two lanes can never receive the same function, and records accepts, deferrals and batch statistics. It was built against the independent function estimate, cross-checked against the finished Ghidra analysis, and proven with a six-lane simulation.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Design and write the first version of the work queue and the per-function context packet as real project tooling: game functions only, easiest first, atomic claims expiring after two hours, capped attempts with a no-improvement stop, deferral with a fixed set of blocker tags, an end-of-batch sweep with a ledger, and context packets carrying disassembly, resolved references, class information and the best earlier attempt. Storage is one SQLite database in write-ahead-log mode; the repository tracks a deterministic text export instead.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The queue builds from the lane estimate: tens of thousands of game functions queued, a few thousand library functions excluded, nothing claimed yet.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The Ghidra function list finished during the lane and was compared entry by entry: the two lists agree on most of Ghidra's entries, the lane list has far more plain-code functions, and Ghidra's entries inside the encrypted region are correctly excluded by the queue's range rule. Importing Ghidra's list over existing queue state reproduced the comparison counts exactly while accepted, deferred and claimed rows survived.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Address forms differ per source file and one value can be a valid address in both forms, so the tools declare the form per source instead of guessing. Guessing had merged hundreds of distinct functions; after the fix every row imports exactly once.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Context packets resolve callees, data references and virtual-method class and slot correctly on real functions, and class-grouped claiming serves one class's methods together.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The verdict contract refuses failing verdicts and unknown blocker tags with the claim left intact; the text export is byte-identical across runs.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Prefer the lane function list for coverage and Ghidra for names, caller counts and library flags; the queue merges both without losing state.</li>
      <li>Unmeasurable zero-size entries sort last so lanes never trip over them first.</li>
      <li>Tool-generated placeholder names are never stored as function names.</li>
      <li>Next steps for later lanes: a subsystem range map, similarity from masked-byte hashes before full search integration, consuming the call graph and cross-reference exports, and a ruling on the functions only the lane list contains.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>From the queue tools folder: run the unit suite, build the queue from the estimate, claim a function for a test lane, write its context packet, accept or defer it, sweep the batch, and run the simulation. Each tool prints usage with the standard help flag, and every script documents its inputs and outputs at the top of the file.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The address-form bug above: automatic detection silently merged functions and mislabelled plain code as encrypted. It surfaced through row counts that did not add up, and the fix was verified by exact cross-checks between the comparison and the import.</li>
      <li>The Ghidra export was still being written when first read and parsed as truncated JSON; waiting and retrying resolved it.</li>
      <li>The first simulation decided slightly more functions than requested through a stop-condition race in the harness itself; the queue stayed correct, and reserved slots fixed the count.</li>
      <li>Two small implementation slips (a miscounted header unpack and a stray test fragment) were caught by the first runs and fixed.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="capture-tool">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tool that reads the encrypted code from the owner's running copy</h2>
      <p>The capture tool is built, self-tested, and ready: once the owner has the game sitting at its main menu, one command reads the decrypted code out of the running process, checks it against the file on disk, and writes the results to the private folders in about five seconds. Nothing leaves the machine, and the game itself is only ever read, never modified.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>The first megabyte of the game's code section is encrypted on disk and decrypted in memory at start-up by a wrapper library that ships with the game. The task was to write a small tool that reads that range back out of the owner's own running copy so it can be analysed like the rest, with strict limits: open the game read-only, never write to it, suspend it, inject into it, or attach a debugger, and write the outputs only under the private originals folder. A dry-run self-test against a small test program of our own had to prove the tool before it ever touches the game.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The tool works end to end. Its self-test builds a tiny 32-bit test program, launches it, captures it through the same code path the game capture will use, checks the capture byte for byte, and terminates it. The code section matched the file exactly, including across a nonzero load-address shift, which proves the relocation-undoing step does its job on a live process.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row">
      <th role="columnheader">Check</th>
      <th role="columnheader">Result</th>
      </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row">
      <th role="columnheader">Synthetic relocation round-trip</th>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Result">Pass, four load shifts including zero and overflow</td>
      </tr>
      <tr role="row">
      <th role="columnheader">Live code section vs file</th>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Result">Exact match, zero unreadable pages</td>
      </tr>
      <tr role="row">
      <th role="columnheader">Live read-only data vs file</th>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Result">Small differences, all in loader-resolved import tables, as expected</td>
      </tr>
      <tr role="row">
      <th role="columnheader">Loaded modules seen in test process</th>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Result">Twelve, main module confirmed by two independent listings</td>
      </tr>

      <th role="columnheader">Estimated full game capture time</th>
      <td role="cell" data-label="Result">About five seconds for twenty-six megabytes</td>
      </tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The encrypted range shows zero standard function-entry patterns on disk, so any such patterns in the future capture will confirm readable code. <span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The live capture is expected to take about five seconds, from timings measured on the file's own bytes and on timed memory reads. <span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Whether the running game carries any run-time patches outside the encrypted range, and which helper libraries are loaded while it idles at the menu. Both questions are answered the moment the tool runs against the real game.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>A plain script on the project's existing Python setup was chosen over a compiled tool, because the cross-bitness memory reads it needs are supported by design and the self-test proves them on this machine. No new dependencies and nothing to build.</li>
      <li>Differences outside the encrypted range are recorded as findings, never as failures: a mismatch there would mean the game or its wrapper patches code at run time, which is itself valuable to know.</li>
      <li>The reconstructed executable the tool produces is for static analysis only and must never be launched, since the start-up wrapper would try to decrypt already-decrypted code.</li>
      <li>Any future code that lists a 32-bit process's modules from a 64-bit tool must query both the toolhelp snapshot and the process-modules call with the 32-bit filter, or it will silently miss half the process. The first version of this tool did exactly that.</li>
      <li>The capture outputs never leave the private folders and are never published; the public record carries only counts and conclusions.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the tool's self-test subcommand with the project Python from the repository root: it prints each stage and ends with a pass or fail line. A second script in the same folder replays the game-scale timing benchmark without needing the game. The lane folder also holds a run-book with the owner's steps, the coordinator's single command, and how to tell the live run worked.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The module-listing gap was the real surprise: the first listing looked complete at seven modules, and only the absence of the most basic system library gave away that every 32-bit library was missing. It took a second enumeration call to see them. Less dramatically, the test program kept landing at the same shifted load address on repeated launches, so the retry loop built to catch varied shifts never saw variation; the synthetic round-trip covers that gap instead. The live game capture itself remains undone because the game was not running during this work and starting it was out of scope.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-rsc5">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: the RSC5 resource container</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The container that wraps nearly every binary game asset now has a clean Rust reader: header, size flags, decompression, the two memory segments, tagged pointers and the block-map slot. All 938 loose resource files in the game folder parse with zero failures.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write the foundation crate that asset-specific readers will build on: parse the resource header, decode the flags word into the virtual and physical segment sizes, decompress the payload, split it into segments, resolve the tagged pointers used for internal references, and read the block-map slot. Test against every loose resource file, and correct the public documentation where the files disagree with it.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every loose resource is one header plus a single compressed stream running exactly to end of file. The inflated size matches the size the flags word promises, to the byte, in all 938 files.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Five asset types occur as loose files: web pages (most numerous), texture dictionaries, two effects package variants, and two drawable dictionaries. The ids match the values public tool sources list for those assets.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Internal pointers use two tag values selecting the processor-side or data-side segment, with zero meaning null. Every pointer at a documented position in all 207 dictionaries resolves inside its segment, including every entry of every member list.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The block-map slot is never populated in shipped files: dictionaries carry a reserved-but-empty slot, effects packages leave debug fill, and web-page resources are not rooted in the paged-object type at all. The engine evidently builds the map when loading.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> An earlier report of a truncated compressed stream in one effects package did not reproduce: the file inflates normally. The earlier failure was a short read in that probe script.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> No decryption is involved at this layer: loose resources are only compressed. The archive key belongs to the archive layer, which a parallel lane is handling.</li>
      </ul>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Check</th><th role="columnheader">Result</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Loose resources found</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">938</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Parsed without error</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">938</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Unit tests (hand-built inputs)</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">11 passed</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Linter warnings left</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">none</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The crate rejects anything that does not inflate to exactly the promised size, caps inflated output well above the largest real file, and returns errors instead of panicking, so hostile input cannot crash or exhaust memory.</li>
      <li>The block-map reader reports three honest states (absent, reserved-but-empty, populated) and exposes the raw words of any populated map it ever meets, since no shipped file has one to learn the entry layout from.</li>
      <li>Next: run archived model, fragment, collision and navigation resources through the same reader once the archive lane delivers their bytes, and look there for a populated block map.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate and run its test suite; the integration test walks the game folder when the game directory environment variable is set and is skipped otherwise. A worked example prints a one-file summary (kind, sizes, block-map state, pointer counts) for manual inspection. The per-file census of all 938 resources is stored alongside the lane report as tool-readable data.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two things cost time. First, the test compressor initially wrote a different stream header variant than the game uses, so every new unit test failed until the tests were pinned to the same variant. Second, a naive scan of every four-byte value for pointer-like tags drowns in false hits from floating-point numbers, hashes and texture bytes; only pointers at documented field positions mean anything, and the dictionary walk that checks those positions is the real validation.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-rpf-img">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: RPF and IMG archives</h2>
      <p>A new Rust crate called lf-archive now opens every archive the game ships, all 49 RPF files and all 254 IMG files, with no parse failures. It lists every entry, reads entry bytes, decrypts tables with a key found at run time, and decompresses where the format allows it.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the two archive containers the game ships, RPF and IMG version 3, covering headers, tables of contents including encryption, entry records, directories, and reading entry bytes. The reader had to be original work, platform independent, return errors instead of panicking, and prove itself by opening every archive in the game folder.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game ships two RPF versions: version 3 for the 45 audio banks and version 2 for the three model archives and the single game data archive. All tables of contents are encrypted, and one small data archive also encrypts its file contents.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> IMG archives are all version 3. All but four are encrypted; the four open ones are small path and script index files. Five archives are empty headers with no entries.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Across all archives there are about three and a half thousand RPF files and fifty two thousand IMG entries. Roughly nine in ten IMG entries are engine resources in the RSC container, which uses standard zlib compression. No shipped RPF entry uses the archive-level compression flag.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> RPF version 3 stores name hashes instead of names, so file names must be resolved through an external hash table. Directory hashes in those archives do not resolve through public tables.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Three header words remain unknown: one in the RPF header that is always zero, one in RPF directory records, and one in the IMG header where a single file differs from all the rest. None affects reading.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The crate exposes one shared archive interface so later code can open either container the same way. The encryption key is located in the owner's game executable at run time by its published identifier and kept in memory only. Name resolution for hashed archives takes an external table rather than embedding one. The next step is wiring that table up and handing payload decoding to the model and texture work.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate and run its tests with the game folder pointed to by an environment variable. Unit tests use hand-built fixtures only; the integration test walks the whole game folder, parses every archive, checks every entry range, and reads back small entries. A bundled example prints a per-file summary, and a second example emits the per-archive census used for the counts above.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>An early probe applied decryption to a file that needed none and produced a nonsense entry count; the full survey was already correct and the probe was fixed. A hand-built test archive accidentally gave one record two parents, which real archives never do, and the fixture was rebuilt as a strict tree. The shell reports failures for successful build commands because build progress goes to the error stream, so every result was confirmed from the tool's own summary lines instead.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-models">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: drawables and fragments (WDR, WDD, WFT)</h2>
      <p>A new Rust crate reads the game's model files end to end, and every file in a 112-file sample now parses with all indices in range and all positions inside their stated bounds.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the drawable, drawable-dictionary and fragment formats, covering shader groups and parameters, skeletons, level-of-detail groups, models, geometries, vertex and index buffers and vertex declarations, with vertex data decoded into positions, normals, colours and texture coordinates. Validate on real files and report counts.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game ships tens of thousands of model files: drawables are the most numerous by far, followed by dictionaries and fragments. A sample of just over a hundred files, plus the two dictionaries that ship loose, was extracted with key-handling tools and parsed two ways, in Python and in Rust, with identical results.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Measure</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The most surprising finding concerns fragments: their child records carry no models at all. All render geometry lives in the main drawable, and the per-child record that one open-source reader labels as a drawable is really a small transform node with empty bounds. The new reader exposes the node without misparsing it.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Several documentation details needed correction along the way: vtable figures on the wiki mix byte orders from row to row, the so-called codec word is just the start of the compressed stream, and the primitive-type list starts counting at zero, not one.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The new crate is original code with a single permissive dependency, no unsafe blocks, and unit tests built from hand-made byte patterns plus an integration test over real files.</li>
      <li>It carries a minimal private copy of the resource-container logic until the shared container crate lands, at which point the private copy should be deleted.</li>
      <li>Fragment physics, skinning palettes, half-float vertices and texture dictionaries inside model files are parsed as far as offsets and left for later lanes.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build and test the crate from its own folder with the normal Rust commands, then run the integration test with the game folder path set so it can read the two loose dictionaries and the extracted sample. An example program prints a one-file summary of names, counts and sizes without writing anything.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first Rust draft failed on every file with an absurd collection count. The cause was passing an already-resolved item list where the collection header was expected, so padding bytes were read as a count. A second early mistake undercounted triangles by assuming the primitive list started at one; reading the actual enumeration fixed it. Both mistakes were invisible until the real-file test ran, which is why the sample comparison against the independent Python walk mattered.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="format-map-data">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Rust reader: map definition and placement files (IDE, WPL, IPL-style text)</h2>
      <p>A dependency-free Rust crate now reads every loose map definition and placement file in the game folder: all item definition files, all binary placement files and all text placement files parse with no failures, yielding typed records for well over three hundred thousand rows.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Write a clean Rust reader for the map formats from public documentation and direct inspection: plain-text item definitions with all their sections, binary placement files with all their record arrays, text placement files, and the load-list manifests that name them in load order. Verify it against every such file outside the archives and list every uncertain field.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The binary placement files store their record arrays in an order that is not numeric section order: the ignored stamp section sits between the modifier data and the level-of-detail data. Reading the sections in numeric order misaligns the rest of the file.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One documented record size is wrong: the time-cycle modifier record is smaller than stated, matching the documentation's own field table rather than its headline size. Every shipped file agrees with the smaller size.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Text placement files declare over twenty sections but only six ever hold records; instance placement moved to the binary files. Two item-definition sections are likewise always empty.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The shipped files confirm several engine text quirks: rows with missing commas, rows cut at the documented line-length limit, and two files missing their final terminator. Unused padding in several binary records holds the uninitialised-memory pattern of a debug build, dating the tool that wrote them.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Item definition files parsed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">all found</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">object, vehicle, pedestrian, weapon and interior rows typed</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Binary placement files parsed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">all found</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">instances, garages, modifiers, stamps, level-of-detail and slow zones typed</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Text placement files parsed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">all found</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">path nodes and links, occlusion, effects and stamps typed</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Parse failures</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">none</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">every record in every file matched its typed shape</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Value">External dependencies</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">none</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">only the Rust standard library; builds anywhere</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The reader tolerates the shipped quirks (missing commas, truncated lines, missing terminators, trailing padding) and keeps one bad row from hiding the rest of its file, while unknown fields stay explicitly marked rather than guessed. Two binary record kinds never appear in shipped files, so their documented layouts are implemented but flagged unverified. The next step is naming the remaining unknown columns from the per-section wiki pages and confirming the two unobserved record kinds.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the crate with the normal Rust toolchain and run its test suite: unit tests use hand-built inputs, and the integration test walks every map file in a local game install when pointed at it, reporting file counts, record counts and each distinct failure. A bundled example prints a per-file summary for manual inspection.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first survey miscounted text placement records because one section name contains a plus sign the section matcher did not allow; fixing the matcher revealed the empty-section pattern. The binary section order took three rounds of probing to pin down, because file sizes alone fit several orders and only the record contents distinguished them. A first draft of the path-node type assumed integer-only fields until the integration test showed float and large unsigned values in real files.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="reloc-reconcile">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>The relocation table is fine; three lanes read it wrong</h2>
      <p>Earlier lanes disagreed about the executable's relocation table: one called it garbage, one found twenty thousand anomalous entries scattered through the code, one counted exact import matches, and one saw no entries at all in the encrypted region. A verified from-scratch parser shows the table itself is healthy, with just under two hundred ninety-two thousand entries that all check out, and each earlier disagreement traces to a concrete reading error, all now corrected.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Settle the contradiction between four earlier lanes about the relocation table, produce the definitive relocation list and statistics, and map the whole code section page by page to find every encrypted or non-code pocket.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The relocation table parses cleanly: only the two expected entry types appear, the bytes consumed match the directory size exactly, and every fixup site is backed by file content.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The "garbage table" verdict was a scripting bug: the lane added the page address twice, scattering all sites to wrong locations. Re-running the bug reproduces its numbers digit for digit.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All twenty thousand odd-looking entries sit inside the encrypted first megabyte, and their on-disk values are ciphertext, confirmed by uniformity tests. There are no scattered high-entropy pockets; an earlier lane misread its own location histogram.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The encrypted region holds over twenty thousand fixup sites, not zero as reported; only their values are opaque, while their positions are exact and probably form the start-up stub's own fixup list.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The import-table cross-check of about two thousand entries reproduces exactly, and a handful of references from code to the file headers are genuine.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Page-by-page mapping finds no second encrypted region: two hundred fifty encrypted pages, sixteen pages of jump and pointer tables, and everything else code, including some zero-heavy initialisation code and tiny stub functions first mistaken for padding.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Both function inventories contain entries inside ciphertext that must be excluded: several hundred in the new Ghidra export (which at least labels the region) and a few thousand in the lane estimate.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The new relocation list replaces all earlier counts as the source of truth, with on-disk values inside the encrypted region marked as ciphertext. Downstream tools must drop ciphertext function entries from both inventories. The stub-fixup theory and the exact table seams inside mixed pages are left for a runtime lane and the function-inventory lane.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane scripts in order with the project Python: a boundary scan by page entropy, a manual relocation-directory walk cross-checked against the parsing library, a bug-reproduction script, uniformity tests on the odd values, and a per-page classifier combining entropy, pointer density and aligned fixup runs. Outputs are a compact relocation list and one record per code page.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two page-classification metrics failed before the third worked: plain linear disassembly misfires whenever a page starts mid-instruction, and resync disassembly then proved too permissive since nearly any bytes decode as something. Pointer density plus runs of consecutive aligned fixups turned out to be the reliable table signal. Separately, several dense initialisation pages first classified as tables or padding and were only corrected by reading their bytes.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="library-ranges">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Library code mapped to exact function lists</h2>
      <p>The third-party libraries in the executable are now mapped to exact lists of functions instead of rough address ranges: just over a thousand functions, about half a megabyte, are identified as library code that the rewrite queue can skip or replace, and the two middleware packages that must be rewritten from scratch are sized with entry points.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Turn the earlier library inventory into exact, function-level exclusion ranges by expanding from evidence anchors through the call graph, identify open-source library versions against public sources, name zlib and jpeg functions where the correspondence is clear, estimate the C runtime extent, and report for each library its size and whether an existing Rust crate can replace it.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A verified direct-call graph of the readable code holds about seventy-two thousand edges; a naive byte scan for call instructions overcounts by roughly thirty percent, so every edge used here was confirmed by disassembly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The linked zlib is the compress side only, twenty-four functions: the checksum, the window filler and the three compression levels were confirmed by reading the code, but the decompressor, the checksum-table code and the gzip helpers are absent from the readable code. Pinning down where decompression happens is left open.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The jpeg codec core is forty-nine functions reached from two entry points, with the standard error table and its six handlers confirmed; the table size and message set point to a 6b-era release. Most codec internals are reached through method tables rather than direct calls, so the full extent needs indirect-call analysis.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The TLS stack covers about three hundred functions with dozens of callers from game code; hash code is present but the symmetric cipher is not found in readable code. The collision subset of the physics library and the animation middleware were mapped from their class tables to under a hundred and about five hundred functions respectively.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Earlier estimates needed correction: the alleged jpeg code range pointed at unrelated data due to an address conversion mistake, the supposed checksum-table constants turned out to be coincidental byte patterns, and most copies of the compression version string sit in game data pools rather than in the library.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The compression library, the jpeg codec and the TLS stack can each be replaced by an existing Rust crate; the physics collision subset needs a careful port against a modern engine crate; the animation middleware has no replacement and must be rewritten from observed behaviour.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The per-function lists ship as data files for the queue builder, with confidence levels and far-flung members marked for review. The independent Ghidra analysis agrees with over ninety-three percent of the listed functions, so either source can be used where they agree. The C runtime beyond the mapped core, the jpeg indirect-call extent, and the missing decompressor are queued for the next lanes.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>All scripts live in the lane scratch folder and run against the game file with the project Python environment. The main pipeline builds the verified call graph with a disassembler library, anchors each library in exact relocation targets and class-table slots, expands through verified caller edges only, and emits the function lists and statistics as JSON. Message tables were dumped to JSON for the version comparisons.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The raw call scan produced confident-looking but false edges, including jpeg helpers apparently calling the compression checksum; only disassembling the actual functions exposed the errors, and the whole analysis was rebuilt on verified edges. The target neighbourhood turned out to mix library code with game code that parses text formats, so every range-based assumption had to be replaced with call-graph evidence. The decompressor hunt ended empty despite its strings being present, which was the biggest surprise of the lane.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="tools-shaders">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tools: shaders</h2>
      <p>All of the game's shaders can be extracted and translated to validated SPIR-V with free tools that now live in the project's tools folder. The game ships 102 shader programs in 6 graphics-card variants (612 files), all using shader model 3.0 bytecode inside a simple container. After removing duplicates there are 969 distinct shader programs. The recommended path is a small extractor, then the DXVK project's shader compiler to SPIR-V, then SPIRV-Cross to Metal shading language, with the official SPIR-V validator as the gate.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Establish the game's shader container format from file headers and public documentation, count the shaders, and find, test and where allowed install the tools the project needs: an extractor for the container, disassemblers and translators for Direct3D 9 shader bytecode, and SPIR-V tools. Recommend a pipeline from the game's shader files to SPIR-V and to Metal shading language.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The shader files sit as loose files in the game's shared shader folder, so no archive tool is needed for them. Each container starts with a four-character magic word, then a list of vertex-shader fragments, then pixel-shader fragments; every fragment carries its parameter names and a size-prefixed bytecode blob, followed by technique metadata. A purpose-written extractor parsed all 612 files with zero failures and every blob checked out as well-formed shader model 3.0 bytecode with full parameter tables.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The six card-specific folders are mostly copies of each other: two are byte-identical, two more differ from the base set in only one or two files, and the remaining two carry cheaper variants of a few dozen shaders. Deduplication leaves 969 distinct programs out of 10,134 blobs.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Tool</th><th role="columnheader">Job</th><th role="columnheader">Result on all 969 programs</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">dxbc-spirv (the DXVK shader compiler)</td><td role="cell" data-label="Job">Bytecode to SPIR-V</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result on all 969 programs">All outputs pass the official validator with no fixes needed</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">MojoShader</td><td role="cell" data-label="Job">Bytecode to GLSL, SPIR-V and Metal</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result on all 969 programs">Reads everything, but its SPIR-V needs trailing junk trimmed and 4 programs fail validation on a gradient bug</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Job">SPIRV-Cross</td><td role="cell" data-label="Job">SPIR-V to Metal and HLSL</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result on all 969 programs">Emits both languages; some shaders need a newer Metal version flag</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Job">SPIRV-Tools</td><td role="cell" data-label="Job">Validate and inspect SPIR-V</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result on all 969 programs">Used as the pass/fail gate for every translated shader</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Job">fxc from the Windows SDK</td><td role="cell" data-label="Job">Disassemble for inspection</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result on all 969 programs">Clean disassembly with parameter tables; inspection only</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Job">rage_fxc_extractor</td><td role="cell" data-label="Job">Container extraction (reference)</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result on all 969 programs">Despite targeting console files, it reads every PC file and matches the purpose-written extractor byte for byte</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row"><td role="cell" data-label="Job">glslang and naga</td><td role="cell" data-label="Job">General shader compilers</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result on all 969 programs">Both work, but neither fits this chain: one cannot read the generated GLSL dialect, the other rejects fragment shaders</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One named candidate was rejected after testing: a DirectX 11 shader decompiler errors out on these older bytecode files and its disassembler crashes on them. It only understands a newer bytecode format, so it was removed again.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The PC and console containers share one layout, since the console-oriented extractor reads every PC file including its quirks.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The technique and pass tables at the end of each container are not fully decoded yet, only their name strings. The Metal output from both translators is unvalidated because no Metal compiler exists on this machine.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Standardise on this offline pipeline: extract and deduplicate to 969 programs, translate with dxbc-spirv, require every module to pass the SPIR-V validator, then convert to Metal shading language with SPIRV-Cross.</li>
      <li>Keep MojoShader as a second source for cross-checking, with workarounds for its two known defects, and keep glslang and naga only for newly written shaders.</li>
      <li>Use the SDK disassembler for inspection. Do not adopt the DirectX 11 decompiler.</li>
      <li>Before translated shaders can run, not just validate, the renderer team must settle how shader resources and inputs are bound, because the translator's output follows DirectX 9 conventions the new renderer has to mirror.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane's extractor over the game's shader folder (read-only), which should report 612 files parsed and 969 distinct programs. Then run each translator over the extracted programs and check every output with the SPIR-V validator. The exact scripts, command lines, tool versions and licences are recorded in the lane's report and tool manifest in the project scratch area.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>An earlier survey reported a different container magic word; re-reading all 612 files showed it was misread, and its shader count had double-counted each program. Both are corrected in the lane report.</li>
      <li>The first batch test reported hundreds of MojoShader failures that turned out to be a bug in the test script's file mapping, not in the tool. After the fix all three language profiles passed everything.</li>
      <li>MojoShader's own example programs corrupt binary output on Windows by printing it as text. A 40-line helper that writes bytes to a file fixed it, and that helper is what all validation here used.</li>
      <li>Two plausible pipeline links failed for instructive reasons: generated GLSL uses too old a dialect for the Vulkan compiler, and the Rust shader compiler rejects fragment shaders from both translators. Both findings are recorded so the next lane does not retry them.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="tools-runtime-debug">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tools: running, debugging and tracing the game</h2>
      <p>All eight runtime tools are installed from their official sources and start on this machine, and scripted tracing with Frida is verified end to end against a 32-bit test program. The bad news is graphics: the display driver ships no 32-bit Vulkan support, so the translation layer that could make frame capture possible has almost no chance of working here.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools the project needs for running, debugging and tracing the game later: an interactive debugger, a scripted instrumentation toolkit, a frame capture tool, a Direct3D 9 translation layer, two system and API tracers, a plugin loader and a community patch baseline. Every download had to come from the project's own official release page, install portably without admin rights, and be tested without touching the game.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Frida attaches from emulated 64-bit Python to a 32-bit test process and runs full instrumentation: architecture detection, module listing and memory reads all returned correct results.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The 32-bit debugger GUI and the API tracer GUI both start under emulation, respond and show a main window. The frame capture tool prints its version cleanly. The system tracer was deliberately not launched because its first run loads a kernel driver; its package includes a native ARM64 build.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A small probe program showed that 32-bit processes on this machine see exactly two Vulkan devices, both provided by the system's Vulkan-on-Direct3D-12 layer at Vulkan version 1.2, and no native graphics driver device. The installed driver ships Vulkan support for ARM64 processes only.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> That finding blocks two tools. The frame capture tool does not support Direct3D 9 at all, so it can only see the game through the translation layer. Current translation layer releases need Vulkan 1.3 or 1.4, which the 32-bit path does not offer; only the legacy 1.10 line, which needs Vulkan 1.1, passes the version check, and running it stacked on emulation is untested by its authors.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The plugin loader, the community patch and both translation layer builds have the right architecture and the expected entry points. The community patch bundles its own loader, its own translation build and about two hundred megabytes of replacement assets.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Tool</th><th role="columnheader">Result</th><th role="columnheader">Limit on this machine</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Interactive debugger</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">starts, untested against the game</td><td role="cell" data-label="Limit on this machine">emulated build only, no native ARM64 version</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Scripted instrumentation</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">attach, script and memory read all pass</td><td role="cell" data-label="Limit on this machine">controller runs emulated; native ARM64 targets would need a native build</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Frame capture</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">starts, cannot see Direct3D 9</td><td role="cell" data-label="Limit on this machine">needs the translation experiment to succeed first</td></tr>

      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Standardise on the interactive debugger for interactive work, Frida for scripted traces, the native system tracer for file and registry activity, and the frame capture tool for any future Vulkan or newer Direct3D work. Run exactly one translation layer experiment with the legacy 1.10 build; if it fails, stop and evaluate the open-source Direct3D 9 call tracer as the fallback. Keep three game configurations strictly separated and label every future trace with which one it used: unmodified, unmodified plus loader, or community patch.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Fetch each tool from its official release page into the project's ignored tools folder, recording version, size and checksum, and confirm each program starts without attaching to anything. Rebuild the two probe programs with the C++ toolchain's 32-bit cross compiler: a Vulkan device enumerator that loads the system Vulkan loader at run time, and a sleeper program that serves as a safe attach target for the Frida probe script. The exact download list, checksums and per-tool command lines are kept with the lane's data files.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first Vulkan probe crashed reading the second device, which briefly looked like a broken driver install but was a bug in the probe: its properties buffer was too small and the driver overwrote the stack. The Frida API examples found on the web failed with a type error because the current major version removed several long-standing helpers; the working forms are documented in the lane report. The API tracer's test process ignored a forced stop command despite declaring no need for elevation, and had to be closed through its window instead. None of these affected the conclusions.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="emulator-harness">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Original functions can be executed for comparison, but not with Unicorn on this machine</h2>
      <p>The planned checker approach works, with a different engine than planned. The Unicorn CPU emulator crashes on every execution attempt on this machine, so the lane built a small 32-bit harness that runs original functions natively through the operating system's own compatibility layer instead. Fifty small functions were executed with hundreds of random inputs, most ran cleanly, and two trial Rust rewrites matched their originals on all 200 inputs each.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Prove or disprove that original game functions can be executed outside the game for comparison testing of Rust rewrites. The plan named the Unicorn emulator: map the executable, set registers and stack inputs, run each function until it returns, and record the return value and memory effects. The lane was also asked to cover harder cases (calls between functions, global data, system imports, floating point, object methods), measure speed, and design what agreement between original and rewrite means.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The emulator engine is unusable here. Every execution attempt crashes the whole process, including a minimal test of one trivial instruction with no hooks attached, and including non-x86 guest code. The fault is inside the emulator's own library, with a different crash code on different runs.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A 32-bit helper program built with the project's Rust toolchain runs original functions correctly. It loads the executable's bytes with standard relocation fixups (a count cross-checked against an independent tool, matching exactly), calls one function at a time with chosen inputs, and reports registers, flags, floating-point state and changed memory as structured output. Faults are caught inside the process and reported with the failing location instead of crashing.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first of the code section's megabytes is encrypted or compressed on disk (entropy near the theoretical maximum, undecodable as instructions), while the remaining nine megabytes are normal code. Functions in the encrypted part cannot be executed from file bytes at all.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of 50 sampled small leaf functions run 8 times each, naive random inputs completed only about one run in eight, while shaped inputs (pointers aimed at scratch memory) completed over half, and a follow-up with better stack inputs brought 43 of 50 to fully passing. All failures were memory access faults, never illegal instructions. Repeated runs were bit-identical.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Harder cases behave as needed: a real nested call between two game functions executed end to end; a global data read returned the correct startup value; an unresolved system import faulted deterministically at exactly the expected address, which is what makes it interceptable; legacy and modern floating-point instructions both work and their outputs are captured.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two hand-written Rust twins of original functions agreed with the originals on all 200 random inputs each, including calling-convention stack accounting on a stdcall function.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Small leaf functions found</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">About 1800 in the readable code</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Plenty of easy first targets for the checker</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Leaf trials passing with shaped inputs</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">43 of 50 functions fully passing</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Input shaping matters more than engine choice</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Relocation entries applied</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">About 292 thousand, matching an independent count</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">The harness loads the program the way the OS loader would</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Single call cost</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Roughly a tenth of a millisecond</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Execution is cheap; process setup dominates and should be batched</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">End-to-end trial cost today</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">A few hundred milliseconds</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">A persistent worker running many trials per process is needed for speed</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Twin agreement</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">200 of 200 on both trial rewrites</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">The full compare loop works in principle</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The checker should use native 32-bit execution, not Unicorn, on this machine: one worker process owns the relocated original plus the linked rewrite, calls either side through the same trampoline, and compares return values, stack accounting, written memory, outgoing calls with arguments, and floating-point state. Bitwise floating-point equality should be the default, with per-function tolerance only where declared. Functions in the encrypted region and functions needing live operating-system state are out of scope for the checker and should be tracked as blocked rather than failed.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Build the scratch helper and twin crates for the 32-bit Windows target with the installed Rust toolchain (offline build, no extra dependencies), then run the driver scripts in the lane's scratch folder: one maps the executable and samples leaf functions with a disassembler, one runs each leaf with random and shaped inputs and records structured results, and one compares the two Rust twins against their originals over 200 seeded inputs. The design document in the same folder describes the contract, the input generation policy, and the per-case handling.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first leaf scan produced nonsense instructions because it started inside the encrypted region; an entropy map showed the boundary clearly and the scan was restricted to readable code. The emulator failure looked at first like a harness bug and was only settled by a minimal one-instruction test with no hooks. The native harness then crashed in its own trampoline for several rounds: the fault addresses first suggested an emulation quirk, but disassembling the generated bytes plus an in-process fault handler proved it was an ordinary stack bookkeeping bug (the host stack pointer saved on the wrong side of two push instructions). Low memory also turned out to be unmappable in 32-bit processes on this host, which forced relocation support earlier than planned. Each of these cost time but left a checkable artifact in the scratch folder.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="swarm-speed">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>How fast an agent swarm went through phase 0, and what that does and does not say about the rest</h2>
      <p>In the first 33 minutes of phase 0, 37 agent lanes finished 545 lane-minutes of analysis and wrote about 104,000 words of findings: roughly sixteen times faster than one agent working through the same tasks in sequence. That speed is real, but it was measured on the kind of work that parallelises best. The rewrite itself has not been timed yet.</p>

      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>The owner noticed the project was moving faster than expected and asked for an analysis, an estimate of when it could finish, and a note on what swarm working is like in practice.</p>

      <h3>What was measured</h3>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader" scope="col">Measure</th><th role="columnheader" scope="col">Value</th><th role="columnheader" scope="col">Note</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Lanes launched in the first 33 minutes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">56</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">In four waves: executable analysis, subsystem surveys, tools, then Rust format readers and follow-ups.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Lanes finished in that time</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">37, none failed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">Every lane delivered its report, its data files and a devlog entry.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Time per lane</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Median 13 minutes, shortest 7, longest 33</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">Subsystem surveys were quickest at a median of 11 minutes. The longest lane overran because the tool it was told to use did not work and it had to build a replacement.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Parallel speed-up</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">16 times</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">545 lane-minutes of work in 33 minutes of wall-clock time, with between 16 and 28 lanes running at once.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Concurrency limit reached</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">None yet</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">Up to 38 lanes ran at once with no rate limiting from the model provider. Each lane used about 180 MB of memory; the laptop had 9 GB free at the peak.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Mistakes caught by a second lane</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">3 in the first hour</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">The encrypted code range the coordinator missed, an emulator that crashes on this machine, and a disagreement about the relocation table that is still being settled.</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>

      <h3>Why it was fast</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The tasks were independent. Each lane read the same file and answered a different question, so no lane waited for another.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every lane got the same written contract: where it may write, what it must deliver, how to label evidence, and a progress log to keep. The coordinator did not have to explain anything twice.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Publishing was automated behind a check. A script refuses any devlog fragment containing addresses, local paths, byte dumps or code, so the coordinator could integrate fifteen entries at a time without reading each line first.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Overlap between lanes was useful, not wasteful. Lanes that measured the same thing a different way are what caught the three mistakes above.</li>
      </ul>

      <h3>What slowed it down or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The coordinator is the bottleneck. Lanes finish faster than one coordinator can read their reports properly. In the first hour most lane reports were read only as fifteen-line summaries.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Lanes cannot be corrected once they are running. When the encrypted code range was discovered, sixteen lanes had already started without knowing about it, and their numbers have to be checked afterwards.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Pushing every commit separately broke the project site for several minutes. See the entry on site build collisions.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Lanes disagree. Two independent function counts differ by about fourteen thousand, and two lanes describe the same relocation table as clean and as mostly garbage. A swarm produces contradictions at the same speed as findings, and each one costs a further lane to settle.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Quality varies with how much of a lane's evidence comes from running code against the real file. Lanes that measured were reliable; the one lane that worked mostly from forum posts was corrected within hours.</li>
      </ul>

      <h3>The estimate, and how much to trust each part</h3>
      <p>These are estimates made on the first evening, before any function has been rewritten through the full pipeline. The pilot in phase 2 replaces them with measurements.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader" scope="col">Phase</th><th role="columnheader" scope="col">Estimate</th><th role="columnheader" scope="col">Basis and main risk</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">0. Measure</td><td role="cell" data-label="Estimate">Finished within a day</td><td role="cell" data-label="Basis and main risk">Measured: most of it took an hour. One megabyte of code is encrypted on disk and can only be read once the owner has started the game.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">1.       <tr role="row"><td role="cell">2. Pilot</td><td role="cell" data-label="Estimate">1 to 2 days</td><td role="cell" data-label="Basis and main risk">Measures functions per lane per hour and the false-accept rate. Every estimate below is a guess until this exists.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">3.
