      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">4. Standalone</td><td role="cell" data-label="Estimate">2 to 4 weeks more</td><td role="cell" data-label="Basis and main risk">Integration debugging is serial and does not speed up with more lanes. The Xbox 360 recompilation projects spent months here.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">5. 64-bit and platform layer</td><td role="cell" data-label="Estimate">3 to 5 weeks more</td><td role="cell" data-label="Basis and main risk">No comparable project to measure against.</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">6. Renderer and macOS</td><td role="cell" data-label="Estimate">6 to 12 weeks more</td><td role="cell" data-label="Basis and main risk">The longest phase in every comparable project. Shader translation already works, which helps.</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p>Added up: a rewritten game that runs on its own with the original renderer in roughly 6 to 11 weeks, and a 64-bit build with a new renderer on three platforms in roughly 4 to 6 months. The first figure rests on one comparable project, the agent-driven Modern Warfare 2 decompilation, which took about ten weeks to become playable with fewer agents, fewer functions and the benefit of symbols.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Keep lanes independent and overlapping. Do not remove overlap to save tokens; it is the swarm's error correction.</li>
      <li>Measure before estimating. The phase 2 pilot is short on purpose.</li>
      <li>Move routine coordination, such as integrating finished lanes and posting status, onto cheaper models or scripts, and keep the coordinator for decisions and review.</li>
      <li>Treat phase 0's speed as the ceiling for analysis work, not as a forecast for the rewrite.</li>
      </ul>

      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Each lane's log records when the coordinator launched it and when it exited. Subtract the two for each lane, add up the durations, and divide by the wall-clock time between the first launch and the last exit.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="tools-xplat-build">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tools: building for the three target platforms</h2>
      <p>One Rust code base can already build and run for both Windows targets on the project machine, and macOS builds belong on macOS runners, not on this machine. A hello-world crate compiled for all three Windows targets and each binary ran. A macOS binary also linked locally through a cross-linker, but only a Mac can run, sign, or ship it.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Work out how the project builds one Rust code base for Windows on x64, Windows on ARM64, and macOS on Apple silicon, from the project machine and from continuous integration. Test the local toolchain, try cross-compiling to macOS, and research runners and their cost, the Vulkan SDK and MoltenVK in CI, macOS signing, and how similar projects set up their builds.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The local machine builds and runs all three Windows targets with no extra setup. The compiler ships native linkers for each one.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Target</th><th role="columnheader">Build</th><th role="columnheader">Run</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Windows ARM64</td><td role="cell" data-label="Build">yes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Run">yes, native</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Windows x64</td><td role="cell" data-label="Build">yes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Run">yes, emulated</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Windows 32-bit x86</td><td role="cell" data-label="Build">yes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Run">yes, emulated</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Static linking of the C runtime removes the need for a redistributable install. The test binary then depends only on core system libraries.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Cross-linking a macOS Apple silicon binary on Windows works for a trivial program using the Zig linker driven by cargo-zigbuild, with no Apple SDK installed. The output has the right Mach-O header for an ARM64 executable.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> That cross-linked binary is a compile check, not a shippable build. Anything using macOS frameworks needs the real Apple SDK, whose licence restricts it to Apple hardware, and nothing here can run the result. Real macOS builds must happen on a Mac or a macOS CI runner.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Standard CI runners are free with no minute cap for public repositories, so the three-platform build matrix costs nothing once the project is public. Suitable runners exist for each target, including an ARM64 Windows runner and current Apple silicon macOS runners.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The Vulkan SDK is a free download and MoltenVK is permissively licensed, so neither needs buying. Both install in CI through maintained setup actions or direct downloads, and macOS runners can also install them from Homebrew.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Ad-hoc signing is enough for development builds on macOS, but a clean first launch of a downloaded release needs paid developer membership, a distribution certificate, and submission to Apple's notarisation service, which is itself free.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Three similar projects were read: a Sonic recompilation, an open game engine, and a GTA IV recompilation. All build each platform natively on its own runner, cache dependencies and compiler output, pin tool versions, sign macOS builds ad-hoc in CI with real signing reserved for releases, and ship Apple bundles as compressed tarballs rather than zip files.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Build Windows targets locally and in CI with plain cargo; keep the C runtime statically linked so there is nothing to install.</li>
      <li>Use the Zig-based cross-linker locally only as a macOS compile check, and do every real macOS build on a macOS runner.</li>
      <li>Standardise CI on one runner per target, a pinned Rust toolchain with a shared build cache, a pinned Vulkan SDK installed by a setup action, and ad-hoc macOS signing, adding paid signing and notarisation only for tagged releases.</li>
      <li>Organise the Rust code as one workspace with a crate per boundary: shared types, platform layer, renderer, engine subsystems, the 32-bit replacement library, the checker, and packaging tasks.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Install the missing Windows target with rustup, then build a hello-world crate for each of the three Windows targets and run each binary. Rebuild with the static C runtime flag and confirm the system library list shrinks. Install cargo-zigbuild, add the Apple silicon Rust target, and cross-link the same crate for macOS, then inspect the output header to confirm it is an ARM64 executable. The full commands, versions, hashes, and CI sketches are in the lane report.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The cross-linker first failed to find its own Zig binary because a system launcher stub shadowed the real interpreter; pointing it at the project interpreter fixed it. The first Zig download arrived truncated and had to be retried with hash verification. A system tool that locates compiler installs reported nothing even though the compilers work fine, which cost a short detour before plain builds proved the linkers were there all along.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="tools-reverse-tools">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tools: reverse engineering helpers</h2>
      <p>Most of the helper tooling works on this machine, but two things failed plainly: neither demangler handles bare type names without a wrapping trick, and the bundled emulator crashes on every run. The project now has tested commands for diffing, listing, disassembling, parsing and demangling, and a clear note on what to avoid.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Find, install and test the tools that complement the main disassembler for this project: an object differ, a relocatable-object exporter, shipped library-identification and similarity data, LLVM-style listing tools, two portable analysis suites, seven Rust crates for disassembly, parsing, hooking, emulation and demangling, plus the demangler in the installed build tools. Every tool had to be run on this machine, not assumed to work, and the demangling command had to be proven on twenty class names from the executable.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The object differ runs natively and diffs 32-bit objects correctly, flagging a single changed constant with a near-total match score, but it refuses 64-bit ARM objects. The relocatable-object exporter ships an exact build for the installed disassembler version, confirmed from its manifest but not yet activated.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The disassembler ships ready-made library fingerprints for five compiler generations in both 32- and 64-bit flavours, including the one matching the executable's linker generation, plus similarity-search scripts and weights. No queryable database exists yet; one must be built after analysis finishes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The installed build tools contain native listing and demangling programs but no LLVM listing tools. An official portable LLVM build for this processor exists (a large download) and was deliberately skipped.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One portable analysis suite runs natively and reads the executable fully (machine type, section count, debug path, build date); the other runs emulated and agrees, additionally naming the linker generation. All Rust parsing and disassembly crates built and agreed with each other on headers, sections, imports and entry code.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Both hooking crates refuse to build for the native processor and both build and run their tests for the 32-bit target the game uses, including an enable-and-disable hook round trip. The emulator package imports and maps memory but crashes hard on every emulation start in both 32- and 64-bit modes, so it is unusable here; its Rust twin shares the same engine core and licence and was not built.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A scan found 1688 type names in the executable (1579 classes, 109 structs). Neither demangler reads a bare type name directly: one echoes it back or emits garbage, the other errors or keeps a prefix. Wrapping each name in the type-descriptor form before demangling fixed both engines, scoring twenty out of twenty on each, with matching results.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Use the object differ for object-level comparisons, the build tools lister for headers and imports, and the native portable suite for second opinions.</li>
      <li>Use the tested Rust crates for disassembly and executable parsing, and the tested demangling wrapper recipe in both Rust code and one-off commands.</li>
      <li>Use the safe Rust hooking library for 32-bit targets with the C-based one as fallback, both fenced off from native builds.</li>
      <li>Tag library code with the shipped fingerprints matching the executable's linker generation, and run similarity search against a local database once analysis lands.</li>
      <li>Do not install the portable LLVM bundle, do not use the emulator on this host, and do not link copyleft-licensed emulation code into the project.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <ol>
      <li>Run the differ with two 32-bit objects, one symbol and dash for stdout; expect a structured diff naming the changed instruction.</li>
      <li>List the executable with the build tools lister and either portable suite; all three should report the same machine type, section count and import count.</li>
      <li>Build the small Rust test programs from pinned crate versions and run them against the executable; parsing results should match the listers exactly.</li>
      <li>Demangle twenty type names by stripping the leading dot, wrapping each name in the type-descriptor form, and running either demangler; expect a plain class line from each after removing the descriptor suffix.</li>
      <li>Build the hook tests for the 32-bit target and run them; expect the detour to reroute and then restore the call. Confirm the native build of the same tests fails.</li>
      <li>Start any emulation call in the bundled emulator package; expect the process to die without an error message.</li>
      </ol>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Downloads silently landed outside the repository because a child shell did not inherit the working directory; the files were moved back and re-verified by hash. Future work should use absolute paths everywhere.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first disassembly test decoded from the wrong offset and produced nonsense; decoding from the real entry point produced a clean result. The first demangling tests also failed until the wrapping trick was found by trying the descriptor form directly.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The emulator failure was silent: no exception and no output, only a dead process. Unbuffered step-by-step runs isolated the crash to the emulation start call itself.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="p0-injection">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>How our code can get into the game</h2>
      <p>Our replacement functions can ride into the game as a proxy system library placed next to the executable, the same way community plugins already load, and nothing in the game's own checks looks at such a library or at patched code. The one thing that needs care is the start-up wrapper: the entry code loads a helper library from the game folder that prepares hidden start-up data before the real game begins, so our loader must wait until that finishes before touching anything.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Work out, by research and static analysis only and without launching the game, how a project-built 32-bit library can be loaded into the running game and replace individual functions: which community mechanism to reuse, which libraries the game loads early enough to proxy, whether any integrity check would notice, and how the loader itself should be designed.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game statically imports three proxyable system libraries early enough to carry our loader, and none of them ships in the game folder, so a file placed next to the executable is picked up automatically. The community loader defaults to one of those names and recommends it in its readme; our loader should take a different one so both can coexist.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Community plugins load inside library initialisation, before any game code runs. The community loader also has a deferred mode that waits for the game's first system call, but only other game titles use it; this game uses the default early path.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game's signature verification checks exactly one thing: the Rockstar Social Club library in the Program Files folder, confirmed as Take-Two signed. Save-game encryption uses the data-protection API and is unrelated. No code path was found that verifies the game executable itself, lists loaded modules for checking, or watches for patched bytes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The entry code resolves system functions by hand, loads a helper library from the game folder, calls into it in a retry loop, then invokes start-up callbacks that are all zeros in the file on disk (so the helper must fill them in at run time) before jumping to the real game code. The helper's imports show process and module inspection, memory reading, debugger checks, and the ability to end the process.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The community fix project finds game code purely with named byte patterns (over a thousand collected, with per-version alternatives and no hardcoded addresses or version checks) and waits with watcher threads when code is not visible yet. Searched against our build, about half match exactly once and form named anchors; the rest belong to other game versions, plus a small set matching more than once that needs disambiguation.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Proxyable early imports</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Three system libraries</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Our loader can enter before any game code runs</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Files the signature check verifies</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">One: the Social Club library</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Our library and patched code are not covered by it</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Named patterns collected</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Over twelve hundred</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">A large pool of candidate anchors</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Patterns matching exactly once</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">About six hundred</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Usable anchors for the hook table</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Helper library reaction to our code</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Not known statically</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Top question for the first live run</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Build the loader as a project-owned proxy under the system library name the community loader does not use, with the small set of used functions forwarded to the real system copy; also support running as a community-loader plugin from the same codebase as a fallback.</li>
      <li>Do almost nothing at load time; wait with an anchor-watching thread until game code is provably final, then install hooks, each behind an on/off switch driven by a start-up file and a local command channel, failing closed on any mismatch.</li>
      <li>Use the pure-Rust detour library (permissive licence, native per-hook enable and disable) as the primary hook mechanism, small assembler adapters for class methods on the stable toolchain, direct slot writes for virtual tables, and mid-hooks only for observation.</li>
      <li>Never touch the helper library's memory or threads, and assume it can see our module until a live run proves otherwise.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>List the executable's import table with a PE parser and confirm which system libraries it resolves at load time and which files exist beside it in the game folder. Disassemble the few hundred bytes at the entry point and note the hand-rolled library loading, the helper-library calls, and the manual start-up callback invocation. Map every cross-reference to the signature and crypto imports and disassemble around each call site to see which file path is built and checked. Collect the community fix project's pattern strings, match each against the code section with wildcard support, and count exact, multiple, and zero matches.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The start-up callbacks being all zeros in the file looked like missing data until the entry code's manual callback loop made clear they are filled in at run time. Two early readings of the entry code were wrong on first pass (how the helper name is encoded, and an address-range slip that briefly suggested odd export locations) and were corrected by re-parsing the bytes precisely rather than by hand. Web page fetches kept truncating, so both community projects were read as local copies in scratch instead, and only the pattern facts were kept. Most pattern variables in the community source share one generic name, so anchors are identified by file, line, and bytes rather than by a meaningful name.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="function-count-estimate">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Counting the game functions without Ghidra</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The executable holds about 45,200 functions in its readable code, with at least 1,170 more hidden in an encrypted first region, measured by recursive-descent disassembly with capstone. The readable code is 95.6 percent covered; the rest is padding, switch data kept inside the code section, and code reachable only from the encrypted region.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Produce an independent estimate of the function count and sizes without waiting for the Ghidra analysis: recursive descent from the entry point, direct-call targets, relocated code pointers, and exception tables; then size and complexity distributions, duplicate detection, and a comparison with the public Xbox 360 counts.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The code section has two sharply divided regions. The first 1,000 KiB is encrypted and unreadable on disk; the remaining roughly 9.5 MiB is ordinary compiled code. A small loader stub at the entry point resolves imports at run time and jumps to the real entry; it was not reversed further. Switch tables live inside the code section rather than in data, which the scan had to learn (see below).</p>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The size distribution below covers 2.59 million instructions. Most functions are small; 134 exceed 1,000 instructions and the largest is about 19 KiB. About 2,400 switch tables were resolved, SSE floating point outweighs x87 by over four to one, and some 900 functions (2 percent) read arguments from unexpected registers.</p>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Duplicate code is significant: 1,108 byte-identical groups covering 13,423 functions and about 400 KiB, including one constructor-like function copied 481 times. <span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The total sits above the public Xbox 360 range of roughly 31,800 to 36,400 functions, which is expected before library code is tagged and removed, and given PC-only code and different inlining.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The wrapper is treated as out of scope: no decryption was attempted and none should be. The per-function data file is ready for the library-tagging lane, which should shrink the count, and for Ghidra cross-checking once that analysis lands. Unresolvable indirect jumps and the encrypted region stay open problems.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable headers, split the code section by per-block entropy, and collect seeds from direct-call targets, relocated pointers with trustworthy sources, and the exception handler table. Run capstone recursive descent over the plain region, resolve index-scaled jump tables validated by relocations, merge case blocks back into their owners, and hash functions with address bytes masked. The lane's scan script repeats the full pass in about two minutes.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first entropy sample covered only the start of the code section and briefly suggested the whole thing was encrypted; a full block scan corrected that within minutes. A 256-byte entropy threshold then missed the boundary entirely because small samples cannot reach high entropy values, and the first full run decoded 64 KiB windows through a disassembler call that decodes eagerly, running twenty times too slow. Both bugs were fixed the same hour. The genuine surprise was switch tables stored in executable code, including one region of 481 identical functions that first looked like a data island.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-physics">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: physics and collision</h2>
      <p>The game's physics is RAGE-native collision code over a statically linked Bullet broadphase and narrow phase, with NaturalMotion Euphoria driving ragdolls, and no Havok anywhere. The survey counted 94 physics-owned classes, 792 related strings, and at least 789 physics functions in readable code, concentrated in one large engine block plus fragment, material, and entity-glue regions.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey the physics and collision subsystem of the original executable by working directly on the file with Python: extract its classes from run-time type information with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code through relocation references, identify its operating system and library dependencies, compare against public knowledge, note frame-rate dependencies, and leave rewrite notes with a ranked list of what to understand first.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The subsystem owns 94 classes: 19 collision bound types from boxes and spheres up to composite, mesh, and octree bounds; live instances, three collider types, joints, rope, constraints, archetypes, materials, a simulator, sleep management, a level world, broadphase variants, Bullet narrow-phase algorithms, and a fragment family for breakable objects. Sixteen more classes in other systems carry physics names, and 24 Euphoria behaviour classes plus two fragment render dictionaries sit at the boundary.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Both the broadphase and the narrow phase are Bullet-derived, with Bullet class names appearing both under the engine namespace and without any namespace. Euphoria appears as behaviour, effector, and engine classes in a dedicated animation namespace, reached through dedicated physics instance types. No Havok class or string exists in the binary.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Game entities attach through a single physics entity class with 72 virtual functions, the parent of pedestrians, vehicles, and objects, with matching network mirror classes. Fragments use multiple inheritance with the largest tables in the subsystem at 65 and 66 slots, while the simulator exposes only 8 virtual functions and the level world only one, so most of their interface is non-virtual.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of 792 related strings, the most revealing are resource paths for fragments and natural motion data, ragdoll state messages, task parameter asserts for ten Euphoria behaviours, debug dump formats for collision state and velocity, 19 wheel friction surface names, tuning keys for damage, inertia, and self collision, and broadphase debug text. Collision file extensions, Havok names, and physics source file paths are all absent.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Relocation clustering plus virtual function targets attribute at least 789 functions and about 309 kilobytes of code to the subsystem across 168 clusters, with disassembly spot checks passing on 94 percent of sampled sites. About two-thirds of the attributed functions sit in one large engine block covering bounds, colliders, joints, rope, archetypes, both Bullet phases, and the simulator, with separate regions for fragments, materials, and game-side glue.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The subsystem calls almost no operating system functions directly: only thread synchronisation primitives and a thread affinity query were found in its code. The C library is statically linked, file access goes through the resource system, and both Bullet and Euphoria are statically linked.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The physics stepper takes variable frame time as a parameter rather than using a fixed-step constant, since no frame constant is referenced from physics code. This matches public reports that running above 60 frames per second breaks vehicle handling, ragdolls, object physics, and helicopters, which community fixes address by restoring frame-rate scaling.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Physics-owned classes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">94</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">The core type surface a rewrite must cover</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Virtual function floor</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">789 in readable code, 32 in the encrypted prefix</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Minimum function count; the true total is estimated at 1200 to 2000</td></tr>

      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Third-party physics code</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">Bullet broadphase plus narrow phase, Euphoria behaviours</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Both statically linked; no Havok present</td></tr>

      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>A rewrite should proceed from bound primitives and mesh bounds with a bounds-file reader, through instances, broadphase, narrow phase, colliders, joints, the simulator, the level world, fragments, and game attachment, leaving the Euphoria bridge for last together with the animation work. Pure geometry queries, solver steps, and broadphase operations can be checked in a CPU emulator in isolation, while stepping, level queries, streaming, entity glue, and behaviours need the running game. Fixed-step-only simulation would be a behaviour change, so the rewrite must reproduce variable frame-time quirks, and field layouts, file formats, and the behaviour interface still need to come from debugger work or community sources.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Four scripts in the lane scratch folder run in order with the project Python environment: an environment check that verifies the encrypted prefix against its mirror section, a class scan that filters the shared type inventory and measures every virtual table through relocations, a string scan that filters the shared string inventory with physics patterns, and a cluster scan that groups code references with slot targets and spot-checks them with the disassembler. Each script reads only the original executable and the shared probe inventories and writes only to the scratch folder, finishing in about ten minutes. The class, string, and cluster data files it produces hold every address and count behind this entry.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Several name filters misfired before review caught them: audio hardware voices, pixel-shader fragments, render phases, camera graph parameters, and a particle attribute all matched physics patterns and had to be excluded by hand, while one iterator class lost its enclosing scope to a name printer bug and had to be re-read from its mangled form. Tiny clusters pairing two type descriptors turned out to be data tables embedded in code rather than functions. A text search over the single-line string inventory hung and had to be replaced with a JSON load. Two Euphoria behaviour name strings looked like noise until the matching behaviour classes confirmed them, and the absence of collision file extensions was checked three ways before being trusted.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="tools-scripts">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tools: mission scripts and the script format</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The project now has a working script pipeline: an open-source tool built from source on this machine decrypts and disassembles mission scripts from our own copy of the game, and a small project script extracts all 940 of them from the game archives without needing any key material.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools for the game's script files: decompilers, compilers and disassemblers. Establish where the scripts live, and the script file header and encryption used on PC. Clone the public decompiled-scripts repository as reference and report its coverage and most-used native functions. Finish with at least one script from our copy disassembled.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Scripts ship inside two archives per episode (main and network), six archives in total, holding 940 scripts. The archives use a newer format than the classic one: only their directory is encrypted, while the script data itself sits raw, so scripts can be recovered by their headers alone.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Every script on this PC build is encrypted but not compressed, with a versioned header carrying code, statics and globals counts. The decryption key is derived locally by the tool from the owner's own executable at run time; no key material was copied, printed or stored anywhere.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The decompiled reference set holds 869 scripts and about 3.8 million lines across the three episodes, making 621,220 calls to 2,206 distinct native functions. The most called natives are injury and death checks, debug print helpers, the timer, and the wait call, which appears in 829 of 869 scripts. The reference predates our game build, so its counts differ by two scripts and its native names need re-mapping.</p>

      <tbody role="rowgroup">

      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">SCO ToolBox</td><td role="cell" data-label="Licence">BSD</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">for the owner: old visual editor, no command line</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Scocl</td><td role="cell" data-label="Licence">proprietary freeware</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">for the owner: closed source, targets old patches</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">OpenIV script tools</td><td role="cell" data-label="Licence">proprietary</td><td role="cell" data-label="Result">for the owner: closed source with installer</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Standardise on the built tool for disassembly and any future script compilation; it is the only candidate that is open source, builds here, and is verified against our copy.</li>
      <li>Keep the project carving script as the extraction path until the archive work delivers an extractor that preserves real script names.</li>
      <li>Leave interactive and high-level viewing tools (archive browser, visual editors) for the owner to install.</li>
      <li>Do not adopt the unlicensed compiler or the old-build binaries into the pipeline.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Clone the tool source, publish its command-line project with the installed .NET SDK, point its configuration at the owned game executable so it can derive the script key, then run its dump command with the GTA IV target from the folder holding the scripts. Carve scripts from the game archives by scanning for the script magic headers and validating their length fields. Count reference coverage by matching all-caps call names across the decompiled text files.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The archives did not start with the expected classic magic, which first looked like corruption; the directory turned out to be encrypted while the data is raw.</li>
      <li>The tool rejected absolute file paths with a file-missing error; its inputs are patterns matched against the current folder, so it must run from the scripts folder.</li>
      <li>The tool targets an older .NET version than the installed runtime, so every run needs a roll-forward setting.</li>
      <li>Disassembly shows native call hashes, not names; a name table for this game build still has to be made.</li>
      <li>Two scripts differ in count between our copy and the older reference set; the cause is still unknown.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="tools-engine-crates">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tools: the future Rust engine's libraries</h2>
      <p>A survey of Rust crates and C libraries for the future 64-bit engine found a maintained, permissively licensed crate for nearly every need, with three licence flags and one platform risk to resolve. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Seventy-three crates were checked against the package index, twenty-two repositories had their build configurations read, and every recommendation below names its version, licence and maintenance state as of the survey date.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Find the best maintained Rust crate or C library with bindings for each need of the future engine: Vulkan bindings and allocators, Metal bindings, windowing and input, audio output and 3D audio, decoding, physics, maths, compression, archive parsing helpers, networking, scripting, profiling and the upscaler SDKs. Check which build for Windows on ARM64 by reading build configurations, flag every licence outside the permissive set, and end with a recommended dependency list. Research only; nothing was installed.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p>Most of the stack is uncontroversial. Vulkan goes through the long-standard binding whose repository is still active, with a pure Rust allocator beside it. Windowing and gamepad input collapse into a single C library that already supports Windows on ARM64 and Apple silicon. Audio output, the game mixer, physics, maths, compression, parsing helpers, networking and the profiler each have a maintained crate with recent releases. The 3D audio answer is the maintained wrapper around the now open source Steam audio SDK.</p>
      <p>Four findings needed more care. First, only one crate in the survey tests Windows on ARM64 in its build configuration; everything else is trusted there because it is pure Rust on what is now a top-tier compiler target, while crates with C build steps each need one compile check. Second, the audio decoding library is pure Rust and complete but carries a weak copyleft licence that needs sign-off, and it cannot decode the game's videos, so a video library is still required for those. Third, the physics engine the original game derived from has only tiny or stale Rust bindings, so the maintained pure Rust physics engine wins despite the family resemblance. Fourth, upscaler bindings are new or placeholder, except for the Metal ones, so thin project-owned bindings are expected later.</p>

      <p>Licence flags, all <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> from package metadata or primary sources:</p>
      <ul>
      <li>Audio decoding: weak copyleft, file level. Usable inside a larger work but needs an explicit decision.</li>
      <li>Video library: copyleft terms that depend on build options; a minimal build keeps obligations small but they still exist, and only this library decodes the game's videos.</li>
      <li>OpenAL: rejected. Its Rust bindings are frozen since 2019, the maintained implementation is copyleft, and the system framework is deprecated on the Mac.</li>
      <li>Upscaler and store SDKs: proprietary redistribution terms each; relevant only at the upscaling phase.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Standardise on the table above. Prefer the single C windowing library over the three-crate windowing plus gamepad plus audio combination. Prefer the pure Rust allocator over the C++ one for the simpler ARM64 story. Take the maintained pure Rust physics engine and drop the idea that matching the original engine's physics family buys fidelity, since behaviour is rewritten rather than carried over. Write thin project-owned upscaler bindings at the upscaling phase instead of waiting for the ecosystem. The full versioned list with reasons, risks and rejected alternatives lives in the lane report.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <ol>
      <li>Query the package index API for each candidate crate and record version, licence, release date and download counts.</li>
      <li>Run package searches for the binding families where the crate name is uncertain (physics, spatial audio, video, networking) and confirm the maintained candidate by release date and repository activity.</li>
      <li>Read the build configuration files of each main repository and note which target triples and machine types are tested.</li>
      <li>Read the platform tables in the audio, windowing and physics project readmes, and the licence files of the profiler, the spatial audio SDK and the video library.</li>
      <li>Compare against the existing upscaling reference for the upscaler SDK state rather than re-researching it.</li>
      </ol>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two searches returned misleading names. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A crate named exactly for the physics engine turned out to be an unrelated virtual machine project, and the crate named for the game's video format is a reserved-name stub; both wasted one lookup each before the package descriptions gave them away. Build configuration scanning missed several projects that use non-standard workflow filenames, which was corrected by listing one project's workflow directory directly. The oldest Vulkan binding release looked stale until the commit history showed active maintenance without recent releases, a reminder that release date alone misleads. Several platform claims rest on consistent secondary sources rather than primary documents because the time budget did not stretch to reading every upstream manual; those are marked as inferred in the report.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="tools-archives">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Tools: archives and compression</h2>
      <p>Every game archive now opens: all 49 package files and all 254 disc images list cleanly with a scripted tool, and the one build quirk found along the way, an encrypted sidecar file nobody had flagged, decrypts with the same method as everything else.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Establish which container and compression formats this build uses from file headers, then find, test and where allowed install the tools to list and unpack them, and prove the pipeline by extracting samples.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The build uses two package-file versions: the audio banks use the newer one and the player-model archives plus one small data archive use the older one. Nearly all disc images are encrypted; four small ones are stored open. All loose resources share one container version and are zlib compressed. No lossless-console compression appears anywhere in this PC build, and no package entry uses the format's own compression flag.</p>
      <ul>
      <li>Package files list 3,522 contained files; disc images list 52,718 entries, with zero failures in either set.</li>
      <li>Audio bank entries carry content hashes instead of names; a public hash table resolves 99 percent of them to readable names.</li>
      <li>Scripts ship only inside archives: 941 compiled scripts across eight archives, none as loose files.</li>
      <li>The small data archive was the surprise: unlike every other package file, its file content is encrypted as well as its table, and it decrypts to a readable text file.</li>
      </ul>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Tool results: the Rust archive crate builds but cannot open this build's encrypted tables, so it is not usable alone. The Python audio-bank library resolves names and extracts correctly for audio banks but misreads model archives. The classic C# archive browser was evaluated from its source only; it supports this exact game version but needs a desktop install. The zlib libraries in both languages inflate identical bytes.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Scripted work should use the lane's small independent reader plus the Python crypto library: it is the only tested path covering all archive kinds, compression and the encrypted sidecar.</li>
      <li>Audio-bank names should come from the MIT-licensed hash table behind a quiet wrapper.</li>
      <li>Rust code should use the standard zlib crate; the LZX crate is recorded for console reference work only.</li>
      <li>The desktop archive browsers stay owner-installed tools for interactive browsing, not part of the pipeline.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Run the lane's listing script from the repository scratch area: it loads the archive key from the owner's executable into memory, validates it by trial decryption without ever displaying or storing it, then lists every archive into a JSON file and extracts a handful of small samples into the asset cache. The Rust check builds a scratch project against the archive crate and the compression crates and inflates one loose texture dictionary three ways for identical output.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Two naming traps cost time. The audio-bank name table looks empty at first because its entries are hashes, not broken offsets; comparing against the Python library's hash table confirmed the bytes match. The script-archive samples also came from an episode archive at first because its folder path ends the same way as the base path; per-archive counts in the report use exact matches. A first Rust attempt failed on a wrong argument type for the LZX crate and a bad relative path; both were fixed by reading the crate source and using an absolute path.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-vehicles"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Subsystem survey: vehicles</h2><p>Vehicle code is scattered across the executable rather than living in one module, with about one hundred thirty RTTI classes, six drivable vehicle types, and handling data held in plain structs with no RTTI at all. Helicopters and planes turn out to be subclasses of the automobile class, all network replication code for vehicles sits in the encrypted part of the file, and the shipped data files match binary format strings exactly, which gives the rewrite free parser tests.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Survey the vehicle subsystem of the original executable by static analysis only: extract its RTTI classes with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code through relocation references, list its operating system and library dependencies, summarise public knowledge, note frame-rate dependencies, and write rewrite notes with a ranked list of what to understand first.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The class tree is small and single-inherited: a base vehicle class with six descendants (automobile, bike, boat, heli, plane, train), plus a vehicle model info class, a factory, a scanner, task info, two network events, a paint shader effect, wheel render data, and two audio entities. Helicopters and planes derive from the automobile class, and the multiplayer mirror classes repeat the same shape.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Handling, wheel, suspension, transmission, chassis, and siren classes do not exist in RTTI. Their behaviour is reachable through strings instead: six suspension position names, three transmission position names, per-wheel suspension health formats, force-transmission script tunables, wheel friction surface names, and a thirty-seven-field handling file with one hundred seventy-eight entries.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One thousand fifty-nine code references cluster into one hundred fifty fine groups and fifty-two broader regions spanning the readable code, holding roughly eight hundred virtual methods as a firm lower bound and an estimated one to three thousand functions in total. The largest regions are vehicle and police audio, car driving and door tasks, drive-by flags with seat and door logic, damage audio, and the get-in and get-out task family.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Vehicle code makes essentially no direct operating system calls; its dependencies are internal engine systems (physics, fragments, audio, rendering, tasks, networking, streaming). Third-party markers found are Bullet broadphase collision, zlib, Bink video, and NaturalMotion animation. Havok, PhysX, FMOD, Granny, SpeedTree, and Scaleform markers are absent.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Six loose data files were read: handling data, vehicle definitions, car colours (hot-reloadable according to its own header), car groups per city district, vehicle extras with boat boarding points, and train camera nodes. A boat boarding-points format string in the binary matches the extras file line for line.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Public bug reports tie vehicle behaviour to frame rate: acceleration and top speed change above ninety frames per second, helicopters and cameras misbehave past sixty, and the standard advice is to cap at sixty or thirty. The binary holds frame-lock settings, slow-motion effect names, and time-scale strings, but no explicit per-frame vehicle constants were found.</p><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Group</th><th role="columnheader">Count</th><th role="columnheader">Note</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Core classes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">18</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">vehicle tree, factory, model info, audio, shader, wheel data</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Network classes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">18</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">replication, parsers, blenders, task clones; all code encrypted</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Task classes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">67</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">driving, entry and exit, doors, police, combat in cars</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Event classes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">15</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">damage, collision, fire, theft, ped entry</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Camera classes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">9</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">follow, cinematic heli chase, fire truck, script instructions</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Unique strings</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">1735</td><td role="cell" data-label="Note">file paths, audio keys, debug formats, shader and particle names</td></tr></tbody></table><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><p>Recover the handling, wheel, suspension, and transmission layouts from parser code and the data files rather than from RTTI, since no such classes exist. Rewrite in the order data parsers, factory and spawning, base vehicle update, automobile physics, per-type behaviour, tasks and events, audio glue, and networking last. Check file parsers, damage maths, task transitions, and packet units in the CPU emulator, and leave frame integration feel, deformation visuals, and multiplayer sync for the running game. Treat per-frame vehicle integration as frame-rate-sensitive until proven otherwise and validate handling at thirty, sixty, and above sixty frames per second.</p><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>Parse the executable headers for section and relocation tables, reuse the shared RTTI inventories of type descriptors and object locators, filter class names by vehicle keywords with a hand-pruned false-positive list, find virtual tables by scanning data sections for locator pointers, extract printable strings from data sections and filter by subsystem keywords, then join relocation targets in readable code against string and virtual table addresses and cluster nearby hits. Capstone spot checks over virtual method targets confirm each region holds real code.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><p>An early function-estimate lane had concluded the code section was unreadable on disk, but per-window entropy and disassembly showed clean code after the encrypted first megabyte, so the survey proceeded on the readable remainder. Keyword matching needed about ninety manual removals, with the worst offenders being mouse wheels, game clocks, uptown business districts, shader planes, and primary clans. One filter typo briefly hid a car-scream task class, and an animation keyword polluted the file-format group with over a hundred unrelated animation classes before it was fixed. All network vehicle code points into the encrypted range, so its size and behaviour stay unknown until emulator work begins.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-network">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: networking</h2>
      <p>The executable still contains the complete multiplayer stack even though this edition removed multiplayer: entity replication, session management, presence and clan services, leaderboards, voice message types, and socket, HTTP and TLS transport. Games for Windows Live is gone without a trace, and the backend points at Rockstar Online Services instead. About half of the game replication layer appears to sit in the encrypted part of the code section, so it cannot be studied statically.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey the networking subsystem from the executable alone: the classes, strings, code locations, operating system dependencies, public knowledge, timing behaviour, and rewrite notes, with a ranked list of what to understand first.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Class names recovered through run-time type information show two layers: a game replication layer with per-entity-type sync wrappers, sync parsers, several dozen network event types, replicated task types, interpolation helpers, and array replication for pickups, player info and script variables; and an online services layer with session tasks, session events, wire message types, and a live-services manager with a Steam backend.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Leaderboards dominate the class count: nearly fifteen hundred template bindings covering several hundred multiplayer mode schemas across ranked and standard boards for races, episodic content, team, competitive and co-operative modes.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> No reference to the old PC online platform remains anywhere: not in strings, class names, or imports. The replacement backend is named throughout: presence, party, invite, clan and sign-in events, matchmaking and clan web service endpoints, and Rockstar service hosts for auth, online services and cloud.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Transport is raw sockets plus the engine's own HTTP client and statically linked TLS. Most socket imports are referenced from readable code in a select-loop client pattern with no listening sockets; all crypto imports are used for certificate checks and protected session-id storage.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The game replication layer and socket startup live mostly in the encrypted code region: most of its class tables and all of its diagnostic strings have no references from readable code. Session, presence, HTTP, stats upload and leaderboard code is in the readable region, in on the order of two dozen code areas totalling roughly a quarter of a megabyte.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Voice chat is a leftover surface only: message types, menu tokens and error text exist, but no voice transport was found, and the similarly named audio engine classes are unrelated sound synthesis voices.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>A rewrite should start with the pure serialisation pieces (bit buffers, message framing and ids, sync data layouts), then session state machines against a fake transport, and leave sockets, NAT traversal and the defunct server endpoints for last with loopback harnesses. The next step for this subsystem is to prove whether any network code is still reachable from the menus, and to recover sync data layouts from the readable parser code.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable headers for sections, imports and relocations; scan read-only data for run-time type descriptors and validate complete object locators and class hierarchies against the relocation table; extract printable strings and filter by network keywords; resolve every relocation in the unencrypted code and keep targets matching network class tables, strings or socket and crypto import slots; group nearby hits into clusters; spot-check samples with a disassembler used only as a verifier.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first clustering pass matched every class table in the binary instead of only network ones and produced hundreds of meaningless clusters; restricting targets to the curated network class list fixed it.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Keyword filters kept catching false friends: police dispatch orders, gamepad names, menu selection tokens and sound synthesis voices all matched naive network keywords and had to be excluded by hand.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The exact third-party TLS library could not be pinned down: the cipher list suggests one family while an error string suggests another, and the version is unknown.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="p0-natives">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>The script native table: just over three thousand natives, all named</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The executable registers 3034 script natives into a single hash table, and every one now has a name from public databases. The older of the two known name-hash generations is the common Jenkins hash and checks out on all 2878 old pairs; the newer generation, which this build uses, is still unidentified, though its hashes have an unusual two-halves structure that constrains the search.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Find the script engine's native function table using byte patterns published by the open-source script debugger scrDbg, enumerate every registered native as a hash plus handler pair, confirm the name-hashing function, and name as many natives as possible against public name lists.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Script-engine anchors located</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">10 of 10, each exactly once</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">The published patterns fit this build precisely</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Native registrations</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">3034, each hash registered once</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">The complete set this build can run</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Named</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">3034 of 3034</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">No unknown natives remain in this build</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Distinct handlers</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">2945</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Most natives have their own code; 20 handlers are shared</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Shared debug stub</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">46 natives, one handler</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">Stripped debug natives point at one shared handler</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Public names absent</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">86 database entries plus 24 mod-added ones</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">The 86 look like entries whose new hash was never recorded</td></tr>

      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Registration takes two shapes that both reach the same table insert routine: a small group carries its own failure check per native, while the large group calls through a shared wrapper that holds the check once. The table routines match the published open-table design entry for entry, including the probing rule and the empty-slot markers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Native name strings are absent from the executable, so scripts and the engine meet only through hash values. Seven cases where the two public databases disagreed on a hash were settled against the registered values: three favour one database, one was a misattributed name, and three turned out to be genuine alias pairs where both hashes are registered.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Roughly the first megabyte of the code section reads as high-entropy bytes rather than code, so it is likely decrypted by the start-up stub at load. Only the shared debug handler points into that region; everything else registered sits in readable code.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>The enumerated hash-to-handler list is the ground truth for this build's natives; later work should consume it rather than re-derive it.</li>
      <li>The new name-hash algorithm stays open. The recommended next step is to extract the hashes that compiled game scripts actually call and attack the algorithm from those pairs, using the two-halves bit structure as the main constraint.</li>
      <li>Handler code clusters into a few regions, which should make per-subsystem handler mapping straightforward.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <ol>
      <li>Search the executable's code for each published scrDbg pattern with wildcard bytes; each should occur once, pointing at the script-engine data.</li>
      <li>Read the table insert routine next to the table anchor and note its two-argument shape and probing loop.</li>
      <li>Find every push of a known native hash immediate followed by a call to the insert routine or its wrapper; pair each hash with the handler address pushed just before it.</li>
      <li>Match the collected hashes against the public SCO-Toolbox and HappinessMP lists to attach names, and hash the old list with the Jenkins function to confirm the old generation.</li>
      </ol>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Each hash in the small registration group appeared twice, which first looked like dual registration into two tables; disassembly showed the second push belongs to a failure-logging path, not a second table. The new hashes first appeared to have two bits structurally clear, which sent the analysis down a blind alley of masked and split-hash theories; the full-bit entries in the same list turned out to be old-hash placeholders, but the true new hashes really do keep those bits clear and the algorithm still resisted some sixty candidates plus seed-inversion, suffix, modulus and shift-family attacks. The shared debug handler points into the encrypted code region, so its runtime behaviour could not be checked statically.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="pages-build-collisions">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>GitHub Pages fails builds when pushes arrive seconds apart</h2>
      <p>Pushing once per commit broke the project site for several minutes. Of 28 site builds in the first hour of phase 0, 23 failed, each with a duration of zero seconds. The owner noticed before the coordinator did.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>The owner reported that the published site did not seem to be working. The pages returned normally when checked a few minutes later, so what had happened?</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The coordinator had just started integrating lane results one commit at a time, pushing after each. Twelve commits went up within about a minute.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The build history shows each push starting its own site build, and every build except the last of a burst ending immediately with "Page build failed". Only the final push of each burst produced a working site.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> A build that is still running is cancelled or rejected when a newer push arrives, and it is reported as a failure, not as superseded. While a burst is in progress the site can serve an old version or fail to load.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Each failed build probably also sends the repository owner a notification.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Commits stay one change each, but a batch of commits is pushed once, after the last one. The agent rules and the commit tooling now do this.</li>
      <li>The status tick makes at most two pushes: one for the batch of integrated lane results and one for the progress files.</li>
      <li>After a batch, check that the newest build reports "built" before telling anyone the site is updated.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>List the repository's Pages builds through the GitHub API and compare their creation times, statuses and durations with the times of the pushes.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Tools: models, textures and collision</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A working asset pipeline for models, textures and map placement now runs on the project machine: a community map extractor built from source converts game map archives to open glTF models and standard texture files, and the long-standing archive browser SparkIV runs for day-to-day inspection.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools the project needs for drawable, fragment, texture dictionary, collision, animation and map placement formats, test each one on this machine, collect the best public format documentation, and recommend which tool to standardise on for each job.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nine candidates were examined. Three were installed and tested successfully:</p>
      <ul>
      <li>SparkIV, the archive browser and viewer for game archives, models and textures. The latest prebuilt release launches and stays running on this machine.</li>
      <li>A community map extractor plus its pinned game-asset parsing library. It compiled with no errors and converted a small map sector (62 archive entries) into 41 out of 41 models with textures, with nothing skipped.</li>
      <li>A Rust parsing crate for a newer game in the series. All 108 of its self-contained tests pass here. It cannot read this game's files directly, but its structure is the best template for a new loader.</li>
      </ul>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Four more were collected as reference but could not be fully tested: a Blender add-on whose code needs Blender itself (not installed), a maintained SparkIV source fork (the prebuilt release covers the need), and two recompilation-project resource readers, one without a licence statement and one under a restricted licence, so both are read-only references.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The public wiki documents several formats field by field (drawables, collision dictionaries, placements, and the two text map formats), but the texture dictionary and vehicle fragment pages are stubs with no layouts; the parsing library source fills that gap.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The project should standardise on SparkIV for browsing archives, the extractor plus parsing library as the asset pipeline, and a new clean-room Rust loader modelled on the Rust crate's design using the documented layouts. The closed-source editor OpenIV, the 3ds Max plugins, a paid modelling tool and Blender itself are left for the owner to install.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <ol>
      <li>Fetch the latest SparkIV prebuilt release from the project's own release page, unpack it into the tools folder, and launch the browser.</li>
      <li>Clone the map extractor and the pinned asset library revision, build the extractor with the installed .NET SDK, and run it against a copy-safe output folder with framework roll-forward enabled.</li>
      <li>Clone the Rust parsing crate and run its test suite with the Rust toolchain; no game files are needed.</li>
      <li>Read the public wiki pages for the drawable, collision, placement and text formats, and the parsing library source for the texture and fragment layouts.</li>
      </ol>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One named Blender add-on repository no longer exists on its hosting site, so it could not be evaluated. One candidate name in the task turned out to be a different game series' recompilation project, not a texture tool; its resource reader was still useful as documentation. A first extraction test silently used an archive with no matching map files and produced nothing; re-running against a real map sector worked. The main closed-source editor's website showed an expired certificate on the day, so its details were confirmed from secondary sources instead.</p>
