      <article class="entry" id="tools-audio-video"><div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div><h2>Tools: audio and video</h2><p>The project now has a tested open toolchain for all of the game's sound and video: FFmpeg reads every cutscene video, vgmstream reads the game's audio banks, and a small Python library extracts those banks from the archives. All sampled game audio turned out to be a single simple codec, which makes the port's audio job smaller than expected.</p><h3>What was asked</h3><p>Find, evaluate and where allowed install the tools the project needs for audio and video: the game's audio containers and codecs, speech and radio streams, Bink video files, and user music. Test whether vgmstream supports this game's PC audio, install a portable FFmpeg build and use it to identify the Bink files without converting them, identify the audio container format from headers, and name the Rust crates that could decode each format in the port.</p><h3>What was found</h3><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game ships nine Bink version 1 videos: two long TV channels for the base game, four shorter ones for the two episodes, and three small clips. FFmpeg's Bink support reads all nine, reporting resolutions from 256 by 192 to 512 by 384 at about 30 frames per second, with Bink DCT audio at 22050 Hz (one small clip uses 11000 Hz mono; two clips have no sound).</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> All game audio lives in encrypted RPF version 3 archives: forty in the base game plus three per episode. The entries inside are Rockstar AUD banks holding between one and over a hundred streams each. Every sampled bank, across ringtones, ambient radio, a music station and speech, uses IMA 4-bit ADPCM at 24000 to 32000 Hz. No MP3, Vorbis, XMA or Miles audio was found in the PC game audio path.</p><p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> vgmstream supports this game's PC audio: it reported correct metadata for all five sampled banks and decoded one stream to WAV. FFmpeg cannot open the AUD banks at all, so the two tools complement each other rather than overlap.</p><p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> User music works by scanning a user music folder for WMA and MP3 files, and a small encoder program beside the game exports replay clips to Windows Media Video 9. Both conclusions come from program text strings, not from running the game. <span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The exact folder path on a player's machine was not checked.</p><table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Job</th><th role="columnheader">Tool</th><th role="columnheader">Licence</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Bink video and audio</td><td role="cell" data-label="Tool">FFmpeg, native ARM64 build</td><td role="cell" data-label="Licence">LGPL</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Game audio banks</td><td role="cell" data-label="Tool">vgmstream command-line tool</td><td role="cell" data-label="Licence">permissive MIT-style</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Archive extraction</td><td role="cell" data-label="Tool">pyrpfiv Python library</td><td role="cell" data-label="Licence">MIT</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">User music and replay formats</td><td role="cell" data-label="Tool">FFmpeg decoders</td><td role="cell" data-label="Licence">LGPL</td></tr></tbody></table><h3>What was decided or recommended</h3><p>The project should standardise on FFmpeg for video and Windows Media formats, vgmstream for inspecting and decoding game audio banks, and pyrpfiv for scripted archive extraction. The closed-source OpenIV editor is left as an optional install for the owner; nothing in this phase depends on it.</p><p>For the port itself, the lowest-risk path is the Symphonia crate family (MPL-2.0, pure Rust) for the ADPCM game audio and MP3 user tracks, plus a project-written AUD container reader, with FFmpeg bindings covering Bink video and the WMA edge case. There is no maintained pure-Rust Bink or WMA decoder, and the one Bink-aware Rust framework found is under the AGPL and therefore excluded.</p><h3>How to reproduce it</h3><p>Install a portable FFmpeg build from one of the Windows build sets linked on the <a href="https://ffmpeg.org/download.html">FFmpeg download page</a>, the command-line build from the <a href="https://github.com/vgmstream/vgmstream/releases">vgmstream releases page</a>, and pyrpfiv from PyPI. Point FFmpeg's probe tool at the game's movie files, extract audio banks from the sound archives with pyrpfiv using the owner's own game executable, and run vgmstream in metadata mode on the extracted banks. Full commands, versions and checksums are in the lane report.</p><h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3><p>The extraction library's documentation names older game versions, but it parsed the current version's archives without complaint, so the version list is out of date rather than the code being broken. The same library prints thousands of log lines and fills in its file list through a side channel instead of returning it, which needed a small wrapper. The word ivaud, the community's name for the PC audio format, appears nowhere in the game executable, which briefly suggested the format might be absent until vgmstream identified the banks directly.</p></article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-world-pools">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: world, entities and object pools</h2>
      <p>The entity hierarchy survived intact in the executable's type data, but the world container, the pools and the population manager left no type traces at all, which means they are almost certainly static code with sizes baked in as plain numbers. Map data on disk uses text definition files plus binary placement files, and the public placement format matched the bytes on disk.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey the world, entities and object pools subsystem working directly on the executable file: list its classes with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code through relocation references, note its operating system dependencies, check public documentation, note frame-rate dependencies, and rank what to understand first.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The run-time type data holds thousands of classes, of which about two dozen belong to this subsystem. The entity tree runs from a common root through dynamic and physical entities down to objects, buildings, dummy placeholders, interior and portal instances, with seven model definition classes and a set of world query helpers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> No trace of a world container, pool collection, population manager, file loader or placement class exists anywhere in the type data or the strings, so these are most likely static classes with no virtual tables. Pool sizes appear nowhere as text and must be plain numeric constants in code.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Useful strings include pool exhaustion errors, population manager startup and shutdown messages, portal and room tracking text, placement provenance wording, level-of-detail distance settings, and pickup save and load errors. Map files on disk come in per-district triplets of definition, archive and binary placement files, and the placement header matches the public format documentation.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Code references to this subsystem are scattered across the whole program by link-time code generation, with the densest spots around model definitions with portal tracking and around generic objects. About sixty direct references group into eighteen small clusters totalling tens of kilobytes, with a lower-bound estimate of roughly two hundred functions. Entity code itself calls no operating system functions directly; timing and threading calls live in neighbouring code.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Start the rewrite with the model definition table and the text definition parser, then binary placement loading, then the pool allocator, then the world grid and scanners, then pickups, portals, population and detail policy.</li>
      <li>Parsers, pool allocation sequences and handle encoding can be checked in a CPU emulator in isolation; streaming interplay, render equivalence and population timing need the running game.</li>
      <li>Public format documentation for placement files is confirmed and can be relied on; pool capacities and the world grid layout are undocumented anywhere and are the highest-value unknowns.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable's type descriptors, object locators and virtual tables from its data sections, extract printable strings, and join the relocation table against those targets, keeping only reference sites in the unencrypted part of the code section. Cluster nearby sites, validate standard function prologues with a disassembler, and curate out audio, interface, task, camera and network classes before clustering. Scripts and data files are kept with the survey.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first clustering attempt produced hundreds of meaningless clusters because audio, interface and task class names share the same substrings; only curation first made the picture usable. The encrypted first megabyte of the code section contains no relocation entries at all, so this method is blind there and the world and pool code may sit in that hole. One vehicle class slipped through a name filter and was caught on review.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-streaming">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: streaming and resources</h2>
      <p>The streaming subsystem splits into a readable edge and an opaque core: 49 related classes were identified through type information, but the central file-device and archive code has all of its virtual methods in the encrypted part of the executable, while the media readers, one loader variant and the resource-dictionary plumbing are readable.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey how the game loads assets at run time: the streaming request system, resource files and pointer fix-up, archives, file devices, asset dictionaries and memory budgets. The work was done by direct analysis of the executable file with Python, without the pending Ghidra analysis and without decrypting or running anything.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 49 classes belong to this subsystem, 47 with measurable virtual tables totalling 597 slots. The file layer is a virtual filesystem family of 8 device classes with 34 to 38 virtual methods each: local disk, memory buffer, relative path remount, network stream, growable buffer, caching decorator, archive files and a streaming device.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the pageable resource system centres on a small base class with 8 typed dictionary instantiations covering animations, textures, drawables, physics bounds, particles and render mesh fragments, plus typed cross-file references that are resolved at load time.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> the main streaming scheduler classes have no type information at all: no descriptors exist for the streaming controller, the streaming module, the asset stores, or archive and resource manager classes, so they must be static classes or plain structures and can only be found through strings and code references.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> every virtual method of all 8 file-device classes and all parameter-stream classes points into the encrypted region, as do nearly all asset-loader methods. Readable code covers the media stream readers, the direct loader variant, dictionary plumbing and file-system call sites.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> 533 distinct subsystem strings, revealing a slot-based request model with active and requested state, per-area streaming set files, an on-disk cache with validation and a defragmentation pass, virtual paths split between shared and platform-specific data, streamed fonts, and a heavily duplicated resource-validation failure message in five languages.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> about ten code regions attributed to streaming through 492 specific references plus 73 direct file-system calls, all sample-checked as genuine code. They cover dictionaries, archives, async streaming, low-level file access, caching and cross-file references.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> compression uses a statically linked zlib, movie playback uses Bink and Windows Media components, and audio streaming uses DirectSound plus the multimedia timers.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> the readable streaming code is on the order of low hundreds of functions; the encrypted region holds most of the archive and scheduler method bodies, so no exact total can be measured from the file on disk.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite work should start with the readable and documented parts in this order: local file device and virtual paths, archive reader checked against public format notes, decompression, resource block loading with pointer fix-up, dictionary containers, cross-file references, then the cache and the request scheduler last, since the scheduler needs dynamic analysis or a decrypted image. The archive format and the general resource design are publicly documented, but the streaming set files, the cache format, the defragmentation pass and the scheduling and eviction policy are not and remain the unknowns.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable headers and relocation table, scan the data sections for C++ type descriptors and object locators, resolve base classes through the hierarchy descriptors, measure virtual tables by counting consecutive relocated code pointers, filter class names for streaming and resource keywords, filter the string table to trustworthy sections only, and collect relocation fixups in the unencrypted code that target subsystem tables, strings and file-system imports, then group nearby references into clusters and validate a sample by disassembly.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two traps cost time. First, a case-insensitive name filter matched unrelated classes such as camera script instructions and destroy-car tasks, and a word-boundary pattern silently missed the whole file-device family; both were caught by inspecting the candidate list and the filter was rewritten case-sensitively. Second, clustering code by synchronisation calls produced bogus mega-clusters because every subsystem uses locks; synchronisation was excluded from attribution and the clusters were recomputed from subsystem-specific references only. Public sources were thinner than expected: the archive format page is thorough, but the canonical modding SDK repository and the resource-format notes could not be located in the time available and stay open leads.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-script-vm">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: the script virtual machine</h2>
      <p>The script virtual machine was surveyed directly from the executable without disassembling the encrypted region. <span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Its interpreter core was located through a tight block of error strings and matching virtual tables, 11 core classes and 127 adjacent script-driven classes were catalogued with their inheritance and virtual table sizes, and 231 code references were grouped into 44 clusters. The network half of the virtual machine lives entirely in the encrypted region, the classic container names from later engine generations are absent, and the interpreter core makes no direct operating system calls.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey the bytecode interpreter that runs mission scripts: thread and program classes, script globals, native function dispatch, the script file format, and script resource handling. Deliver class hierarchies with virtual table sizes, the strings that belong to the subsystem, the code ranges where it lives with a function and byte estimate, its operating system dependencies, public documentation, frame-rate dependencies, rewrite notes, and a ranked list of what to understand first.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The class hierarchy starts at rage::scrThread, a root class with five virtual functions, with GtaThread inheriting two slots and overriding three. Native commands are served by a CScriptCommands pair, mission entity lifetime by a CMissionCleanup pair, each with an episodes variant that overrides one slot. Script host and client variable replication plus a host-variables verification event account for 80 virtual functions whose code sits entirely in the encrypted region. A further 113 virtual tables belong to a queued camera-instruction family, one subclass per camera command, with smaller bridges to audio, script 2d drawing, tasks, and in-game html objects.</p>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The interpreter announces itself through ten adjacent messages: unknown opcode, missing native command, unknown script name, three thread-reset diagnostics covering argument size, static variables versus stack size, and program identity, plus thread kill, array overrun, and clean exit notes. These confirm fixed-size thread stacks, id-indexed programs, name-based lookup, and abort-on-bad-opcode behaviour, matching the <a href="https://gtamods.com/wiki/SCO">public script container layout</a> of code plus statics plus globals. Mission and ambient script slots, a dozen script entity and event-argument type names, network reservation states, and pool flags marking objects usable from scripts round out the vocabulary.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Several expected things are absent: the classic container names from later engine generations have neither type records nor raw bytes anywhere credible, and the executable never names the script file extension, the wait intrinsic, a hash function, or any frame-timing term in a script context. The interpreter address range contains no direct operating system calls at all, which makes it a good candidate for isolated emulator testing. No third-party library code was found in any script cluster.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Scripts load by plain name or hash through the streaming layer, waits are opcode numbers rather than named calls, and whatever the virtual machine needs from the operating system arrives through engine memory, threading, and streaming layers. Public bug reports say several missions are frame-rate dependent and fail above capped frame rates, which fits a model where each script advances once per frame.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The rewrite should start with the thread context and reset and kill paths, then the interpreter step and opcode table against the public container documentation, then native dispatch, the loader and slots, mission cleanup, the event bridge, and finally the encrypted network replication and the audio, camera, render, and task bridges once the pending analysis finishes. The next lane should trace the users of the ten interpreter messages to name the step, reset, kill, and load functions, and hunt the native hash table, the scheduler, and the globals table, whose locations remain <span class="evidence">Unknown</span>. The 112 camera instructions should be generated from their enumeration, not hand-written.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane scripts in order with the project Python environment: layout and candidate scan, hierarchy and full virtual-table scan, string filtering with independent raw-byte term checks, relocation-based clustering with spot disassembly checks restricted to the unencrypted range, message-neighbourhood and import-reference scan, then curation into class, cluster, and string data files. Every script asserts the unencrypted-only rule before disassembling anything. The relocation table, the runtime type records, and the credible-section string pool are the only inputs.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The substring scr matches screen, describe, and discrete, and mission matches transmission, so the first candidate list was mostly noise and needed two curation passes. The prior lane string inventory mixes garbage decoded from encrypted bytes with real strings, so only three sections were trusted. About three of forty spot disassemblies decoded to implausible instructions where the sample landed mid-instruction, which was treated as sampling noise rather than evidence. The short tokens sitting inside the interpreter message block and the single throw message next to them could not be identified and are recorded as unknown rather than guessed at. Open format references and one engine-documentation set were left unchecked for lack of time.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-peds-tasks">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: pedestrians, AI and the task system</h2>
      <p>The pedestrian and AI subsystem is the largest surveyed so far: 511 core classes built around a task tree of nearly 330 task types, 99 event types, per-ped brains with Liberty City variants, and a distant-ped stand-in system, with combat behaviour driven by versioned data files rather than code.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey the pedestrian, AI and task subsystem of the game executable by reading the file directly: list its classes with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its revealing strings, locate its code through cross references, identify its operating system and library dependencies, check public knowledge, note frame-rate dependence, and advise a rewrite.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The class census, from the executable's own runtime type information, counts 511 core classes and 81 shared boundary classes out of 3,243 classes in the binary, holding 10,334 virtual table slots between them.</p>
      <table role="table"><thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Family</th><th role="columnheader">Count</th><th role="columnheader">What it is</th></tr></thead><tbody role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Complex tasks</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">194</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it is">Sequenced behaviours: combat, movement, scenarios, wandering, driving, player roots</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Simple tasks</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">130</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it is">Leaf behaviours, including ragdoll leaves</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Task metadata</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">About 33</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it is">Serializable task descriptors and factories</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Events</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">99</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it is">Stimulus types plus group, scanner, handler and factory classes</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Ped classes</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">37</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it is">Ped entity, player ped, intelligence, data, model info, factory, formations, attractors</td></tr><tr role="row"><td role="cell">Dummy system</td><td role="cell" data-label="Count">10</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it is">Cheap distant-ped entity with stub tasks</td></tr></tbody></table>

Task ownership appears folded into the per-ped intelligence object, and decision makers are data files on disk with a version migration path, including separate police behaviour per wanted level.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Movement tasks use multiple inheritance: 39 classes carry a second virtual table for a movement interface. Distant pedestrians run as cheap dummy objects and convert back to full peds near the player, with explicit handling for peds yanked out of vehicles and ragdolls.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> About 2,400 code references to the subsystem's tables and strings were grouped into 195 clusters across the readable code, with the densest regions holding task methods and the string-heavy regions holding logging and event text. Direct operating system calls could not be attributed: the import table has no on-disk content, so which system functions ped code calls is unknown from static analysis.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The ragdoll task leaves drive a statically linked third-party dynamics library, which will be the hardest part to reproduce. No frame-timing strings were found in the subsystem, but a well-known community fix documents broken pedestrian pathfinding above 60 frames per second, so movement timing needs re-validation at every frame rate.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite in this order: task base classes, then the event scan and dispatch loop, then ped intelligence wiring, task metadata, simple leaf tasks, the wander and movement family, scenarios, combat and cover, ragdoll leaves once the dynamics question is settled, the dummy stand-in system, wanted level and police, and network task mirrors last. Task metadata, event groups, decision tables and formation calculators should be checkable in a CPU emulator in isolation; movement, combat, scanners, ragdoll and wanted behaviour will need the running game or a rich harness.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable's runtime type information to enumerate classes, read base-class lists and count virtual table slots through the relocation table; extract printable strings and filter by subsystem keywords; then map relocation sites in the readable code that point at the subsystem's tables and strings, cluster them by address gap, and validate a sample of function starts with a disassembler. The class list, string list and cluster list are kept as data files with the survey for later tooling.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>An early pass double-counted movement task classes because each has two virtual tables; recognising the multiple inheritance layout fixed the count. A first string filter caught hundreds of unrelated matches on short keywords and had to be tightened with word rules. The import scan repeatedly found zero calls until it became clear the import table itself is not present on disk, which closed off per-subsystem dependency attribution. Public documentation for this subsystem in this game turned out to be thin: community headers target older builds, and the decision-maker file format appears undocumented.</p>
      </article>

      <p>The engine's file, config, memory and save subsystem splits in two: a RAGE core of virtual file devices, memory allocators and an XML and binary parameter system whose code sits mostly in the encrypted part of the executable, and game-side users such as the replay recorder, video editor interface, statistics and save handling whose code is openly analysable and clusters cleanly.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey one engine subsystem working directly on the executable with Python: extract its classes from run-time type information with base classes and virtual table sizes, collect its strings, locate its code by following references in the unencrypted code only, list its operating system and library dependencies, compare against public knowledge, note frame-rate dependencies, and write rewrite notes with a ranked list of what to understand first.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The binary holds about three thousand seven hundred type descriptors and about three thousand two hundred classes with virtual tables. About one hundred classes belong to this subsystem.</p>

      <li>The generated leaderboard family belongs to the network side and should be stubbed behind an interface, not rewritten with this subsystem.</li>
      <li>The encrypted core classes need the running game or decrypted analysis before their virtual table slot order can be trusted.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable headers with pefile, extract printable strings from the data sections, parse the MSVC type descriptors, object locators and hierarchy descriptors to rebuild each class with its bases, measure each virtual table as the relocated run of code pointers following its locator reference, then scan every relocation in the unencrypted code for values matching subsystem strings, virtual tables and import slots, merge nearby hits into clusters, and validate sampled function entries with capstone.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>A generated leaderboard family with over a thousand classes merged into one giant meaningless cluster on the first pass, so it was aggregated separately and the clustering re-run.</li>
      <li>Disassembling at relocation sites produces garbage because a relocation points at an instruction operand, not an opcode, so validation moved to function entries taken from virtual tables.</li>
      <li>A short string that looked like a save file magic turned out to be a frontend text label on closer inspection, and no save magic was found in the executable.</li>
      </ul>

      <h2>How the game was built: reading the Rich header</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game is C++ built with Visual Studio 2012 Update 1, with whole-program optimisation enabled on about half of its C++ code, stack cookies on, run-time type information on, and the C runtime statically linked. It was linked in January 2023, a decade after its toolchain was current, and a post-link wrapper stub owns the entry point.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Decode the executable's Rich header completely: map every entry to its tool and toolchain release using public tables, decide whether link-time code generation was used, corroborate that from sampled disassembly without Ghidra, and infer the compiler options.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The header holds 21 entries covering 2293 objects. Every tool mapping was checked against three independent public tables, which agree on all of them.</p>

      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Stack cookies (<code>/GS</code>) are on, confirmed three ways including over a thousand cookie references in the code. The C runtime is statically linked with no debug leftovers, matching a release build.</li>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The rewrite should target Visual Studio 2012 Update 1 semantics for matching purposes, and must account for whole-program optimisation effects such as custom register passing and missing frame pointers rather than expecting standard calling conventions everywhere. The thousands of type names are a ready-made class list for later naming work. A Ghidra-equipped lane should attribute the unstamped objects and the older libraries, confirm where virtual tables live, and identify the wrapper stub without running it.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Read the bytes between the DOS stub and the PE header, unscramble them with the four-byte key stored next to the Rich marker, and split the result into eight-byte records of tool id, build number and object count. Map the tool ids with the <a href="https://github.com/dishather/richprint">richprint table</a>, the <a href="https://github.com/horsicq/Detect-It-Easy">Detect-It-Easy database</a> and <a href="https://github.com/kirschju/richheader">kirschju/richheader</a>, and map build numbers to releases with the compiler version table on Wikipedia; the background format is documented in <a href="https://www.ntcore.com/files/richsign.htm">Pistelli's Rich signature notes</a>. For corroboration, collect candidate function starts after padding bytes in the code section, disassemble the first dozen instructions of a few thousand of them, and measure frame setup, register argument passing and vector register use.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>An early check seemed to show the parsing library dropping the last Rich record. It was a bug in my own debug print, which truncated the list for display. The library and the hand decode agree on all 21 records.</li>
      <li>The type names all sit in the writable data section instead of the read-only constants section, which is unusual and unexplained. Disabled string pooling is one hypothesis; a follow-up lane needs to confirm it.</li>
      <li>The first register-argument measurement counted register saves as argument passing and overstated the result. Excluding save and restore instructions fixed it and the corrected numbers still support the optimisation finding.</li>
      </ul>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="imports-api">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>What the import table says the engine needs from the platform</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The executable imports 329 functions from 21 system and middleware libraries, and counting every use site shows the engine leans hardest on synchronisation, threading and its millisecond clock, while graphics, audio and online services arrive mostly through libraries loaded at run time. The scan is provably complete: every reference found in code matches an entry in the relocation table exactly.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Turn the import table into a specification for the platform layer: list every imported function, group the imports by purpose, rank them by counting call sites, find libraries loaded at run time instead of imported, and recommend a maintained Rust replacement with a verified licence for each group.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of the 329 imports, 264 are called directly, 12 are used only through a register, and 53 are fully dead: their slots are referenced nowhere in the file. The 2,274 references found in code equal the 2,274 matching relocation entries, so no use site was missed. Sockets are imported almost entirely by ordinal rather than by name, as is the whole of DirectSound.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The platform layer needs, in order of weight: full synchronisation primitives with exact wait semantics, threads with priorities and affinity, a millisecond engine clock, client sockets with a select-style loop, synchronous file and directory access plus file mappings, a window with minimise semantics, gamepad input, and decoders for Bink video and the existing audio formats. Registry, power queries, version stamps and signature checks can be dropped or replaced with config files. Video and audio replacements carry licence notes: the FFmpeg wrapper is permissive but FFmpeg itself is LGPL or GPL depending on build options, and the audio decoding library is MPL-2.0. The largest unknown is the window creation path (see below), which does not block the specification: the window group itself is certain.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable import directory, then scan the executable sections for indirect calls, jumps, pushes and pointer loads through each import slot, and cross-check every hit against the relocation table: the counts must agree exactly. Recover run-time loads by listing loader call sites and the string arguments pushed near them, then cross-reference every library-name string in the image. Ordinal imports were resolved against the export tables of the matching system libraries, and crate licences were checked against the crates registry and lib.rs. The lane scripts and the resulting machine-readable tables are kept with the lane scratch work for the coordinator to integrate.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The biggest surprise is that every window-creation and message-pump import is dead, with no dynamic name string either, yet the program has a live window procedure and window-state code, and no shipped module creates the window for it. <span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The call path is hidden from static analysis; the leading hypothesis is that the start-up stub resolves a window-API table that game code calls through, and a later lane should check cross-references to data pointer tables plus dynamic observation. Two smaller traps: the linker folds some string literals together with the import table own name entries, which at first looked like dynamic resolution reusing import names, and naive call counting misses a dozen imports used only through registers, including the two path-building functions that turned out to be among the heaviest shell users. Register-indirect counts stay approximate because some calls sit further from their pointer load than the pairing window.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="data-sections">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Mapping the executable's data sections</h2>
      <p>The executable's data is now mapped: read-only data holds imports, over three thousand validated virtual tables, string and float pools; the writable area is mostly an eleven megabyte zero-initialised region with a few very heavily referenced globals; and the binary contains no C++ exception tables at all, which means later lanes never have to model C++ unwinding.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Map every data section of the game executable so later lanes know what lives where: describe each section, break read-only data into regions with byte counts, count functions with C++ exception unwinding, find the most-referenced globals, list every resource, analyse relocations, and report anything unusual.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The nine sections do not overlap. The code section is about eleven megabytes and the read-only data section about two megabytes. Writable data is thirteen megabytes in memory but barely over one megabyte on disk, so most of it is zero-initialised. The small entry-point stub section is writable and executable, and the one megabyte blob beside it is uniformly maximum-entropy, so encrypted or compressed.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Region</th><th role="columnheader">Size</th><th role="columnheader">What it holds</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Import tables</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">about nine kilobytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it holds">twenty-one libraries, three hundred twenty-nine functions, no delay imports</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Type and table data</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">about five hundred forty kilobytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it holds">three thousand seven hundred type descriptors, three thousand two hundred virtual tables with forty-two thousand slots</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row">String pools</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">about three hundred eighty kilobytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it holds">twenty-four thousand strings plus wide strings</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="row">Float pools</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">about sixty kilobytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it holds">constant runs referenced directly from code</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Zero-initialised data</td><td role="cell" data-label="Size">about twelve megabytes</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it holds">unreferenced gaps of hundreds of kilobytes, probably static arrays or object pools</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Zero functions use C++ exception unwinding: no exception tables exist anywhere in the image, and only plain system exception imports are present. The build was most likely compiled with C++ exceptions disabled.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The most-referenced global is used from over two thousand code sites. The top fifty globals are nearly all in the zero-initialised area; the few named ones sit beside engine class names and a view-matrix global next to what look like viewport dimensions.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Resources are seven icons, version information reading 1.2.0.59, a manifest, and one large embedded achievement database carried over from the console build, with achievement text in several languages. The manifest still asks for a much older C runtime, which looks vestigial.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Of almost three hundred thousand relocations, about one hundred fifty-three thousand are code-to-data pointers and about forty-six thousand are data-to-code pointers, mostly virtual table slots. Seven percent of code relocations point at values that are not valid addresses and sit in maximum-entropy pockets spread across the whole code section.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The anomalous relocations are either stale linker output or bytes the startup stub restores at runtime. The small extra read-only section looks like a vector-constant pool from a statically linked library. Code also reads its own file headers, which suggests an integrity or version check.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Treat C++ exceptions as absent: no unwinding support is needed in the checker or rewrites.</li>
      <li>Treat the twenty thousand anomalous code relocations as untrusted input until a runtime lane diffs the code section after the startup stub runs.</li>
      <li>Use the region map and the top-fifty globals list as the starting point for naming global variables.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>All analysis ran directly on the executable file with small Python scripts using a PE parser and a disassembler library, without starting the game. The scripts parse section headers, directories, resources and relocations, scan for runtime type structures and exception records with pointer validation, and cross-check every structure against relocation references. The lane outputs are a full report, a region map file with start, size, kind and evidence for each region, and per-area detail files.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first type-information scan found nothing, because the type descriptors live in writable data rather than read-only data, which is not the usual compiler layout. The locator scan then failed too, because the hierarchy descriptor here is four words wide rather than the documented three; decoding one known class hierarchy by hand revealed the extra field. The version-information library call also failed and had to be replaced with a manual parse. What remains unknown is why the descriptors sit in writable memory and what restores the high-entropy pockets in the code section, if anything does.</p>
      </article>

      <h2>Tools: public documentation of the game's file formats</h2>
      <p>The public documentation for the game's file formats is now indexed in one place, and spot checks against real game files matched it: the archive split, the resource wrapper, the text database and the shader packaging all look the way the wiki and tool authors describe. The gaps are also mapped: everything packed inside archives still needs an extraction tool before its documentation can be checked.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Build a complete index of public documentation for every file format the game uses, starting from the modding wiki and the open parsers, and verify at least one documented detail of each format against a real file header. Research and writing only; install nothing.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A read-only census of the game folder counted over five thousand files in four dozen extensions. Two archive families hold nearly all the bytes: dozens of general archives for audio, player models and one data pack, and hundreds of image archives for maps, vehicles, scripts, animation, navigation meshes and paths. The most numerous loose files are vehicle path recordings, fragment tuning files, in-game web pages and compiled shaders.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Header checks matched the documentation for the formats stored as loose files: the general archives use one format version for audio and another for everything else, all loose binary resources share one container with a different version word per resource kind, the text database opens with its documented version and table directory, and the compiled shaders are wrapped platform blobs around standard shader bytecode. Text formats for vehicles, peds, placement, zones, decisions and configuration are plain readable files with commented headers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The documentation landscape, ranked by usefulness, is: the modding wiki prose specs; the open RageLib parser set inside the Unity reimplementation project; the SparkIV archive editor sources; the web-map project, which holds the only navigation-mesh documentation because no other reader exists; the FiveM format library's container reconstruction; script tools; audio tools including a scriptable archive reader on the Python package index; and the closed-source reference viewer with its interchange specs.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Several formats have no prose documentation at all and are only described by reader source code or not at all: effects packages, streaming request lists, control mappings, binary audio configuration, vehicle recordings, save-game internals and the benchmark capture files.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Every format that exists only inside archives could not be header-checked, because checking them needs an extraction tool this task was scoped not to install.</p>

The scripts and raw outputs live in the lane scratch folder.</p>

Licence labels for most open tools could not be confirmed in the time available, so every reuse must check the repository licence file first — two key parsers are reported as copyleft and are reference-only under project rules. The most numerous loose format, vehicle recordings, has the thinnest usable documentation of any common format.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-mainloop-timing">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: start-up, the main loop, threads and timing</h2>
      <p>The engine's start-up, thread and timer machinery is now mapped from the file alone, and the headline is a split picture: the synchronisation and timing calls are all visible, but the main loop itself, render-thread startup and command-line parsing live almost entirely in the encrypted first megabyte of the code section, so a rewrite must validate them behaviourally.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey one engine subsystem working directly on the executable with Python: process start-up after the C runtime, command-line parameters, initialisation order, the main loop, every thread created, synchronisation primitives, timers and frame-time globals, the game clock and pause handling.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game-layer classes of this subsystem left no run-time type information at all: of several thousand class records in the file, none is a game, app, timer or thread class, and the expected names occur nowhere as byte strings either. The only timer-related classes with type records are the engine time manager and a thread-pool work item, plus script-thread classes owned by the script survey.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Strings name one render thread and four audio threads, two timer names, an eight-field game clock (weekday, hours, minutes, seconds, days, months, seconds-per-minute and a bird-cycle field), a crash reporter built on Windows error reporting, frame-pacing settings including a frame limiter and a 15 to 120 frames-per-second automatic quality range, and per-frame logging of frame index, game time and delta. Only two command-line switches survive as strings.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> There is exactly one thread-creation call in the readable code, and it follows a fixed sequence: create suspended, set normal priority, disable priority boost, resume. There is one high-resolution-timer wrapper that caches the counter frequency, while the coarse millisecond timer is called from dozens of sites and is the dominant tick source. Locking is pervasive, with several hundred critical-section calls, and the synchronisation set is era-typical: critical sections, mutexes, semaphores, events and interlocked operations, with no newer primitives imported.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Referencing analysis shows the render-thread name, the frame-timing log strings, the surviving command-line switches and several timer imports are referenced only from the encrypted region. Startup proceeds through numbered checkpoints with fatal exits after reading the command line once.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Public bug reports and mod fixes agree the simulation step is coupled to frame rate: vehicle handling, ragdolls, rotors, ladders and several interface speeds all change above console frame rates, so the rewrite's time step must reproduce the original arithmetic, not just the wall time.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Fact</th><th role="columnheader">Value</th><th role="columnheader">What it means</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Class records scanned</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">a few thousand</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">game-layer timer and thread classes have no type records</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Named threads found</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">one render thread, four audio threads</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">thread inventory for the rewrite to reproduce</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Thread-creation call sites</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">one wrapper with a fixed four-step sequence</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">all engine threads are born the same way</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Timer call sites</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">dozens for the millisecond timer, one wrapper for the high-resolution counter</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">coarse timing everywhere, precise timing in one place</td></tr>
      <tr role="row"><td role="cell">Code clusters attributed</td><td role="cell" data-label="Value">about three hundred, roughly half a megabyte</td><td role="cell" data-label="What it means">mostly shared locking; a handful of small clusters are the true subsystem core</td></tr>
      </tbody>
      </table>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>Rewrite the timer wrappers and command-line handling first, since both are small and checkable in isolation, then the thread-creation wrapper, crash handling and game clock, and the main-loop skeleton last because it sits in encrypted code. The millisecond-timer semantics, including its wrap behaviour, must be reproduced exactly. Two open questions go to follow-up work: whether the few named synchronisation objects have fixed names, and what a counter-gated self-termination sequence near the sleep calls is for.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the relocation table and resolve every fixup inside the readable code to its target; collect targets that are subsystem strings, virtual tables or import slots for thread, time and synchronisation functions; merge nearby referencing code into clusters; confirm the key call sites by their call bytes and short aligned disassembly windows; and search the whole file for the expected class names to establish the negative result. All counts come from these machine steps, not from estimates.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first class filter matched over eight hundred classes because gameplay words like event, task and frame collide with subsystem vocabulary; it took a second pass to show that almost all were other lanes' classes and the true subsystem set is tiny. A verification script re-ran the clustering step through an unguarded import and wiped the function counts, which had to be recomputed. Disassembly windows placed at an offset from each call site usually started mid-instruction and looked like garbage until re-aligned to the exact call address.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-input-ui">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: input, front end and HUD</h2>
      <p>The front end, HUD and input of the game are driven by a large in-house UI widget framework of about fifty classes, a small set of 2D draw commands, and a device layer that reads the keyboard and mouse through the operating system, gamepads through DirectInput and XInput, and all display text through per-language dictionary files. Classic names from older titles in the series do not appear as polymorphic classes, so the menu and HUD code was substantially rebuilt for this engine.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey one engine subsystem directly from the executable: keyboard, mouse and gamepad input, control mapping, the pause menu and front end, the HUD and radar, text and fonts, the phone, subtitles and help text, loading screens, and the localisation text format. The deliverables were the subsystem classes with their base classes and virtual table sizes, its strings, the code regions where it lives, its operating system dependencies, public knowledge about it, frame-rate dependencies, rewrite notes, and a ranked list of what to understand first.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A full scan of the run-time type information found a few thousand classes in the executable, of which about one hundred and ten belong to this subsystem. They fall into a UI widget framework of about fifty classes with very wide virtual tables, fifteen viewport and render-phase classes for the radar, phone, in-game web browser and menu backdrops, seventeen 2D and HUD draw commands, ten HTML browser classes, eight video-editor overlay classes, and a small group for fonts and text.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The text renderer itself has no virtual table, but helper classes leak the names of its two key operations, one that lays a string out for display and one that counts its lines. The in-game web browser parses pages with the engine XML parser, and its text flows through the same text pass as everything else.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> About seven hundred subsystem strings were collected. Gamepads are handled two ways: a built-in list of roughly twenty named DirectInput devices, and an XInput interface loaded at run time rather than linked. The keyboard path reads raw key state plus layout information so several keyboard languages work. A family of named input actions maps devices to game controls, and preference keys cover inverting the mouse and look, controller and mouse sensitivity, vibration, subtitles and keyboard language.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Display text comes from one dictionary file per language, with seven languages present. Fonts are engine texture pages plus metrics files, with separate sets for two of the languages. Menu layout is partly data driven, with an XML menu file, several data files for the HUD and front end, and named texture sets for fonts, blips and radar tiles. Button icons inside text use tilde-delimited tokens.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Cross-referencing the subsystem strings, virtual tables and imported functions against the relocation table produced just over five hundred strong references in the readable code, grouped into nine regions: viewport and HUD setup, HUD text with blips and the HTML browser, input devices, the largest region holding menus, dictionaries, HUD, radar, fonts and input actions, the window hook with 2D effects, two video-editor regions, the UI framework classes, and the title menus. A spot check by disassembly confirmed nearly all sampled references sit inside real instructions.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The subsystem imports only a small operating-system surface: keyboard state, layout and translation, mouse capture, the window message loop, a windows hook, cursor control, one DirectInput entry point, and a millisecond timer. There is no raw-input, no polling key-state, and no operating-system text drawing, so all text is rendered through the 3D interface.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> A rewrite should start with the dictionary format and the font metrics, then the text layout pass, then the 2D draw commands, then the UI framework, then input devices, and last the browser, phone and video editor, because each layer only depends on the ones before it. The dictionary loader, token substitution and input-action mapping are isolated enough to test in a CPU emulator, while anything touching the UI framework, the renderer or the window needs the running game.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The missing classic class names mean the next lane should search the encrypted half of the code after the analysis tooling finishes, rather than assuming the names are gone entirely.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable headers to find the readable code range, walk the run-time type information from type descriptors through object locators to virtual tables to get class names with base classes and slot counts, extract readable strings outside the encrypted range and filter them by subsystem keywords, dump the import tables for the relevant system libraries, then match every relocation in the readable code against the collected string, table and import addresses, verify a sample by disassembly, and cluster nearby references into regions.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The expected class names from older games in the series were absent from the type information, which first looked like a parser bug until exact-name probes over all descriptors confirmed the absence. Early clustering was polluted three ways: a camera-instruction family slipped in through an over-broad name filter, a millisecond timer used by the whole program created false clusters across unrelated code, and physics and audio strings sharing words like axis and rumble matched the keyword list. All three were removed by weighting targets and re-running the attribution, which cut the hit count roughly in half and left clean regions. One sampled reference in twelve failed to decode under the disassembler, most likely a fragment alignment artefact rather than a bad reference.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="subsystem-animation-euphoria">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Subsystem survey: animation and the Euphoria ragdoll system</h2>
      <p>The animation subsystem is large, mostly readable, and cleanly layered: a codec layer for compressed clips, a motion-tree composer with worker threads, a game layer that plays named animations through tasks, and a statically linked Euphoria integration with eighteen named behaviours. Nearly all of its code sits outside the encrypted region.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Survey one engine subsystem working directly on the executable: skeletons, clip playback and blending, inverse kinematics, the Euphoria middleware and its integration, ragdolls, and the hand-off between animation and physics. Deliver class, string, and code-cluster inventories plus rewrite notes.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The survey found about two hundred animation-related classes out of roughly thirty-seven hundred runtime type records in the executable, with just over two hundred virtual tables and around nine hundred distinct method addresses.</p>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Euphoria arrives as a statically linked framework under an internal ART namespace, with an engine root, a per-character instance, a physics-side instance, end-effector drivers, and eighteen behaviour controllers with descriptive names covering balance, falling, impacts, injury reactions, grabbing, head look, and arm gestures.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Animation clips are stored as compressed per-track channels with a family of about fifteen codec variants over floats, integers, booleans, quaternions, and vectors, evaluated through a motion tree of blend, filter, mirror, and frame nodes.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game drives animation through script-visible task types that run named, dictionary, timed, and script animations, plus dedicated fall, get-up, death, injury, and balance tasks, and a ragdoll request event type.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Error and debug text shows animations are looked up by dictionary and id pairs, ragdoll state is guarded with explicit failure messages, blending exposes speed and amount parameters, and Euphoria data lives under its own asset path.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Code references cluster into about ninety tight groups spanning roughly one hundred eighty kilobytes, plus a looser view of about fifty groups spanning roughly five hundred kilobytes. Two apparent clusters turned out to be data embedded in the code section rather than code.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The only operating system functions referenced from animation code regions are thread synchronisation primitives, matching a named scheduler that evaluates motion trees on worker threads. There is no Euphoria dynamic library; the middleware is linked directly into the executable.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The subsystem holds a few hundred functions and a few hundred kilobytes of code, with about nine in ten method addresses outside the encrypted region.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> No runtime type record exists for the skeleton itself or for the core blender, so both are probably plain data or non-polymorphic types; likewise there are no message classes under the expected middleware messaging name, so the script-side message wrapper must live above the ART interface.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> A rewrite should proceed bottom-up: channel codecs first, then frame filters and bone masks, then motion-tree nodes and the composer, then the clip player and task glue, with the Euphoria behaviour layer and the physics hand-off last as the hardest part. The codecs, filters, and blend math are pure buffer functions that can be checked in a CPU emulator in isolation, while scheduling, tasks, ragdoll transitions, and anything streamed needs the running game.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Public bug reports confirm the physics and ragdoll simulation assume a narrow frame-rate range and break above it, so the rewrite must pin down timestep handling early rather than treating it as a detail.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Parse the executable's runtime type records and relocation table with standard binary tooling, filter class names by animation and middleware keywords, expand one round through inheritance, find virtual tables by scanning data sections for hierarchy pointers, and cluster code references found at relocation positions in the unencrypted code only. Capstone spot checks at virtual table targets confirm real function starts. Full class, string, and cluster inventories are kept as data files with the survey.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The system symbol decoder returned garbled output for runtime type names, so a small hand-written pretty printer was used instead. One analysis run died early when its output was piped through a truncating pager and had to be rerun. Broad keywords swept particle-system and video strings into the results and had to be excluded by hand. Import attribution picked up unrelated one-off system calls from shared utility code overlapping the clusters. The expected middleware messaging classes do not exist in the binary, which cost a search round before the real interface namespace was identified.</p>
      </article>

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The executable holds about 163,000 text strings, and they yield around 12,800 naming hints, enough to suggest names for roughly 560 functions plus nearly 3,700 engine class names from runtime type data. The binary is otherwise almost fully stripped: only three source file paths survive.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Extract every ASCII and wide-character string of length four or more from all sections of the game executable, classify them into naming categories, trace each name back to the code that uses it through the relocation table, and estimate how many functions could be named this way.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> String counts by category, with distinct texts in brackets: uncategorized 140,820 (61,960), script-facing identifiers 10,417 (6,068), runtime type names 3,727 (3,727), asset names 2,582 (1,022), format strings 2,381 (1,656), config keys 1,236 (622), error messages 1,159 (575), Class::Method names 307 (107), shader names 199 (128), console commands 110 (75), registry and URL strings 33 (23), source paths 10 (8).</p>

The main code is not encrypted, since thousands of its embedded addresses resolve to real strings.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The hint table is ready for the disassembly lane to join against its function map: each hint carries the referencing code address, so attaching a name is a matter of finding the containing function. Class names from runtime type data should be propagated separately through virtual tables. Strings from code, relocation, resource and packed sections should be distrusted unless they carry a reference.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Run the lane script named mine.py from the scratch folder with the project Python environment. It reads only the original executable, scans every section for ASCII and wide-character runs, classifies them with documented patterns, resolves the relocation table to string cross-references, and writes the string list, the hint table, the source tree and the statistics files in under a minute.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first classifier pass produced thousands of false hits from machine code bytes that happen to look like text. Filtering by section and by whether anything references the string removed nearly all of them. Runtime type names initially showed zero references because the recorded pointer aims eight bytes before the name, at the type record header; accounting for that offset resolved all of them. A quirk worth knowing: two anti-tamper label strings contain the letters HKCR by coincidence and were briefly mistaken for registry keys.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="renderer-survey">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Renderer survey: what the executable and shader files reveal</h2>
      <p>The game uses a deferred renderer on Direct3D 9 with shader model 3 throughout: a four-target geometry buffer, stencil-masked deferred lighting, cascaded shadow maps, and a full high dynamic range post chain. All shaders ship precompiled in per-graphics-vendor variants, and the executable talks to Direct3D only through one creation call plus interface calls.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Gather everything the executable and game folder reveal about the renderer, to prepare a later renderer rewrite. Static reading only: Direct3D-related strings and rendering class names from the executable, how the graphics device is called, the shader files in the game folder with their format and versions, the render phases and their likely order, public write-ups of the pipeline, and what a new renderer would need that the original does not produce.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The executable imports a single graphics function and loads no shader compiler library, so every shader is precompiled and all drawing goes through graphics interface calls.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The geometry buffer has four targets, lit by a dedicated deferred lighting shader with about thirty light parameters, with stencil masking for light volumes.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Shadows combine a cascade atlas in two depth formats with cube shadow maps for point lights and a separate shadow conversion pass.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The post chain includes exposure adaptation, bloom, depth of field, motion blur, light shafts and tone mapping, fed by quarter-size and blur scratch targets.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game folder holds just over one hundred unique shaders in six graphics-vendor variants, plus small text preset files, text vertex declarations, and an ordered preload list. Every shader is vertex and pixel shader model 3, nothing older.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Class names show resource wrappers for textures, render targets and buffers, a dozen model and shader classes, twenty five render phases, thirty five small draw-command classes, and bucket-sorted draw lists built on worker threads.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The likely frame order is shadow depth and reflections, then geometry buffer, then lighting, then transparent and forward effects, then post processing, then interface drawing.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>A new renderer needs per-pixel motion vectors and a jittered projection, since the original produces neither; its motion blur is camera-parameter based.</li>
      <li>The six vendor shader variants should be diffed and collapsed to one set, and the geometry buffer channel packing read from the decompiled shaders, before any rewrite.</li>
      <li>Exact graphics call counts need a running capture, not the file, because the executable code section is packed and all device calls are indirect.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>List printable strings in the executable and filter for graphics, shading and phase names; list the class names embedded for run-time type information and group them by prefix; confirm the import list shows one graphics creation call and no shader compiler; walk the shader folders in the game install, count files per variant directory, and scan the compiled shaders for shader-model version markers. Public cross-checks are the well-known <a href="https://www.adriancourreges.com/blog/2015/11/02/gta-v-graphics-study/">graphics study of the newer engine entry</a>, the <a href="https://github.com/robi29/GTA-IV-Shaders">decompiled shader collection</a> with its fix notes, and the <a href="https://github.com/ThirteenAG/GTAIV.EFLC.FusionFix">community fix project</a> documenting shadow, depth precision and water issues.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first disassembly attempt produced nonsense, and a byte-entropy check showed the start of the code section is encrypted by the executable packer, so the planned call-site counting had to fall back to a raw byte-pattern estimate with wide error bars. The first class-grouping script silently dropped whole groups because of a name-prefix parsing bug, caught by comparing group counts against a direct search. One shipped reference file dumped far more listing text than expected and truncated a tool result, so later passes wrote to files and printed summaries only.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="pointer-tables">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Pointer tables: the functions calls alone cannot reach</h2>
      <p>Most of the game's indirectly called functions are now mapped: about three thousand virtual tables confirmed through type data, two dozen dispatch tables dominated by online-service handlers, over two thousand switch jump tables, and nearly fourteen thousand code targets that no direct call reaches. The planned method failed first — the relocation table turned out to be unusable — and the first pages of the code section are encrypted, so everything below comes from value-based scanning of the readable parts only.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Find the function pointer tables in the executable's data, because functions reachable only through pointers are easy for analysis tools to miss. The task named five classes to look for: C++ virtual tables, C runtime initialiser arrays, callback and dispatch tables, switch jump tables, and anything unclassified, plus counts, the functions reachable only through pointers, the static constructor count, and the largest dispatch tables with string evidence.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The relocation table cannot be used as a detector. Of roughly 292,000 entries, nearly half sit at unaligned offsets a linker would never emit, and under 3% of the values they point at land anywhere inside the image. Detection was rebuilt on values instead: runs of consecutive words in data sections whose contents fall inside the code section.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first 250 pages of the code section are encrypted or obfuscated: per-page entropy near maximum and no decodable instructions, against normal code entropy everywhere after a page-exact boundary. A separate section holds a byte-identical copy of that encrypted prefix plus one page. Table slots landing in the encrypted region, about sixteen hundred of them, have unknown reachability.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Raw value scanning found over eleven thousand runs, but three fifths were text, not pointers: lowercase prose and UTF-16 strings fall numerically inside the huge code range all the time. A byte-pattern filter removed nearly seven thousand text runs, including every large fake dispatch-looking and fake initialiser-looking run.</p>

      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row"><th role="columnheader">Table class</th><th role="columnheader">Tables</th><th role="columnheader">Slots</th><th role="columnheader">Standing</th></tr>

      <tbody role="rowgroup">
