      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The confirmed virtual tables name just over three thousand distinct classes, mostly engine and audio names. <span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The largest dispatch table, with just over two thousand slots, points at evenly spaced stubs that each push an identifier, which reads like a script-native registration table. Nearly every other large dispatch table sits beside online-service strings: presence, matchmaking, tickets, authentication, clans, friends, and net messages, each handler scattered across its own subsystem with a repeated default entry.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Jump tables use plain 32-bit absolute addresses: for over a thousand tables the address baked into a nearby table-jump instruction equals the table address exactly. Their targets are case labels inside functions, not function entries, so they are counted separately. Three data-resident jump tables have byte-identical twins elsewhere in data, presumably backup copies like the encrypted code copy.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nearly fourteen thousand distinct readable-code targets appear in data tables but in no direct call instruction; all but a small fraction also appear in no direct jump. These are the functions reachable only through pointers, as an upper bound, since calls from the encrypted region are invisible. There are zero TLS callbacks. <span class="evidence">Unknown</span> The static constructor count could not be established: every large null-delimited run proved to be something else, and the startup code that would anchor the real initialiser groups sits in the encrypted region.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Later tools must not trust the relocation table for pointer detection; the lane's value-based tables ship as JSON instead.</li>
      <li>Backup copies (the encrypted code duplicate and the twinned jump tables) should be deduplicated by content hash before any function counting.</li>
      <li>The small unclassified runs still mix string fragments with real pointer pairs and need per-item review, starting with the ones flanked by encrypted-region pointers.</li>
      <li>Static constructors stay unknown until an unpacking or dynamic lane reads the startup code; candidate groups are listed in the lane report.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Work only on a copy of the executable with read-only scripts. Map the sections and confirm the encrypted prefix by per-page entropy, then scan the file-backed data sections for runs of consecutive aligned words valued inside the code range. Drop runs whose bytes are UTF-16 or printable ASCII, confirm virtual tables through the type-descriptor name behind each table's header pointer, census direct calls by scanning readable code for call and jump opcodes, and verify jump-table encoding by comparing each nearby table-jump instruction's embedded address against the table address. The lane's scripts run in this order: layout survey, relocation probe, encryption probe, value scan, bridged and filtered passes, then relabelling.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>The first full analysis trusted the relocation table and reported sixteen tables; the real count was thousands. That failure took one probe to diagnose and forced the value-based rewrite. The value scan then reported over eleven thousand runs, most of them strings, and the classifier initially labelled nearly three hundred string runs as initialiser tables — the byte-pattern text filter fixed that but certainly left string fragments among the small unknowns. Two self-checks were built on flawed reasoning and caught before shipping: a span comparison meant to test address encoding is translation-invariant and proves nothing, and a merge pass for split runs was unnecessary because runs already spanned encrypted-region slots. Both were replaced with direct evidence.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="p0-libraries">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Library inventory: what the executable borrows, and what it owns</h2>
      <p>The executable statically links six third-party or runtime code bases (zlib, libjpeg, a CyaSSL-era TLS stack, Bullet collision detection, NaturalMotion Euphoria, and the C runtime), keeps three more behind external DLLs or services (Bink video, Steamworks, Social Club), and encrypts its first megabyte of code with an unidentified packer. Roughly one fifth of the code section is library code; the rest is engine and game.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Identify the third-party and runtime library code statically linked into the game executable so it can be excluded from the rewrite queue, with evidence, versions where stated, code locations, Rich-header toolchain clues, an estimate of the library share of the code section, and a note of which middleware has no source and no open replacement.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> zlib 1.2.3 (2005) is linked in, identified by its inflate and deflate banners, its error strings, and its checksum constant used as code immediates.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> An IJG JPEG codec is linked in, identified by its full error-message table including encoder warnings. No version string survives, so the exact release is unknown.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A TLS stack is linked in, identified by a large table of cipher-suite names and error strings plus a bundled set of CA certificates. <span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The string set matches CyaSSL 2.x, the library later renamed to wolfSSL, circa 2012 to 2014. Hash support is confirmed present but the AES tables could not be found in any readable section, so part of the crypto may sit inside the encrypted region.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Bullet Physics is linked in as collision detection only: broadphase, dispatcher, and a handful of narrowphase algorithms, with RAGE-written wrappers. No rigid-body dynamics, no soft bodies, and no Havok anywhere.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> NaturalMotion Euphoria is linked in behind a Rockstar-authored layer, with dozens of behaviour classes for shot reactions, falls, balance, grabbing, flinching, and stairs. This is the largest middleware item and the only one with neither source nor an open replacement.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The C runtime is statically linked: no runtime DLL is imported. Standard C++ library use is essentially zero; the engine uses its own containers.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Bink video, Steamworks, and the Social Club SDK contribute only small glue code in the executable (a video-player wrapper, a Steam API loader with callbacks, COM-shaped stubs). The real code lives in external DLLs and services.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Absent as linked code: PNG, Ogg Vorbis, Speex, MP3, FLAC, Miles, FMOD, OpenAL, curl, Lua, any script language, Scaleform or any UI middleware, any XML parser library, LZX or other compression beyond zlib, Havok, PhysX, Granny, D3DX, OpenSSL banners, and all Games-for-Windows-Live traces. Audio decode is the engine plus operating-system codecs, with user MP3 tracks transcoded by a separate helper process.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first megabyte of the code section is encrypted and a second section holds a verbatim copy of it. The entry point sits in a tiny unpacker stub. No known packer or DRM brand markers were found, so the protector is unidentified.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Library and runtime code is about fifteen to twenty-five percent of the code section, best guess one fifth. The mapped libraries account for roughly one eighth in readable code; the rest of the estimate allows for runtime startup and crypto inside the encrypted megabyte.</p>

      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <p>The mapped library ranges should be excluded from the rewrite queue, and Euphoria plus the Social Club online layer should be planned as clean-room reimplementation rather than ports. The encrypted first megabyte must be revisited after a runtime memory dump before its contents can be queued or excluded. The Rich header shows a 2012-era rebuild with a small residue of older prebuilt objects, consistent with most middleware having been rebuilt from source.</p>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>All checks run offline against the executable with Python and a PE parser. Extract printable strings and search for version banners (zlib), error tables (JPEG, TLS), interface names (Steam, Social Club), and import names (Bink, runtime). List class names from runtime type information to confirm Bullet, Euphoria, and the absence of standard-library use. Scan for well-known constants such as hash tables and cipher boxes. Walk the relocation table from each identifying data block back to the code that references it, then follow class tables to member functions to bound each library's code range. Measure per-block entropy of the code section to find the encrypted region, and compare the spare section against it byte for byte.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Two keyword hits looked like libraries but were game words: bullet impact effects are ammunition, not Bullet Physics, and toggle text is not the Ogg container. A Lua hit turned out to be random bytes inside encrypted code. The SHA-256 table first looked like a false positive because it sits directly after a text translation table, but the surrounding finished-message labels confirmed it belongs to the TLS code. The Steam DLL name appears nowhere in the file even though the API names do, which remains unexplained. The vtable walk initially matched nothing because class tables point eight bytes before the name string, not at it; the windowed pass before that fix overstated every range. About one tenth of the relocation targets read as garbage until the encrypted region explained them.</p>

      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Ghidra compiles scripts at run time, so mistakes only surface when a script executes. The first real run caught a naming clash: two scripts defined a helper with the same name as a built-in script method, and neither compiled until the helper was renamed.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The JSON library silently drops fields whose value is null, which made the first schema ragged. Enabling explicit null output fixed it.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first cross-reference dump was mostly noise from stack references and the first call graph pointed at import entries with no function records. Both were fixed by filtering to memory targets and exporting imported functions, as described above. No game data was touched at any point; the game project stayed locked by its own analysis throughout.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="startup-stub">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>The start-up stub: a tiny loader, an encrypted first megabyte, and an external unlocker</h2>
      <p>The game does not start in its own code. A loader stub of about six hundred bytes runs first, loads a Rockstar wrapper module shipped beside the game, lets it prepare the process, then hands control to the normal C start-up routine. The first megabyte of the code section is encrypted on disk and a read-only section holds an identical backup copy of it.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Explain what happens between process start and the game's real entry point: what the stub in the small executable section does step by step, what the one megabyte high-entropy section is, what runs before the real entry point, how the shipped launcher starts the game, and whether any of this interferes with analysis or with loading extra code into the process.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The entry point sits at the first byte of a tiny writable and executable section. The stub finds the system library through the process loader list instead of using imports, then loads a wrapper module by name and resolves two single-letter functions from it by walking its export table by hand.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The stub calls the first wrapper function once with no arguments, then calls the second one in a loop until it reports success, passing it the locations of the thread-storage and relocation tables. It then unloads the wrapper and jumps to the real entry point.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The one megabyte section is byte-for-byte identical to the first megabyte of the code section, and that first megabyte is encrypted: maximum entropy, incompressible, and disassembles as nonsense. The boundary between encrypted and normal code falls exactly on a page boundary one page before the end of the copy.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The encrypted region holds heavily used code: tens of thousands of call sites and over sixteen thousand linker-confirmed pointers from the rest of the program reach into it, including the call to the main window function from the C start-up code. It must be decrypted before the game can run.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> No game code references the backup copy. It is mapped read-only, so the game cannot corrupt it. It is most likely the wrapper's pristine reference for decrypting and integrity checks.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nothing runs before the stub except the operating system loader. The thread-storage callback list is empty, and the stub's own callback-dispatch code can never execute because its guard condition is always false.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The real entry point is an ordinary C start-up routine of the expected compiler generation: cookie check, exception-handler setup, a check of the program's own headers, command-line retrieval, then a call into the main window function.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The wrapper module exports only the two functions the stub calls. Its own code is obfuscated, and its imports show it can scan processes and modules, change memory protection, read process memory, terminate processes, and detect debuggers.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Signature-checking functions are called from one cluster of game code far from the stub. The code verifies an Authenticode signature, treats a missing or bad signature as not verified rather than fatal, and inspects the signer certificate and timestamps. A separate pair of data-protection calls sits elsewhere and looks like save-data encryption.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The game is normally started through a 64-bit launcher stub that reads two metadata files, supports store-specific launch paths with documented command-line flags, enforces a single instance, and hands off to the Rockstar Games Launcher, which starts the game itself.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Static analysis of the first megabyte of code is blocked until it is decrypted; disassemblers will show garbage there, while callers elsewhere in the program stay visible. The import table is intact, so API usage remains readable.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Loading an extra module into the process is not blocked by the stub itself, but the wrapper scans the process before the game starts, so injected modules may be noticed. This needs live testing to confirm.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Replacing functions in memory at run time is mechanically normal, but the pristine backup copy and the wrapper's memory-reading ability mean integrity re-checks are plausible. Whether any run after start-up is unknown.</li>
      <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The wrapper's retry loop and the signature checks deserve dynamic observation in a sandbox before any lane depends on start-up behaviour.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>All results come from static reads of the game executable and the two files shipped beside it, using a PE parser and a disassembler library from throwaway scripts. The checks were: section table and entropy survey; full disassembly of the stub section with manual decoding of its five embedded strings; byte comparison of the backup section against the code section; a page-by-page entropy scan to find the encryption boundary; counting linker relocation records that point into the encrypted range; reading the thread-storage directory and its empty callback list; disassembly of the real entry point; import-table review of the wrapper and launcher; and string and metadata review of the launcher. No game code was executed and no protection was defeated.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Linear disassembly of the stub initially misread its embedded strings as instructions, which hid the real control flow until a raw dump revealed the call-and-capture pattern. A first scan for references to the backup section returned dozens of hits that all turned out to be misaligned decoding artefacts and coincidental numbers in graphics data, which only became clear after checking each one against aligned disassembly and the relocation table. The wrapper takes the thread-storage and relocation locations as arguments for reasons that remain unknown.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="game-folder-inventory">

      <h2>What the game folder contains</h2>

The loose tree around them is mostly plain-text tuning data, compiled shaders in six graphics-vendor variants, and a surprisingly talkative set of developer leftovers.</p>

Headers, counts and sizes only; no archive contents were to be extracted.</p>

A third bundled installer, a Visual C++ redistributable, is present but referenced by neither install script, so it no longer runs.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The shipped tree still contains developer material: spreadsheet sources of tuning tables, a test script, test-rig names, 3D-editor source paths in map files, and a console development-kit path in an audio settings file. None of it is needed by the game.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Format lanes can start on the loose text formats and the resource container now; the format table in the lane data file lists magics, versions and public references for every extension.</li>
      <li>Script and model inventories need a lane that can read the encrypted disc-image archives without extracting game content into the repo; the loose tree gives no script coverage at all.</li>
      <li>Two binaries need a follow-up lane: one support library exports only two single-letter names with no stated purpose, and the game program carries no visible reference to the multiplayer-platform library shipped beside it.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Walk the install folder read-only, group by extension, and sample the first bytes of a few files per type; compare magics against the public format pages on the community modding wiki and the video codec vendor page. Analyse the nine shipped programs with a portable-executable reader for architecture, imports and exports, and read the two Steam install scripts as text. The lane data file records every count, magic word and import list.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> One archive breaks the encryption pattern: all disc images but one look random, while the navigation-script image starts with a readable structured header. Also surprising: none of the nine shipped programs contains version information, so link dates are the only build dating, and the game program neither imports nor names two of the libraries shipped next to it. A first attempt at dumping version strings failed on the reader library's nested list layout and was fixed by probing for the string table defensively. Nothing was left half done except the five open questions listed in the lane report.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="public-names">
      <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
      <h2>Public engine class names collected and checked against our build</h2>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Nearly all of the engine classes named inside our executable have no public documentation: 1596 of 1664 distinct class names found in our build appear in none of the public sources, while 68 publicly documented names were confirmed present, so the project now has a ranked list of the 100 most important classes with the best public source for each.</p>
      <h3>What was asked</h3>
      <p>Collect public class and structure names for this game's engine from other builds and projects so they can later be matched to our executable: the RAGE API notes and investigation documents in <a href="https://github.com/OZORDI/LibertyRecomp">LibertyRecomp</a>, the <a href="https://github.com/Zolika1351/iv-sdk">IV-SDK</a> headers, IV-SDK .NET, the <a href="https://github.com/Neproify/ivmultiplayer">IV multiplayer</a> client headers, <a href="https://github.com/DK22Pac/plugin-sdk">plugin-sdk</a> GTA IV headers, and <a href="https://github.com/Yimura/GTAV-Classes">GTAV-Classes</a>. Then extract the class names from our own executable, cross-reference the two sets, rank the 100 most important classes, and record every source licence. Names and layouts only, no code copying.</p>
      <h3>What was found</h3>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Our executable names 3723 distinct RTTI types, demangled into 1664 distinct class names, of which 478 sit in the rage namespace. The largest families are tasks, cameras, network messages, animation, events, audio, physics, rendering commands, and particles.</p>
      <table role="table">
      <thead role="rowgroup">
      <tr role="row">

      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The core entity, physics, streaming, model info, camera, task, event, network and render-command names match across sources and our build, including all thirteen named render-command subclasses from the LibertyRecomp investigation. Two independent public readings of the player-info layout agree field for field.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Four sources are GPL licensed (LibertyRecomp, IV-SDK, IV-SDK .NET, IV multiplayer), plugin-sdk is permissively licensed, and GTAV-Classes has no licence and no content: it was emptied by its owner and archived, so the rage primitives came from plugin-sdk and LibertyRecomp instead.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Several SDK struct names with a temporary air about them have no footprint in our build and are probably invented by SDK authors rather than real engine names; they remain useful as layout hypotheses but not as vocabulary.</p>
      <p><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> A handful of engine classes the public headers describe as central, including the audio engine, graphics device, script program, and page streamer, have no type entry at all in our build. They may be renamed here, built without type info, or described from a different version.</p>
      <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
      <ul>
      <li>Every layout from an older build stays marked as unverified here until re-measured against our build, since IV-SDK itself warns that classes differ between versions.</li>
      <li>Where two public sources disagree on a layout, both readings are recorded and neither is trusted; the next lane re-measures rather than picking a winner.</li>
      <li>After the entity core, the highest-value documentation targets are the thirty top-100 classes with type entries here but no public documentation anywhere, mostly physics, rendering, audio, and task classes.</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
      <p>Scan the executable for the standard MSVC runtime type descriptor string prefixes, keep the terminated names, and demangle the simple and template cases; then fetch the listed public headers and documents as plain web pages and match unqualified class names, mapping the multiplayer client's mirror prefix to the game prefix. The lane's scratch folder holds the scan script, the raw name inventory, the public class data, and the cross-reference with the ranked hundred.</p>
      <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
      <p>Large public files arrived cut off partway, so three big headers and two long documents are only partially collected; the gaps are listed in the lane report for a follow-up with full-file fetching. Two guessed header paths returned not-found, which corrected the inventory rather than costing much: vehicle subclasses have almost no public PC layout, and the player-info mirror lives under a different filename than expected. The most confusing result was the missing type entries for supposedly central engine classes; absence of a type entry proves nothing for types without virtual functions, but for virtual-heavy classes it is a genuine puzzle left open for a string and vtable hunt.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="encrypted-prefix">
        <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
        <h2>Correction: the first megabyte of the code is encrypted</h2>
        <p>About 9% of the code section is encrypted on disk, and the first look at the executable missed it. The first 1,028,096 bytes of the code section are indistinguishable from random data, and a separate section named <code>.tbm</code> holds a byte-for-byte copy of the same bytes. The remaining 9.9 MB is ordinary compiled code.</p>

        <h3>What was asked</h3>
        <p>A lane estimating the number of functions reported that the code section looked encrypted, which contradicted the coordinator's earlier reading. Which was right?</p>

        <h3>What was found</h3>
        <ul>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Measured in 256 KB windows, the first four windows of the code section have an entropy of 8.00, 8.00, 8.00 and 7.97 bits per byte. Every window after that is between 5.6 and 6.6, which is normal for compiled code.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The first four windows contain no standard function prologues and no padding between functions. Every later window contains hundreds to thousands of each.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The <code>.tbm</code> section is exactly 1,028,096 bytes and is identical to the first 1,028,096 bytes of the code section.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> The start-up stub in <code>.rkstr</code> probably decrypts this range in memory before the game runs, as part of Rockstar's protection for this build. A lane is analysing the stub; this has not been confirmed.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> What code lives in the encrypted range, how many functions it holds, and why the same bytes are stored twice.</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>What was confusing or went wrong</h3>
        <ul>
          <li>The coordinator computed one entropy figure for the whole section, got 6.71, and wrote "not packed or encrypted". An average over 10.95 MB cannot show a 1 MB anomaly. The fix is to measure in windows, always.</li>
          <li>The mistake was caught within minutes because an independent lane measured the same thing a different way. Two lanes looking at the same file from different angles is worth the duplication.</li>
          <li>The Ghidra analysis had already started and was disassembling the encrypted bytes as if they were code, producing nonsense functions and call targets. It was stopped and restarted with that range split into its own block and marked non-executable.</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
        <ul>
          <li>Until the range has been read from a running copy, every tool treats it as opaque data. It is excluded from function counts, from the queue and from the code map, and the progress figures state its size separately so the percentages are honest.</li>
          <li>The coordinator first wrote that the project would never read this range from the running game, citing the anti-piracy rule. That was the coordinator's own over-reach, and the owner corrected it the same day: the anti-piracy rule is about piracy, not about analysing a copy the owner bought. The range will be read from the owner's own running, purchased copy and analysed like the rest of the code.</li>
          <li>What is read that way is game code. It stays in the private, ignored folders and is never committed or published, like all other game code.</li>
          <li>The project still distributes no game files, keys or cracks, and does nothing to help anyone run the game without buying it.</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
        <p>Read the code section with <code>pefile</code>, cut it into 256 KB windows and compute the Shannon entropy of each. Count the byte sequence of the standard function prologue and runs of padding bytes per window. Compare the first megabyte of the code section with the contents of <code>.tbm</code>.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="ghidra-dot-path">
        <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
        <h2>Ghidra refuses project folders that start with a dot</h2>
        <p>Ghidra will not create or open a project if any folder in the project's path has a name starting with a dot. This repository keeps all generated files under a folder named <code>.artifacts</code>, so the first headless analysis failed immediately.</p>
        <h3>What was found</h3>
        <ul>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Ghidra 12.1.4 headless aborts with "Path element starting with '.' is not permitted" when the project location is under a dot-prefixed folder. The check is on the path text, not on where the data physically lives.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Script folders passed with the script path argument may live under a dot-prefixed folder. Only the project location is checked.</li>
        </ul>
        <h3>What was decided or recommended</h3>
        <p>The Ghidra project is addressed through a directory junction whose path has no dot, <code>tools/ghidra-db</code>, which points at <code>.artifacts/cache/ghidra</code>. The data stays with the other caches and Ghidra sees a path it accepts. Any lane that needs a Ghidra project must use the junction path.</p>
        <h3>How to reproduce it</h3>
        <p>Run the headless analyser with a project directory under any folder whose name begins with a dot.</p>
      </article>

A search for 2026 results showed agent-driven decompilations finishing in weeks. The working estimate now rests on one comparable agent project and will be replaced by measured throughput after the phase 2 pilot.</p>
        <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The coordinator reasoned from the GTA III decompilation, which took a small team about two years, and arrived at a multi-year effort. A web search on 2026-10-03 produced the figures below and the estimate was revised. Lesson: search for current evidence before estimating agent throughput.</p>

      <article class="entry" id="route">
        <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
        <h2>Why the route is direct to Rust</h2>
        <p>Lanes read decompiler output from a private folder and write Rust directly, with no committed C++ stage. Each rewrite is checked by running the original function and the Rust version in a CPU emulator from the same state. This follows from the owner's rule that no decompiled code may be committed, and from the goal that the game becomes 64-bit and portable.</p>

        <h3>The route changed three times</h3>
        <ol>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A from-scratch engine that loads the original assets. Rejected once the evidence showed that decompiling is fast and carries mission logic, AI and ragdoll behaviour across intact.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Decompile to C++, rebuild, then port to Rust. Rejected because only structures, symbols and Rust rewrites may be committed, so a C++ stage cannot be kept, and an uncommitted months-long intermediate is a loss risk.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Rewrite directly to Rust. Current route, and one phase shorter.</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>What the direct route costs</h3>
        <ul>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Byte-matching against the original compiler is impossible for Rust, so every byte-matching tool in the reviewed projects is out. The check is an emulator comparison: results, memory writes and outgoing calls must agree. Both sides run in the emulator, so it does not depend on the game running on this ARM64 machine.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The second check swaps accepted functions into the running game through an injected 32-bit DLL with a per-function switch. A regression is found by switching replacements off in halves.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Known weakness: floating-point results can differ in the last bits, so those comparisons need a tolerance, and a tolerance can hide a real difference. The in-game switch is the backstop.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence">Unknown</span> Whether the emulator comparison works at scale. It is our own design and no other project has proven it. The phase 1 gate of 50 accepted functions tests it.</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Why Rust, and what that forces</h3>
        <p><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> The Rust port exists to make the game 64-bit and portable to Windows x64, Windows ARM64 and macOS. That forces the following work, which is why 64-bit and renderer work wait until after phase 4.</p>
        <ul>
          <li>Euphoria, the animation and ragdoll middleware, is statically linked 32-bit code with no source. It must be rewritten like game code.</li>
          <li>Bink video needs a replacement decoder.</li>
          <li>Resource files hold 32-bit pointers, so a converting loader is needed.</li>
          <li>The script virtual machine needs pointer handles.</li>
          <li>All Windows and Direct3D 9 calls go behind a platform layer.</li>
          <li>The renderer must output motion vectors, depth and jitter for upscalers.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Path tracing on macOS would need native Metal, because MoltenVK does not expose ray tracing as far as we know.</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Xbox 360 static recompilation against function-by-function rewriting</h3>
        <p><span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Lane D compared the routes. Its facts about the 360 projects come from their repositories (<a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hedge-dev/XenonRecomp/main/README.md">XenonRecomp</a>, <a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OZORDI/LibertyRecomp/main/LibertyRecomp/api/RAGE/README.md">LibertyRecomp RAGE API</a>). Its PC column is its own assessment. It concluded that the 360 route is the better base for a quick playable port and the worse base for reconstructing source.</p>
        <table role="table">
          <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row">
            <th role="columnheader">Dimension</th>
            <th role="columnheader">Xbox 360 recompilation</th>
            <th role="columnheader">PC rewrite</th>
          </tr></thead>
          <tbody role="rowgroup">
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">Output</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Xbox 360 recompilation">Unreadable by design. Every function takes a machine-state context.</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="PC rewrite">The product is the readable code. No second lifting phase.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">Rust suitability</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Xbox 360 recompilation">Hostile. Big-endian memory, reversed vector lanes and goto control flow would carry into Rust.</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="PC rewrite">Clean. Only names and layouts come from the 360 side.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">Memory model</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Xbox 360 recompilation">Byte swap on every load and store, permanently.</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="PC rewrite">Little-endian 32-bit x86, like for like with modern hosts.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">Time to playable</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Xbox 360 recompilation">Fastest demonstrated. One independent port reached gameplay except collision.</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="PC rewrite">Slowest. Playable only after a critical mass of rewrites.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">New gameplay</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Xbox 360 recompilation">Constrained. Patches wrap original functions and the engine stays a black box.</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="PC rewrite">Unconstrained, at the cost of understanding everything.</td>
            </tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
      </article>

      <article class="entry" id="harness">
        <div class="entry-meta"><time datetime="2026-10-03">2026-10-03</time></div>
        <h2>Harness design taken from other projects</h2>
        <p>Thief 3 (MSVC 7.1, x86) has the closest toolchain and the most developed agent harness, so the plan copies its structure. The parts that make a compiler reproduce original bytes do not apply, because Rust cannot. The byte-match gate is replaced by the emulator comparison.</p>

        <h3>Parts taken, with the real numbers</h3>
        <ul>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Queue. A script orders functions easiest first and lanes do not choose. Thief 3 scores instruction count plus 3 per branch, 2 per call, 10 per switch, 10 per exception frame and 1 per x87 instruction (<a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Veradictus/Thief3-Decomp/main/tools/agent/next.py">next.py</a>). Snowboard Kids 2 later fitted its weights by logistic regression, and stack size predicted nothing (<a href="http://blog.chrislewis.au/the-unexpected-effectiveness-of-one-shot-decompilation-with-claude/">blog</a>).</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Claims. One file per claimed function, created atomically, expiring after 2 hours and renewed by every attempt.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Context packet: the target, resolved references with names, structures touched, the most similar accepted functions with source, names that accepted callers already use, the family, and the best earlier attempt on a second pass (<a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Veradictus/Thief3-Decomp/main/tools/agent/context.py">context.py</a>).</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Attempt budget: cap of 12 per claim, stop after 4 counted attempts with no new best. The code comment cites replayed ledgers: 3 would have refused 10 of 1,219 matches to save 36 attempts, and 4 refuses 2 to save 18 (<a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Veradictus/Thief3-Decomp/main/tools/agent/common.py">common.py</a>). <span class="evidence">Inferred</span> Another lane read the workflow document and recorded 3, so sources disagree. The code is more likely current. Snowboard Kids 2 reportedly gives up after about 30 attempts, seen only in a fork.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Deferral is a normal outcome, recorded with a blocker tag. Permanently unworkable functions move to an exclusion list.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Routing by size. Functions up to 31 bytes: 20 per worker, cap 5. From 32 to 79 bytes: by class, cap 8. From 80 bytes: the stronger model, cap 10. A second pass uses the other model. Workers stay under about 100 tool calls and up to 20 run at once.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Families. Functions identical after masking references are grouped. One accepted member is stamped onto the rest and passed through the same gate with no model call.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Guard rails live in tooling. Thief 3 workers write only under a scratch folder and run only four scripts, enforced by a pre-tool hook that also denies git (<a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Veradictus/Thief3-Decomp/main/tools/agent/guard-settings.json">guard-settings.json</a>).</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> A lint runs on every candidate, and every batch ends with a sweep that releases stale claims and appends cost, attempts and deferral reasons to a ledger.</li>
          <li><span class="evidence verified">Verified</span> Smaller ideas. Nigel defines a lane as a candidate command, a prompt template, and verify, success and reset commands (<a href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cdlewis/nigel/main/README.md">README</a>). The asmlift prompt demands two deliverables of equal standing: merged work and a tool defect log ranked by cost.</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>What applies to us</h3>
        <table role="table">
          <thead role="rowgroup"><tr role="row">
            <th role="columnheader">Part</th>
            <th role="columnheader">For LibertyFlux</th>
            <th role="columnheader">Reason</th>
          </tr></thead>
          <tbody role="rowgroup">
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">Queue, claims, guard rails, sweep</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="For LibertyFlux">Unchanged</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Reason">Independent of language and of the check.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">Lint</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="For LibertyFlux">New rules</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Reason">No inline assembly, no hard-coded original addresses, no stubs.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr role="row">
              <td role="cell">Attempt cap and patience</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="For LibertyFlux">Starting values</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="Reason">Remeasure in phase 2. Our failures differ from register-allocation near misses.</td>
            </tr>

            </tr>

              <td role="cell">decomp.me</td>
              <td role="cell" data-label="For LibertyFlux">Not allowed</td>

            </tr>
          </tbody>
        </table>
